The US warned allies of missile delivery delays of up to five years — this could complicate aid to Ukraine

The US warned allies of missile delivery delays of up to five years — this could complicate aid to Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
The US is replenishing depleted missile stocks, which could delay deliveries by up to five years. This makes it more difficult for Ukraine to obtain Patriot systems.
The United States has warned its allies that deliveries of some key missiles and air defense systems could be delayed by up to five years due to the need to replenish its own depleted stockpiles. The shortage could also complicate Ukraine’s efforts to obtain more Patriot interceptor missiles ahead of winter, Bloomberg reports, according to UNN.
Details
U.S. stockpiles have declined significantly during the war with Iran. According to estimates, the United States has used more than half of its stockpile of the most advanced variants of Patriot missiles, one-third of its Tomahawks, and nearly half of its precision-strike missiles and THAAD interceptors.
In particular, Germany asked the United States to expedite the delivery of Tomahawk cruise missiles and Typhon ground-based launchers. However, given the state of U.S. stockpiles, the missile manufacturer is unlikely to be able to fulfill the order within the next five years.
The shortage could affect deliveries to Ukraine
The Pentagon’s decision to prioritize replenishing its own arsenals complicates Kyiv’s efforts to obtain additional Patriot interceptor missiles. Strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses is expected to be one of the key topics during meetings of world leaders in New York next week.
U.S. President Donald Trump previously said that the possibility of transferring a "much less complex version" of the Patriot to Ukraine, or granting European countries licenses to produce the weapon, was being discussed.
According to Bloomberg, U.S. defense companies are already trying to sharply increase production. Lockheed Martin is working to raise annual capacity from approximately 600 to 2,000 PAC-3 MSE missile segments.
Despite the shortage, the United States continues to supply Ukraine with weapons purchased by European allies through NATO and EU mechanisms. European leaders also plan to urge Trump during next week’s meetings to provide Ukraine with more Patriot missiles.

What Russia attacked Ukraine with this night and how many targets were shot down
Kyiv • UNN
Russia launched two Tsirkon missiles and 174 drones. Air defenses shot down or suppressed 141 targets, but hits were recorded at 15 locations.
During the night of September 19, Russia attacked Ukraine with 2 Zircon anti-ship missiles and 174 strike and other drones, half of which were jet-powered Shaheds. Air defense forces shot down or suppressed 141 aerial targets, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported, according to UNN.
Details
The main directions of Russia’s attack were Odesa and Kyiv regions. The enemy launched the Zircon missiles from Russia’s Kursk region, and the drones from Oryol, Millerovo, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, and the temporarily occupied Donetsk and Crimea.
For the attack, Russia used Shaheds, Gerbera drones, Bandеrol/Dan-T loitering munitions, and Parody imitation drones. The aerial attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups.
How many targets air defense neutralized
As of 08:00, air defense had shot down or suppressed 138 Shahed-, Gerbera-, and other types of drones, as well as 3 Bandеrol/Dan-T munitions.
The Air Force recorded strikes by aerial attack weapons at 15 locations; at another 9 locations, downed targets or their debris fell. Neither of the two Zircon missiles reached its target; the locations where they fell are being clarified.
As of the time of publication of the report, the attack was ongoing—more than 10 enemy UAVs remained in Ukraine’s airspace.

What happens if a solar farm catches fire? Europe’s biggest battery test centre is finding out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:02:38 UTC
14:02:38 KST

Battery ‘torture testing’ simulates car washes, sandstorms and wildfires for the benefit of the energy transition.
Eastern Germany is home to some of the world’s most advanced ‘torture chambers’. Here, water, fire, high-voltage current and even dust are used to press and squeeze, twist and strike, shake and hammer the beating hearts of the technology we use every day, like electric vehicles.
At Europe’s largest battery testing centre, they put batteries into every imaginable situation to see what happens. Whether they explode, survive or thrive, it’s better to find out here than in a consumer’s garage.
Batteries are subjected to extreme temperatures and full-blown sandstorms
I am standing beside a long row of garage-sized boxes inside the DEKRA facility in the small town of Klettwitz in Lusatia. Each box has its own unique purpose. Head of DEKRA, Thomas Hucke, is showing me around. Thermometers and warning lights surround me – what do they mean?
“We’re testing how battery prototypes behave at very low temperatures, or at very high temperatures. From Siberia to the Sahara,” Hucke explains. “In other words, the classic environmental conditions that a battery like this experiences over its lifetime.” He then walks over to a control panel and, with grim determination, turns it all the way to the minus max level: “Right, minus 40 degrees Celsius – let’s take it right down to the limit…”
Full-blown sandstorm? No problem for Hucke and his team. If a specialised battery is to survive use in the desert, its suitability must be certified before it can be marketed and sold. For that, the DEKRA team naturally have some particularly gruelling dust chambers.
We cross an industrial road and enter a hall on the opposite side. A few staff members hurriedly push plastic crates in front of a prototype that has just been delivered to block the view. “Camera off!” they say. This is top secret.
“We also test very large batteries,” says Hucke, explaining the enormous size of the test hall, “such as stationary energy storage systems, for example.
“Over there,” Hucke points to another test chamber, “we carry out vibration tests. In vehicles, batteries are usually subjected to vibrations. What happens when a vehicle drives over a curb, or when it receives a mechanical impact?” All of this is tested, documented and reported to the manufacturer. Certification is only granted once the new battery model has met all stress parameters to Hucke’s complete satisfaction.
Consumer safety is a top priority in the European Union. “The EU has drawn up a Battery Regulation which sets out the tests that must be carried out on batteries. It’s about sustainability, the value chain, and ultimately, always about safety.”
Hucke elaborates: “The energy transition isn’t just about electric mobility. At the test centre, we naturally also test vehicle batteries. But beyond that, we are increasingly testing energy storage solutions for stationary applications. These are mostly intermediate storage systems for renewable energies, namely solar and wind. That is the future.”
Batteries are crushed and burnt – to find out what happens
Hucke smiles as he leads us into the next fiery circle of battery hell.
“What happens in the event of a fire? In an accident? Or if batteries are overcharged or discharged improperly? Batteries must remain safe even in these situations,” he says. “The energy transition [and the associated electrification] must function safely and sustainably. This requires testing service providers who ensure that certain rules and standards are adhered to.”
Hucke nods towards the ‘fire hall’. There, they recently tried to set an entire battery container alight. This is not an unrealistic scenario: planet-heating fossil fuel emissions are leading to increasingly extreme temperatures. Europe experienced this first-hand in a scorching summer filled with devastating wildfires and drought.
It cannot be ruled out that one day a major fire might also reach the buffer electricity storage facility at a solar or wind farm. Up to certain temperature levels, a large-scale battery storage facility must be able to withstand this.
Opening a high-security airlock, Hucke leads me into a room with a cathedral-high ceiling. Massive metal blocks are firmly bolted to the floor. This is the bunker hall of the ‘crush bed’.
“We’ve got an oversized vice here,” says Hucke, where batteries are clamped to be stress tested. “The battery is squeezed – and the regulations stipulate that absolutely nothing must happen.”
But what if it does? What if the new prototype can’t take any more, after the water, dust, heat and cold tests? What if it really does crash and explode in the crushing bed between the jaws of the steel clamps?
Hucke points to the special fixtures on the thick walls. “We have pressure relief flaps here – and outside the building, a complete flue gas scrubbing system that extracts the gases in an emergency.”
Batteries are key to a safe and sustainable energy transition
Wind and solar power are a rapidly growing source of energy in Europe. Grid constraints and the intermittent nature of these renewables means the need for flexible storage is rapidly increasing.
Battery test centres are “a key component” of the energy transition, says Hucke, ensuring that this renewable power can be stored safely.
“Standards and regulations have been in place in the automotive sector for some time now. And the same is now happening in the field of stationary battery storage solutions for renewable energies,” he tells me. “This requires state-of-the-art testing laboratories. We ensure that batteries entering service meet all safety requirements.”
What about the test centre’s own sustainability? A huge, ultra-modern battery test centre like this requires a lot of energy. “We’re expanding our solar PV systems,” emphasises Hucke, “and using stationary battery storage to ensure we can recover energy”.
The DEKRA Group also took a stand at the World Economic Forum (WEF) in Davos, joining the Alliance of CEO Climate Leaders. “In an increasingly disruptive global environment, in which the urgency and even the existence of the climate crisis is, in some quarters, being called into question once again, we emphasise the strategic importance of jointly combating climate change,” states the Group headquarters.
The DEKRA Climate Impact Programme includes internal decarbonisation and support for external climate projects that make a measurable contribution to the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

Drums, dancing and definitely no tears: Here’s why you need to experience Nepal’s Sa: Paru festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:00:48 UTC
14:00:48 KST

Euronews Travel’s Dianne Apen-Sadler headed to the ancient city of Bhaktapur in Nepal for the Sa: Paru festival honouring those that have died in the past year.
The sound I most associate with death is silence. Not just the obvious one, in that the dearly departed will never speak, never yell, never cry, never laugh again.
Smaller silences, like post-funeral, when the last guest is gone and all you’re left with are your thoughts and an inordinate amount of food shared by well-wishers. Or when weeks have passed and you go to call or text them about your day before you stop yourself because you can’t do that any more.
Even years later, it lingers in that awkward pause when you reveal someone close to you has passed away and the other person doesn’t quite know what to say in response.
Drums and bells, it is not. Music, beyond the songs chosen for the service, feels incongruous. The loud, chaotic energy of a festival? Never.
Yet that’s exactly what Sa: Paru, an annual festival honouring those that have died in the past year, is all about, as I discovered on my recent trip to Nepal’s Bhaktapur.
Celebrated across the Kathmandu Valley by the Newar people, the festival turns the western idea of grieving on its head, giving the dead a joyous farewell as they head towards salvation.
“When people pass away in western societies, people wear black. They grieve in silence – it's a very somber moment,” says Ajay Bahadur Pradhanang. “But in Nepal, everybody comes together and it's turned into this carnival, a real joyous moment of farewell.”
A community coming together
While the festival also takes place in other cities like Lalitpur as well as the capital Kathmandu, which is around 13 kilometres away, the celebration in Bhaktapur takes its own unique form.
Prior to the festival’s main day, which takes place after the full moon during the 10th month of the country’s lunisolar calendar in August or September, neighbours – whether they’ve lost someone or not – gather to create taha: sa.
The bamboo structures, which replaced the cows that would traditionally have been used as part of the procession, are wrapped before a painting of the sacred animal is placed at the top.
It takes skill, and manpower, to complete the whole affair. After the cloth (generally red for women, and white for men) and cow portrait are added, various decorations follow, like a photograph of the deceased, depictions of Shiva, and, finally, an umbrella to shield them from sun and rain – a sign of respect.
“For Sa: Paru, we have to have certain rituals, and these would be impossible if it was just me, or just my family, without the wider community to help us,” Ajay notes.
It might take a village to raise a child, but the celebration in Bhaktapur goes to show that it takes a community to mark the other end of somebody’s life, too.
I’m here at the invitation of The Nanee, a boutique hotel near the city’s centre. Ajay, the hotel’s chairman, lost his mother this year, which means I can see the work underway in the neighbouring courtyard, but any visitor to the city will easily be able to find taha: sa being constructed throughout the day.
The festival starts early the following morning, with a steady stream of taha: sa passing through the streets accompanied by music, drums, bells and the sound of sticks clashing together as pairs take part in the Ghintang Ghisi dance.
The procession follows a set route, and at the beginning, it seems each troupe is moving to its own beat – some rush, causing the structures to sway, giving the effect of a drunken cow passing by; others march slowly, pausing to dance together. It’s only as the streets begin to clog up and movement reaches a snail’s pace that they move as one.
While some attendees don traditional wear, or modern interpretations of it, you’re just as likely to see people wearing football kits and Hawaiian shirts. Come as you are – you’re welcome to get involved in the festivities, provided you don’t mind crowds.
After taking a pause to catch my breath, I get chatting to Mano Dhaubhadel, a Nepali living in the US who recently lost his younger brother and has returned for the festival.
“This is something you don’t see anywhere else in the world,” he told me. “The culture here is just magnificent, and it’s there for everyone to enjoy, not just Newars. The best way to learn is to get involved.”
Of course, you can also attend the festival with a guide. I’m joined by The Nanee’s curator, Peepul Subedi, a priest and PhD student who is more than happy to explain the meaning behind the festival’s various elements, and its importance.
"The whole city comes together for this festival, and every household who has a family member who has passed away in the past year will take out this sort of structure,” he tells me.
“It represents the message that everyone has to die, and all of us are going through the same sort of sorrow – that's life. We're not celebrating death by dancing and singing, we are celebrating the fact that the departed soul is moving towards salvation.”
Celebrations in most of the valley last just a single day – here in Bhaktapur, the festival continues on for eight, with different dance performances throughout the city.
The exact origins of Sa: Paru, which is also known as Gai Jatra, aren’t precisely known, but historians believe that the tradition may have started in the 14th century.
The name most commonly associated with the festival is King Pratap Malla, who is said to have expanded the festival to cheer up his wife following the death of their son Chakravartendra Malla with the inclusion of satirical elements, which today sees people don satirical masks of political figures like US president Donald Trump and Russian president Vladimir Putin.
A reason to linger in Bhaktapur
Travel itineraries for tourists visiting Kathmandu often include a detour to Bhaktapur – but they typically only mention a visit to the Durbar Square, with its various temples and the 55 Window Palace.
Similar to the cruise ship tourists who swarm cities in Europe for a few hours in the summer months, climbing back on board having contributed nothing to the local economy beyond the cost of an ice cream and a fridge magnet, these visitors will spend an hour or two in town before heading back to the capital.
It’s a real shame – not just for the locals, who fail to see the financial benefit, but for the tourists themselves, who miss out on the best Bhaktapur has to offer.
Life is slower here, and the city is best experienced in the early mornings, when you’ll see folks milling about, praying at the Hindu and Buddhist temples, or buying produce at the market.
Aside from the Durbar Square, you can see ceramics drying under the sun at Pottery Square, give pottery a go yourself at one of the workshops, or pick out some pieces to add to your homeware collection.
The Peacock Shop is another must visit, where the chatty owner is more than happy to talk, and walk you through the traditional Lokta paper making process.
The Nanee was founded by Ajay and Shailaja Pradhanang with a view to encourage people to linger longer while enjoying the comforts of a luxury boutique hotel.
“Bhaktapur is a living heritage site, and we wanted that to continue,” Ajay tells me.
“With The Nanee, we offer guests a small oasis in the beautiful city of Bhaktapur while ensuring that the community, which has done so much to preserve and conserve its heritage, benefits from their stay.”
Experiences offered by the hotel are in partnership with locals, like the morning walk with a housewife, or the evening dinner with an artisan.
Aside from Sa: Paru, there are numerous festivals throughout the year, including the famed Bisket Jatra, celebrated for eight nights each April.
A note on the recent floods
Just hours before landing in Kathmandu for the festival, a series of flash floods near the border with Tibet saw the loss of at least 1,369 lives, with some 5,000 people missing.
Naturally, many people have cancelled or are thinking about cancelling their trips to Nepal as a result, which will have a serious impact on a tourism industry that is already dealing with the impact of the Iran war on flight routes to the country.
Popular tourist spots like the Kathmandu Valley, as well as Mount Everest and other trekking trails, were unaffected by the tragedy, and your tourism dollars are more needed than ever.
Dianne Apen-Sadler was hosted by The Nanee during the Sa: Paru festival. You can reach out to the hotel directly to enquire about your potential stay in order to align your trip with one of Bhaktapur’s many festivals. For more information about Bhaktapur, visit the official tourism board website.

European education powerhouses rocked by falling scores in global study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:00:42 UTC
14:00:42 KST

France’s were its worst ever. Germany’s, too. In the Netherlands, results also tumbled to all-time lows. Even in Finland, Europe’s much-vaunted schools champion and a global leader for decades, scores plummeted.
The 2025 Pisa scores, which assess how effectively 15-year-olds apply school-learned knowledge and skills in reading, mathematics and science to real-life situations, have rocked some of western Europe’s education powerhouses.
While the UK bucked the trend, results on the continent continued a slide that began in 2018. In France, Germany, the Netherlands and Finland, the proportion of 15-year-olds lacking basic functional literacy and maths skills rose to nearly one in three.
Pandemic learning losses accelerated the drop, but education experts say the roots of the problem run much deeper: chronic teacher shortages, repeated curriculum reforms that have neglected basic skills and widening inequalities within increasingly segregated systems.
Compounding it all, incessant smartphone use has dramatically reduced attention spans, replacing “deep reading” with scrolling, and pupil motivation has collapsed.
Pupils in Germany got their worst-ever Pisa report card, reviving a decades-old debate about the country’s weaknesses in schools, integration and closing the wealth gap. Samuel Greiff, the German Pisa study coordinator, noted an alarming rise in youngsters who lack basic skills for citizenship and employment, including the ability to understand a written text and do rudimentary consumer maths.
The study found that in Europe’s top economy the link between academic performance and socioeconomic status was particularly strong: only 2% of pupils from low-income families achieve high levels of competence, against 25% from higher-income families – a correlation twice as strong as in Denmark or Norway.
“Other countries are far more successful in decoupling educational success from family background,” Greiff told local media, noting that class had a far greater influence on teens’ academic success than whether their family had immigrated.
Germany endured a first “Pisa-Schock” in 2000, when the report’s dismal ratings triggered a nationwide effort to raise performance. The 2012 report identified significant improvement, putting the country above the OECD average.
But the 2025 edition showed Germany slipping back to average, with about one in four pupils lacking competency in natural sciences and one in three in reading and maths. About one in five demonstrated insufficient capabilities in all three areas.
The number of teens deemed “at risk” because they lacked the reading and maths skills for further education has doubled over the last decade, and reading for pleasure has declined at a faster rate in Germany than in other industrialised countries: one in two 15-year-olds said they only read when it was required.
Strikingly, pupils from the most socioeconomically privileged neighbourhoods recorded the sharpest decline in reading comprehension. Education minister Karin Prien said the report required an urgent response, highlighting the negative influence of excessive social media use and pledging to present new measures to protect younger children by the end of the year.
In the Netherlands, the scores marked a historic low point, setting troubling new records in reading literacy, where a record 39% of 15-year-olds now lack the basic skills required to navigate modern society, evaluate the credibility of sources or process multi-page texts, up from 33% in the previous 2022 edition.
Researchers noted that the Dutch reading score has plunged by more than 60 points over the last decade, meaning today’s 15-year-olds are effectively reading at the level that 12-year-olds achieved 10 years ago.
The decline was less marked in maths, where Dutch pupils once dominated the European rankings, but still represented a record low only marginally higher than the OECD average, while the science score was also below its previous level.
The Dutch education ministry promised urgent action, acknowledging that the assessment “confirms our decline was not a temporary post-pandemic dip, but a structural issue. We can’t accept a society where a third of our youth leave school unprepared for basic reading in daily life.”
However, teachers’ unions and literacy advocates reacted with frustration. The AOb teachers’ union argued reading levels would never improve as long as “classes are routinely cancelled, non-qualified staff are filling gaps, and the workload is driving experienced educators out of the profession.”
The reading advocacy group Stichting Lezen added that the failure lay “not with pupils, but with an approach that has turned reading into a set of mechanical comprehension tricks rather than fostering deep reading habits”.
In France, the scores were similarly grim. “It’s worrying, but it’s unfortunately not a surprise,” said Édouard Geffray, the education minister. Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate, called the outcome a “catastrophe” and a reflection of the nation’s decline.
French education analysts have long warned of a lack of state investment, particularly in primary schools, as well as a highly unequal system where socioeconomic status dictates results, while governments have tended to approach education failings by debating timetabling and how many hours children sit at their desks.
Over the past decade, a succession of eight different education ministers has resulted in constant policy changes and reversals, leaving teachers feeling more stressed by the avalanche of directives than by teaching in class. Mid-career salaries, meanwhile, remain below the OECD average and another recent report found just 4% of French teachers felt valued.
Éric Charbonnier, an OECD education analyst, argued that the focus should shift away from debates over desk hours toward greater autonomy to explore teaching methods, and more method-focused training.
In Finland, average results were lower than in 2022 in maths and reading, and stable in science. Dr Arto K Ahonen, Pisa national project manager at the Finnish Institute for Educational Research, said the results had prompted serious discussion over pupils’ perseverance and effort.
“The goal remains to reverse the decline and return to a rising trend,” Ahonen said. “Meanwhile, we recognise the universal decline we are part of.”
Ahonen noted that the Finnish system had seen “no major change in our education system in 50 years,” warning that “curricula must be renewed as times and society change. It’s unlikely that any school system could operate with the same curricula for decades, even a successful one.”
In neighbouring Sweden, record-low results spurred heated political debate ahead of recent elections, with party leaders blaming everything from screens to immigration and insufficient teaching staff. But experts say there is no single explanation.
In its report on the latest scores, Skolverket, the national education agency, said several changes were already under way aimed at reinforcing pupils’ knowledge and the classroom role of teachers in creating a “safer and more equal environment”.

Henry Harris’ recipe for tomatoes, creme fraiche and herbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:00:41 UTC
14:00:41 KST

Forty years ago, an antiquarian bookseller recommended to me Edouard de Pomiane’s La cuisine en dix minutes, a selection of recipes that could be cooked at home in less than 10 minutes. A scientist and food lover, de Pomiane stripped back what was then viewed as a very complicated craft, and also gave the time-poor an opportunity to cook and enjoy a good meal made from good ingredients. This was the first recipe I cooked from that book, and it is still a great favourite that has punctuated my menus ever since.
Tomatoes, creme fraiche and herbs
This is a perfect end-of-summer supper that I have never quite managed to do at the speed of de Pomiane – it usually takes me about 15 minutes. Use proper creme fraiche for this, ideally a French one, because there are some very poor British-made equivalents out there that have no natural tang and tend to coagulate when heated.
Prep 5 min
Cook 15 min
Serves 2
1 good tbsp unsalted butter
Salt and black pepper
  4 ripe plum tomatoes, cut in half lengthways
200g creme fraiche, or more if you like a lot of sauce
2 thick slices sourdough
  A few basil leaves, or 1 small handful mixed soft herbs
Melt the butter in a medium frying pan until foaming. Generously season the tomatoes, then put them cut side down in the hot butter and leave to cook on a medium heat for at least five minutes, until the butter colours to a light nut brown (if at any stage it looks as if it may be going too dark and at risk of burning, turn down the heat and proceed more gently).
Spoon the creme fraiche into the pan, bring up to a low simmer and cook for another two minutes. Turn over the tomatoes, cook for a further minute or two, then taste the tomato-rich cream and adjust the seasoning as required. Meanwhile, toast the sourdough.
Put four tomato halves on each slice of toast, spoon the sauce all over the top and serve topped with torn or roughly chopped basil.
- 
  Henry Harris is chef/co-owner of Bouchon Racine, London EC1. His book, The Racine Effect, is published by Quadrille at £40. To order a copy for £36, go to guardianbookshop.com

‘Cost of housing’ crunch looms for low-income families, warns Resolution Foundation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:00:40 UTC
14:00:40 KST

More than 1.1 million low-income families in rented homes face a “cost of housing” crunch without action from John Healey in next month’s budget, the Resolution Foundation thinktank has warned.
Local housing allowance (LHA) has been frozen in cash terms since autumn 2024.
In a new report, Saving Private Renters, the thinktank found that rising rents since then have led to a widening gap between what families claiming LHA can afford, and the realities of the market.
It said a low-income family renting a typical two-bedroom flat now faces an average shortfall of £158 a week. That rises to more than £300 a week in parts of London.
The Resolution Foundation rejects the suggestion that relinking LHA with local conditions would mainly benefit private landlords, by driving up rents.
By analysing previous changes in LHA, it finds that 90p of every £1 tends to fall to tenants, instead of feeding through into price changes.
Resolution Foundation economist Stephen Hunsaker said: “The gap between average rents and Local housing allowance levels is set to reach a record high this October, and failing to repeg LHA to actual rents in next month’s budget could lock in a freeze for another year, and see the gap reach 30% by March 2028.”
He added that “with many tenants receiving housing support already going without essentials to pay their rent today, the government should restore the automatic annual linking of LHA to relieve the pressure on low-income families in the private rented sector.”
Relinking LHA to rents would cost £2bn a year by the end of this parliament in 2029-30. The Resolution Foundation suggests funding that change by increasing the “taper rate” at which universal credit (UC) is withdrawn as recipients’ income rises.
The report argues this would involve a transfer within the UC system, towards claimants with the most need.
The thinktank pointed to survey evidence suggesting one in five working-age adults in families on housing support in private rental accommodation were unable to afford to keep their homes warm, and one in eight were unable to afford three meals a day.
When LHA was first introduced in 2008 it was pegged to the median level of local rents, and in 2011 that was reduced to the 30th percentile. It has been frozen for nine of the past 14 years.
A chorus of charities and campaigners have called for the restoration of the link, including Crisis, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation and Citizens Advice.
The chancellor will present his budget on 28 October. He is under pressure to fulfil Labour’s promise of giving voters a “breathing space” amid rising costs, but likely to be constrained by rising inflation and interest rates.
A government spokesperson said: “Local housing allowance rates are reviewed annually, and future decisions will be taken in the context of the government’s welfare priorities, and the fiscal context.”

Here’s how Germany can defend its democracy – banning the AfD isn’t the answer | Timothy Garton Ash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:00:38 UTC
14:00:38 KST

Far-right nationalist populist parties are making the running everywhere from Washington to Warsaw. So why be so alarmed about a little regional electoral victory for one such party, the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), in one federal state, Saxony-Anhalt? “Because it’s Germany!” is the almost instinctive answer in many heads around the world.
But that “because it’s Germany” needs to be taken apart, like the segments of an orange. Yes, because of Adolf Hitler, two dictatorships (Nazi Germany until 1945, communist-ruled East Germany until 1989) and two world wars. And yes, some of the language used by the AfD will give anyone familiar with Nazi rhetoric a cold shudder down the spine.
Then there’s the fact that Germany is Europe’s central power. The AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel says that when her party gets into government after the federal election scheduled for 2029, Germany will abandon the euro and leave the Schengen border-free travel area. What would be left of the EU then?
The great German liberal social and political thinker Ralf Dahrendorf, who died in 2009, told me more than once that he would only feel really confident of the resilience of German democracy when it had withstood the test of a big economic crisis. Well, the country is close to that now.
The final segment of “because it’s Germany!” is perhaps the most interesting. The federal republic’s entire constitutional, political and educational system is designed to prevent anything like the collapse of the Weimar republic into Hitler’s dictatorship in 1933. The federal republic should be a wehrhafte Demokratie – a democracy capable of defending itself.
So how Germany will defend its democracy is a question not just of European but of global significance. Looking at all the answers being frenetically canvassed in Berlin, I think the most convincing formula is: neither ban the AfD nor embrace it, but instead constrain it legally and fight it politically.
The German constitution provides for political parties that are “hostile” to its basic liberal democratic principles to be banned. Senior German politicians have called for an application to be made to the constitutional court to ban the AfD, or at least its most extreme parts, on those grounds. But it’s too late for that. The AfD has been a major force in the Bundestag since its success (off the back of the migration crisis) in the 2017 general election and, like Reform UK in Britain, has led nationwide in opinion polls. To suddenly tell so many citizens “you’re not allowed to vote for the party you support!” would itself be an assault on democracy.
But this is not democracy as the tyranny of the majority: the people have spoken, off with your head! It’s liberal democracy, meaning the outcome of any popular vote is constrained by the rule of law, human and minority rights, and pluralist, anti-majoritarian institutions. The real threats to German democracy today are less like Weimar in 1933 than Budapest in 2010 (when Viktor Orbán took over) and Washington DC in 2025. The mini-Donald Trumps of the AfD have reportedly been quietly exploring Trump-like executive and administrative devices they might use to consolidate their control. The Federal Republic of Germany has the right, the power and the duty to stop them.
Article 37 of the constitution, which allows federal authorities to overrule anti-constitutional behaviour by the states, has never been used in the 77-year history of the republic. Assuming, as now seems likely, the AfD forms the state government in Saxony-Anhalt, all federal powers, up to and including article 37, should be used wherever necessary. For example, they should prevent sensitive intelligence about Russia’s increasing aggression being shared with a Saxony-Anhalt branch of the domestic security service controlled by the pro-Russian AfD; secure the independence of courts and prosecutors, as well as the neutrality of police and civil service; and, I would add, stop any extreme politicisation of education and public service broadcasting. Of course, AfD politicians will cry “foul!”; tough. If, as they say, they want “another republic”, they can go and live in Russia.
Yet even more important than these legal and administrative constraints is the political response. At the opposite end from those calling for the party to be banned are Christian Democrats calling for the “firewall” to be abandoned and AfD politicians to be embraced as part of the normal political process. Letting them take responsibility in a state government will, it’s argued, expose their incoherence, incompetence and lack of real policy answers.
Talking and working with them will end up moderating them, as apparently happened with Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy. I’ve been tempted by these arguments myself. But evidence collected by political scientists suggests that a strategy of inclusion is just as likely to put more wind in the nationalists’ sails. And AfD activists are themselves warning against the danger of Melonisierung (Melonisation).
So Christian Democrats should not be tempted to get half into bed with the AfD, like a middle-aged man nervously edging into an extramarital affair. Instead, starting already this weekend with elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, they should more effectively combat it politically. Rather than defining Christian Democracy by what it’s against (the AfD and the far-left Linke), they should say what it’s for. To renew Germany’s social market economy, they should implement all the labour market, pension, tax and other reforms agreed this summer with their Social Democrat coalition partners – and more. Faced with huge external challenges, from Russian aggression to US and Chinese AI, the Christian Democrats – historically the party of Europe – should boldly advocate the European-scale answers which alone will give any European country the strength to stand up to giants.
But besides AI, Germany’s mainstream parties badly need EI (emotional intelligence). The key to the success of the AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund in Saxony-Anhalt, as with Trump and Britain’s Nigel Farage, is a kind of emotional communication. I’m here with you; I hear you and see you; I share your anger. With me, you can say what you really think and be yourself, because – whether or not I’m a millionaire – deep down I’m a normal bloke like you. So let’s all have a beer and march forward to an imagined past.
It’s fascinating to re-read the exiled German political scientist Karl Loewenstein’s influential 1937 article on “militant democracy” and find him insisting that democracy cannot “devise emotional formulas capable of competing with the fascist Pied Pipers”. Hence the emphasis on constitutional constraints. But in our transformed information environment, with its premium on attention, drama and passion, democracy can’t be defended simply by legal constraints and rational policies. Democrats everywhere need to compete with today’s Pied Pipers on the emotional plane, too. Constant presence on social media and physical presence on the ground are both essential.
Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, and to some extent the UK’s, Andy Burnham, have shown how it can be done. So much will now depend on German democrats, and especially Christian Democrats, proving they can do the same.
- 
  Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnist. His new book, Europe in 7 1/2 Chapters, is published in October

Fear of AI job losses now outweighs hope of new jobs, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

In the midst of calls for an AI development slowdown, the fear and uncertainty over AI's impact on the job market remain present worldwide, study finds.
People’s view of a country and trust for its artificial intelligence (AI) regulation tend to be closely linked, Moira Fagan, senior researcher at the Pew Research Center and one of the authors of a new study on AI, told Euronews Next.
According to the report, in Bangladesh, Malaysia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the West Bank and East Jerusalem, people trust China more than the United States (US) or the European Union (EU) with AI governance.
And, taking into consideration the other seven middle-income countries where this question was asked, a median of 43% trust China to regulate AI, 35% trust the US and 34% trust the EU.
“Favourable views of China tend to be quite high in middle-income countries – and opinion has risen in many places since last year, likely contributing to some of the high marks we see for trust in China on this particular dimension,” Fagan said.
The report, which was built on a survey conducted between February and June 2026, polling over 50,000 people from 37 countries, also examines people’s opinions on AI’s impact on the job market.
Specifically, more people expect AI to lead to fewer jobs than to job creation, according to the study. A good share of respondents, though, also report uncertainty about the impact AI will have on the number of job opportunities.
The survey also shows that worries about job losses due to AI are particularly high in wealthier countries.
For instance, in Australia, South Korea and the US, around seven-in-ten adults or more believe AI will result in job loss over the next 20 years.
Similarly, richer countries are more concerned about AI increasing economic inequalities than middle-income ones, the report highlights.
According to Fagan, these tendencies appear to be linked to other data, including people’s familiarity with the technological tool.
“People in wealthier countries are more likely to say they have heard or read a lot about AI. And we also found that people with higher AI awareness are more likely to believe it will lead to job loss,” she told Euronews Next.
However, some high-income and middle-income nations are brought together by a shared thread: young adults aged 18 to 34 are more concerned about AI-related job loss than older generations. And this is the case for countries like Canada, France, Singapore, Sweden, Indonesia, India and Malaysia, according to the survey.
Opinion divides are less pronounced when it comes to the rise of AI in daily life. Across the 37 countries, a median of 37% are more concerned than excited, while 41% median are equally concerned and excited, the survey found.
Although the survey was conducted in the first half of 2026, its publication arrives at a very crucial moment for AI.
Leaders of major AI companies, including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei, are increasingly concerned about the risks their AI creations pose to humanity and are calling for a slowdown in the pace of AI development.
President of the European Commission, Ursula Von der Leyen, also backed the deceleration effort in her landmark State of the Union address to the European Parliament earlier this week. On this occasion, she also pledged closer safety cooperation with Canada, the UK, and other like-minded partners.

EU fuel prices hit records as ECB experts see diesel margins peak in October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:00:17 UTC
14:00:17 KST

EU petrol and diesel prices hit record highs this week, according to the European Commission. Refining margins—the cost of turning crude oil into fuel—are partly to blame, and prices could remain elevated as ECB experts tell Euronews that diesel margins are expected to peak only in October.
Filling up a car has never cost more on average across the European Union, according to European Commission data going back more than two decades. At the latest average prices, it costs about €103 to fill a 50-litre tank with petrol and €108 with diesel.
Retail fuel prices have surged since the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, adding to inflationary pressures. Eurozone energy inflation rose to 14.3% in August, up from 10.3% in July, according to the European Central Bank.
A litre of petrol cost a weighted EU average of €2.063 as of 14 September, while diesel reached €2.159 per litre. Both were the highest readings in the Commission’s series, which begins in 2005. Petrol’s previous peak was recorded in 2022, while diesel last approached its current level in April this year.
Prices varied considerably across the EU. Petrol was cheapest in Malta, at €1.34 per litre, and most expensive in Denmark, at €2.56. Diesel ranged from €1.21 per litre in Malta to €2.51 in Finland.
The figures come from the European Commission’s latest Weekly Oil Bulletin, published on 17 September using prices reported for 14 September. They include taxes.
Fuel prices have been rising for months since the war with Iran broke out at the end of February and disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz. International benchmark Brent crude prices rose above $126 at the height of the conflict and were trading at more than $104 a barrel for delivery the following month on Friday. Brent cost about $72 per barrel before the war broke out.
European crude supplies face further disruption after Saudi Aramco told at least two European refiners that they would receive no oil under long-term contracts in October following an attack on the kingdom’s key pipeline to the Red Sea, Bloomberg reported, citing people informed of the decision who said it applied to all European buyers.
What makes European fuel prices expensive?
But international crude prices are not the only factor driving petrol and diesel prices higher. Refining costs and margins have also risen significantly, putting further pressure on prices at the pump.
Refining margins reflect the difference between the cost of crude oil and the price of refined products such as petrol and diesel. While petrol margins appear to have peaked, ECB experts told Euronews Business that diesel margins are not expected to reach their highest point until October.
“Looking ahead, based on refined diesel futures from LSEG on 16 September, the margin for diesel is expected to peak in October. Based on refined petrol futures from LSEG on 16 September, petrol margins peaked in August,” they said.
Since the beginning of 2026, the weighted EU average petrol price has risen by about 29%, while diesel has surged by almost 40%.
Higher crude prices have also fuelled energy inflation across both the eurozone and the wider EU. According to an ECB blog published in July, increases in crude-oil prices generally feed through fully to pre-tax pump prices within one or two months. Governments can temporarily cushion the impact through measures such as cuts to fuel duties.
Crude oil accounted for less than a quarter of the euro-area pump price in the ECB blog’s July calculations. The remainder included refining and distribution costs and margins, excise duties and value added tax, helping to explain the significant differences between countries.
The blog’s calculations indicated that excise duties and VAT together represented around 44% of the euro-area diesel price and 52% of the petrol price in July.
ECB experts told Euronews Business that refining margins are now making a large contribution to diesel prices.
“At the current juncture, we have estimated that in the third week of September refining margins have contributed €0.41 (19% of the pump price) and €0.17 (8%) per litre to the retail diesel and retail petrol prices in the euro area, respectively.”
Could fuel prices rise further?
The ECB’s monetary policy statement, published on 10 September, warned: “Renewed disruption of energy supplies could cause energy prices to rise further and for longer than currently expected.”
ECB experts said an end to the Middle East conflict and the restoration of energy and refining flows would be central to bringing prices down.
“For petrol and diesel prices to decline, the key factor would be a cessation of the war in the Middle East, a normalisation of flows through the Strait of Hormuz and a restoration of global refining activity to allow oil inventories to rebuild,” they said.
Such a normalisation could quickly lower crude oil and retail fuel prices. However, disruptions to Russian refining capacity could keep margins elevated even if the Middle East conflict were resolved.

Russians leave before election ends, fearing mobilisation to follow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:00:16 UTC
14:00:16 KST

Requests for emergency emigration assistance from Russia have surged eightfold since July, with searches for "how to leave" and "mobilisation" at their highest since early 2023. An electronic summons register now automatically triggers an exit ban, documented cases show.
Russians fearing a new military mobilisation are leaving the country in advance of possible restrictions on departure, according to the anti-war project Ark, after requests for emergency assistance and emigration advice from Russia have nearly octupled since the start of the summer.
The surge coincides with Russia's State Duma elections, which began on Friday and run through Sunday.
Kremlin critics and several Western governments have accused Moscow of planning to announce a new call-up to beef up its troops in its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine after the vote concludes, allowing an unpopular measure to avoid affecting the election.
Russia's Vladimir Putin has dismissed mobilisation rumours as "utter nonsense," but independent Russian media have counted 17 official denials of an imminent draft since the summer.
Jan Slovitsky, a human rights activist and coordinator of the Ark project, said the current wave was driven by lessons learned from 2022.
"Since mid-July a wave of panic has been rising in Russia, linked to the risk of mobilisation, fuel shortages and lack of internet access," he told Ark's network from Yerevan, where he is assisting new arrivals.
"People are leaving in advance because they have seen what happened during previous waves. And Armenia is facing a migration crisis, if we are not already in the thick of it."
'How to leave' online search spikes
The number of daily requests for relocation assistance has risen from around 70 to 120 since July, according to organisations helping Russians move abroad.
Yandex and Google searches for "how to leave" and "mobilisation" reached their highest level since early 2023 during the summer and the first ten days of September, according to independent Russian media analysis.
Preparations for a possible call-up are already visible. Tens of thousands of people have received mobilisation notices setting out the steps required if called up, and an electronic register of summonses has been introduced under which an exit ban takes effect automatically when a notice is issued.
In early September, passport control officers in Krasnodar detained a 24-year-old resident of Rostov region who had completed his military service in 2024 and served him with a notice banning him from leaving the country, the first such case reported at that crossing.
Daniil Neonov, a former candidate for municipal deputy in the Moscow City Duma, described leaving at the last moment.
"If I had waited another day or two, they would most likely not have let me leave, because they would have blocked my exit," he said. "I received an electronic summons. But I still managed to get out."
Fear of mobilisation has also spread to members of the elite and draft office staff, according to international media reports claiming officials have begun opening foreign bank accounts and moving assets abroad.
In August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned of the risk of mobilisation in Russia, citing intelligence data.
Kyiv described a Kremlin plan to rapidly call up several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year, with at least as many again the following year. Moscow has not commented on those claims.
Neighbouring countries first
Arrivals are heading primarily to visa-free destinations: Armenia, Georgia and Kazakhstan. Yerevan said in recent days it was ready to assist Russians arriving in the country.
The exact scale of the current wave is unknown, but it is likely less intense than the exodus of 2022, when between 600,000 and 700,000 people left Russia within weeks of the partial mobilisation announcement, according to independent estimates.
That mobilisation has never been formally cancelled, and those called up then have not been demobilised.
"It is very sad to leave Russia," said a 28-year-old marketing specialist, whose name was withheld for security reasons.
"My family lives here, my elderly grandparents live here. My girlfriend is here too, she is still in her medical residency, and it is very hard for me to leave her behind."
Russia's Duma elections, running from 18 to 20 September, include only parties that back Moscow's war in Ukraine. Yabloko, whose platform called for an immediate ceasefire and peace talks, was barred from standing by the Supreme Court in August.

Could Latin become Europe’s common language? A young group thinks it can
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

It may sound improbable: Latin, often described as a dead language, becoming a common language understood across Europe.
Yet a group of young Europeans believes the ancient language could one day become a shared means of communication – and even an official language of the European Union.
The goal is ambitious. The EU currently has 24 official languages, and making Latin one of them would require a long political and cultural journey.
For the founders of Via Nova – Latin for “new way” – that journey is measured not in years or decades, but generations.
“It all started with a four-month backpacking trip around the world,” said Timi Celcer, the organisation’s leader. “Ironically, it all started outside Europe.”
Celcer, a self-described pan-European who studied political science, worked at Google and founded a startup, said the trip prompted him to think about how other cultures relate to their traditions.
He was particularly struck by India and China, where he said linguistic integration had helped create broader national identities.
“First of all, I was inspired by how much these cultures valued their traditions and how closely they were connected to them, in contrast to Europeans today, who have increasingly distanced themselves from theirs,” Celcer said.
He came to believe that the European project needed a third pillar alongside political and economic integration: culture.
“My eureka moment was realising that Latin historically played this role and is not associated with any particular country or region,” he said. “It is our collective heritage, connected to our shared traditions, and could play this role again.”
Latin was originally spoken by the Latins of Latium, in central Italy. It spread throughout territories conquered by the Roman Republic and later the Roman Empire. Although it eventually ceased to be a native spoken language, Latin profoundly influenced European languages, including Italian, French and Spanish.
During the Middle Ages, written Latin became a major language of scholarship and administration across Western and Central Europe. It remains an official language of the Vatican.
Celcer also points to the revival of Hebrew in the 19th and 20th centuries as evidence that languages can return to everyday use after long periods of decline.
“Hebrew was revived from a more difficult position than Latin is in today, and it became the foundation of the emerging Israeli identity,” he said.
Via Nova was founded last autumn by three Slovenians, including Celcer, and a Frenchman. The organisation is seeking members from across Europe, including Lithuania, where Celcer said it currently has no supporters.
One of its founders, Pierre Gorsky-Mieze, teaches Latin at Oxford Latinitas and speaks the language fluently. The other founders are learning it.
“We are growing together,” Celcer said. “Three of the four of us in the founding team speak Latin about as well as the average European. But we are learning, Pierre teaches us, and we are trying to bring Latin increasingly into everyday use.”
Gorsky-Mieze argues that Latin is not as difficult as many people assume.
He estimates that reaching B2, or upper-intermediate proficiency, on the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages could take about two years with two hours of study a week, some exercises between classes and regular conversation.
“Latin can be spoken in everyday life,” he said. “For example, with my girlfriend, who is not French, we don’t speak English. We speak Latin to each other.”
Via Nova also rejects comparisons with Esperanto, the artificial language created in the 19th century to facilitate international communication but which never became Europe’s dominant lingua franca.
Celcer argues that Latin has an advantage because it is a historical European language rather than an invented one. Until the 18th century, it was widely used in academic, diplomatic and religious settings, and in some places remained in use into the 19th century.
He recalls an episode from the European Parliament in 1979, when Italian lawmaker Mario Capanna unexpectedly addressed the chamber in Latin. Otto von Habsburg responded in Latin, praising it as a distinctly European language.
Gašper Mlakar, another Via Nova founder, said Latin remains embedded in Europe’s collective cultural memory.
“Even today, I think Latin is still somewhere in Europe’s collective subconscious,” he said. “People who try to create European organisations often use Latin names for them.”
Via Nova has outlined a four-stage process for its project.
The first is what Celcer calls democratic legitimacy: persuading Europeans to view Latin as a potential symbol of European unity rather than primarily associating it with classical studies or religious traditions.
The second is symbolic adoption through culture and everyday language. Later stages would involve broader institutional use, potentially through programs such as Erasmus and European cinema.
The final goal would be recognition as an official EU language while preserving Europe’s national languages.
“We always emphasise that this project could take several generations,” Celcer said. “It is a very long road.”
“Europe should think in generations,” he added.
Tilen Božič, another Via Nova founder and its marketing director, said the project is not about bringing the past back to life but using Europe’s linguistic heritage to build something new.
“The Latin we are trying to promote is not about bringing history into the present,” he said. “It is about taking a modern path – bringing people together and creating a common culture, common art and inspiration, and working with the idea of Europe and what it means to be European.”

FBI suspended cooperation with Canada over 9/11 language – NYT
Unknown

FBI suspended cooperation with Canada over 9/11 language – NYT
The FBI temporarily suspended some cooperation with its Canadian counterpart this month after the country’s public broadcaster instructed journalists not to refer to the 9/11 attacks as terrorism without attribution to experts or authorities, the New York Times reported on Friday, citing officials familiar with the matter.
According to the Times, FBI officials canceled meetings with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP). Normal cooperation was restored around the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, after the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) reversed its stance.
In response to the Times report, RCMP Commissioner Mark Duheme said: “We value our relationship with our US counterparts, as we work closely to respond to threats to national security and maintain situational awareness of emerging risks.”
The controversy erupted late last month when a CBC memo was leaked to the Canadian press. The broadcaster explained that its “longstanding language guidance regarding the terms ‘terrorist’ and ‘terrorism’ is a preference for the use of these words with attribution, a practice shared by many of the world’s top journalistic organizations.”
The memo sparked outrage in the US, where nearly 3,000 people were killed 25 years ago when Al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four passenger planes and crashed two into the World Trade Center towers in New York and one into the Pentagon outside Washington, DC. The fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. FBI Director Kash Patel described the CBC’s stance as a “bastardization of history” and an insult to the victims.
Following the backlash, the CBC said it was updating its language guidance to “clarify that direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism.” The broadcaster denied, however, that any of its news reports had implied that the attacks were not terrorism.
The incident added to a broader feud between the neighbors after talks on a new trade deal abruptly collapsed last month, with both sides blaming each other. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada should become “the 51st US state” and recently instructed federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario, which straddles the US-Canada border, as Lake America.
The talks broke down after the two sides failed to agree on tariffs and other issues, including US objections to Canadian rules protecting French-language and domestic cultural content.

China Focus: Scars, love, and message of peace carried by Japanese war orphans
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
12:38:44 CST
13:38:44 KST

SHENYANG, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Not until 1986 did Katsu Takahashi, then 43, learn that she was a Japanese war orphan. Growing up in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, she was treated as her father's favorite child, always the first in the family to wear new clothes and shoes and the one who received the largest share of candy.
In 1945, when Japan surrendered and began to retreat from occupied Chinese land, many Japanese women and children who had arrived in northeast China as settlers during the war were abandoned by the Japanese militarists. Takahashi's biological family was among those left behind.
"Later I learnt that in 1945, Japanese militarists had distributed poison to Japanese households in northeast China and told them to commit mass suicide," said Takahashi.
Unwilling to sacrifice her two-year-old daughter, Takahashi's mother secretly left her outside. She was luckily found by the Chinese couple who later became her foster parents.
Takahashi is one of many Japanese war orphans. Records show that over 4,000 Japanese war orphans were left in China and adopted by Chinese families, who raised them despite their own suffering during the Japanese invasion and the harsh postwar environment.
Today, many of these orphans, including Takahashi, have returned to Japan without severing ties with their Chinese foster parents. Their stories continue to call for public attention to the brutality of a war fueled by Japanese militarism and the borderless love shown by ordinary Chinese people.
SURVIVING ABANDONMENT AND SUICIDE CALLS
Ninety-five years ago, on Sept. 18, Japan launched its invasion of China in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, marking the beginning of China's 14-year War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression.
In the following years, Japan sent not only troops to China but also a large number of Japanese settlers, uprooting countless Chinese people from their homes.
In 1936, Japan tried hard to encourage its farmers to migrate to northeast China, promising them access to large tracts of fertile farmland.
With great expectations, some farmers migrated there, only to find themselves serving as pawns in Japan's economic and military expansion, said Cui Xuesen, a professor at Dalian University of Foreign Languages in Liaoning, who has long studied Japanese war orphans.
The villages they lived in were placed under close surveillance and guarded by Japanese troops around the clock. As the war expanded, young and able-bodied men were increasingly drawn into military service, according to Fumiko Wada, whose husband was drafted.
In 1945, as Japan faced defeat, the Japanese forces secretly withdrew, abandoning most of the elderly, sick, women and children among the settlers in the war zone.
Wada, among the women left behind, recalled in her memoir that she took her two young children to the railway station to leave, only to find that the Japanese troops had already disappeared.
"A Japanese official even urged us to 'die for Japan' rather than be captured and humiliated, and soon grenades and poison were handed out," Wada wrote.
Amid gunfire and cries, some took the poison, while others threw themselves into the burning train. Wada shielded her children and fled south to the mountains, but her two-year-old daughter and three-year-old son died on the journey, due to hunger.
Disease, hunger and suicide claimed countless lives among those abandoned. In the turmoil, some Japanese children were left in China. Many of them were later raised by Chinese people.
"The war of aggression waged by Japanese militarism brought immense suffering not only to people of other countries, but also to people of its own," said Cui.
Since 2022, he has traveled to Japan multiple times, interviewing nearly 300 Japanese war orphans and documenting their oral histories.
The stories of these orphans, who serve as both witnesses and survivors of the war, are a vivid reflection of the tragedy caused by the atrocities of Japanese militarism, Cui noted.
Before Takahashi left for Japan, her foster father handed her a faded photo of her biological father. However, when she finally stepped on that unfamiliar land, Takahashi suffered a double blow: her biological father had already died, while her stepmother refused to acknowledge her.
Many Japanese war orphans faced a similar plight. Separated from their families at a young age for decades, these orphans struggled to obtain official recognition of their identities. After returning to Japan, many found it hard to reach their biological parents, struggled to rebuild a life there due to language and cultural barriers, and were trapped in a lifelong identity crisis.
DEFEND TRUTH VIA ACTIONS
After the normalization of diplomatic relations between China and Japan, Chinese authorities allowed the war orphans to choose freely whether to remain in China or return to Japan, and provided assistance accordingly.
After relocating to Japan, Yoshinori Tomii, who was adopted by a family surnamed Dong and graduated from a university in Beijing, still traveled a lot to Heilongjiang to see his foster family. With strong language skills and a cross-cultural background, he has founded businesses in several parts of China, contributing to China-Japan trade and local economic development.
Many other orphans were committed to promoting peace and opposing war, as another way to give back to their foster parents in China.
Sumie Ikeda, also known by her Chinese name Xu Ming, was adopted by a Chinese family in 1945. She became a teacher after graduating in China. When conditions allowed, her foster mother encouraged her to return to Japan and reunite with her biological parents.
Although she chose to return to Japan, Ikeda never forgot her years in China. In 2008, when a magnitude-8.0 earthquake hit southwest China's Sichuan Province, she immediately raised donations among war orphans across Japan. Together, they also helped build a primary school in Sichuan.
In 2009, Ikeda organized a group of Japanese war orphans to return to their "hometowns" in China. She remembered that many of them burst into tears when they set foot on the land they had long missed.
"My Chinese parents gave me a second life, and I grew up in the kindness of many other ordinary Chinese people," she said. "Therefore, my sincerest wish is to see the two peoples live in friendship."
Notably, the orphans' efforts to preserve memories of the war have gone beyond telling their own stories to helping ensure the history is told as it truly was.
For years, some Japanese textbooks and publications have downplayed the colonial nature of the settlement in northeast China, glossing over land seizures and the abandonment of settlers after Japan's defeat, while portraying it as a positive effort to build new lives overseas.
Since 2002, the war orphans have filed a series of lawsuits seeking compensation from the Japanese government. Their lengthy legal battles have prompted the Japanese public to reconsider the nature of the war and Japan's responsibility for it.
Today, an increasing number of artistic works based on this history are also helping more young people learn about the past, while even inspiring new creations.
For years, the dance drama "Chinese Mothers," themed around stories of Japanese war orphans, has been staged across cities in China and Japan.
In November 2025, Japanese documentary filmmaker Ryo Takeuchi held a special screening in Japan for his new work "The Nameless Child." The film tells how Chinese people took care of Japanese war orphans despite the bitter conflict between the two countries.
Having often read news reports about Japanese war orphans when he was a child, Takeuchi hoped to record their stories through his own lens.
"Only by understanding from where we came can we tell where to go," said Takeuchi. ■

Capella Taipei was conceived as a “modern mansion,” welcoming guests into salon-style living spaces rather than a traditional lobby, with books, art, and curated furnishings. The 2026 selection added nearly 470 hotels worldwide, as “hoteliers are reinventing the stay experience through more immersive, personalized, and experiential concepts.”
The Michelin Key system evaluates hotels through anonymous and independent visits by inspectors using five universal criteria. The assessment focuses on the overall accommodation experience rather than individual facilities or services.
Michelin Keys are awarded across three levels, with one Key recognizing a “very special stay,” two Keys an exceptional stay, and three Keys an extraordinary stay. The selection was launched in 2024 across 15 destinations in North America, Europe, and Asia, and now covers 79 destinations worldwide.

Japan has record 100,000 people aged over 100: How societies are ageing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
04:31:06 UTC
13:31:06 KST

Japan has record 100,000 people aged over 100: How societies are ageing
Fewer births and deepening labour shortages are placing mounting pressure on Japan’s social care system.
Japan is now home to more than 100,000 people aged 100 or older, marking a new longevity milestone for a country confronting an accelerating demographic crisis.
The number of centenarians reached a record 107,677 this year, according to Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare – an increase of 7,914 from 2025 and the 56th consecutive annual rise. Women account for almost 88 percent of the total.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4The view from Russia: ‘No party can be antiwar’ in parliamentary election
- list 2 of 4How fantasy fans are keeping a Turkish blacksmithing tradition alive
- list 3 of 4Why does Canada want to join the Europe-led JEF military partnership?
- list 4 of 4As Houthis grab Bab al-Mandeb, US appears willing to watch from sidelines
Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno said he was “very pleased that many people are living long, healthy and active lives”, citing advances in medical technology as well as healthy lifestyles and diets.
But behind the celebration lies a profound imbalance. Japan’s elderly population continues to grow while the number of births remains at an all-time low, leaving a shrinking workforce to plug mounting pension, healthcare and social care costs. Here is what we know.
How rapidly is Japan ageing?
Japan has one of the world’s oldest populations, with almost three in every 10 residents now aged 65 or older. That proportion is projected to approach 40 percent by 2070.
Furthermore, more than 800,000 people were aged 95 or above in Japan last year while only 700,000 babies were born, according to government figures.
The country’s population is, therefore, also declining increasingly quickly. Preliminary census figures show that the population was lower in 45 of Japan’s 47 prefectures in 2025 than five years earlier, with only Tokyo and Okinawa recording increases.
Japan’s population peaked at about 128 million in 2008, with the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research projecting that it will fall to 87 million by 2070 – a decline of roughly 30 percent.
Why are there so many over-100s in Japan?
There is no single explanation for this longevity but researchers have pointed to a combination of diet, activity and healthcare.
The traditional Japanese diet tends to contain large amounts of fish, vegetables and rice, and comparatively low levels of saturated fat. Obesity rates are also significantly lower than in many Western countries.
Daily routines may play a role as well, with many people out walking, cycling and using public transport, including older people, while group exercise is widely practised.
Japan’s universal health insurance system also provides broad access to treatment and medicines at relatively low cost compared with other countries such as the United States.
Why is longevity a problem for Japan?
While living longer is an achievement, in Japan, it is also occurring alongside one of the world’s lowest birth rates. The country’s total fertility rate – the average number of children a woman is expected to have during her lifetime – fell to a record low of 1.14 in 2025. A rate of about 2.1 is generally considered necessary to maintain a stable population without requiring immigration to bolster working-age numbers.
As a population ages, more people of pension age, who may require higher levels of social care and medical intervention, are being supported by fewer working-age people. Over time, this becomes a major economic problem.
Japan has introduced child allowances, subsidised childcare, parental leave programmes and other incentives intended to encourage couples to have children. None has yet reversed the long-term decline, however.
Furthermore, social scientists say, fewer Japanese people are marrying – or they are marrying later when they are less likely to be able to have children – and many younger adults are worried about insecure employment, stagnant wages and demanding working hours, making having a family harder.
Women’s increased participation in the workforce has not always been matched by an equal sharing of childcare and household responsibilities, making parenthood particularly difficult to combine with a career for women.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has identified population decline and the falling birthrate as major national challenges, while Japanese officials have repeatedly warned that the trend threatens the country’s economic and social foundations.
What does this mean for Japan’s economy?
A shrinking working-age population means fewer people paying income taxes and social-security contributions, as spending on pensions, healthcare and elderly care rises in tandem.
That imbalance places mounting pressure on public finances and on the younger workers supporting the system through taxes.
Labour shortages are also affecting industries ranging from construction and agriculture to transport, healthcare and social care. Rural areas face a particularly severe challenge as younger residents move to cities, leaving ageing communities with fewer workers and declining public services.
Immigration can help to offset labour shortages, and Japan’s foreign population has risen in recent years. Foreign nationals, however, still account for only about 3 percent of the population, and proposals to accept substantially more migrants remain politically contentious.
Are other countries also growing older?
Longer life expectancy is one of humanity’s greatest achievements all around the globe, according to the World Health Organization. “Advances in social and economic development as well as in health have lowered mortality rates, particularly among older people,” the WHO said. “Most people can now expect to live into their 60s and beyond.”
Global life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2024, an increase of 8.4 years since 1995, according to the WHO. The number of people aged 60 or older is projected to rise from 1.1 billion in 2023 to 1.4 billion by 2030.
But the transition is considerably more advanced in some countries than others. The latest historical estimates in the United Nations’ World Population Prospects put Japan’s median age at 49 in 2023. Among other countries, Italy followed with a median age of 47.5. Portugal’s stood at 46.2, Greece’s at 45.7 and Germany’s at 45.1.

Cuba's electrical grid collapses again, plunging island into darkness
HAVANA, Sept 18 - Cuba's electrical grid suffered a total collapse on Friday, plunging the nation into darkness and leaving millions without power amid a US pressure campaign that has largely blocked oil from reaching the Caribbean's largest island.
Friday's collapse was triggered by a failure in high-voltage transmission lines in central Cuba that occurred around 2 p.m. local time, authorities said.
"Protocols are now in place to begin the gradual restoration of the system," said Felix Estrada, an official with Cuba's National Electrical Union (UNE).
Power had returned to a handful of scattered neighborhoods in Havana by late evening, primarily around hospitals, but much of the city remained completely dark under cloudy skies and rain.
The nationwide blackout, the latest of at least six partial or total grid collapses since January, hardly registered in a country accustomed to long hours, or even days, without power.
Many exhausted residents of the capital Havana were already without power when the blackout hit.
"Yesterday I'd gone without power for 24 hours. They turned the lights on for an hour, and then the grid collapsed," said Frank Lorenzo, a 23-year-old Havana resident looking forward to a long night of sweating and slapping mosquitoes.
Cuba's aging power generation system has been under severe strain from fuel shortages and decrepit infrastructure for years, but a US-imposed oil blockade that began in January has vastly worsened blackouts and led to more frequent grid collapses.
The grid collapsed three times in July and rolling blackouts have since spanned 30 hours or more across most of the country.
United Nations human rights experts have condemned the US oil blockade, calling it a violation of international law and warning that Cuba risks becoming a "silent Gaza" as shortages and blackouts grow ever more critical. REUTERS
