I live in the ‘coolest neighbourhood’ in the world. It’s not as great as you’d think
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
03:16:30 UTC
12:16:30 KST

In 2021, I was asked by Time Out to nominate a Seoul neighbourhood for its annual list of the world’s coolest. I didn’t think much of it and put forward the one I live in, Jongno 3-ga, in the old centre of the city. Somehow, it got ranked third.
This week, the same area was named the coolest neighbourhood in the world. I should be pleased, but instead, I’m devastated.
All these lists seem to celebrate the same idea of “cool”: expensive conceptual art galleries, high-end restaurants, and the sort of places that cater to a narrow demographic of people who read lifestyle magazines. Most cities have these places.
But when I moved to Jongno 3-ga, I chose somewhere that was the opposite: humble, raw and completely unpretentious.
I was first drawn to the neighbourhood 20 years ago, fresh out of school. I recollect with sweet nostalgia being one of the few tourists at a time when South Korea was not “cool”, and people often advised me against travelling there, confusing South Korea with North Korea.
There were no English menus, but restaurants were welcoming. Shopfronts were rusty but full of artisanry, while alleys that went nowhere and were slightly dilapidated felt cosy. There were men getting drunk over bottles of soju who occasionally got into a brawl, but nothing that ever felt particularly threatening. I felt at home and eventually made it my home.
It was a refuge for society’s rejects: people with nowhere to go, some of the poorest in Seoul, residents of the city’s tiny-room settlements and people with disabilities. In Tapgol Park, elderly women sold sexual services to older men in plain sight. Outside the park, pensioners played janggi, Korean chess, on the pavement. Around them lived musicians and artists. In Jongno 3-ga, everyone was welcome.
For years, the pojangmacha, the street-food tents that serve everything from fried squid to kimchi pancake, catered to older people drinking through to the early evening. Then at some point – around 9pm – there was an unofficial handover to the gay scene.
South Korea is socially conservative and the LGBTQ+ community is still very much frowned upon. But come the weekend, hundreds of excited men of all ages came to let off steam out in the open, as well as in one of the area’s more than 100 gay bars and karaoke rooms. Jongno 3-ga was a place where people could be themselves, without fear of being outed, harassed or judged.
None of that was cool. But that was the entire point: people could mind their own business in a safe haven amid a culture addicted to consumerism and keeping up appearances.
That all changed after Covid. The street barbecues and pojangmacha are still there, but now they have queues, some up to an hour long. People line up for a seat, take their Instagram shots, and the neighbourhood that used to hide people has become a place to be seen.
With the crowds came the displacement. Gay patrons no longer take over the streets at night. The older drinkers have largely gone. The sex workers have been pushed out. The chess boards outside Tapgol Park were cleared away. Rents have risen sharply.
The area is now littered with kitschy tourist shops, claw-machine arcades and unmanned photo-booths, and, in the streets nearby, bakery after bakery, coffee shop after coffee shop. One by one, the small merchants have left, to be replaced with another dessert shop. It’s now hard to find the humble rice-and-soup places that fed this neighbourhood for decades. The once shabby and unremarkable place is now heavily curated, and doesn’t feel very “Korean” any more.
Locals complain about lost identity and gentrification but put on a brave face for the hordes of tourists, both local and international, who come to gorge on this area.
None of this is the fault of the visitors either. They were told the place was worth seeing, and they are buying exactly what they were sold. K-culture has never been more popular. From the likes of BTS to Squid Game, the whole world is looking to South Korea and keeps coming – and things are changing to accommodate for these tourist dollars.
But in a way, I feel part of the problem. I highlighted a place I loved for being overlooked, and feel I helped create a monster. Now, as the neighbourhood becomes almost unrecognisable, I wonder what effect these rankings have on the people who live in the listed destinations.
Jongno 3-ga becoming the “world’s coolest neighbourhood” is nothing to celebrate. I feel guilty for calling it cool. I’d take the word back if I could.

China Focus: Chinese AI-driven telescope earns place in Stanford AI Index Report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:51:03 CST
11:51:03 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China's StarWhisper Telescope has been cited in Stanford University's AI Index Report 2026 as a leading 2025 example of AI agents in physics, astronomy, chemistry and materials science, signaling growing international recognition for the country's AI-driven observation efforts.
Led by the National Astronomical Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NAOC), the telescope explores how large models and AI agents can be integrated with telescope control systems, enabling agents to help plan tasks and carry out observations based on researchers' requirements, scientific objectives, equipment status and observing conditions.
As large models, AI agents and embodied intelligence advance rapidly, AI is moving beyond data analysis into the operation of scientific instruments and the conduct of research. The NAOC launched its AI for Astronomy program to seize this shift.
The program explores AI applications in astronomical data processing, scientific discovery, telescope control and coordinated observations across multiple facilities. Its goal is to move from isolated algorithms to an intelligent tool system spanning the entire research process.
Recently, the team reported new progress centered on the StarWhisper Telescope in three areas: digital simulation of research-grade telescopes, coordination between scientific models and observation-control systems, and autonomous observation by AI agents.
The telescope has expanded its simulation capabilities with a digital simulation system for large-aperture research telescopes, creating an experimental environment where AI agents can take part in observation planning and validate control strategies.
Research-grade telescopes are complex instruments whose observation processes are shaped by the optical tube, mount, camera, sensors, control systems and weather. For AI agents to play a substantive role in telescope operations, they first need an environment that can sense equipment status, understand observation conditions and test control strategies.
Drawing on its long experience in telescope operation and control, along with an agent toolchain developed in recent years, the NAOC research team built the digital simulation environment quickly.
Without consuming actual telescope observing time, the system can simulate telescope components, sensor states, environmental changes and observation workflows, laying a foundation for testing control strategies, training agents and optimizing observation procedures.
The team is also exploring a system that links scientific models, environmental models, telescope control systems and AI agents, enabling agents to monitor and invoke different tools and devices.
AI agents can further weigh scientific-target priorities, the telescope's real-time status and target visibility windows to autonomously complete a closed loop of state perception, task planning, plan generation and workflow validation.
To date, the agents have flagged eight very early supernova candidates, two of which triggered follow-up observations when weather conditions permitted. ■

Mongolia's national book festival opens in Ulan Bator
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:50:56 CST
11:50:56 KST

ULAN BATOR, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- The 40th edition of Mongolia's National Book Festival officially opened in Ulan Bator, the capital of Mongolia, on Friday, bringing together hundreds of authors, publishers, readers and book lovers from Mongolia and abroad.
The festival is being organized by the non-governmental organization Nomiin Soyolt Yertunts (World of Book Culture) at Sukhbaatar Square in the heart of the capital.
The festival aims to promote a culture of reading and appreciation for books, encourage children and young people to read more, and provide an opportunity for readers to meet and interact with authors and writers, according to the organizer.
Held under the motto "Let's read more and love our planet," the book festival features more than 300 authors and over 200 publishing houses, as well as representatives from countries including China, India, Japan, South Korea and Kyrgyzstan, it said.
The three-day event includes book fairs featuring both new and previously published titles, meetings and discussions with Mongolian writers, presentations of new books by foreign authors, and mass public reading sessions.
Visitors can also explore a wide range of books and take part in activities designed to encourage reading among children and young people.
The National Book Festival was first held in 2007 and has since been organized twice a year, in spring and autumn. Over the years, it has grown into Mongolia's largest book-related cultural event, attracting increasing numbers of readers, writers, publishers and international participants.
The festival has also become an important platform for promoting literature, supporting the publishing industry and fostering a stronger reading culture among Mongolia's younger generation. ■

Putin approves takeover of French and Swiss giants’ Russian assets. Why now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
02:46:31 UTC
11:46:31 KST

Putin approves takeover of French and Swiss giants’ Russian assets. Why now?
President Vladimir Putin has ordered the Russian subsidiaries of Nestle, Auchan and Leroy Merlin placed under temporary management owing to Western support for Ukrainian strikes on Russian civilian and economic infrastructure.
Moscow introduced the temporary management mechanism in 2023 in response to Western companies leaving Russia and the seizure of Russian state and private assets abroad. Officials said it was intended to keep strategically important businesses operating and shield the economy from decisions by “unfriendly” countries.
On Thursday, Putin amended the 2023 decree to add the Russian assets of Nestle, Auchan and Leroy Merlin to the list. All three were transferred to L.E.V. Management, a business and management consultancy.
Why now?
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the companies’ home countries and their support for Kiev were major factors behind the decision.
“We are talking about European companies, companies from unfriendly countries,” he told journalists on Friday. “These are unfriendly countries that are actively involved in military actions against our country,” Peskov said, adding that some also support Ukrainian strikes “against our civilian economic infrastructure.”
Why these companies?
Auchan and Leroy Merlin are controlled by France’s Mulliez family through ELO Group and ADEO respectively. Nestle’s Russian business was controlled by subsidiaries of the Swiss food giant.
France has been one of Kiev’s major military backers throughout the conflict. President Emmanuel Macron also pushed a “forward deterrence initiative” earlier this year that could see French nuclear weapons deployed elsewhere in Europe.
Moscow has warned that such a strategy could backfire, saying it cannot “ignore an obvious buildup of the nuclear component of NATO’s joint potential.”
Switzerland, meanwhile, has backed EU sanctions against Russia, prompting Moscow to designate it an “unfriendly nation.” Bern has also considered easing restrictions on the re-export of Swiss-made weapons to Ukraine, sparking criticism from the country’s largest party that its longstanding neutrality is being eroded.
Strikes on Russian infrastructure
The takeover also comes amid continued Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian and energy infrastructure.
Ukraine has recently targeted warehouses and logistics facilities belonging to Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, and its rival Ozon. Kiev has acknowledged deliberately striking the facilities, claiming their networks are used by the Russian military to procure, store and transport dual-use goods. Moscow rejects the allegations and has denounced the attacks as terrorism.
Ukrainian media reported in July that French intelligence was providing “critical targeting assistance” for strikes on at least eight Wildberries facilities, as well as refineries and other infrastructure.
How important is Russia to the companies?
Russia has been a significant market for the French retailers. At its peak, Auchan Russia was one of the country’s largest foreign retail chains and was still operating around 230 stores as of 2025. ELO reported in 2023 that Russia generated 10% of its revenue, making it the group’s third-largest market after France and Spain.
ADEO relinquished operational control of its Russian subsidiary in 2023, handing management to local executives. However, documents obtained by French investigative outlet L’Informe indicated that ADEO continued to classify the operation as a subsidiary and an “autonomous business unit.”
Leroy Merlin, rebranded as Lemana PRO in Russia in 2024, remained a major source of revenue for ADEO. L’Informe reported that Russia was the group’s second-largest market by revenue after France in 2024 and accounted for around 18.5% of its worldwide revenue in 2025.
Nestle has less exposure. Its Russian operations account for about 1% of global sales, according to Jean-Philippe Bertschy, an analyst at Swiss investment bank Vontobel. RBK estimated Nestle Russia’s revenue at 258 billion rubles ($3.06 billion) in 2025.
How have the companies reacted?
Auchan and Lemana PRO said they had received no official notification from the Russian authorities about the status of their assets and had requested clarification. Both said their stores were operating normally as of Friday.
Nestle said it “takes note” of the presidential decree and is “assessing the situation and its options.” The company said it would take “all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders.”
What happens to the assets?
Under the 2023 framework, foreign owners temporarily lose control of assets placed under management but do not automatically forfeit ownership.
Some assets have been transferred directly to Russian state bodies. In 2023, the Russian operations of Germany’s Uniper and Finland’s Fortum were placed under the Federal Property Management Agency.
In other cases, Moscow has authorized sales. Putin approved the sale of Goldman Sachs’ Russian subsidiary to Balchug Capital in January 2025.
The system also allows assets to be returned. In March 2025, Italian appliance maker Ariston regained control of Ariston Thermo Rus after announcing its return to the Russian market. The subsidiary had been placed under the temporary management of Gazprom Household Systems the previous year.
Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said in 2025 that cases would be assessed individually. Companies that left under government pressure but preserved jobs, contacts and technology, as well as a buy-back option, could be allowed to return, he said.

Belarus Reactivated Drone Relays, Helping Russia Strike Diplomatic Train Route Near Polish Border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
02:34:20 UTC
11:34:20 KST

Belarus has reactivated signal relay stations that help Russian Shahed and Gerbera drones reach deeper into western Ukraine, reversing a June shutdown that followed a direct warning from President Volodymyr Zelensky.
State Border Guard Service spokesman Andrii Demchenko said in a televised interview early Saturday that Belarusian relay activity had intensified in recent days.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Since the end of last week, we have essentially been detecting the activation of signal relays that amplify the signal for Russian drones that the enemy directs at our western regions,” he said.
The systems allow Russian drones entering from Russia to stay close to the Belarusian border, pick up stronger signals and then move deeper toward the Rivne, Volyn and Lviv regions.
Demchenko said the activity shows Belarus is continuing to help Russia attack Ukraine despite statements from Belarusian Alexander Lukashenko seeking to distance Minsk from Moscow’s war.
Kyiv forced the relays offline in June
In June, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had identified four Russian signal relay stations operating in Belarus’s Gomel and Brest regions.
He said the equipment had helped Russia strike the Zhytomyr, Rivne and Volyn regions, including Ukrainian energy infrastructure, railways, cities and villages.
Zelensky gave Lukashenko one week to remove the systems, warning that Ukraine would destroy them if Minsk failed to act.
Within days, the equipment went silent.
Trump Signs Sweeping Russia Sanctions Bill Into Law
On June 24, Zelensky said military and intelligence reports showed that the relay stations had stopped operating as of June 22, although Kyiv could not confirm whether they had been dismantled or merely switched off.
Ukraine’s Air Force later said the shutdown had significantly weakened Russia’s ability to control Shahed drones in real time, including changing their routes and targets while airborne.
Now, they are back.
Belarus helped Russia strike near diplomatic train
The renewed relay activity follows a familiar and dangerous pattern.
Demchenko linked Belarusian support directly to Russia’s Sept. 13 drone attack near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk crossing with Poland.
A Russian drone struck a locomotive on the Kyiv-Warsaw route roughly two kilometers from the Polish border, while another hit near the crossing itself.
The passenger train carried 206 people and was evacuated before impact. A diplomatic train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt and other Western officials had passed through the station shortly beforehand.
“As of now, Belarus is actively assisting Russia” in strikes on Ukrainian territory, Demchenko said while discussing the Yahodyn attack.
Kyiv watches northern border
While the electronic threat has returned, Ukraine is not currently seeing a Belarusian ground force near the border capable of launching a conventional invasion, the State Border Guard Service said.
Kyiv nevertheless remains alert, closely monitoring frequent Belarusian military exercises and readiness checks.
Belarus as Russia’s launchpad
In February 2022, Belarus served as one of the main launchpads for Russia’s full-scale invasion. Since then, Minsk has hosted Russian tactical nuclear weapons, held repeated joint military exercises and provided military infrastructure that helps Moscow sustain pressure on Ukraine.
For Kyiv, the issue is not only whether Belarusian soldiers cross the border. The deeper concern is whether Belarusian territory, bases, radar systems, relay stations and logistics continue to support Russian attacks.
That makes Belarus part of the battlefield, even if Lukashenko insists he is not part of the war.

What is celebrated on September 19 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:33:11 EEST
11:33:11 KST

What is celebrated on September 19 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
In Ukraine, Inventors’ Day and Pharmaceutical Workers’ Day are celebrated. Around the world, World Smiley Day and the independence of Saint Kitts and Nevis are commemorated.
On September 19, Ukraine observes Inventors’ and Rationalizers’ Day and Pharmaceutical Workers’ Day; worldwide, people celebrate Digital Smiley’s Birthday and the Independence Day of Saint Kitts and Nevis, while according to the church calendar based on the new style, the holy martyrs Trophimus, Sabbatius, and Dorymedon are commemorated, UNN writes.
Inventors’ and Rationalizers’ Day of Ukraine
An official professional holiday established by a decree of the President of Ukraine in 1994, observed annually on the third Saturday of September.
The event honors Ukrainian scientists, engineers, designers, and innovators whose technical developments, patented inventions, and rationalization proposals advance the country’s industry, defense-industrial complex, medicine, and IT sector.
Pharmaceutical Workers’ Day of Ukraine
An official professional holiday established by a decree of the President of Ukraine in 1999, which also falls on the third Saturday of September.
The holiday is dedicated to representatives of the pharmaceutical industry—pharmacists, pharmacy professionals, scientists, drug developers, and medicine manufacturers—who ensure the country’s medical security, develop innovative medicines, and provide an uninterrupted supply of essential products.
Digital Smiley’s Birthday (Smiley Face / Emoticon Birthday)
An unofficial international observance dedicated to the event of September 19, 1982, when Carnegie Mellon University professor Scott Fahlman first proposed using the sequence of symbols :-) to mark humorous messages on an electronic bulletin board.
This simple symbol became the textual ancestor of modern emoji culture and the digital expression of emotions in online communication.
World Bone Marrow Donor Day
A global medical observance under the auspices of the World Marrow Donor Association (WMDA), held on the third Saturday of September.
It aims to express gratitude to millions of volunteer donors and raise public awareness of the importance of expanding hematopoietic stem cell donor registries to save patients with leukemia and other serious hematological diseases.
International Talk Like a Pirate Day
An unofficial parody holiday invented in 1995 by Americans John Baur and Mark Summers.
On this day, fans of pirate themes and popular culture around the world communicate using the slang of 17th–18th-century pirates, use characteristic exclamations, and dress in themed costumes.
Independence Day of Saint Kitts and Nevis
The main national holiday of the Caribbean island nation, established to commemorate the proclamation of full independence from Great Britain on September 19, 1983. The country gained sovereignty as a federal constitutional monarchy within the Commonwealth of Nations.
The Day of Remembrance of the Holy Martyrs Trophimus, Sabbatius, and Dorymedon
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate the holy martyrs Trophimus, Sabbatius, and Dorymedon, who suffered for the Christian faith in Antioch in the 3rd century during the persecutions under Emperor Probus.
This day also commemorates the Venerable Alexei of Holosiiv (Shepelev), a renowned Kyiv elder and ascetic of the 19th–20th centuries who became famous for his gift of clairvoyance and prayerful assistance.
According to the old calendar, believers observe the Commemoration of the Miracle of the Archangel Michael at Khonae (Colossae)—one of the best-known folk-religious holidays, known as Michael’s Miracle.
According to tradition, in the 4th century in Phrygia, the Archangel Michael appeared near a church and, striking the rock with his staff, split it open, directing into the fissure two mountain rivers that pagans had unleashed to flood the shrine.
The holy martyrs Eudoxius, Zeno, and Macarius are also commemorated on this day.

Flock Offers Employees Buyouts as Customers Flee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
02:22:54 UTC
11:22:54 KST

Flock Safety announced a voluntary employee separation program on Friday, offering a “generous” severance package to those who want to leave amid growing backlash against the surveillance technology company, according to an internal email shared with WIRED.
Applications for Flock’s voluntary severance program opened Friday, and employees have until October 2 to decide whether to leave the company. Flock expects to grant buyouts to the majority of workers who apply, according to the email. People familiar with the program but not authorized to discuss it publicly say they believe that a significant number of the startup’s roughly 1,500 employees may try to depart.
Flock is making the severance offers as it continues to lose customers amid growing frustration across the US about its sprawling network of license plate readers, which have raised concerns about privacy and misuse. In the last month, WIRED has documented officers allegedly abusing Flock to track former romantic partners and colleagues, exposed how widely some agencies share access to the system, shown how little is known about the manufacturing of the devices, and revealed in new detail how much information Flock’s cameras collect based on data from a dismantled Flock device.
Founded in 2017, Flock raised money at a valuation of more than $8 billion in a funding round that closed in April. The company has had many of its contracts either not extended or dropped this year, which could leave it short of revenue goals, according to two of the people. A wave of vandalism targeting its cameras has unexpectedly increased expenses. Without buyouts, Flock almost certainly would have to lay off some staff, one of the people believes.
In an internal announcement, Flock said the separation program provides “greater agency” for its workers and “treats employees with transparency, respect, and choice.” It also described the package as the “most generous” ever offered by the company, roughly double its previous severance offers.
Flock did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Some Flock employees have said they have received buyout offers in the range of tens of thousands of dollars, one of the people said. The package also gives employees several months of health care coverage and the ability to exercise stock options within two years after separation, a longer period than the company typically offers resigning employees, according to the email and people familiar with the offer.
Flock employees are expected to learn whether their applications were accepted on October 9, according to the email. Most accepted employees would leave the company by October 29, though in some cases Flock may ask employees to remain for another one to three months.
People familiar with Flock’s severance plan tell WIRED that some employees may take the offer amid speculation that the company, which has raised about $1.2 billion in venture capital, might resort to selling off parts or all of its business to stay afloat. “When you see enough of the vandalism” targeting Flock cameras this year, one of the people says, “you know the writing is the wall” that something has to change.
Flock CEO Garrett Langley said on the All-In podcast last month that “the biggest damage” caused by the backlash against the company had been “internal morale.”
“Because you go on to X or you go on to Reddit and you go, why are people so mad at us when we've been doing the same thing for nine years?” Langley said. “And why are they so mad at us for things we don't do? And we just want people to be safe.”
One advocacy group identified 93 city and county governments that cut ties with Flock in August alone. Overall in 2026, roughly three times as many local governments have dropped Flock compared to the previous five years.
Flock has recently been building products that extend the company beyond its core license plate reader offering. WIRED reported last month that the company has developed AI-powered investigative software to identify drivers, find potential associates based on patterns of movement, and search across police records and other data.
A separate WIRED analysis of Flock’s software found tools designed to continuously search camera feeds for people matching written descriptions. WIRED’s analysis of Flock’s code also found potential integrations with drones and other surveillance systems.

US clears way for US$2.7 billion sale of air-defence development upgrades to Ukraine
WASHINGTON - The US State Department approved a potential US$2.7 billion military sale to Ukraine for air defence development upgrades and related equipment and services, the department said in a congressional notification late on Sept 18.
If the purchase is concluded, Ukraine would finance it using a combination of European contributions and US Foreign Military Financing (FMF) appropriated during the administration of former US president Joe Biden, the State Department said in the notification.
FMF provides grant assistance that enables countries to purchase weapons and defence equipment produced in the United States.
“The FMF will be counted as a US capital contribution to the Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund via a 1:1 reimbursement,” the State Department said.
The US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund was established as part of a minerals deal signed between the US and Ukraine last year.
The package includes S-300 clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, range-extended air defence laser-guided rocket missile systems, launcher and mobile launching system modification kits and counter-drone system radars, among other weapons systems, the State Department said.
The proposed sale is still subject to congressional review.
President Donald Trump had said he would end Russia’s war in Ukraine when he took office early last year but the goal remains elusive 20 months into his presidency. 
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
Earlier on Sept 18, Trump signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill into law, paving the way for increased economic pressure on Russia.
Earlier this month, Trump said he would ask European nations to pay back the United States for military aid and munitions previously sent to Ukraine. REUTERS

US court blocks Trump plan to deport migrants to third countries
US judges affirm migrants must have opportunities to voice safety concerns before deportation to unfamiliar nations.
A US federal appeals court has rejected the Trump administration’s policy of rapidly deporting migrants to countries other than their own – a ruling that could next go before the Supreme Court.
On Friday, a three-judge panel of the 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston largely upheld a February decision that found the Department of Homeland Security’s so-called third-country removal policy unlawful.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Why are election officials in the US preparing for chaos before midterms?
- list 2 of 3US judge blocks Trump’s latest effort to limit birthright citizenship
- list 3 of 3Trump administration proposes excluding certain immigrants from US census
The case stems from a class-action lawsuit testing what due process migrants are owed before being sent to nations with which they have no ties.
Writing for the panel, US Circuit Judge Seth Aframe said migrants must be given a “meaningful” chance to raise safety concerns before removal, rejecting the Trump administration’s narrower reading of the law.
The court did overturn part of the ruling on procedural grounds, concerning whether officials must first try deporting migrants to countries they have ties to.
Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said the decision confirmed that “due process and the protections Congress enacted against persecution and torture cannot be circumvented by putting someone on a plane to a country that was never part of their removal proceedings”.
The DHS did not immediately comment. The Trump administration is expected to appeal the ruling.
Under Trump, the US has struck agreements allowing it to send more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, most often Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a tracker run by the rights groups Refugees International and Human Rights First.
The policy, adopted in March 2025, allowed removals with only minimal notice if officials had diplomatic assurances against persecution.
The controversial programme has reached the Supreme Court twice.
In 2025, the justices cleared the way for eight men, including nationals of Cuba, Myanmar and Vietnam, to be deported to South Sudan, a country the US State Department advises against visiting because of “crime, kidnapping, and armed conflict”.
The DHS called the removals “a win”, while rights groups said they flouted basic protections.
The Trump administration’s immigration agenda has faced a string of setbacks this month.
A federal judge blocked planned caps on student and journalist visas, calling the government’s justification “exceptionally weak”, while a coalition of 22 states and Washington, DC, sued to stop a separate rule that would let officials deny green cards to immigrants who lawfully use public benefits.

Chinese scientists find first evidence of ancient nose-chopping punishment for cattle thieves
Unknown

11:00:10 KST

Chinese scientists find first evidence of ancient nose-chopping punishment for cattle thieves
Under the rule of the King of Qin (247 BC–221 BC), severed noses accumulated like mountain peaks, and carts overflowed with amputated feet
Stealing someone’s cattle is a serious crime, and in many places, the thief would end up in jail. However, ancient Chinese justice could result in a truly horrific form of mutilation: the amputation of the nose.
This harsh consequence has been well-documented by historians as one of the infamous “five punishments” from the penal system of the Xia dynasty (2070 BC–1600 BC). Until now, no physical evidence of this punishment had been discovered.
A team of researchers from China and the US recently announced the finding of a female skeleton dated between 1298 and 1404 (from either the Yuan or Ming dynasties) that showed clear evidence of nose removal as part of a criminal sentence.

How Germany’s far right learned to put on a smile to win elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Five years ago, the Alternative for Germany’s campaign posters in Saxony-Anhalt carried a single bleak word: “Enough.”
This month, the far-right party won a historic landslide in the eastern German state by offering something different: “Everything is Possible.” Arguably, it was an AfD version of Barack Obama’s 2008 rallying cry: “Yes We Can.”
That change — from grumbling exasperation to upbeat optimism — helps explain why the AfD has surged at the ballot box, putting its first state government within reach earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt and setting it up to hit historic highs in two further state elections on Sunday, in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Advertisement
Others have taken note, and it might well serve as a new campaigning template for far-right populists across Europe — at least for those able to flash a credible smile.
“I call it feel-good populism,” said Johannes Hillje, a Berlin-based political consultant who managed the European Green Party’s 2014 European Parliament campaign. “What we saw was a new type of AfD campaign.”
“In the past it has been mainly negative rhetoric, scapegoating migrants, attacking the elite, evoking fear and rage,” Hillje added. “If you really want to mobilize people, it’s not enough just to attack others. You also have to offer a positive perspective.”
At its core, the AfD continues to hold a dark vision of Germany’s path — depicting the country as on the brink of catastrophe due to the destructive forces of migration and deindustrialization. The party’s intellectual ideologues espouse an almost apocalyptic view of the decline of Germany and the West.
Yet in recent elections, the party has papered over this ideological core with a cheerful, reassuring facade, seeking to marry hope with fear.
In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD’s lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund was labeled by one magazine “Germany’s most dangerous man.” But at campaign stops and in television appearances, he projected another image: He kept an almost permanent smile on his face, was invariably polite and friendly, took selfies with voters and rode his sky-blue vintage East German-era scooter.
Advertisement
Siegmund combined the forward-looking “Everything is Possible” with another slogan, “Bring Back the Good Old Times,” fusing nostalgia and hope, a powerful combination for people worried about the rapid pace of disruptive change and an uncertain future.
“He’s become a bit of a pop star, and that explains a lot about why the AfD doubled its vote,” said the German-British historian Katja Hoyer. “It also helps explain why there was a smaller gap between men and women in Saxony-Anhalt. In the national vote, far more men than women vote for the AfD.”
Hoyer believes the appeal won’t be confined to Germany. Others will learn from it.
Alice Weidel, Ulrich Siegmund and Tino Chrupalla celebrate following state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6, 2026. | Omer Messinger/Getty Images
In the summer of 2024, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen declared that “the center is holding.” Following that year’s European Parliament elections, it seemed voters still largely backed centrist parties, despite significant gains by right-wing populists and national conservatives. But a succession of elections since then, including Saxony-Anhalt, has suggested that Europe may be further from peak populism than many centrists hoped.
Marco Tarchi, an Italian political scientist at the University of Florence, believes populism in Europe still has further to go. “Political narratives rather than policy details drive voter behavior,” he told POLITICO. For right-wing populists, he said, it will be crucial to ensure that their narratives focus on the issues potential voters deem most important.
Hoyer’s latest book, “Weimar,” chronicles interwar Germany and the rise of the Nazis through Weimar, the birthplace of the country’s first full democracy. She has closely observed this month’s state elections and, while dismissing comparisons with the late 1920s, acknowledged some parallels.
Advertisement
“There’s certainly something in the air that causes lots of politicians to refer to Weimar and to the Nazi era,” she said.
But she cautioned that the periods were very different, particularly when it came to political violence. “Whatever the similarities, we don’t see the AfD running around with armed people on the streets intimidating and murdering opponents,” she added.
But Hoyer sees one important echo: Voters worried about the future are looking to parties that offer a clearer vision than moderates. After the Wall Street crash, Germans got austerity from Chancellor Heinrich Brüning. Hitler, by contrast, promised: “Give me four years, and I will sort it all out,” she said.
“I fear there’s a similarity now,” she added. “People don’t see solutions coming from the mainstream parties, who point to geopolitics and say, ‘What can we do?’ Meanwhile, the AfD and some other right-wing populists say, ‘We will do X, Y, and Z.’”
“It doesn’t even have to be realistic,” she said. “I think people just want to feel that somebody has got some sort of plan.”

Berlin election campaign centers around radical-left drive to seize properties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

BERLIN — Berlin’s leftist parties have a radical answer to the capital’s worsening housing crunch: seize the properties of the real estate giants they blame for ruining the city.
That plan has become the most hotly contested issue in an election that takes place Sunday, with a coalition of left-wing parties poised to oust the conservative mayor of Germany’s capital and potentially usher in the first far-left mayor since the fall of the Berlin Wall.
“The housing issue is the central social issue facing our city, and I have always said that, if I become mayor, I will pull out all the stops to make Berlin affordable again and lower rents,” said Elif Eralp, the lead candidate for the Left party.
Advertisement
Eralp’s far-left party maintains a narrow lead in polls heading into the vote Sunday in Berlin, just ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which currently holds the mayor’s office. If her Left party is able to eke out a win, it’s likely to lead a coalition of left-wing parties that excludes the conservatives, who have fought such plans.
The Left party, which traces part of its history to East Germany’s communist party, is enjoying a political revival after winning a new wave of support from young voters mobilized by the far right’s rise. For its Berlin campaign, the party has taken inspiration from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, employing his focus on cost-of-living issues as a model.
Once a city known for cheap rents that helped cultivate an international, bohemian culture, affordable housing has become a particularly pressing issue in the German capital in recent years. Fewer than one in six residents of the city own the home they live in, while rents have risen by about 70% over the past decade.
The Left party is running on a plan to expropriate properties from real estate companies that own more than 3,000 apartments. It’s an idea that has widespread support in a city that has historically leaned left.
Nearly 60 percent of voters backed expropriating properties from major real estate companies in a 2021 referendum. The organization that initiated that referendum estimates that the city could forcibly buy as many as 220,000 apartments for up to 60 percent of their market value — amounting to a total of €18 billion. That money, they argue, could be recovered by the city over the course of a century from rental income.
Stefan Evers, the CDU’s lead candidate in Berlin, says fear of a Left party win is already causing harm to the city’s real estate market.
Advertisement
“Many housing companies are steering well clear of Berlin simply because this debate is already taking place today, because there is a political party that may come to power and actually wants to implement this,” he told RTL television. “It will prevent new apartments from being built — apartments that are already in short supply today. And it will drive up rents. And that is exactly the opposite of what we want.”
Leftist ‘paradigm shift’
The Greens in Berlin, polling in fourth place with around 15 percent support, are the only other party to fully support the expropriation plans, and have expressed their ambition to push it through in coalition with the Left party.
“The question is whether, after this election, the right policies will finally be put in place and we can usher in a paradigm shift,” said Katrin Schmidberger, a Green lawmaker sitting in Berlin’s state parliament.
That leaves the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), polling fifth with 12 percent support, as a potential moderating force. The Left party would need both the Greens and SPD to have enough seats to form a government in Berlin. But the SPD’s lead candidate, Steffen Krach, opposes expropriation, favoring other measures to lower rents.
Krach may have somewhat limited scope to hinder the plans following a corruption probe involving accusations he accepted illicit campaign donations while he held an earlier office in Hanover. Krach, who denies any wrongdoing, has lost political capital as a result of the accusations.
Right-wing parties have meanwhile railed against the expropriation plans in Berlin, including the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is polling at an unexpectedly strong 18% — putting it in third place, just a few percentage points behind the Left party.
Advertisement
“With the Left party, above all, what you get is new socialism,” Kristin Brinker, the AfD’s lead candidate in Berlin, told Welt TV. “We know — if we look back — that Berlin has already experienced socialism, and given the state of the real estate market at that time, that’s something many people don’t want.”
Legal hurdles
The AfD has no chance of taking real political power in Berlin, as all other parties have ruled out working with the far right. But a potential left-wing coalition would still need to overcome many hurdles.
Although an expert commission concluded in 2023 that the expropriation proposal is legally feasible, implementing it would be tricky.
Such a move be founded on Article 15 of Germany’s constitution, which allows “land, natural resources, and means of production” to be transferred to “common ownership.” But that provision has never been applied.
If implemented, the expropriation policy would almost certainly be challenged before the constitutional court, with experts arguing the judges could rule either way.
Merz’s government has vowed to prevent the expropriation of real estate companies at the state level by adopting a national law against the practice. But that text hasn’t been drafted and experts are, once again, divided on whether the federal government would have the legal ability to block local efforts.
Despite the obstacles, the Left party, believes it will prevail.
“As for the federal government’s proposal, I’ll say this very clearly: we don’t want any interference … And as a lawyer, I’ll also say clearly that I have very serious doubts about whether that is constitutional,” the party’s lead candidate Eralp told reporters in Berlin earlier this month. “That’s why we stand by our position: We want to expropriate.”

Harry Kane (front) of Bayern Munich takes a penalty to score during the German first division Bundesliga football match between FC Bayern Munich and 1. FC Union Berlin in Munich, Germany, Sept. 18, 2026. (Photo by Philippe Ruiz/Xinhua)
BERLIN, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Harry Kane became the fastest player to score 100 Bundesliga goals, while Michael Olise hit a hat-trick as Bayern Munich thrashed Union Berlin 7-0 on Friday.
Union, with captain Christopher Trimmel replacing the ill Josip Juranovic, defended deep under coach Mauro Lustrinelli and kept Bayern at bay during the opening 15 minutes.
Jamal Musiala broke the deadlock in the 18th minute, drilling a low shot into the right corner for his first Bundesliga goal since Bayern's 4-3 win over Mainz on April 25.
Union goalkeeper Frederik Ronnow produced a sharp save to deny Jonathan Tah before Olise won a penalty after being fouled by Tom Rothe inside the area in the 38th minute. Kane converted from the spot a minute later to score his 100th Bundesliga goal in just his 98th appearance, setting a competition record.
Olise made it 3-0 in the 43rd minute, firing into the top corner after receiving a pass from Musiala.
Manuel Neuer was called into action twice shortly after the restart, denying Janik Haberer and Rothe, but Bayern soon resumed its dominance. Olise crossed for Kane to head home his 101st Bundesliga goal in the 54th minute.
Kane was denied a hat-trick by a defensive block, while Rothe cleared substitute Ismael Saibari's effort off the line. Saibari responded moments later, collecting a pass from Alphonso Davies, beating several defenders and firing Bayern's fifth goal into the net in the 70th minute.
Olise then took center stage. Tom Bischof released the Frenchman, who rounded Ronnow to score his second goal three minutes later. The same pair combined again in the 76th minute, with Olise curling the ball home to complete his hat-trick and seal the 7-0 rout.
Serge Gnabry came off the bench in the 77th minute as Bayern comfortably saw out the closing stages.
"Top performance on the highest level from start to finish. To reach 101 Bundesliga goals makes me proud," Kane said.
Union remains without a victory after four rounds, while Bayern will travel to Augsburg after the international break. Union will host newly promoted Elversberg on October 10. ■

Anthropic picks Accenture for in-house AI safety evaluation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

10:40:00 KST

Anthropic picks Accenture for in-house AI safety evaluation
NEW YORK – Anthropic said it is partnering with consulting giant Accenture to have outside evaluators work inside the artificial intelligence company, a step towards fulfilling a pledge by chief executive Dario Amodei to have independent observers evaluate its most powerful models.
The partnership will be led by Faculty, Accenture’s specialist AI business. Its work will include evaluating and “red-teaming” Anthropic’s models, the company said on Sept 18.
Red-teaming is the practice of deliberately trying to make AI systems misbehave to expose flaws.
Anthropic and Accenture each expect to invest at least US$1 billion (S$1.28 billion) over the next five years for the effort.
The pledge was made in a Sept 12 essay in which Amodei argued that AI companies must slow the pace at which they improve their models’ capabilities.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has said his company would give outside evaluators similar access, while Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella welcomed embedded evaluators but cautioned that a handful of entities should not control oversight.
Given the “importance and urgency of this work”, Anthropic said it will fund Accenture’s work directly, but that in the long term, “funding should come from pooled or government sources”.
Anthropic said it is in talks with Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), a California-based non-profit organisation, to participate in elements of embedded evaluation using METR’s own funding.
Critics, including David Sacks, a former White House AI adviser, have questioned METR’s independence because of its ties to Anthropic’s investors and staff.
METR says it takes no funding from AI companies or their executives.
On Sept 18, more than 100 AI researchers, including Geoffrey Hinton, who is considered an AI “godfather”, signed a public letter calling for evaluators embedded in AI companies to be “meaningfully independent”.
That includes, at a minimum, that such organisations “should not be owned or governed by frontier AI companies, should not have other significant commercial business with them, and should not accept any form of payment or other reward contingent on the evaluator’s findings”, the letter said. AFP

Japan’s wartime kamikaze pilots remain among the most recognisable symbols of the Pacific war: young men flying aircraft into Allied ships on missions from which they were not expected to return.
Far less well-remembered are the fukuryu – suicide frogmen trained in the closing months of World War II to walk into the sea with mines on bamboo poles, then wait beneath the waves for an Allied invasion fleet.
Kanade Hamamoto was one of many Japanese people who had never heard of them, despite spending years on the same stretch of coast where they once trained.
The 25-year-old photographer knew Inamuragasaki, on the Shonan coast south of Tokyo, only as a scenic seaside spot until a friend mentioned that the remains of a military base could still be seen near the cape, in tunnels cut into the cliff face.

Trump signs broad Russia sanctions bill

Trump signs broad Russia sanctions bill
September 19, 2026
US President Donald Trump signed into law a package of new sanctions against Russia named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, the White House said on Friday.
Earlier, the bill passed Congress with large bipartisan majorities: 86-11 in the Senate and 262-159 in the House.
The comprehensive sanctions package is intended to punish and pressure Moscow for its ongoing war against Ukraine.
In addition to the sanctions on Russia, the law establishes a framework to maintain sanctions on Iran until 2031.
What sanctions does the bill include?
The bill targets Russian officials and key sectors of the Russian economy, including banks, and a fleet of shadow tankers that transport Russian energy.
It also instructs Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas. However, some countries are exempt.
The US president can also impose sanctions on the five countries that do the most to help Russia circumvent energy sanctions.
These measures could further strain US trade relations with China and India, both of which buy significant amounts of Russian oil.
What are the reactions?
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked Trump for signing the bill, as well as all the senators and members of the House of Representatives who supported it.
"When Lindsey Graham was here in Ukraine, he would always talk about how important it was not to ease pressure on Russia, to strengthen sanctions and seek a path to peace," he wrote on X.
Graham, who played a leading role in advancing the bill, was a staunch supporter of Ukraine. The senator had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly passed away in July.
"The best way to honor Lindsey's memory will be to implement the provisions of this law fully and swiftly. And the best reward for everyone helping us put pressure on Russia to end its war will be peace," Zelenskyy added.
Before Trump signed the bill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned that additional US sanctions would hinder efforts to achieve a peaceful resolution in Ukraine.

The Iran war has cost US$43.6 billion as of this month, the highest official estimate to date, the Pentagon told Congress’ defence oversight panels this week.
The cost estimate comes as polls show Americans increasingly oppose the war, partly over its impact on the economy, and the issue is looming large as the November midterm elections approach.
The Pentagon’s latest figure comprises US$11.2 billion already obliged for operating expenses – for fuel, combat pay, aircraft, medical care, parts and the like – plus US$32.4 billion in unfunded replacement costs for munitions, damaged aircraft and other assets, according to a Pentagon document submitted to Congress.
The estimate does not include the cost of addressing potentially billions of dollars in damages to US military facilities in eight Middle East countries.

US and Denmark reach security deal after Trump’s threats to take over Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
01:01:37 UTC
10:01:37 KST

Donald Trump announced on Friday that the US had struck an Arctic security pact with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, after threatening for much of his second term to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory by force.
The full scope of the deal Trump described as “very important, historic, and special” was not immediately clear. But soon after his announcement in a post on Truth Social, the leaders of Denmark and Greenland issued statements indicating the deal would be signed by the three governments on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York City next week.
In his social media post, Trump cast the deal as a personal triumph, claiming that the agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns”.
“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” Trump added. The US already has a presence on the island, and the right to expand bases, through Nato.
The announcement comes just weeks before November’s midterms, giving the president a foreign policy accomplishment he can tout to voters as the deeply unpopular war with Iran becomes an increasing political liability for Republicans vying to hang on to their narrow majorities in the House and Senate.
The US has long had a military presence in Greenland – a self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, a fellow Nato member – and has had a military base at Pituffik since the cold war.
In his post, Trump said that the agreement means “no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval”.
Statements from Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and the leader of Greenland’s government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, posted online late on Friday, emphasized that the agreement would fall far short of Trump’s previously stated desire for “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States”.
Frederiksen said that what she called “a great agreement” for all three parties “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”.
Nielsen said it was “joyous” that the agreement “ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western Alliance”, suggesting that the deal might possibly just reiterate the existing US rights through Nato to use the island as a security base.
Once agreed to, the pact would need to go through parliamentary procedures to be enacted, the Danish and Greenlandic statements said.
Earlier in his term, Trump argued that the US needed control of Greenland for “economic security”, and has described ownership and control of the territory as an “absolute necessity”. The island had long been on the president’s radar as a target for purchase, and during his first term, in 2019, Trump confirmed reports he had been urging aides to find out how the US could buy Greenland, describing any sale as “essentially a large real estate deal”.
Trump’s claims deepened divisions among the western alliance, with the Danish government repeatedly stating that Greenland was “not for sale”. When concerns over Trump’s annexation threats reached a fever pitch last year, the Guardian reported that the Danish government set up a “night watch” in the foreign ministry to monitor the US president’s pronouncements while Copenhagen sleeps.
At a Nato summit in Ankara earlier this year, Trump renewed his bid for the US to acquire Greenland. He threatened to pull all American armed forces out of Europe after the continent repeatedly pushed back.
Strategically positioned between the US and Russia, Greenland is viewed as increasingly important for defense and is emerging as a geopolitical battleground as Arctic ice melts.
The US vice-president, JD Vance, and his wife Usha, received a frosty reception when they visited US troops stationed at Pituffik space base last year, amid the White House’s aggressive campaign to take the mineral-rich island with roughly 56,000 inhabitants.
Polling has found Greenlanders strongly oppose any effort to make Greenland a part of the US.
Even so, a Trump administration insider dropped a hint online that the US side intends to present whatever the deal actually is as an American triumph. Katie Miller, a former White House aide whose husband is Trump’s closest adviser, posted a map of Greenland covered in the American flag, with the caption: “ITS [sic] HAPPENING”.
Miranda Bryant contributed reporting

The world is arguing about migration. Here's where Australia fits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
00:56:31 UTC
09:56:31 KST

IN BRIEF
- Australia is targeting students, backpackers and overstayers as it seeks to bring net overseas migration down.
- Canada, the US, UK and countries across Europe are also tightening parts of their immigration systems.
Australia has unveiled a major shake-up of its migration system, targeting visa-hoppers, overstayers, international students and backpackers as the federal government seeks to bring migration down further.
The changes come as governments in several other major migrant destinations — including Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States and Europe — also tighten parts of their immigration systems.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced the reforms on Thursday, which include restrictions on international students bringing family members, new rules aimed at preventing "visa hopping", and caps on working holidaymakers seeking to extend their stays.
The government is also strengthening enforcement against visa overstayers and migration agents who lodge applications without merit, while changing the skilled migration system to prioritise workers in areas including healthcare, construction and education.
The government wants to bring net overseas migration down from 292,100 to 245,000 in the year to July 2027, and to 225,000 each year thereafter.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The changes include caps on working holidaymakers extending their stays, with 45,000 second-year places and just 5,000 third-year places — down from 57,000 and 31,000 respectively.
There will also be a crackdown on the 77,000 people who are believed to be overstaying their visas: they will face tougher enforcement, including detention.
So, how does Australia's approach compare with migration changes elsewhere in the world?
United States
The United States has pursued what US President Donald Trump has promised to be the "largest domestic deportation" operation in US history, built on aggressive enforcement.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been tasked with that crackdown after its annual budget more than tripled, with heavily armed agents facing worldwide backlash for aggressive tactics, including the fatal shootings of two US citizens this year in Minneapolis.
The Department of Homeland Security says the Trump administration has deported more than 605,000 "illegal aliens", with a further 1.9 million "self-deporting".
Trump has also focused on border security, particularly in the south, primarily targeting Mexican migrants and those crossing the border illegally — as well as the construction of the continued and expanded construction of the Mexico-United States border wall.
He has also worked to restrict the entry of foreigners who do follow the rules and has gone after those who overstay their visas after they expire.
The US government plans to revoke the visas of foreigners who came to the country for tourism or business but sought to stay longer by applying for asylum.
The administration also paused visa approvals for people from 75 "high-risk" countries — Afghanistan, Brazil, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Nigeria, Somalia, Thailand and Yemen — a move a federal judge struck down last month.
He also saw another legal setback this week after a federal judge blocked his attempt to impose stricter limits on how long foreign students and journalists can study or work in the US.
The Trump administration has also expanded vetting of visa applicants' social media accounts, with a State Department spokesperson saying: "A visa is a privilege — not a right."
In August, the department said that since President Donald Trump returned to power in January 2025, some 175,000 foreigners had seen their US visas revoked on grounds ranging from criminal offences, including driving under the influence, to praising the killing of the right-wing activist Charlie Kirk.
Canada
Canada has long held a reputation for welcoming immigrants, with foreign-born people making up almost a quarter of its population.
But that reputation, and its appeal relative to the US' immigration crackdown under Trump, hasn't stopped Canada from hardening its own approach.
Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, Canada has cut its temporary resident target to 385,000 this year, down 25 per cent from the 516,600 previously planned for 2026.
Canada aims to reduce its temporary resident population to less than 5 per cent of the total population by the end of 2027.
Of the 385,000 temporary resident arrivals targeted this year, 230,000 are workers and 155,000 are international students.
International students have been particularly affected by Canada's migration tightening. The government expects to issue up to 408,000 study permits in 2026 — including extensions for existing students — down 7 per cent from its 2025 target and 16 per cent from its 2024 target.
Canada's temporary population has already begun to fall, declining from a peak of 7.6 per cent of the country's population to 6.5 per cent.
Immigration plans for 2026-28 focus on a "return to sustainable immigration levels", with a focus on decreasing temporary resident arrivals and stabilising permanent resident admissions.
While reducing temporary migration, Canada plans to stabilise permanent migration at 380,000 admissions a year between 2026 and 2028.
Its plan places greater emphasis on economic migration and workers in high-demand occupations, while continuing to prioritise family reunification and refugee resettlement.
Canada is also increasing its target for French-speaking permanent residents settling outside Quebec, from 9 per cent of admissions in 2026 to 9.5 per cent in 2027 and 10.5 per cent in 2028.
It will also focus on attracting workers in high-demand occupations, increase the target for Francophone admissions, while aiming to continue to be a "global leader in refugees" and prioritise family reunification.
Former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau sought to attract more immigrants to the country, but the increase in migration was blamed for housing pressure and unemployment rates, resulting in a sharp cut in the number of immigrants allowed into the country.
UK
The United Kingdom is also moving to tighten its migration system, with the government proposing to double the standard qualifying period for permanent settlement from five to 10 years.
Under an "earned settlement" model, some legal migrants could face waits of up to 20 years, depending on factors including their reliance on benefits, while high earners and other applicants deemed to have made significant contributions could qualify sooner.
The proposals could affect an estimated 2.6 million people who arrived in the UK since 2021, while separate reforms to the asylum system would replace permanent refugee status with temporary status subject to review every 30 months.
Europe
Europe is cracking down harder on migration amid rising anti-immigration rhetoric in recent years, the surging popularity of far-right parties, and unfolding humanitarian crises.
In June, the European Parliament approved a new migration plan that would allow the return of illegally staying third-country nationals, with the possibility of detention if they don't comply.
The same law doubles detention times for irregular migrants, speeds up deportations, toughens entry bans, and gives authorities the power to search migrants' homes.
One of the changes includes the creation of so-called "return hubs", which would see migrants without legal residency, including rejected asylum seeker claims, hosted in centres in non-EU nations — a model the Lowy Institute says borrows from Australia's own offshore detention approach.
Five countries — Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands — are working on the "return hub" plan, with Denmark's immigration minister saying he expects to send the first people to a partner country by the end of 2027.
But not every EU member is on board, with French President Emmanuel Macron dismissing the approach as ineffective and out of step with European values.
The push lands amid a broader rightward shift on migration across Europe.
In Germany, far-right political party Alternative for Germany (AfD) — who vow to heavily restrict immigration — topped state elections, putting a far-right party within reach of power at the state level for the first time since World War II.
Swedish elections on Thursday saw the centre-left Social Democrats win a slim majority — but they have still vowed to maintain a hardline immigration policy, inspired by their Danish counterparts who have one of Europe's toughest and most restrictive immigration policies.
Spain, meanwhile, is dealing with its own migrant humanitarian crisis after at least 72,000 people crossed into the North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco in July. More than 10,000 migrants remain stranded.
Just this week, the European Commission pitched a new emergency response framework following the Ceuta crisis, which could translate into a temporary suspension of the right to asylum in the event of "mass movements" which are "engineered and weaponised".

Extremely speedy action by probe agency can create doubt: SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
00:54:25 UTC
09:54:25 KST

The Supreme Court acquitted the RPF official, saying the CBI failed to prove that the intermediary accepted the bribe on his behalf.
New Delhi: The speed at which CBI sprang into action on a bribery complaint and laid a trap within hours to catch a public servant could give rise to suspicion, which, Supreme Court said, could not be brushed aside and had to be examined.Finding fault with CBI's investigation, Justices Dipankar Datta and N K Singh acquitted the official in a two-decade-old case as he was not caught with the bribe money. It was an intermediary who accepted it and CBI failed to prove it was meant for the accused, SC said.The complaint made in 2005 alleged that the accused, working as a divisional security commissioner in Railway Protection Force, had demanded illegal gratification from subordinate officials for transfers and postings. CBI immediately lodged an FIR and laid a trap just hours later, catching the intermediary.The intermediary, who alleged that he accepted the bribe on behalf of the official, was given a pardon.SC said since the FIR was lodged on Aug 4, 2005, at 2pm and CBI decided to lay the trap on the same day, the agency must have verified the authenticity of the complaint before the trap was planned. "It is surprising that CBI started the investigation of a cognisable offence by way of verifying the complaint of bribery even before the formal FIR was lodged...
The entire trap was arranged between 2 pm to 4.30pm. While the investigating agency cannot be faulted for organising the trap in such an extraordinarily speedy manner, it can raise certain doubts. The trial court, however, brushed aside the doubts raised by the appellant," the bench said.The court said criminality under Prevention of Corruption Act did not arise merely because money changed hands. "Before criminal liability can be fastened upon the public servant, the prosecution must establish by reliable evidence that the intermediary was acting under the authority, direction or for the benefit of the accused and that the demand itself was attributable to the accused. Mere receipt of money by a third person cannot automatically result in criminal liability being imputed to a public servant," it said.

Google says its Gemini AI model hacked three other companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
00:53:20 UTC
09:53:20 KST

In a first for Google, the company confirmed that its AI model, Gemini, breached the security of three other companies in May. The hacks occurred during a cybersecurity evaluation by AI-security firm Irregular.
Irregular, an Israel-based startup that scrutinizes the security of advanced AI systems, was also at the center of some of the recent OpenAI and Anthropic hacks of third-party entities, including OpenAI’s breach of AI software company, Hugging Face.
The circumstances that enabled the models to hack other companies in some of these cases are similar: Irregular was testing the models in a closed testing environment with fake companies. The testing environment was not supposed to be internet enabled, but internet access was made available unintentionally, according to the Wall Street Journal. Once connected to the internet, the models unexpectedly hacked into real firms.
Irregular disclosed the hacks to Google at the end of July after discovering OpenAI hacked into Hugging Face. Google confirmed to the Guardian that the hacks occurred, but that the company did not feel it required public disclosure because the models did not damage the companies. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the breaches and revealed for the first time that they occurred.
“In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test,” Heather Adkins, vice-president of security engineering at Google, said in a statement. “In all three of these instances, the model stopped.”
In one of the security breaches, Irregular was testing Gemini’s cybersecurity capabilities by prompting the AI model to obtain information from a fake company’s software. The fake company had the same name as a real company. When the model unintentionally gained access to the internet, it correctly guessed the password of and breached a real company’s service, Irregular told the WSJ. Google said once it figured out it had hacked a real company, and not the simulated one, it stopped.
In two other tests, the model searched the web for and found public repositories containing credentials to two other companies. The model used those credentials to access real companies. When it figured out they were real companies, it stopped, according to Google.
Anthropic and OpenAI chose to voluntarily disclose the hacks but Google did not. However, the company said it ensured the three companies that were hacked were made aware.
“These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly,” Adkins, the Google spokesperson, said.
Anthropic and OpenAI’s disclosures prompted the independent senator Bernie Sanders to demand the companies pause development of their technology, saying it signaled the company was no longer able to control their models.
OpenAI paused development of their models for two weeks, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a collective slowdown of AI development to ensure that its most advanced models are being built with enough safeguards.

NEW DELHI: Questioning the efficacy of prohibition, Supreme Court Friday pointed to five "evils" associated with the ban on liquor - revenue loss, money spent on its enforcement, corruption in police, illegal distilling, and result-ant drug menace - while also referring to a number of hooch tragedies in Gujarat and other states over the years.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said this while quashing Rules 18A and 18B of Maharashtra Poisons Rules restricting purchase of methanol and making it mandatory to add bitterant and colourant to it before selling to non-drug manufacturers. The rules were framed following the deaths of 93 people from spurious liquor containing methanol in Mumbai in 1991.While allowing the plea of various chemical manufacturing companies, including Indian Chemical Council, the bench dwelled upon the efficacy of the prohibition policy. The court said recent hooch tragedies in Bhavnagar (Gujarat) and Sagar (MP), which claimed 13 and 15 lives respectively, were a reminder for the authorities to wake up and act."History bears eloquent testimony to the fact that complete alcohol ban often drives the liquor trade underground, increasing the prevalence of unregulated, lethal brews. The state of Gujarat has a strict prohibition policy... It has witnessed at least 10 major mass hooch tragedies since the state's formation and independence, claiming the lives of over 600 people," the bench said.
SC rejected Maharashtra govt's plea and said the rules had no rational nexus with the objective sought to be achieved to prevent hooch tragedies. The court said it was not doubting the intention of the state but intention solely would not pass the test of manifest arbitrariness."The state failed to indicate that this practice of putting such additives would discourage or rather dissuade continuous usage of methanol or affect its chemical composition so it cannot be used in making spurious liquor. Further, the state has also failed to indicate how mixing of the additives would definitively prevent deaths. Another question that is left unanswered is how the respondent plans to prevent manufacturing of spurious liquor by the use of other adulterants," the bench said.

Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions over Ukraine war
New law allows tariffs of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil, including China and India.
US President Donald Trump has signed into law a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russia over its war in Ukraine, days after Congress sent the bill to the White House with rare bipartisan support.
Signed on Friday, the legislation, known as the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, honours the late Republican senator who spent more than a year negotiating it before his sudden death in July. It was co-written with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Russia, China veto UN mandate to monitor Iran sanctions
- list 2 of 3Russia’s parliamentary election: Who’s on the ballot, and why it matters
- list 3 of 3Why the Kremlin fears even the ‘managed opposition’ in Russia
The bill sanctions Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior officials and oligarchs, along with Russian banks and financial institutions. It also targets Moscow’s energy and defence sectors and the so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to move Russian oil around Western sanctions.
A key provision gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, a measure expected to fall hardest on China and India, the top two importers of Russian crude. The bill separately extends sanctions on Iran’s energy and weapons sectors.
The bill passed the Senate last month and the House on Wednesday, with 58 Democrats crossing party lines to back it.
It marks the first major Ukraine-related bill to clear Congress in more than two years.
Supporters say the aim is to starve the Kremlin of the funds sustaining its war effort and push Putin towards negotiations. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who had lobbied lawmakers ahead of the vote, called the legislation “an extremely powerful tool”.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said the bill placed “maximum pressure” on what he called “the Russian war machine”, while Blumenthal said he hoped it would help bring Moscow to the table, telling Putin: “We have your number.”
Not all Democrats were on board. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries opposed the bill, warning that its tariff powers would raise costs for American families and calling its sanctions provisions full of “loopholes”.
India, one of the countries most exposed to the new tariff threat, said this week that it “remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people”.
Trump’s decision comes about a week before he is due to host Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House.
