Anthropic considers releasing new AI model ahead of IPO, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
00:40:00 UTC
09:40:00 KST

Anthropic considers releasing new AI model ahead of IPO, sources say
Anthropic is considering rolling out a new AI model to counter OpenAI’s momentum since its competitor’s launch of GPT-6 Astra, according to three sources, ahead of an expected initial public offering (IPO) and after its CEO called for an industrywide slowdown.
The timing of a potential launch aimed at addressing competitive pressure from a direct rival follows Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei’s call on the global AI community to slow down the pace of releasing new capabilities to address safety concerns, the sources said.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he wrote in a 3,800-word essay on Sept 12.
The essay, which painted a bleak picture of swarms of AI agents taking over the internet and outpacing human control, drew support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, released this month, has gained traction among businesses, prompting concerns among some investors who told Reuters they are re-evaluating Anthropic’s position as the leading provider of enterprise AI tools.
Anthropic is evaluating the safety of its next model as part of its deliberations over a release, one of the people familiar with the matter said.
Some of the discussions involve how to balance investment in releasing new models with efforts to strengthen the company’s profitability as rising interest rates make investors more focused on the timing of expected profits, said people familiar with the company’s thinking.
The debate over spending highlights the increasing pressure on the firms at the centre of the AI boom to produce sustainable cash flows sooner, thanks both to rising rates and tough competition from open-source AI providers, especially in China.
Anthropic declined to comment for this story.
The potential launch would test how Anthropic can defend its enterprise market position against OpenAI while maintaining the safety-first identity that has distinguished it from competitors.
OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra gains enterprise traction
OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on Sept 3, touting gains in computer use, software engineering, cybersecurity and professional work.
The model has received a strong response from enterprise users and developers, prompting potential Anthropic IPO investors to scrutinise whether OpenAI could begin taking market share from Anthropic, which has been viewed for months as the leader in enterprise AI.
Astra accounted for about 13 per cent of enterprise AI spending tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp, compared with about 8 per cent for Anthropic’s Claude Fable, according to the latest data.
Astra has also pulled ahead on OpenRouter, a widely used platform that routes developer traffic across AI models. 
OpenRouter said its users spent more on OpenAI models than on Anthropic models last week, the first time OpenAI has led on that measure in more than 2½ years.
Anthropic maintains revenue advantage
Some existing investors and those who expect to invest in both Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPOs said they do not believe Astra poses a significant threat to Anthropic, given the size of its lead in the market for enterprise AI tools and the amount of time it takes to unseat incumbent vendors to large companies.
Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate topped US$65 billion by the end of July, up from about US$9 billion at the end of 2025. 
It is also projecting a 2028 revenue of roughly US$190 billion to US$200 billion, Reuters previously reported. 
OpenAI’s annualised revenue run rate passed US$40 billion in July.
Investors also expect leadership among Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet’s Google and other major AI developers to shift repeatedly as companies release new generations of models, making any advantage potentially short-lived.
Bigger challenges ahead
A potentially bigger challenge for Anthropic and other leading AI providers is the rise of open-source and open-weight models, which can lower token costs and allow companies to build more of their own AI infrastructure rather than rely on providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI, investors said.
The shift could put pressure on the economics of the AI industry as companies have more options to develop and run models outside the leading commercial providers, broadening the competitive threat beyond the race between Anthropic and OpenAI.
Meta Platforms has been among Anthropic’s largest customers, but is looking to reduce its use of Anthropic’s models as it develops more AI capabilities internally, people familiar with the matter said. 
Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
OpenAI, meanwhile, has taken some pressure off the race to public markets. 
Its CEO, Altman, confirmed on Sept 12 that the company would not go public in 2026, saying concerns around AI safety made this an ill-advised time for a listing.
Anthropic could push its IPO to after the November US midterm elections, with the elections not expected to have a major impact on the offering, according to two people familiar with the matter. 
The IPO has already been pushed back from earlier plans, with Reuters previously reporting that marketing was expected to begin in mid-October at the earliest. REUTERS

South Korea, US discuss Seoul’s role in Middle East and investment pact

But he said Seoul was reviewing whether to play a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region.
Cho said before leaving Seoul on Sept 17 that investment plans under the trade deal had been delayed while procedural issues were clarified, without elaborating.
Lee told a news conference on Sept 18 that concerns over the commercial viability of the package had become a sticking point in negotiations, although the two sides were nearing an agreement.
He said some elements of the package were difficult for Seoul to accept, but the government would continue discussions to ensure any deal protected South Korea’s interests while benefiting both countries and the broader US-South Korea relationship.
Seoul committed in 2025 to invest in US manufacturing in return for lowering tariffs on imports from South Korea to 15 per cent.

North Korea also featured in the talks, amid speculation over a possible summit between Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

A 63-year-old man has died after being bitten by a shark off Sorrento beach in Perth’s north.
Emergency services were called to the popular beach at about 10.30am on Friday after reports of a shark-related incident.
Western Australia police said a man had been bitten by a shark while swimming along the coast. He died as a result of his injuries, police said.
Emergency services, including water and air personnel, conducted an extensive search of the area. The swimmer’s body had not been found.
The Alkimos Surf Life Saving Club said Sorrento beach would remain closed until noon on Saturday. Locals were urged to stay out of the water until the beach was declared safe for swimming.
The City of Wanneroo closed all other beaches along its coastline until noon on Saturday.
WA police continued searching the shoreline on Saturday morning but said the 63-year-old still had not been located.
The local state MP, Liam Staltari, extended his condolences to the man’s family, friends and loved ones.
“Like all locals and people from across WA, I’m deeply saddened by the tragic death of a man following today’s shark attack at Sorrento beach,” he said.
“Our entire community is thinking of you at this incredibly difficult time.”
A witness, Darrel Haythornthwaite, told 7News that he could not believe the incident had occurred, “especially in a place like this”. He said the man’s friend, who was swimming with him, made it back to shore but was inconsolable.
“He felt bad because he didn’t go back to save his mate and I said, ‘Nah you couldn’t have done that’,” he told the outlet. “There’s nothing that anyone could have done.”
Another witness, Ingrid Mitchell, told 9News she swam at the beach every day and did not expect sharks to attack outside dawn and dusk.
“There was other swimmers in there … just near the seaweed, and there was one poor girl there who was sun-baking, and she saw the whole lot as well,” she said.
A third witness, Jacqui Rapaic, told the ABC she was walking along the beach with a friend when the incident occurred.
“My friend said, ‘Jac, I think there’s been a shark attack,’ and I looked out to the ocean and I could see a pool of blood,” she said.
“I hugged on to my friend … [we] felt rather traumatised at that point. It happened so quickly.”
The fatality followed a shark attack on Monday at the remote Glenfield beach, north of Geraldton on WA’s mid-west coast, which left a surfer with serious injuries.
He was taken to the nearby Geraldton health campus and was in a stable condition.

Trump extends push for $128,000 H-1B visas by another year
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump has extended an executive order that would impose a fee of US$100,000 (S$128,000) for H-1B non-immigrant visas by another year, the White House said on Sept 18.
US employers seeking to hire skilled foreign workers can use the federal government’s H-1B visa programme for a fee, allowing tech and other professionals from abroad to work in the United States for a few years.
Trump, who has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown, has criticised the programme and wants to permanently raise the fee from between US$2,000 and US$5,000 to at least US$100,000, though the attempt has faced legal challenges.
A Boston-based appeals court is reviewing a June decision by a federal judge who deemed the higher fee imposed by the Trump administration illegal and blocked the government from collecting it.
Another court is considering whether a judge properly rejected a challenge to the fee by the US Chamber of Commerce, the largest US business lobbying group.
Trump’s initial order for a fee hike, first released in September 2025, was set to expire in September 2026.
It did not apply to visas granted to foreign citizens already in the United States on student visas, who make up a large share of new H-1B recipients, or to renewals of current visas.
Despite criticism that some companies use the visas to hire lower-paid foreign workers instead of Americans, business groups and companies say they help recruit highly skilled professionals and address a lack of qualified US workers in some industries.
The visas, established by Congress in 1990, are especially critical for tech companies seeking to recruit from India and China.
Changes to how potential visa holders are scrutinised and processed have impacted companies’ hiring and expansion plans, with some top H-1B users, such as Google parent company Alphabet, moving to increase operations in India. REUTERS

Why relying on university students skews global psychological research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
00:00:31 UTC
09:00:31 KST

An analysis of the World Values Survey (2005-2022) data found that individuals with more education tend to be culturally similar to people from the Anglosphere and Western Europe. Interestingly, education level was not associated with cultural similarities to other large and influential countries such as China, Russia, or India. The paper was published in Nature Communications.
Psychological research has traditionally relied heavily on participants from Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic societies. This is so common that the acronym WEIRD has been coined to refer to such groups. However, this has raised concerns about how well findings on such groups generalize to the wider world. Although cross-national research has expanded substantially, many international studies still depend disproportionately on highly educated participants such as university students.
But are university students, even from non-WEIRD countries, really representative of the wider cultures of the countries they belong to? Education itself is an important source of cultural norms. Formal schooling transmits not only knowledge and skills but also particular values, cognitive styles, and patterns of behavior. Studies have found that higher levels of education tend to be associated with traits typically considered characteristic of WEIRD societies, such as individualism, analytic thinking, nonconformity, and generalized trust.
Socioeconomic status may also contribute to the adoption of WEIRD cultural norms through the endorsement of personal freedom, specific styles of thinking, and the availability of resources needed to experience different cultures. However, education may play a particularly important role in determining what kinds of cultural norms a person will actually adopt.
Study authors Cindel J. M. White and Michael Muthukrishna conducted a study in which they explored whether socioeconomic status is associated with a variety of different cultural traits across 95 countries around the world. They note that processes of colonization, globalization, and the adoption of Western-style institutions have led to the diffusion of WEIRD cultural norms around the world. As a result, highly educated individuals could be expected to be more similar to one another across the world, but to also show patterns of attitudes, traits, and behaviors characteristic of cultures of WEIRD countries, including Anglosphere countries like the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Western Europe more generally.
These researchers analyzed data from the World Values Survey (2005-2022), waves 5-7. The World Values Survey is a long-running international research program that measures people’s values, beliefs, attitudes, and social and political views across countries and cultures. These analyses were based on data from 268,992 participants from 95 different countries.
Study authors report that they excluded from analyses any country or group with fewer than 100 respondents. As a result, the number of countries for which data were available differed between analyses and did not always include all 95 countries.
Participants within each country were grouped into high, middle, and low clusters according to three indicators of socioeconomic status: educational attainment, income, and subjective social status. Next, they used a statistic called the cultural fixation index, which quantifies the overall magnitude of cultural differences between groups across a wide range of traits, to measure cultural distance between people with high and low socioeconomic status in 95 countries. Most importantly, they compared all these groups to the U.S., as a prototypical WEIRD country.
Results showed that, across the whole world, highly educated groups and those with only secondary education were more culturally similar to the U.S. than low-education groups. For example, people with high education in Singapore were as similar to the U.S. culturally as highly educated Australians were. However, people with low levels of education from Singapore were culturally quite distant from the U.S. Highly educated Russians were as similar to Americans as highly educated people from New Zealand. However, this was not the case with Russians with low levels of education. This pattern was found in 70 percent of the analyzed countries.
These results seemed to be specific to education. Cultural similarity to the U.S. did not differ between high- and low-income groups, or between groups differing in subjective social status. Additional analyses showed that this observed association between education and cultural similarity becomes even more pronounced when Sweden, the Netherlands, Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, Andorra, Norway, Germany, and Switzerland were used as the reference category. This indicates that the finding might not be about educated people adopting U.S. culture specifically, but about them adopting cultural traits of WEIRD countries in general. Interestingly, education was not associated with cultural similarities to other large, culturally and politically influential countries such as China, Russia, or India.
“Contrary to modernization theories, income and self-reported subjective status did not show the same pattern of WEIRD cultural similarity. Our results suggest that cross-cultural samples of students or university-educated individuals overrepresent cultural values that are typical of WEIRD countries,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of cultural differences across the world. However, it should be noted that the study was based on data about self-reported beliefs and behaviors, which may not be identical to beliefs and behaviors people practice in everyday life.
The paper, “Higher education predicts global cultural similarity to WEIRD countries,” was authored by Cindel J. M. White and Michael Muthukrishna.

China makes progress in 3-nm chips without advanced lithography tools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

China makes progress in 3-nm chips without advanced lithography tools
The breakthrough by the Chinese Academy of Sciences is far from mass production but shows China is tracking the road map of global leaders
Chinese researchers have made early strides in pushing semiconductor processing nodes below 3-nm using older lithography technology, as more advanced extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUV) tools from ASML remain blocked under US sanctions.
The breakthrough marks the latest progress in China’s drive to chart an alternative path to advanced chipmaking amid US export restrictions. Under current export control rules, Dutch equipment giant ASML is barred from selling its state-of-the-art EUV machines – essential for producing chips below the 7-nm node – to Chinese clients.
In the latest development, state-backed Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) has established a preliminary gate-all-around (GAA) device development path using the less advanced deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography, Taiwanese media Digitimes reported on Thursday, citing a speech by Ye Tianchun, a veteran from the academy’s Institute of Microelectronics (IMECAS).
Ye said the institute had finished early integration for stacked nanosheet-channel GAA CMOS transistors using DUV tools. He described the result as a “new early-stage MOS transistor process path for China’s sub-3-nm advanced manufacturing”, according to the Digitimes article.

Father of murdered Spanish student arrives in Mexico after suspect detained
MEXICO CITY, Sept 18 - The father of a Spanish exchange student killed in Mexico arrived in the Mexican state of Morelos on Friday to identify his daughter's body, a day after authorities detained a suspect in her murder.
Claudia Tacoronte, a 21-year-old student, died from stab wounds on September 12 in the city of Cuautla after someone tried to steal her cellphone, Mexican authorities have said.
On Thursday evening, authorities announced they had arrested a suspect, identified as Francisco Javier "N."
The case has caused widespread anger in both Mexico and Spain, with students demanding stronger protections for women. Mexico has long struggled with high levels of gender-based violence.
Spanish newspaper El Pais, citing sources close to the investigation, reported that the suspect had confessed to the killing.
The killing is being treated as a femicide, or a killing motivated by gender, the state prosecutor in Morelos said.
Morelos recorded 21 femicides between January and July this year, according to official data, while 380 were registered across Mexico over the same period.
The suspect was due to appear before a judge on Friday afternoon. Fernando Blumenkron, Morelos' state prosecutor, said his office would seek the maximum penalty for femicide — 70 years in prison.
Blumenkron told journalists that the suspect attacked Tacoronte outside a cultural building where she had been attending a conference and staying. The prosecutor said the suspect had a police record for burglaries, and had spent time behind bars.
Tacoronte was a student at Spain's University of Granada and had arrived in mid-August on an exchange program at the Autonomous University of the State of Morelos.
At least four female students at the same Mexican university have been killed in Morelos this year, according to student protesters, and Spain's Foreign Ministry has urged citizens to avoid non-essential travel to the state, citing rising drug-related violence and kidnappings.
The University of Granada has also canceled exchange placements for three students who had been due to study in Morelos next semester. REUTERS

wendell castle’s family home returns through furniture and artifacts at friedman benda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
23:55:25 UTC
08:55:25 KST

designboom attended the opening reception for Wendell Castle: Living at Friedman Benda, where the gallery had taken on the density of a lived-in home. A Kermit the Frog toy sits on Environment (1972), Castle’s colossal stacked-walnut bed and work station, and family home videos play on a small television alongside it. Books lie beside furniture and personal objects turn up between works that now belong to the history of American design. The exhibition‘s scale can be monumental, but the rooms feel inhabited.
Curated by Castle’s daughter, Alison Castle, the exhibition begins with a June 1973 House Beautiful feature on the family’s Scottsville, New York, home. The magazine caught Wendell Castle and ceramic artist Nancy Jurs living among their own work while much of it was still fresh from the studio.
‘Today, these works are usually seen in museums, but as furniture, they were made to be used,‘ Alison says. Her aim is to let visitors feel how the pieces functioned within the home.
Castle Home, circa 1970s | image courtesy Estate of Wendell Castle and Friedman Benda
the house becomes an archive
Across Friedman Benda‘s gallery space, enlarged photographs from the House Beautiful spread act like murals. Objects pictured in the designer‘s old rooms appear again in front of their own images, bringing the Scottsville interior into the present without turning it into a period reconstruction. The house occupied a former mill that Wendell Castle renovated, and its contents kept changing as work moved upstairs from the studio.
Alison has explained that pieces often entered the living space while waiting for a buyer, sometimes remaining with the family for years. Living with them gave her parents time to study what they had made and think through future work.
The house also recorded the creative world around Castle and Jurs. Their friends’ work entered through purchases and trades, including paintings by Michael Venezia and a ceramic fireplace by Roy Cartwright. Glenn Adamson’s catalogue essay also points to craft artists Tommy Simpson and Ann Sutton as part of the couple’s wider circle.
Alison remembers the atmosphere: ‘Our home became a total environment where furniture, ceramics, color and architecture blur together.‘ Castle appeared in both the wood and plastic sections of Objects: USA, the landmark 1969 Smithsonian exhibition that brought American studio craft to a much larger audience.
Wendell Castle: Living | image courtesy Friedman Benda and Wendell Castle Inc., photography by Izzy Leung
a career written into the grain
The installation also makes Castle’s technical evolution unusually easy to follow. His 1962 Chaise Rocker still lets the eye read oak members meeting through visible joinery, while another early chaise nearby carries the same sense of furniture assembled from distinct pieces.
In 1963, Castle began developing stack lamination, building timber into thick layered masses and carving them back into continuous forms. By Environment in 1972, stacked and laminated walnut had become architecture at the scale of furniture, with a bed and work surface absorbed into a broad horizontal wooden landscape. A lamp and drawers emerge from the same body.
Across the room, Opposites Attract (2017) turns that logic on its side. The massive floor lamp rises from diagonally oriented laminated wood, with a side table and drawer integrated into its body. The grain sweeps upward through the form, making the construction itself part of the visual movement.
Nearby, Arcadia (2010) turns a three-seat bench into one continuous carved body, its openings and raised ends giving the mahogany form an almost anatomical rhythm. Seen together, the works let the eye track decades of experimentation through the direction of the wood.
Wendell Castle: Living | image courtesy Friedman Benda and Wendell Castle Inc., photography by Izzy Leung
family furniture keeps its traces
Some of the most affecting objects are also among the smallest. Castle made a wooden high chair for Alison, carving her name across the back in broad graphic lettering. Elsewhere, a 1973 coat rack carries his own hat, still covered with wood shavings from his final time working in the studio. These details place biography directly onto the furniture. The high chair belongs to childhood; the hat still seems to belong to the workshop.
Nancy Jurs’ presence runs throughout the rooms with equal ease. Her ceramics sit on tables and shelves, echoing the vessels visible throughout the 1973 magazine spread, while friends’ artworks keep the installation open to a wider creative circle.
Jurs would later move further into sculptural ceramics, including her Wall Pouches of the 1980s, but here her vessels retain their place within the household. In the old photographs, Castle’s bright molded seating shares rugs and tabletops with handmade ceramics. Friedman Benda brings that visual density back into the room.
Wendell Castle: Living | image courtesy Friedman Benda and Wendell Castle Inc., photography by Izzy Leung
kermit on a masterpiece
The Kermit toy on Environment may be the detail that explains the whole exhibition best. The piece is huge and technically ambitious, yet here it becomes a bed again. Family videos flicker nearby. Alison’s curatorial premise comes through in these small collisions between canon and use, where a major work can hold a childhood toy and a gallery can briefly take on the looseness of a family room.
By the time Wendell Castle: Living reaches Castle’s later works, the exhibition has become both a chronology and a portrait of the world around the objects. You can follow changes in woodworking through the seams, then look up and find Jurs’ ceramics or a friend’s painting nearby. Before these works entered museum collections and design histories, people sat in them and slept beside them. At Friedman Benda, that earlier life comes back into view.
Wendell Castle: Living | image courtesy Friedman Benda and Wendell Castle Inc., photography by Izzy Leung
Wendell Castle: Living | image courtesy Friedman Benda and Wendell Castle Inc., photography by Izzy Leung
the first stop of our new travelling series brought together designers, architects, collaborators, and friends for a week of conversations and hands-on activities.

Senior US officials to 'Post': Trump-Netanyahu meeting not currently planned at UNGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
23:41:33 UTC
08:41:33 KST

A meeting between US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is not currently on the agenda during Netanyahu's upcoming visit to the United States, a senior US official told The Jerusalem Post on Saturday, with the latest schedules placing the two leaders in New York at different times.
Netanyahu's presence in New York is expected to be "quite limited," the official said, noting that under the most recent schedule available to the administration, the prime minister is not due to arrive until after Trump has already left.
"The latest scheduling that I've seen, he will be here after the president leaves," the official said when asked directly whether Netanyahu was seeking a meeting with Trump.
A senior Israeli official told the Post that Netanyahu is expected to arrive in New York on the morning of his UN General Assembly address and depart for Israel immediately afterward.
At this stage, it appears Netanyahu will fly directly from Israel to New York rather than stop in Texas, and may not spend a night in the United States at all. However, the source stressed that the prime minister’s final itinerary has not yet been finalized.
Netanyahu's UN General Assembly address is expected later in the week, the US official added, while Trump is set to arrive in New York on Monday and depart Tuesday evening.
The US official declined to say whether Netanyahu or members of his team had formally requested a meeting, citing a policy against discussing requests submitted to the White House. In practical terms, however, the current schedule leaves no overlap between the two leaders' time in the city.
The UN's 81st General Debate runs September 22–28 at UN headquarters in New York.
Iran, Gaza at center of Trump's UN agenda
Even without a Netanyahu meeting, Israel and the Middle East are expected to feature prominently across Trump's UN visit.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said Trump plans to stress in his General Assembly address that Iran must never obtain a nuclear weapon, while also highlighting what the administration views as progress under the president's 20-point Gaza peace plan.
Iran is also expected to loom large in Trump's multilateral meeting with leaders of the Gulf Cooperation Council. A senior US official said Tehran would be "a key topic of conversation and diplomacy" throughout the week.
The administration believes pressure on Iran continues to mount, the official said, arguing that Tehran's leverage over the Strait of Hormuz is diminishing as alternative infrastructure and bypass routes come online, compounded by US military and economic pressure. "In one way or another," the official said, Washington expects the Iranian regime to abandon its pursuit of a nuclear weapon.
Officials added that US sanctions against Chinese and Hong Kong entities accused of helping Iran generate revenue - including through oil-related activity - would continue.
Waltz also tied the UN gathering to Gaza, calling the annual session an unusually valuable diplomatic opportunity given the concentration of world leaders in one place.
Trump's publicly announced Tuesday schedule includes bilateral meetings with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, a sit-down with GCC leaders, and a reception for world leaders - but no meeting with Netanyahu. AP separately reported the planned meetings with Burnham, Takaichi and the Gulf leaders.
From New York to Xi Jinping meeting
Immediately after Trump's UN appearance, the diplomatic spotlight shifts to Washington, where the president is set to host Chinese President Xi Jinping for a three-day visit.
On Wednesday, Trump is scheduled to greet Xi and his wife at Joint Base Andrews. The following day, Trump and First Lady Melania Trump are expected to formally welcome the Chinese couple to the White House; after an arrival ceremony, the two leaders will review a military ceremony in the Rose Garden before holding bilateral talks. That evening, the president and first lady will host the Chinese delegation for a state dinner in the East Room.
On Friday, the two couples are expected to hold a private tea at the White House before visiting the National Archives to view founding US documents as the country marks its 250th anniversary.
The visit follows Trump's meeting with Xi in China in May; Trump had previously announced Xi's US visit for September 24.
Several of the most sensitive issues in US-China relations are expected to be on the table. A senior White House official confirmed that artificial intelligence and the current US-China trade truce will be discussed, alongside trade, AI, and rare-earth exports - all expected to feature prominently in preparatory talks between senior US and Chinese officials.
The administration also intends to press China over precursor chemicals used in fentanyl production, rare-earth supplies, and the terms under which Chinese investment can enter the United States. The White House made clear it does not intend to trade away US export controls in exchange for rare earths it believes Beijing has already committed to supply - though officials confirmed discussions have taken place over possible tariff reductions on a "narrow band" of non-sensitive, non-strategic goods.
Musk, Bezos, Altman, Cook in the same room
The state dinner's guest list is expected to draw nearly as much attention as the summit itself.
A senior White House official said expected attendees include Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Michael Dell, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser and Apple CEO Tim Cook, alongside senior administration officials. "It'll be a very popular and hot-ticketed event here in Washington, DC," the official said.
Several major tech executives are indeed expected to attend, while Reuters has reported that Xi may bring a substantial Chinese business delegation of his own.
Within the span of a few days, then, Trump will pivot from Iran, Gaza and the Gulf in the corridors of the United Nations to America's most consequential strategic rivalry - with China, trade, artificial intelligence and Iran all converging on the White House agenda.

25% youths in 250 districts not in education or jobs: Survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
23:31:28 UTC
08:31:28 KST

The situation is of particular concern in northernIndia (Representative image)
NEW DELHI: In nearly 250 districts, more than 25% youth (15-29 age group) are neither engaged in any productive work, nor are they pursuing education or any sort of training for work, highlighting a gap in human capital utilisation.The situation is of particular concern in northern India, especially in states such as Bihar, UP, Haryana, Punjab and West Bengal, where nearly two-thirds of districts have around a quarter of the young population categorised as NEET (not in employment, education or training), showed the first-ever district-level periodic labour force survey (PLFS) for 2025, released by statistics ministry Friday.In Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Assam and Telangana in nearly half the districts, 25% young population is categorised as NEET (not in employment, education or training). A recent Niti Aayog report pegged the number of NEET youth in the country at nearly nine crore, with govt clarifying that these people cannot be crudely termed as unemployed.In around 25 districts, NEET is below 10%, including Kabirdham, Rajnandgaon and Uttar Baster Kanker in Chhattisgarh; Chamba in Himachal Pradesh; Ernakulam in Kerala; and Mandla in Madhya Pradesh. Nabarangpur in Odisha had the lowest NEET rate of 4.1%.
The ministry's report covered around 600 districts in major states and UTs. In some cases, it clubbed a few adjoining districts and treated them as a single unit.
Lowest unemployment rates across India
Generally, high unemployment rate among youth is attributed to their participation in education or their engagement with skilling or vocational programmes. NEET, however, represents those people who are not enrolled anywhere with any educational institution and have also withdrawn from the labour force altogether. This is either due to them attending to domestic unpaid duties, care work in the case of women or those who have stopped looking for work due to no suitable work being available, or in some cases, preparing for exams or having leisure. For young women, nearly three-fourth of total districts surveyed recorded a NEET rate of more than 25%, highlighting the burden of unpaid domestic chores and societal expectations.

Gemini hacked 3 companies in first known breakout by Google’s AI: Wall Street Journal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
23:30:00 UTC
08:30:00 KST

Gemini hacked 3 companies in first known breakout by Google’s AI
Google’s Gemini model accessed the internet and hacked other companies during a test of its cybersecurity capabilities, the first known example of the company’s AI systems autonomously committing such an act.
The hacks occurred in May during a test conducted by Irregular, an independent company that conducts cybersecurity evaluations.
During a standard evaluation, Gemini found public information online and guessed credentials to access three websites it thought were within the scope of its test, Google’s vice-president of security engineering Heather Adkins said in a statement.
In one of the cases, the Gemini model guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system.
In the other two cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that allowed it to access protected systems, according to The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the news on Sept 18.
Adkins said that in all three instances, the model ceased its hacking when it realised it had accessed real companiess.
“We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes,” she said. 
“These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.”
An Irregular spokesperson said the incident involved the same issue that affected other AI labs and that all relevant labs were notified in late July.
“All known issues on our end were remedied and resolved weeks ago,” the spokesperson said.
Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed similar incidents linked to Irregular. 
Meta said in August that the incident did not involve a sandbox escape or sophisticated cyberattack, while Irregular said it was working on best practices for securely conducting AI cybersecurity evaluations.
The incidents have raised questions about the safeguards needed as AI agents gain greater autonomy and access to the internet and computer systems. REUTERS

Trump claims deal with Denmark, Greenland giving U.S. control over security in Greenland
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:23:32 CST
08:23:32 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that the United States has reached an agreement with Denmark and Greenland giving the United States "permanent control" over security and other needs in Greenland.
"At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.
"We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many," he said.
The U.S. president described the deal as an "Infinite Life" agreement with no expiration date and said it would come at no cost to the United States.
The full text of the agreement was not immediately released.
The office of Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said that the agreement is expected to be signed during the upcoming UN General Assembly and requires necessary national parliamentary procedures.
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.
Trump's earlier statements about acquiring the territory met with strong opposition from Denmark, Greenland and several European countries. ■

Trump to meet with Venezuela's interim president Rodriguez in New York on Tuesday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
23:23:28 UTC
08:23:28 KST

Trump to meet with Venezuela's interim president Rodriguez in New York on Tuesday
WASHINGTON, Sept 18 - US President Donald Trump will have a meeting with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez in New York on Tuesday, a senior US official said on Friday, in what will be the first in-person meeting between the two leaders since Washington ousted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January.
Trump's meeting with Rodriguez, Maduro's former deputy, will be on the sidelines of a reception that the Republican president will be hosting, US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told reporters in a briefing call.
"The president will host a UN General Assembly leaders' reception. There, he'll participate in a pull-aside with the acting president Rodriguez of Venezuela," Waltz said. He did not give any details of what they might discuss.
The Venezuelan communications ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Last month, the US and Venezuela signed an energy agreement that would allow the US to take partial control of Venezuela's vast oil reserves, betting that American companies can help revive the South American nation's battered energy industry.
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado is facing a growing dilemma over when to return home to rally support amid reticence from the Trump administration about her homecoming.
Machado left the country late last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after largely living in hiding since a contested 2024 election. She sought to cultivate Trump as an ally well before Maduro's removal. But since the ouster, Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Rodriguez. REUTERS

Maths doesn't add up for Australian parents juggling work and school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
23:22:05 UTC
08:22:05 KST

The lost time of modern parenthood
Australian families are living in work, school and care systems designed for another era. And the math ain't mathing.
Morning scramble. Uniform. Lunch box. Breakfast. Hair. Teeth. Socks. Socks! Drop off. Commute to work. Work. Pick-up. After school sport. The assemblies. The parades. The homework. The appointments. The pings of parent WhatsApp groups. The bottomless laundry basket. The shopping. The dinner. The never-ending list of unpaid work. The endless worry and guilt.
When it comes to working and being a modern-day parent, the juggle is real.
If we look back to family life in the 1960s, or even the 1990s, so much has changed.
In most two-parent families these days, both parents are employed, but the work and school systems are largely set up for a bygone era.
"The maths does not add up," says Kate Harrison Brennan, director of the Sydney Policy Lab at The University of Sydney.
To help us put the numbers in context and talk about real solutions, alongside Dr Harrison Brennan we've enlisted these experts:
- Elizabeth Hill from The University of Sydney Department of Political Economy
- Georgie Dent, CEO of advocacy organisation The Parenthood
- Lyndall Strazdins from the ANU National Centre of Epidemiology and Population Health
- Rowena Ditzell, lecturer at the University of Technology Sydney
So with the introductions out of the way, let's do some rough sums.
The maths
Parents can feel like there aren't enough hours in the day. And when you stop to work out just how much overlap there is between the hours that your children need you, and the hours that you're expected to devote to work, it's easy to see why.
We know that every family arrangement is different.
Let's assume there are two parents at home, and both parents work full-time.
We're going to look specifically at parents of primary school-aged children and compare the average work year with the average school year.
7.5 hours per week
Is the gap between the full-time work week and average primary school hours.
Read more
School often starts about 9am and finishes between 3pm and 3:30pm. The traditional full-time work day is 9am to 5pm or 8 hours. Assuming school finishes at 3:30pm, that's 300 hours per year parents need to find across the 40-week school year.
"What becomes immediately obvious for any parent in the first week of their child being at school is that suddenly there is a cliff when you get to 2 something in the afternoon … and kids need to get picked up," Dr Harrison Brennan says.
After-school care is often relied upon to cover the gap, but that's if parents can afford it. It gets expensive if you have multiple children.
And many people don't have access to it at all.
"I'd say you're part of a lucky one in five in Australia," Dr Harrison Brennan says.
"The reality is: places in subsidised after-school-hours care are incredibly concentrated in Australia's major cities."
"The gap between care and work, and school hours and work hours, isn't an inconvenience; it's a structural tax that parents, most often mums, pay every single day," says The Parenthood CEO Georgie Dent.
The average daily commute is 52 minutes, or about 56 minutes in capital cities. On average, Australians spend 3.8 hours commuting to work each week, which is about 182 hours per year.
While many Australians are now able to work from home, or work a hybrid arrangement, most Australian workers still commute to work.
"For those who work at a distance from their workplace and from their school drop-off, the degree of difficulty in completing that task every day, five days a week, for four terms a year is really, really high," Professor Hill says.
The COVID-19 pandemic did make working from home much more common.
It's one of the things that's made the workplace happier for many women, Dr Strazdins says.
"They're finding that time by cutting back on a commute from work, from home and dovetailing tasks a bit better," she says.
"I think the ferocity with which we embrace work from home and protected it when it looked like it was going to be threatened speaks to how desperate families are to find every last minute because they need them."
But when you throw in the difference between the workday and school day, the commute time makes a lot of work completely inaccessible to many Australians.
"Once you factor in things like the time at which children can be dropped at school and what that's like for a young child in early primary years when they are dropped at school leads to whether that's actually even a solution for parents to be able to drop off when the school gates open," Dr Harrison Brennan says.
"Factor in commute times to an office, and increasingly families needing to move further out in our major cities in Australia.
"As soon as you get out into some of the kind of commuter suburbs, it makes actually commuting into a job in the city or somewhere else in a metropolitan city just not even a thing for families."
While distances are much greater in rural or regional areas, most (78 per cent) primary school-aged parents live within 2 kilometres of their school.
That may be a 2-minute drive or a 15-minute walk.
But if we're conservative and allow 10 minutes for each drop-off and pick-up, which realistically, doesn't also account for the time it takes to get everyone out of the house, settle the kids at school and get back, that's roughly 1.7 hours per week.
Professor Hill says for workers who work a "typical" workday of 9am-5pm or 8am-6pm, the school pick-up is a real problem.
"It's a hard stop, and it typically happens when you're kind of reaching peak productivity in your working day."
It's hard to get the exact figures on how many activities children do and how much time parents spend attending them, but increasingly Australian families are feeling the pressure to enrol their kids in sports, arts, swimming and tutoring.
The last Australian Bureau of Statistics survey into children's participation in cultural and leisure activities found 35 per cent of kids aged 5 to 14 did a cultural activity outside of school hours. About 60 per cent did an organised sport and spent about 5 hours a fortnight training or playing outside of school hours.
Let's be conservative and allow 1 hour of the working week for dropping off and attending extracurricular activities, (even though it's likely to be more for most families).
Often this involves working parents coming up with creative solutions like carpooling, working from the sidelines or logging back on when the children are in bed.
Professor Hill says some parents feel penalised for accessing flexibility for this.
"Just because they pick up their kids from daycare or from school or take them to netball practice, or to piano lessons, does not mean that they're any less committed as an employee and any less deserving of access to training opportunities or promotion opportunities."
24 days per year
For school holidays. And that's if parents take all of their annual leave separately.
Read more
The average Australian worker gets four weeks of annual leave, but there are 12 weeks of school holidays. Then there are at least four pupil-free or curriculum days to cover (in some states there are up to eight).
Even if there are two parents at home who each have four weeks of annual leave and they choose to take all of their leave separately, which means no family holiday time, there's still a gap of more than four weeks.
There are sometimes school holiday program options, but they can be costly.
Dr Harrison Brennan says kids often need this time for downtime at home and with family and friends.
"Many parents, they look to the school holidays and think, 'Oh, finally, this is going to be a chance to regroup.'
"And then the realisation comes in that first year of school, 'Oh no, now we have to look at holiday care options', because even if you have four weeks of annual leave and two parents in a household, that's only going to cover about two-thirds of a child's annual school holidays."
She says it's an outdated set-up we're dealing with.
"It's just such a clear example of our models for the purposes of annual leave for workers and the purpose of school holidays for children being at complete odds with one another.
"It's affecting kids, it's affecting families and extended families as well as grandparents being asked to do more. And sometimes that's possible, sometimes it's simply not."
At least 814 hours
That's how much time parents have to find each year if both parents are working full-time and have primary school children.
Read more
That overlap, when your job and your children need your attention, works out to be about 34 full days every year.
And we know this is being conservative.
Obviously it doesn't take into account the many variables in different family situations.
It doesn't reflect families that have only one parent and/or children with additional needs.
It's not counting the huge amount of unpaid work, cooking, cleaning, washing, planning, maintenance or day-to-day caregiving, that needs to be done for a family to run smoothly.
It also doesn't factor in the assemblies, the medical appointments, the early pick-up days, the school events or homework.
"The numbers are damning but they're not surprising," Georgie Dent says.
"Those additional hours, they're so unseen until you're in the midst of it," Dr Harrison Brennan says.
"Parents are trying to find another 800 hours and they're facing impossible job demands," Dr Strazdins says.
Dr Strazdins says it's time to talk about the broken system.
"We've got lots of reasons why we do need to have this conversation," she says.
"If you're trying to find an extra 800 hours a year, well, what are you actually doing to do that? I mean, what actually are people trying to do if they're trying to find those extra hours?"
There is a lot of evidence to show that time pressure changes how people behave, Dr Strazdins says.
"They're rushing, they're feeling incredibly anxious, they're cutting back on other things that they really need to do.
"It's really a social problem to put this much pressure on citizens."
Professor Hill says society needs to recognise that intensive child care does not end when young kids start school.
"I think it's really good to name it and to shine a light on the quantum of hours that require some form of adult supervision, whether it's parents, whether it's grandparents, whether it's other community members."
Mums are in paid work more, but still carry larger portion of unpaid workload
Between 1990 and 2025, the proportion of two-parent families in which both partners worked rose from 55 per cent to 71-73 per cent, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics data.
Over the past 20 years, the hours of paid work has grown for women.
This chart shows the hours worked when there is a child under 15 in the home, broken down by men and women.
Median hours of working men haven't changed much.
Across the past 20 years, they've sat at about 40 hours per week.
For quite some time, working hours of women hovered between 24 and 25 hours a week.
But since about 2016, those hours have been rising.
ABS data shows the median hours for mums is currently about 30 hours.
And that's the same whether they are in a two-parent or single-parent home.
But the data also shows historically those hours fluctuate a lot and continue to do so.
The dips in hours show that women's work has been more flexible to accommodate the school holidays.
All of the notable downward spikes in this chart appear to align with the four school holiday periods in summer, autumn, winter and spring.
The biggest drop shows a holiday period in 2012/2013 known as the "Angry Summer".
Catastrophic bushfires, extreme heat and devastating floods were simultaneously happening across the country, which may explain the dramatic dip in hours for both men and women employees at this time.
But it hasn't been the norm for both men's and women's hours to change during the holidays.
If we look at 2014 as an example, we can see that men's hours remained unchanged throughout the year, while women's hours zigzag during the school holiday periods.
However, that is changing.
In more recent years, men's hours have been fluctuating during these periods too.
If we fast-forward to 2024, men's hours reduce across the four holiday periods.
This may indicate that more dads are reducing hours to accommodate the school holiday juggle.
However the size of the dips indicate that women are still having their hours disrupted more dramatically.
Increasing financial pressures mean families often don't have a choice about whether or not both parents should work, or work more.
In homes where there is a couple and children aged 0-14 years, about 36 per cent have both parents working full-time.
The way society is built has not kept up with the reality of modern family life, Georgie Dent says.
"There are more parents than ever in paid work, not as a lifestyle choice, but out of necessity, yet so many of our systems, from schools to workplaces to paid parental leave and child care, still reflect an outdated assumption that there's a parent at home to readily absorb the care and domestic load of raising a family."
And not only that, the economy wants women to work more.
Australian women work part-time at higher rates than many other advanced economies.
In an economic roundtable a year ago, economists highlighted that women were an untapped resource for our nation's productivity.
"We've got women working shorter hours, doing the rest, helping men work the long hours and making the money … but it's not in the country's interests and it's certainly not equal," Dr Strazdins says.
This is reflected in the amount of unpaid work mums do, compared to dads.
An ABS survey reveals mothers do more than 2 hours of extra unpaid work and have 24 minutes less leisure time each day than fathers.
Georgie Dent says our economy relies on the unpaid work of women.
"We've built an economy and society that runs on the invisible labour of parents, particularly mums, and called it a 'work-life balance problem' instead of a policy failure."
A flood of comments in a recent ABC social media post highlighted that many mums felt like they weren't juggling, they were struggling.
"Working hours and school hours do not make sense … this is structural inequality that guarantees failings for all parents, but especially mums. We've lost before we even walk out the front door." - @lauren_affairs_and_trade
Another commenter said: "We're not juggling, we're sacrificing our own mental, physical and emotional health to meet the structures of a system designed for a different time." - @otto.von.gram
What society needs to do to keep up
The majority of our workforce are 'worker-carers' — people who have responsibilities at both work and home.
Experts say there is no silver-bullet solution to overhaul the system, but propose a suite of changes to better support modern families.
This can come in many different forms, says Rowena Ditzell, who specialises in the future of work.
"People are talking about working from home and that's certainly a really common way of flexible working, but there's many other ways, whether it's flexible start and finish times, which can really help parents with school-aged children, whether it's term hours, you know, things like that can make a real difference for working parents."
A four-day work week is one possible solution to a more flexible work environment, Dr Ditzell says.
"Certainly in my research I have spoken to women who have told me that because they have been able to do a relatively important role, but been able to do it in four days, they wouldn't have been able to access that role beforehand.
"Rather than thinking to be successful or to be taking your career seriously, you need to be in the office five days a week, it's about: to be successful you need to be delivering your outcomes."
Dr Ditzell says while more Australians are able to access workplace flexibility, it needs to come without the worry of being overlooked for pay increases or promotions.
"We still see what we call either flexibility stigma or flexibility bias and that is the situation where people who use flexibility actually feel that they are disadvantaged as a result of that and they feel that they are judged differently."
Experts say for the gender pay gap to shrink and the glass ceiling to break, more men need to take up the flexibility too and employers need to recognise that mums and dads have equal responsibility for children.
Professor Hill says research suggests men can suffer from flexibility stigma in more extreme ways than women.
"If flexible work arrangements are not taken up by men as well, then they risk becoming just another reason for women to continue doing a disproportionate amount of unpaid care work," she says.
Dr Strazdins says flexibility should no longer be seen as a nice to have under Australian Work Health and Safety laws.
"There's legislation now, and it's called psychosocial hazards … parents are trying to find another 800 hours and they're facing impossible job demands."
She also argues it's time to crack down on working hours beyond the mandated 38-hour work week.
"While we allow long-hour jobs to be so well incentivised and earned, households have to make a really tough choice: who earns the big bucks and works the long hours and then who does the rest?"
Kate Harrison Brennan says reliable after-school care, ideally in the same location the child goes to school, is the backbone to stable employment.
"Quality, affordable care is crucial, particularly for workers who aren't able to be flexible with their working hours."
This could look like extra leave for parents of young children, beyond when they're babies, to give families more time together.
"I think this mismatch between the hours that we are at work and the hours that they are at school really demands that we think in new ways around paid leave away from work in order to provide those supports," Professor Hill says.
"We've always thought about 'paid parental leave' as being something only relevant to the first year of a child's life, but there are countries where there's an expectation that parents have access to paid leave throughout the early years of a child's schooling as well."
In Sweden parents get 480 days of paid parental leave per child, shared between the parents. That can be banked and used flexibly throughout their childhood.
Dr Strazdins says legislating against excessive work hours can level the playing field and reduce the gender pay gap.
"There's a review of the National Employment Standards right now. I would say there's very few employment standards which are so routinely ignored as the work hours per week.
"I'm trying to get people to see that it's really not right for workplaces to expect people to work these excessive hours – even if they reward them for it."
Men need to step up and do more of the unpaid work, and society needs to make that more possible, Professor Hill says.
"It's a big task. It's mostly invisible. It's squeezed in around everything else. It creates huge cognitive, emotional and logistical pressure that is primarily borne by mothers and grandmothers, and we need community and workplace supports that recognise that and allow it to be distributed more equally between all caregivers.
"Importantly, in offering and providing that flexibility, it's really critical that employers don't penalise dads for contributing to the unpaid care load."
We can’t expect families to keep patching over the gaps, Georgie Dent says.
"We're effectively asking parents to run a marathon in shoes designed for someone else and then wondering why they're not keeping up."
She says sytems that don't match modern-day realities are not only leaving parents scrambling, but they're failing children.
And perhaps, one of the biggest changes required is an attitude one.
“Supporting parents isn’t a concession to adult convenience: it’s one of the most powerful things we can do for the next generation," Ms Dent says.
“When we invest in parents, we invest in children."

Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of launching 26 strikes in 24 hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of launching 26 attacks in 24 hours
The war in Yemen intensifies with mounting clashes and reciprocal attacks between Saudi forces and the Houthis.
Yemen’s Houthi rebels have said Saudi Arabia carried out 26 attacks against areas under the group’s control in the past 24 hours, as the two sides continue trading fire amid an escalating war in Yemen, according to the AFP news agency.
On Friday, the group claimed Saudi attacks on Houthi-held territory had reached 300 over the past week alone, hitting positions across the areas it controls, AFP reported.

list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Italy to deploy warships to protect shipping through Bab al-Mandeb
- list 2 of 3Pakistan pledges full committment to defence of Saudi Arabia
- list 3 of 3In Yemen, war at home and in the region drives up prices
Yemen’s government, backed by Saudi Arabia, said on Friday its forces had killed 30 Houthi rebels and wounded more than 60 in clashes in the al-Waziiyah district of Taiz province, one of several fronts where combat has picked up this week.
The exchange has come on the heels of a widening escalation of fighting in Yemen between the government’s military and the Houthi fighters.
Tens of thousands marched through Sanaa on Friday in a show of support for the Iran-backed Houthis and against Saudi Arabia, as the rebels press gains that have brought large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, under their control.
Earlier this week, the intensifying attacks between the Yemeni government and the Houthi rebels killed at least five people, including three children, according to reports from both sides.
Saudi Arabia said one person was killed in the Taif governorate after a Houthi drone was intercepted, while Houthi-linked media reported deaths from Saudi attacks in Taiz and the town of Abs.
The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) condemned the Houthis’ continuing attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying they had caused civilian casualties, including women and children, and damaged energy infrastructure.
In a statement released on Friday, UNSC members said: “The military escalation being carried out by the Houthis in Yemen, their continued attacks on Saudi Arabia, and the attacks and threats to international shipping in the Red Sea, along with the Houthis’ advance near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, are all factors that threaten to widen the conflict, endanger maritime security and international trade, and undermine regional and international efforts to achieve peace in Yemen.”
Members added they were “deeply concerned by reports that at least 125,000 people had been displaced across Yemen since the start of September” and demanded “an immediate halt” to the group’s attacks, voiced solidarity with Saudi Arabia and affirmed the kingdom’s right to self-defence under international law.
The escalation has drawn in Washington, though reluctantly.
United States officials met Houthi representatives at the US embassy in the Omani capital, Muscat, over the weekend after the group’s rapid territorial gains raised concern over shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, a vital corridor for global trade.
The Houthis reportedly assured Washington that vessels not linked to Saudi Arabia would not be targeted.
Despite appeals from Riyadh for US President Donald Trump to strike the Houthis directly, Washington has so far held back, wary of opening a new front while still fighting a costly war with Iran.
Meanwhile, European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Friday the bloc’s Red Sea naval mission, Operation Aspides, had raised its alert level as the situation in the region worsened, the Reuters news agency reported.
“Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are unacceptable and sabotage the global economy,” Kallas said in a post on X.
She added that she had spoken with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud about diplomatic efforts to end the fighting in Yemen and restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

Putin says Ukraine interfering in Russian parliamentary election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:58:28 UTC
07:58:28 KST

Putin says Ukraine interfering in Russian parliamentary election
MOSCOW – Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Sept 18 that Ukraine was deliberately hindering talks aimed at ending the 4 ½-year-old war and accused Kyiv of interfering in Russia’s parliamentary election.
Putin, in comments to Russia’s Military-Industrial commission, also reasserted Moscow’s main defence aim of relying on its “nuclear triad” of weapons and said Moscow also had to move towards improving its anti-missile defences.
In comments reported by Russian news agencies, Putin said Ukraine had “long degenerated into a dictatorship”, referring to the country not holding a new presidential election despite the expiry of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s mandate.
“The Ukrainian leadership is in no hurry to hold elections, as you know, but they are also trying to interfere with us,” Putin was quoted as saying, without providing evidence.
Zelensky and other Ukrainian officials say no election can be held in their country while a state of emergency, in place since Russia’s February 2022 invasion, remains in effect.
Kyiv derides the Russian vote as a “pseudo election” with the result never in doubt.
Election ongoing
Russians began voting on Sept 18 in a three-day parliamentary election that Putin has said will show that millions of people back his army fighting in Ukraine, even though most anti-war candidates were not allowed to run.
The result is likely to be held up by the Kremlin as evidence of widespread public support for Putin’s policies and, in particular, for his prosecution of Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War Two, now in its fifth year.
Putin said Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets meant Kyiv’s offers to hold negotiations to end the war were disingenuous.
He said one recent Ukrainian strike had hit a home in a village in a Russian-occupied part of Zaporizhzhia, killing the head of a local election commission, who had been presented posthumously with a Russian state honour.
“By committing crimes of this kind, they are doing everything to ensure that there is no peace and no negotiations,” Putin was quoted as telling the commission.
In other comments to the commission, Putin said Russia was continuing to rely on the nuclear triad of land-based, sea-based and aircraft-launched weapons, but that it also needed to improve air defence systems.
Ukraine has rapidly developed its drone capabilities and has launched strikes against Russian industrial targets up to 3,000km from its border, disrupting fuel supplies and other aspect of Russian daily life. REUTERS

Presumption of guilt doesn't make prosecution case 'gospel truth': SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:55:22 UTC
07:55:22 KST

A bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and NV Anjaria gave this ruling
NEW DELHI: In a judgment that will impact as many as nine penal laws, Supreme Court has ruled that the stringent provisions of Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (Pocso) Act providing for presumption of guilt of the accused must not persuade trial courts to believe the prosecution's case to be the "gospel truth".A bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and N V Anjaria gave this ruling while setting aside concurrent judgments of a Delhi court and Delhi HC convicting a man, whom a woman had falsely accused of sexually assaulting her minor daughter in a Kalkaji slum in south Delhi in 2015. It said the accusation was part of a long-standing feud over water the woman had with him.The bench said both the trial court and HC appeared to have been swayed by the presumption of guilt provision in Pocso Act and overlooked glaring discrepancies and loopholes in the mother's testimony despite these being highlighted by the accused during cross-examination. Writing the judgment, Justice Anjaria said presumption of guilt in Pocso Act did not operate to eliminate evidence standing in favour of the accused.The statutory presumptions cannot be read to mean that the prosecution version is liable to be treated as gospel truth in every case," he said.The presumptive provision cannot unburden courts from "discharging their essential duty to analyse the evidence on record in light of the features emerging in a particular case", he added.
This ruling will potentially impact provisions of presumption of guilt against the accused, or casting reverse burden on them, in eight other laws - Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, Prevention of Corruption Act, Wild Life (Protection) Act, Essential Commodities Act, Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, Customs Act, Foreign Exchange Management Act, and Negotiable Instruments Act, which were specifically mentioned in the 42-page judgment.
Justices Mishra and Anjaria said, "The court should not mechanically accept the ipse dixit of the prosecution riding on the provisions regarding presumption of guilt to give a stamp of approval to every prosecution even if they are absurd or improbable in its story."It said the provision, or the rule of reverse burden requiring the accused to prove his innocence, did not change the rule of standard of proof as normally applied in criminal cases.

Nayan Sethin Washington
US President Donald Trump on Friday signed a new sanctions bill into law that targets Russia’s leading energy buyers – China and India – just days before Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for a state visit.
The White House issued a brief statement, saying that the President had “signed into law” the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” which “authorises and expands statutory sanctions, tariffs, and prohibitions on Russia and extends existing sanctions on Iran.”
The US House of Representatives passed the bill by a comfortable 262-159 vote on Wednesday. The Senate cleared the bill last month by an overwhelming 86-11 vote.
The legislation, originally backed by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July, gives Trump the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the five biggest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, adding another layer to his tariff-driven approach to foreign policy.

Five Great Reads: End times fascists, battling patriarchy in the climate crisis, and why Kylie still lives in our heads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:30:30 UTC
07:30:30 KST

Hello and welcome to the weekend.
At the moment, it’s easy to feel as if things have taken a turn towards the apocalyptic.
Headlines this week predicted that AI could kill all humans, the climate crisis would exacerbate environmental disasters, and “end time fascists” were plotting their escape from the end of the world.
But there is hope among the pessimism. In this selection of reads from across the Guardian, communities are fighting back, finding joy in music, and staying loyal to the planet as well as each other.
Enjoy.
1. Six experts on whether AI could really wipe out humanity
If the world didn’t feel bleak enough, some startling claims this week made the end truly seem nigh. Warnings from people working in the AI industry that there was a 10% chance humanity could be wiped out by the technology in the next decade was just one of them. But how serious are these claims? Here, six experts give their views.
‘Bizarre nonsense’: Hearteningly, scepticism around the latest claims abounds. Some experts believe the idea that AI bots could take over with their own free will is nonsense, and it’s (you guessed it) the humans who let things go berserk. “The AIs would not decide to do it on their own,” says Prof Alan Woodward from the University of Surrey’s centre for cybersecurity. “It’s the humans that are responsible and the AI is a tool. That is what we need to control, not the AI.”
Should we slow it all down? It appears the industry is divided on what to do, despite loud cries and alarm around the world at how quickly AI is evolving. “The path to better understanding and control of AI is more research, not less,” says Pedro Domingos, an emeritus professor of computer science at the University of Washington. “What would be truly irresponsible is putting up barriers to it.”
How long will it take to read: According to my AI chatbot (kidding!) just under four minutes.
Further reading: How AI ghosts and deathslop are changing the way we mourn, and this very excellent explainer on why tech companies might be only too happy for us to believe AI will “kill us all”.
2. The woman battling fire, patriarchy and super El Niño
As fires burn in Indonesian Borneo, and a looming “super” El Niño threatens to exacerbate already fragile conditions, a local group of women have come together to defend their community and battle the patriarchy. Indonesia’s first-ever all female firefighting team, which goes by the name Power of Mama, is made up of more than 140 women, with some as young as 10 years old. They receive rigorous training – from firefighting to operating surveillance drones – in order to help protect the nearby rainforests and peatlands that make up one of the most biodiverse regions on the planet.
Notable quote: “Because we are housewives, we are the ones that feel its effects most.”
Breaking down the village patriarchy: At first, the all women firefighting team faced criticism from the men in their villages. They would tease the women and ask them if they have “other duties to perform” instead of battling fires on the frontlines. But protecting residential properties and local farmland is gruelling work in unforgiving conditions, and Power of Mama members say they now work hand in hand with local communities.
How long will it take to read: About two minutes. 
Further reading: As the fires destroy precious Indonesian forests, critically endangered Bornean orangutans have no choice but to flee.
3. How do we stop the end times fascists?
The hysteria surrounding tech bros and the super rich at the moment isn’t just because of the rise of AI. As the sharp and thought-provoking author Naomi Klein, and co-author Astra Taylor, write in their new book: “The most powerful people in the world are preparing for the end of the world, an end they themselves are frenetically accelerating.” So what can we do about it? Here they give their vision.
Plotting their escape: “On one side are those of us who have no escape plan, no bunker in the sky or underground,” they write. “On the other are those with rapturous plans to shield themselves and their families from the political and ecological fires burning our planet. Instead of improving conditions for actual people on Earth … end times fascists are plotting their escape, indifferent and oblivious to all that’s worth saving.”
Are we at their mercy? The authors argue that our own human networks could give “basis for a different kind of survivalism”. As they write: “Part of that involves telling new stories, stories that are truthful and inspiring enough to help our depleted fellow humans fall back in love with our one and only home and defiantly recommit to defending it with all they’ve got.”
How long will it take to read: Just over nine minutes
Further reading: This soothing antidote to the ills of the world.
4. The students returning to school after sexual assault
Peer-on-peer violence is on the rise in Australia, with school-age girls making up the majority of sexual assault victims. As cases continue to grow, many victims have no choice but to go back to school and share classrooms with their perpetrators. Experts agree the current frameworks leave educational institutions unable to properly respond to this mounting crisis. Left to manage the aftermath of their assault alone, many female students stop going to campus all together.
Facing abusers at school: One student who experienced sexual assault when she was 14 says: “You go back to school the next day, and you just deal with it.” One social workers says she hears stories of schools not intervening, mishandling a report, or of female students having to keep attending the same school – facing their abuser regularly on the school grounds “many, many times”.
“Hypocrisy”: Prof Michael Salter, a leading researcher into child sexual abuse and exploitation, says if schools are teaching students about respectful relationships and consent, but are not empowered to protect and respond to students who experience sexual assault, “there would seem to be an obvious contradiction, or even hypocrisy”.
How long will it take to read: Just over three minutes.
Further reading: What the research says about choking as a sexual practice, and how to talk to your children about misogyny.
5. Twenty-five years of Can’t Get You Out of My Head
Born on an autumn weekend in a garage studio using a Mac computer-generated drum loop, the minimalist dance-pop opus Can’t Get You Out of My Head would go on to define Kylie Minogue’s career. Twenty-five years later, music writer Michael Cragg looks back on the dance tracks legacy and longevity.
Futuristic escapism: Released in the wake of the 9/11 terror attacks, Can’t Get You Out of My Head seemed to become a “hypnotic balm” for a world trying to make sense of things as the global “war on terror” dominated headlines.
Notable quote: “I really do believe that [Osama] Bin Laden and Kylie represent the polar opposites of human nature; the first all about cruelty without beauty, the second all about beauty without cruelty.”
Posh v Kylie: Back in the early 2000s, music fans were “obsessed with chart battles”, often pitting female songwriters against each other. On the same day Can’t Get You Out of My Head hit the airwaves, Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham was ready to release her own lead single from her debut solo album. Kylie would emerge victorious, beating out Posh whose Not Such an Innocent Girl came in at No 6 on the charts.
How long will it take to read: About five minutes. Enough time to spin Can’t Get You Out of My Head (three minutes and 50 seconds) at least once.
Further reading: Kylie’s 30 greatest singles, and a refreshingly raw and real encounter with the songwriter.
