Gazans face critical shelter conditions as rainy season arrives: UN
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:28:46 CST
07:28:46 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Shelter conditions for the majority of Gazans range from critical to catastrophic as the rainy season arrives, UN humanitarians said on Friday.
Humanitarian partners continue to warn that families are living amid widespread destruction, immense humanitarian needs, and ongoing restrictions on access and the entry of essential supplies, said the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
"An estimated 1.2 million people, or 58 percent of the population, face shelter conditions ranging from critical to catastrophic," said OCHA.
As the first rains of the season fell over Gaza on Friday, humanitarian partners stress that more than 65 percent of families they have assessed are living in tents or makeshift shelters, with over half of those described as being in poor or very poor condition, said the office.
Parts of a war-damaged residential building collapsed on Friday in Gaza City, the second such incident this week. Emergency teams were able to rescue children who were underneath the building, and only minor injuries have been reported, said OCHA.
The first collapse, which occurred on Wednesday, has killed at least 21, including 11 children.
OCHA said that, with its partners, it reached 200 households with rapid assistance last week and provided nearly 6,600 families with routine shelter support, including hundreds of new tents, tarpaulins, kitchen sets, solar lights, sleeping mats and blankets.
Once again, the UN urged Israeli authorities to approve the entry of heavy equipment, engine oil, durable shelter materials and other items necessary to repair damaged buildings and help people secure safer living conditions. ■

Economic Watch: European investors grow wary of U.S. Treasury risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:28:44 CST
07:28:44 KST

BELGRADE, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- European financial institutions are increasingly reassessing risks associated with U.S. government debt, as Treasury yields remain near multi-year highs and U.S. federal debt has surpassed 40 trillion U.S. dollars.
The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield hovered around 5 percent on Friday after hitting its highest level since 2007 earlier this week. Despite the Federal Reserve's first interest rate hike in more than three years and the U.S. Treasury's expanded buybacks of longer-dated securities, long-term borrowing costs have remained elevated.
Against this backdrop, some European investors have moved to reduce exposure to U.S. government bonds, while others have raised concerns over the country's fiscal outlook and the traditional perception of Treasuries as virtually risk-free assets.
Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages Norway's sovereign wealth fund, proposed earlier this month reducing the share of government bonds in the fund's fixed-income benchmark to 50 percent from 70 percent, while increasing exposure to non-government debt, including mortgage-backed securities.
Under the proposal, the weighting of U.S. government bonds in the benchmark would fall to 21.9 percent from 34.1 percent.
Other European asset managers have also adjusted their positioning toward U.S. government debt.
Swisscanto Asset Management said in its September asset allocation update that interventions by the U.S. Treasury in bond and currency markets had unsettled investors. The Swiss asset manager said it was reducing exposure to long-dated U.S. Treasuries after the 30-year yield broke above its previous trading range, while finding Australian government bonds more attractive.
British private bank and wealth manager Brown Shipley has, meanwhile, maintained a tactical underweight position in U.S. Treasuries, citing higher energy prices, elevated government borrowing and persistent geopolitical uncertainty. It said an expansion of U.S. Treasury buybacks of longer-dated debt could provide some technical support to bond prices but would not address underlying fiscal concerns.
The debate has also extended to the traditional status of government bonds as safe assets.
James Turner, head of global fixed income for Europe, the Middle East and Africa for BlackRock, recently told the Financial Times that government bonds were "not as risk-free as they used to be." He noted that a company with a fiscal position comparable to that of the U.S. government would be unlikely to be regarded by investors as risk-free.
Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at London-based global investment manager Man Group, has also identified reduced exposure to U.S. Treasuries among the market trends to watch this autumn. She said uncertainty surrounding U.S. policy was contributing to unease among international investors, while moves by some U.S. allies to relocate part of their gold reserves also reflected broader concerns.
BNP Paribas Wealth Management said in its September fixed-income outlook that the recent rise in Treasury yields had been driven in part by increased capital demand and a higher term premium amid uncertainty over Federal Reserve policy.
The institution said the U.S. Treasury's decision to expand buybacks of longer-dated securities was unlikely to have a lasting impact on yields. It maintained a 12-month target of 4.50 percent for the 10-year Treasury yield, while saying yields could temporarily approach 5 percent in the coming months. ■

Feature: From D-Day to present, HMS Belfast reflects changing political landscape
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:28:38 CST
07:28:38 KST

Photo taken on Sept. 18, 2026 shows HMS Belfast, a former Royal Navy light cruiser, in front of Tower Bridge in London, Britain. (Xinhua/Zhang Feng)
by Xinhua writer Zhang Feng
LONDON, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Near the banks of the River Thames in London, not far from Tower Bridge, a 187-meter-long vessel sits quietly at anchor, its massive hull a reminder of its wartime past.
HMS Belfast, a former Royal Navy light cruiser, took part in major operations during World War II. It entered the Thames in 1971 and later opened to the public as a museum.
Walking through the cruiser, visitors could encounter marks of age everywhere. At the gun turret on the quarter deck, three 6-inch guns remained in place, with rusted shell casings lying nearby.
Inside the turret, a date stood out on the wall: June 6, 1944 -- D-Day, when Allied forces led by Britain and the United States crossed the English Channel and landed in Normandy, opening a major new front in Western Europe against Nazi Germany.
The date stood as one of the defining moments for HMS Belfast, and a symbol of the alliance between Britain and the United States in the 20th century.
But that relationship faces a more complicated political landscape today.
During U.S. President Donald Trump's two-day visit to Ireland recently, he said he would "love" to see the unification of Ireland and Britain's Northern Ireland.
It came as no surprise that the remarks sparked stiff opposition from British politicians, including Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, saying that Northern Ireland is an integral part of the United Kingdom.
Bruce, a staff member aboard HMS Belfast, offered an analogy when asked about the unification comments.
"You have America and you have Canada, they're the same place (continent), but they're different," he said. "Well, Northern Ireland is different from Ireland. Ireland is Irish, Northern Ireland is the UK."
Below deck, another exhibition aimed to showcase the Anglo-American alliance. A compartment of the ship has been turned into a display for Pressure, a film about the tough decision of the U.S. general Dwight Eisenhower over whether to postpone the Normandy landings amid bad weather and military pressure.
More than 80 years on, the relationship between the allies looks markedly different: Trump has repeatedly called on European allies, including Britain, to shoulder more of the European security costs.
On the Malvinas Islands, known in Britain as the Falkland Islands, Trump has suggested that Washington could reconsider its position in the sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina.
When it came to Greenland, former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer said flatly Greenland and Denmark must determine the future of Greenland and "nobody else."
For visitors walking through HMS Belfast, the gap between the past and the present was particularly stark.
The guns at the bow stood silent, but evoked the deafening battlefields where they once thundered. The transmitting station has long since fallen silent, but one could almost hear the hiss of electrical signals. In the sick bay, wards and surgical instruments reminded onlookers of the very human cost.
The cruiser also carried another connection to British politics: its name.
Belfast, capital of Northern Ireland and a city with a shipbuilding tradition, gave its name to the 1998 Belfast Agreement, also known as the Good Friday Agreement which helped bring an end to decades of violence referred to as "the Troubles."
The 1998 agreement established a political framework under which Northern Ireland's constitutional status can change if a majority of people in Northern Ireland vote for a united Ireland in a referendum.
The debates on the future of Northern Ireland, however, have not disappeared. The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland met in Cardiff on Monday to declare "Westminster's time is coming to an end," pushing for independence from Britain and rejoining the European Union.
As the debate continued, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin on Friday reaffirmed "their shared commitment to upholding the Good Friday Agreement."
For many people in Britain, the status of Northern Ireland remains deeply sensitive, touching both Britain's territorial integrity and the fragile peace established by the Belfast Agreement.
"Belfast is part of the UK," Bruce said. "It's not part of Ireland." ■
Photo taken on Sept. 16, 2026 shows a display compartment for the film Pressure on HMS Belfast, a former Royal Navy light cruiser, in London, Britain. (Xinhua/Zhang Feng)

NAIROBI, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Kenya has launched a counter-terrorism hotline to give citizens a confidential channel to report concerns linked to radicalization, violent extremism and terrorism.
Musalia Mudavadi, prime cabinet secretary and cabinet secretary for foreign and diaspora affairs, said the newly launched counter-terrorism hotline will elevate communities as key partners of security agencies in preventing terrorism.
Mudavadi said the toll-free channel allows Kenyans to share confidential tips anonymously without fear of exposure, removing barriers to intelligence reporting and strengthening public safety nationwide.
"Communities and security agencies should closely monitor the activities of such gangs, given the risk of radicalization and their potential evolution into violent extremism and terrorism," he said during the launch of the hotline on Thursday evening in Nairobi.
Mudavadi described the platform as a critical measure to enhance public safety and reinforce community-led approaches to countering violent extremism.
By removing barriers to timely intelligence sharing, Mudavadi noted, the initiative will build stronger trust between citizens and specialized security agencies.
"The hotline provides an essential platform for enhanced cooperation between communities and security agencies in making Kenya a country in which all people can live together safely and peacefully," he said.
Mudavadi urged Kenyans to use the platform responsibly and clarified that it was intended specifically for counter-terrorism reports, rather than general police complaints.
He called for heightened public vigilance ahead of the 2027 general election, warning that political gatherings could be targeted by extremist groups.
He emphasized that vigilance must extend online to counter emerging cyber-terrorism and ransom-seeking attacks.
Mudavadi stated that regional instability across the Horn of Africa continues to heighten security risks, making close cooperation between the public and security agencies vital for identifying and disrupting potential threats.
He warned that organized criminal gangs, including groups involved in violence and intimidation, could evolve into violent extremist and terrorist organizations if their activities are not closely monitored.
Mudavadi said communities and security agencies must increase vigilance to prevent criminal gangs from expanding, becoming entrenched and threatening national security.
The Kenyan official also emphasized that authorities must closely scrutinize organized criminal gangs that terrorize communities, undermine state institutions and threaten democratic processes. ■

Feature: The last 7 dunams -- a farmer's struggle in Gaza
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:28:08 CST
07:28:08 KST

GAZA, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- On a seven-dunam plot near the "Yellow Line," 55-year-old Mohammed Al-Dahdouh bends over a small field of potatoes, a fraction of the more than 40 dunams he once cultivated.
The military demarcation line established under a ceasefire arrangement separates Israeli-deployed areas from the rest of the Gaza Strip, making every planting season a gamble.
Since the war began on Oct. 7, 2023, Gaza's farmland has shrunk dramatically. Water, electricity, fuel, and agricultural supplies are scarce or unaffordable. Yet Al-Dahdouh, a father of six, refuses to abandon the soil.
When shelling nears, he flees; when it stops, he returns.
His struggle mirrors that of farmers across the enclave. In Beit Lahia town in northern Gaza, 42-year-old farmer Ibrahim Abu Samhadana grows strawberries, zucchini, and eggplant while living in a tent beside the ruins of his home.
His family's 22 dunams are gone.
"The war has completely devastated the agricultural sector," Abu Samhadana said.
Still, he plants on.
"I am determined to rely on agriculture, as it is the profession we have known since childhood," the farmer, also a father of six, added.
In southern Gaza, the guava season, normally from September through December, tells a similar story.
Farmer Hani Al-Qudra's land in Khan Yunis has shrunk from about 1,350 dunams before the war to around 200 dunams, and his workforce from about 100 to 15.
"Guava is one of the most important crops in the Gaza Strip; both residents and farmers depend on it for food and employment opportunities," Al-Qudra said.
Consumers feel the loss too. In a Khan Yunis market, 45-year-old Ahmed Al-Najjar, a father of three, said guava, once an affordable seasonal fruit, is now beyond reach for many families.
"It saddens me when my children ask for it, and I cannot buy it," Al-Najjar said.
Experts paint a grim picture. Agricultural specialist Mohammed Abu Shamala said guava cultivation had fallen from about 1,700 dunams before the war to less than 100 in Gaza, while damage to farmland and irrigation systems and rising water salinity have degraded crop quality and limited the cultivation of some varieties.
A Food and Agriculture Organization assessment issued in August found that only about 448 hectares, or roughly 3 percent, of Gaza's cropland remained both accessible and undamaged. Gaza's Hamas-run agriculture authorities have put agricultural losses at about 3.49 billion U.S. dollars.
Before the war, agriculture accounted for about 10 percent of Gaza's economy and supported more than 560,000 people. Today, for farmers like Al-Dahdouh, Abu Samhadana, and Al-Qudra, insisting on cultivating potatoes, vegetables, and guavas has become a struggle to preserve both their livelihoods and what remains of Gaza's agricultural sector.
When shelling subsides, Al-Dahdouh returns to his seven dunams, tending his potatoes and preparing to plant tomatoes in the coming season.
"I insist on farming and earning an income for the sake of my children," he said. ■

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 19, 2026
Trump says he’s banning media outlets CNN, MS NOW, Politico from White House
US President Donald Trump said on Sept 18 he was banning three major news outlets – CNN, MS NOW and Politico – from the White House, in his latest move to crack down on the independent press.
He wrote that he was banning the outlets for allegedly “reporting FAKE NEWS” in a move that is likely to be challenged as conflicting with the US Constitution’s First Amendment guarantees of free speech and a free press.
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
CNN, MS NOW, Politico and the National Press Club did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CNN’s team remains at the White House working as if it were a normal Friday afternoon, CNN reporter Brian Stelter said on air.
OpenAI’s Sam Altman to brief UN Security Council next week
OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman will brief the United Nations Security Council next week during the annual gathering of world leaders in New York for the UN General Assembly, an OpenAI spokesperson said on Sept 18.
The 15-member Security Council is due to meet on Sept 23 on artificial intelligence and international security, just weeks after several AI industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the increasingly powerful technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and slip beyond human control.
“Sam Altman will brief an open UN Security Council meeting in person next week,” an OpenAI spokesperson told Reuters. “His remarks are expected to focus on the steps OpenAI is taking to ensure AI is safe and benefits people globally, along with the need for international coordination and shared safety standards.”
Russia seizes assets of Nestle, French firms over West’s Ukraine support
The Russian authorities have seized the businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestle and three French groups, a move the Kremlin defended on Sept 18 as a justified measure against firms representing “unfriendly countries” that back Ukraine.
A decree signed by President Vladimir Putin transferred the Russian operations of Nestle, French retailer Auchan and the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain, now known as Lemana Pro, to a company called LEV Management.
The decree, issued late Sept 17, also covers the Russian subsidiaries of French logistics group FM Logistic.
Disney taps AI executive Karandeep Anand as first tech chief
Disney on Sept 18 named the CEO of artificial intelligence startup Character.AI as its first chief technology officer, a year after sending the company a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorised use of Disney characters.
Karandeep Anand will join Disney on Oct 2 as senior executive vice-president and CTO, reporting directly to chief executive Josh D’Amaro.
Anand will oversee enterprise technology, infrastructure, data management and AI platforms, product and engineering, Disney said in a statement.
Bayern star Harry Kane becomes fastest player to score 100 Bundesliga goals
Harry Kane scored twice in Bayern Munich’s 7-0 demolition of Union Berlin on Sept 18, becoming the fastest player to reach 100 Bundesliga goals.
Kane scored his 100th and 101st goals in just 98 domestic games, obliterating the previous record set by Cologne’s Dieter Mueller in 1977 by 31 games.
It’s the latest record that the England captain has torn up during his time in Munich, having already become the fastest Bayern player to reach 75, 100 and 150 goals in all competitions.

How can new olim navigate Israel’s 2026 election? French immigrant builds online quiz to help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:10:44 UTC
07:10:44 KST

"I built knesset2026.com to help olim (immigrants) understand Israeli politics. Users can answer 16 questions to discover the candidate that best matches their views, then receive a daily news email about Israel in their language,” said Dan Finel, a recent French immigrant.
The free, user-friendly online questionnaire is available in English, French, German, Italian, Spanish, and even in Hebrew.
“On October 27, I will be voting for the first time in Israel, and I wanted to understand the different candidates and their opinions,” he explained. “There are many candidates I don’t know much about, and I couldn’t find enough information in French or English. I spoke with many olim from different countries, and they told me it’s difficult to find information online in foreign languages.
“So, for those who cannot follow the news in Hebrew, I decided to create a quiz where you answer easy questions about your views. At the end, we tell you the candidate most aligned with your thinking. We update the questions often. And then, every day, you receive curated news about Israeli politics in your preferred language, in an easy-to-understand format. At the end of each newsletter, which is also free, is a review of the latest election polling results.”
Finel, 27, is learning to perfect his Hebrew on the job as a data scientist at Similarweb. Meanwhile, his knesset2026.com platform has attracted more than 50,000 users, mainly between the ages of 25 and 40. (I’m much older than the average user, but I found the website helpful in confirming my choice of candidate.)
Growing up in Paris in a traditional, Zionist family, Finel visited Israel annually from the time he was six years old. Although he is the first in his immediate family to make aliyah, his grandparents live in Ashdod, and he has aunts and uncles in Givat Shmuel and Tel Aviv.
While finishing his studies at a top business school in France, he had the option to do a six-month internship abroad and decided to do it in the start-up nation through the Jewish Agency’s Masa Israel Journey career development program.
The track he chose was Israel Tech Challenge (ITC), a Jewish Agency and Israeli National Cyber Bureau initiative connecting young professionals and students from overseas with the tools they need to break into careers in Israel’s hi-tech industry.
“I loved the country, and I wanted to see what it was like to live in Tel Aviv,” he said.
Originally, his flight had been scheduled for October 9, 2023. For obvious reasons, that flight was postponed, and instead he arrived in November. Despite the wartime situation, his ITC experience cemented his decision to move here.
“I really loved meeting Israelis and people from around the world; in Paris you were only with French people,” he said.
Part of the present and the future
ONE OF THE people he met during his six-month internship, Susana Arditti, was from his past and she’s now part of his present and future – they’re getting married in October.
“Susana and I met in kindergarten in Paris, and we were basically in love,” said Finel. “Then her family moved to London, and we didn’t see each other for 20 years until we met again in Masa. She was going to make aliyah, and I said, ‘I love life in Israel, and I want to leave Paris, so let’s do it.’” Arditti works as a corporate brand designer.
Finel officially made aliyah in September 2024. “Now I’ve been here for more than two years, and I have lived through war and bombings. It’s been quite challenging. Sometimes you can’t sleep at night,” he said.
“One regret I have is that I didn’t do the army; I arrived at 24, a bit too late. But I have friends in the army, and they say it’s hard, but they feel proud to defend the country.”
When asked his favorite aspect of Israeli life, Finel didn’t hesitate to answer: “The people.”
“You feel that even if you don’t know anyone, if something happens to you, people will help. I felt it at work the moment I arrived. I’m a French guy; nobody knew me, and I didn’t speak Hebrew well, but I immediately felt they were like family. They told me if I needed anything, they’d be there for me. And that’s been true.”
The biggest difference he notices between French and Israeli culture is the Israeli directness in communication.
'The sun, the beach, the restaurants, the food'
“Relations between people are much more authentic and honest,” he said. “In France, you don’t say exactly what you think, and there are many topics you don’t talk about. In Israel, nothing is off limits. If you think something, you can discuss it openly. At the beginning that was difficult for me, but you get used to it.”
In addition to the warm culture, he enjoys “the quality of life, the sun, the beach, the restaurants, the food.”
One of Finel’s favorite hobbies is cooking and baking, everything from pasta and fish to chocolate cake. “I love learning and trying new stuff,” he said. He’s also an avid runner and all-around sportsman.
With everything he has going on in his life, he still felt the need to contribute his skills voluntarily toward greater unity among Israelis. Using his favorite Hebrew word, bekitzur (in short), he phrased it like this:
“The country is a bit broken, very divided, and that’s difficult. This is why the election is so important. I feel we should all be together, going in the same direction and helping each other get there, even if we don’t all think the same way. We have so many enemies; we need to be together.” ■
Dan Finel, 27
From Paris to Tel Aviv, 2024

Putting conversation first: Jerusalem ulpan founder reflects on 18 years of teaching Hebrew to olim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:10:22 UTC
07:10:22 KST

Any immigrant who ever struggled to become conversant in Hebrew could rightfully feel a bit jealous of Ami Steinberger.
He grew up in a bilingual home in Los Angeles, speaking English with his mother and Hebrew with his Israeli father. That gave him a huge advantage when he relocated to Israel.
Steinberger felt he could help those without prior Hebrew fluency reach a conversational level that most could not achieve in existing ulpan classes. (“Ulpan” means “studio” but is also used to describe an intensive school for learning Hebrew.)
On August 18, 2008, he held his first ulpan class in his living room in Katamon. He had four students. Two months later, he was asked to hold two simultaneous classes at AACI and had to hire another teacher.
Today, Steinberger’s Ulpan La-Inyan (ulpan.com) employs 80 to 90 teachers in a variety of time zones, teaching private lessons and group courses to roughly 2,000 students annually, online and in person. Companies, embassies, and gap-year programs are among its clients.
In celebration of Ulpan La-Inyan’s 18th anniversary, Steinberger talked with the Magazine about the history of his ulpan, current trends and methodologies for teaching Hebrew, and how Hebrew is increasingly pivotal to Jewish identity outside of Israel.
A new kind of ulpan
Although he officially made aliyah in 1994 at age 14, when his family lived in Ra’anana for a year, and came back for a year after high school and two years after college, Steinberger permanently relocated in 2007. He had earned an undergraduate degree in English literature from Yeshiva University and a master’s degree in clinical psychology.
Ulpan La-Inyan was born of his interest in languages – he had searched for an effective method for mastering Arabic, French, and Spanish as a hobby – combined with his realization that the free ulpan courses offered by the government for new immigrants weren’t always successful.
“I noticed that although some English-speakers would come out of a traditional government ulpan with strong Hebrew, many of them would come out understanding the difference between verb forms but not being able to open their mouths and speak,” he said. “These ulpan classes are too large for the teachers to engage each student, so they rely more on theory than on practice. They’re teaching language as if it’s an academic discipline rather than a social skill.”
He saw this as a gap that needed filling.
“I decided to open my own language school based on the method that had helped me learn foreign languages. And it turned out that the need was real. People would come to me and say, ‘I’ve been to five ulpanim, and this was the first one that worked.’
“Traditional ulpan, for many people, is like taking a horse and buggy to your destination; our ulpan gets you there in a car.”
Grammar drills vs speaking skills
Steinberger creates scripted lessons based on research into how the brain absorbs and processes language. Without going into detail, this method teaches words by repeating them at very specific intervals.
“All of this takes place in a conversation which is relevant and useful, where you feel as if you’re actually participating. We don’t teach words with flashcards but through natural conversation.”
In the past decade, additional private ulpanim in Israel have followed suit, radically shifting the emphasis from grammar drills to speaking skills.
“I like to think we started that trend,” Steinberger said. “However, none of them use our exact method, our secret sauce.”
Along with online quizzes and games, ulpan homework these days might include watching a contemporary Israeli TV show and discussing it in the next class, or meeting up in a Hebrew-speaking environment like a café.
Another trend is online learning. Ulpan La-Inyan is still headquartered in Jerusalem with a branch in Tel Aviv, but the physical location doesn’t matter as much anymore.
“Before corona, we offered only private lessons online, not group lessons, and that segment constituted no more than 10% of our clientele. Since corona, 50% of our students participate online, in private and group classes,” Steinberger said.
Students come from North America, South America, Mexico, and Europe. Not all students are Jewish. For example, clientele includes Jerusalem Arabs seeking to improve their Hebrew for easier integration into academia or the workplace.
Hebrew via AI?
The growing preference for long-distance learning comes in tandem with many options for language acquisition – for example, the popular Duolingo digital language-learning platform and app. Steinberger said Duolingo is fun but not very effective for Hebrew, Arabic, and other non-European languages.
“Then there are AI language-training apps with an avatar acting like a language coach; the learner speaks, and the avatar corrects them.
“However, if someone really wants to progress in a language, it requires discipline. If you have good self-discipline to engage with the app on a consistent basis, AI is great. If you’re somebody who needs a structured learning environment where you feel accountable to the teacher and classmates to show up, that is what will help you progress,” he said.
“Either way, AI is not human, and it’s the human element in conversation that really drives communication.”
Ulpan La-Inyan is developing a hybrid option: a digital course combined with human interaction in real time.
“This enables you to experience fadihot, those embarrassing mistakes, together and get past them,” Steinberger said. “AI can be helpful, but people will always need a sense of human connection because language is ultimately a social activity.”
Pitfalls, pet words, and identity
What are the most common difficulties for new Hebrew-speakers?
“Pronunciation can be difficult to master,” said Steinberger. “English-speakers often confuse the pronunciation of the Hebrew letters hay and het, while French-speakers often confuse raish and het.”
Aside from that, he said, “mostly it’s the verb conjugations that trip people up.”
Steinberger noted that shaky Hebrew skills lead many a new immigrant to feel a frustrating loss of self-esteem. “They may have a PhD, but their Hebrew is on a first-grade level.”
It helps to inject some basic everyday expressions into your vocabulary from day one. Handy exclamations such as sababa, ahla, and yalla – all of which, ironically enough, are borrowed from Arabic – lend ease to daily interactions even if your ability to put a full sentence together isn’t yet up to speed.
Steinberger believes that the ability to interact with Israelis in their own tongue is increasingly essential to Jewish identity formation in the Diaspora, particularly in non-Orthodox streams.
It’s true that many graduates of Orthodox and ultra-Orthodox schools lack conversational Hebrew fluency because Hebrew is often taught as a subject and not a language, he says. But their Jewish identity is tied to Torah values and lifestyle rather than spoken Hebrew.
“However, in the non-Orthodox world, the educational emphasis is on creating a link with peers in Israel. Hebrew could be that bridge, especially in times when Israel’s reputation is in question and Jewish identity becomes complex,” Steinberger said.
“If someone opts to say ‘I stand with Israel,’ then learning the language becomes their opportunity to connect with Israelis. Many people with a strong feeling of Jewish identity abroad feel they don’t belong at all when they’re in Israel because they can’t really have a conversation.”
And that brings us back to the question of how best to acquire a comfortable command of Hebrew.
Studies back up Steinberger’s contention that the old-style approach of memorizing grammatical rules and vocabulary word lists is not nearly as effective as the way babies learn to talk, by listening and speaking.
So, if you haven’t progressed as well as you’d like in a public or traditional ulpan, don’t despair – Ulpan La-Inyan or similar programs may be just the ticket for a faster ride to fluency.■
To sign up for Steinberger’s Daily Dose of Hebrew via WhatsApp or email, or book a 15-minute trial lesson: ulpan.com/your-daily-dose-of-hebrew

Pentagon's US-Iran war fatality accounting may be inaccurate - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:10:17 UTC
07:10:17 KST

The Pentagon's public account of US service member casualties in the Iran war excludes at least four service members killed in the Middle East since the war began on February 28, The Washington Post reported on Friday, citing six US officials familiar with the Defense Department's internal casualty accounting data.
While the Pentagon's public database, the Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), lists 18 US military fatalities, five of the officials told WaPo that there had been at least 22 fatalities, with an additional official saying there had been 23.
The official said that while not all of the undisclosed deaths were directly tied to the conflict, all involved US personnel in the region during the war.
Three US contractors based in the region have also died since the start of the conflict, the official added.
Officials expressed their frustration with the excluded deaths to the Washington Post.
Proper accounting of military deaths essential for families
In addition to public transparency, the proper accounting of military fatalities is essential for service members' families who receive survivor benefits based on whether the death occurred while performing official duties.
As of Friday, 14 fatalities are listed in the system as occurring during Operation Epic Fury, with an additional four categorized under Overseas Operations, referring to the July ceasefire between the US and Iran, which later collapsed, the Washington Post wrote.
Pentagon releases two additional names of service members killed in region
The Pentagon also released the names of two service members who died in the Middle East since February while assigned to missions unrelated to the Iran war, although both deaths occurred at bases attacked by Iranian forces.
Sgt. Devin Seibel died in Irbil, Iraq, during a training accident on May 31 while assigned to the ongoing campaign against Islamic State terrorists, Operation Inherent Resolve, according to a Pentagon press release.
In addition, Maj. Sorffly Davius died on March 6 after suffering an unspecified medical emergency, having been deployed under Operation Spartan Shield, which involved partnerships with regional militaries, according to the Washington Post.

‘Checkout,' ‘Fauda’ test the appetite for Israeli spy stories after October 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:10:13 UTC
07:10:13 KST

Is there still an appetite for Israeli spy stories?
Two productions arriving in the United States this month are testing that question: Checkout, a dark Israeli comedy about an aging Mossad operative, and the fifth season of Fauda, the Israeli action thriller about undercover counterterrorism agents.
One is an indie film that spent years getting to the screen; the other is a global Netflix hit whose new season plunges directly into the trauma of the October 7 massacre.
The two projects are seeking audiences in a challenging climate. A Pew Research Center survey conducted in March found that 60% of Americans had an unfavorable view of Israel, compared with 37% who viewed the country favorably. And Israeli cultural exports have faced increasing scrutiny abroad over the country’s conduct since October 7.
Yet Fauda has returned to Netflix with considerable international attention, while Checkout opened in Manhattan to a sold-out audience.
“It’s hard for Israeli movies right now to find an audience because everything translates to, you know, the ‘P’ [Palestinian] problem,” Jonathan Dekel, the writer, director and executive producer of Checkout, said in an interview. “It’s problematic.”
Checkout premieres to sold-out theater
Checkout opened September 17 to a sold-out audience at the Quad Cinema in Greenwich Village, which Dekel described as a “stalwart of indie cinema.”
Dekel has said the film’s six-year production was almost as difficult as the journey of its protagonist. They shot in Ukraine in November 2020, at the height of the pandemic, and barely escaped with the film’s hard drive after the set was bombed when Russia invaded. They had just finished editing when October 7, 2023, arrived, and Dekel was called up for military service.
Dekel knew that the movie would debut in a world transformed by the war and its aftermath.
“Trying to find a good time to put out a movie, a satire - a dark comedy about the Israeli special forces - was very, very touch and go until we finally decided to go for it,” he told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
Checkout is not a conventional spy thriller. Its protagonist, Dov, is an American-born New Yorker who moved to Israel and is now about to retire from the Mossad.
“The day he checks out of his hotel to retire, someone else checks in, and it turns out it’s Mossad’s number one target - an arch terrorist [code-]named Gilgamesh,” Dekel said. “The entire movie is this weird weekend in a hotel where these two middle-aged men, spy-versus-spy, try to figure out who they are. They’re trying to find out about each other, but they find themselves.”
Josh Pais, who plays Dov, said his character is a man searching for meaning in his life - and comes to believe he can find it by tracking down and stopping a terrorist.
“He is possibly stepping into delusion,” said Pais. “What was appealing to me was that this is a story of what really happens to spies. So many movies tap into, you know, the James Bond of being a spy. Those movies are awesome, but this movie is about what it’s really like to be sent to a distant land, to be on location and to pretend that you’re someone else. Over a certain amount of time these guys start to lose touch with reality because, in truth, the vast majority of time as a spy nothing happens.”
Shai Satran, the movie’s co-writer, said he believes this is the “perfect moment for a movie about the Israeli intelligence community and an operation gone bad.”
“His driving force is not really to catch that guy - he doesn’t care about that guy. The driving force is to be accepted by his peers, the people who sent him - that’s at the core,” said Satran. “I don’t want to be crude about this, but there was something pre-October 7 about the Israeli security forces, maybe the special forces: There’s a certain arrogance in being only worried about your peers and not being aware of” the wider mission. In the lead-up to the Hamas attacks of October 7, “Israel, in a sense, thought that they were more in control of the situation than they were,” he said
Fauda's international success rewarded with fifth season
That idea - of intelligence work as something more complicated than heroic missions and exotic adventures - also runs through Fauda, though in a much more conventional action-thriller format.
The Israeli series has been an international success since its Netflix debut in 2016, and its fifth season, which arrived on Netflix September 8, is now testing whether audiences will follow its characters into a story shaped directly by and set two years after October 7.
Lior Raz, the show’s creator, co-writer and star, said last month at a fundraiser in Lenox, Massachusetts, for Israel’s Magen David Adom emergency service that he was genuinely surprised by the show’s reception in unlikely places: Previous seasons of the show hit No. 1 in popularity in Lebanon and the United Arab Emirates, and it was No. 2 in Qatar.
Season four ran in 2022 in Israel and early the next year on Netflix. The show’s creators had originally begun writing a different fifth season. But after the October 7 Hamas attack, Raz said those scripts were discarded. The new season deals directly with the aftermath of the attack and what Raz described as the nature of revenge. One reviewer called it “gripping, emotionally exhausting and often deeply difficult to watch,” particularly because of its depiction, in flashbacks, of October 7.
Raz, in his MDA talk, said the backlash against Israel was a campaign orchestrated by radical activists and Israel’s enemies. The latest season of Fauda is in part an attempt to depict the Israeli perspective for those open to nuance. “I want them to look in my character’s eyes, and to see what we felt on those days,” he told the New York Times. “If it would happen in their countries, they would feel exactly like we felt and how we feel about the world. So I hope it would open people’s eyes to see what happened on October 7.”
Although its reception abroad is hard to gauge, the latest season was a hit in Israel: The Times reported that it had already been the most-watched season of any show in the history of Israel’s Yes network.
Lacking the backing of a streaming giant, Checkout will have to work harder to find an audience. The Sundance Screenwriters Lab supported the Checkout script, Dekel said, but that was before October 7. Since then, “finding a distributor, finding a Netflix, Amazon or Hulu was pretty much crickets [silence] all over. It might be our movie, but looking around [at] movies from my colleagues - Israelis - I think it’s pretty much a broad phenomenon.”
Asked if he believed the difficulty he faced was because it is an Israeli movie or because it involved Jews, Dekel replied, “Is there a difference?”

Archbishop of Canterbury revokes award from Pakistani cleric who praised Osama bin Laden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:09:58 UTC
07:09:58 KST

The Archbishop of Canterbury withdrew on Thursday an award given to a Muslim cleric who praised Osama bin Laden in comments he made in 2007.
Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi, a Muslim cleric from Pakistan, received the Hubert Walter Award for Reconciliation and Interfaith Cooperation at Lambeth Palace, the residence of the Archbishop of Canterbury, last Friday.
Ashrafi serves as the chairman of the Pakistan Ulema Council, an Islamic umbrella group composed of Islamic scholars from a wide spectrum of Islamic traditions.
The Archbishop’s office said that Ashrafi was being honored for “his outstanding work as an ambassador of interfaith harmony in Pakistan, known for his commitment to promoting religious tolerance.”
The statement continued to praise Ashrafi’s role in supporting “religious minorities in Pakistan, particularly the Christian community.”
Bin Laden was 'fighting for Islam'
The ceremony coincided with the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in New York City. Lambeth Palace announced the withdrawal of the award after Ashrafi's comments resurfaced.
Comments made by Ashrafi emerged from 2007, in which he praised bin Laden, the architect of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, as someone who had “been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans, and British,” and in a different instance said he would give bin Laden the title “Saifullah,” meaning “sword of God.”
Lambeth Palace faced backlash over the resurfaced comments and announced it would withdraw the award.
“It is a longstanding principle of interfaith dialogue and co-operation that we must engage with one another across deeply held differences, and that remains the case,” Lambeth Palace announced.
“However, previous comments made by Imam Ashrafi have come to light that have led Lambeth Palace to reconsider this award, and we can now confirm today that the award has been withdrawn. We have contacted Imam Ashrafi to make him aware of this decision,” the statement continued.
'An unfair campaign' against him
In a statement to the BBC, Ashrafi told reporters that his comments from 2007 had been “totally taken out of context” and the subsequent outcry was “an unfair campaign” aimed at smearing him.
Ashrafi said he made the comments in response to “the hurt felt by many Muslims” after the British government’s decision to knight the “Satanic Verses” author Salman Rushdie.
Ashrafi has also been criticized since the award was first announced for his support of the Pakistani blasphemy laws, which have been criticized by human rights groups.
Ashrafi claimed the laws actually “save lives” by stopping people from taking matters of religious offenses into their own hands.
Human Rights Watch said last year that “the laws perpetuate religious discrimination and are used to target the poor and minorities in unlawful evictions and land grabs.”
The group also called on Pakistan’s government to reform the laws to prevent them from “being weaponized” against any of Pakistan's minority communities.

US granted permanent control over all security needs in Greenland, Trump announces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:09:54 UTC
07:09:54 KST

WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump announced that the United States has reached what he described as a permanent agreement with Denmark and Greenland, granting Washington sweeping and indefinite security rights in Greenland, including the ability to expand its military presence and prevent adversaries from establishing bases, deploying forces, or making sensitive investments there.
Trump said the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” while fully addressing what he described as longstanding American concerns in the strategically important territory.
“There will be NO COST to the United States!” Trump wrote in announcing the agreement.
“At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America,” he said.
Trump also said that under the agreement, no US adversary would be permitted to establish a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without express written American approval.
“For over 100 years, Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but NONE of them were able to do anything about it,” Trump said. “I am proud to be the President that permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation.”
He described the arrangement as an “Infinite Life” agreement, declaring that “there is no end.”
Permanent access, bases, and overflight rights
A US State Department official provided additional details on the agreement, describing it as an unprecedented arrangement that permanently guarantees US security interests in the Arctic at no cost to the American taxpayer.
According to the official, the deal gives the United States permanent security control over Greenland and ensures that the territory will remain part of what Washington describes as the strategic defense area of North America.
The agreement explicitly guarantees the United States “the complete ability to do what it deems is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the American continent,” the official said.
Those authorities include permanent access, basing and overflight rights.
The agreement also allows the US military to increase the number of bases in Greenland as necessary, according to the State Department official.
Trump said the United States would “immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” adding that Washington would work with the people of Greenland on development and construction.
“This solution is a great one for the United States of America, Denmark, Greenland, and all of our Allies,” Trump said.
Non-NATO countries prohibited from building bases in Greenland
The State Department official said the agreement explicitly prohibits any non-NATO country from building a military base in Greenland or maintaining a troop presence there.
The official contrasted that with what the administration described as the previous status quo, under which countries outside NATO could potentially have been allowed to establish military facilities or send forces to Greenland.
The official singled out China and Russia, saying the agreement guarantees that neither country can establish a base in Greenland or deploy troops there.
It also creates mechanisms designed to prevent adversaries from investing in sensitive sectors.
According to the official, only the United States and its allies will be able to make sensitive investments in Greenland under the agreement, replacing what the administration described as a previous system under which adversaries could invest in sensitive areas without investment screening.
The deal, the official said, is intended to remain fully in force even if Greenland one day becomes a fully independent country.
Rubio: ‘A huge win’
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the agreement “a huge win for the United States and the American people.”
“Thanks to President Trump’s vision and leadership, this historic agreement permanently guarantees US security interests in the Arctic at zero cost to the US taxpayer,” Rubio said.
“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” he added.
Rubio said the agreement “permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland.”
Trump framed the deal in similarly sweeping terms, calling it “a dream come true for the United States of America” and describing it as “very important, historic, and special.”
“We look forward to working with the wonderful people of Denmark and Greenland toward a magnificent future with respect to this large, and highly strategic, parcel of land,” Trump said. “We will be very protective of it.”

Trump says deal with Denmark gives US ‘permanent control’ over Greenland
Denmark and Greenland plan to sign a US defence pact next week, pending approval from both parliaments.
United States President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington has entered into an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that gives the US “permanent control over security and all other needs”.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said, “At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the US will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland”.

Screen time isn’t linked to language delays in autistic children, large U.S. study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:00:57 UTC
07:00:57 KST

A recent study suggests that reading books together at home is associated with better language abilities in young autistic children. The research provides evidence that this shared reading time helps explain why children from higher-income families tend to have stronger communication skills, but finds that screen time does not have a negative impact on these abilities. The findings were published in Autism Research.
Language skills vary widely among children on the autism spectrum. Autism is a developmental condition characterized by differences in social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviors. Some autistic children experience challenges producing or understanding spoken language, whereas others develop abilities similar to or exceeding those of their neurotypical peers. To understand this variation, scientists are increasingly looking at environmental influences that shape early development.
Human development is shaped by different layers of a child’s environment. Broad, distant factors include a family’s socioeconomic status, which generally refers to household income and the parents’ education levels. Closer, everyday factors include the specific activities a child experiences at home, such as shared book reading and screen time. Shared book reading involves an adult caregiver looking at and reading a story with a child, encouraging them to actively participate.
Screen time refers to the hours a child spends in front of televisions, tablets, computers, or smartphones. In the general population, researchers have observed that reading together provides benefits for communication skills. For example, a 2026 study of early childhood development indicated that interactive home literacy routines, like reading books and discussing past events, directly promote language growth over time.
However, reading with an autistic child might look different. In fact, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that autistic children tend to focus their attention differently during shared reading than neurotypical children, looking less at the reader’s face and more at background objects. Because autistic children might engage with their environment in unique ways, scientists wanted to see if the typical patterns seen in other children hold true for them.
“Children with autism are likely to experience language delays and other challenges using and/or understanding spoken language that emerge early in childhood and sometimes persist into adulthood,” said lead author Meredith Pecukonis, an assistant professor in the Department of Psychology at Smith College and director of the Autism & Neurodevelopment (AND) Lab. “Identifying how certain aspects of the home environment relate to language abilities in autistic children is an important first step towards understanding how children’s experiences at home are shaping their language development, and developing interventions that lead to stronger language outcomes for autistic children.”
“Prior to publication of our study, only three studies had looked at the association between screen time and language abilities in autistic children,” Pecukonis told PsyPost. “All of these studies were conducted in China, and therefore no studies had been done in the U.S. on this topic. This gap in the literature was surprising to us, given that several studies have linked excessive screen time to language delays in neurotypical children, and autistic children engage in more screen time than their neurotypical peers.”
To address this gap, the researchers aimed to map out how socioeconomic status, reading habits, and screen use connect to language development. They wanted to see if the broader impact of a family’s income and education might operate through the daily routines children experience at home. To investigate this, the researchers analyzed data from the National Survey of Children’s Health collected between 2018 and 2022.
They focused on a nationally representative group of 1,217 autistic children living in the United States. The children in the sample were between the ages of two and five. Data was collected through surveys completed by parents or adult caregivers who lived with the children.
The survey assessed socioeconomic status by recording the highest level of parent education and calculating the family’s poverty ratio based on their income. It also tracked daily habits, asking parents how many days per week they read to their child and how many hours per weekday the child spent on electronic devices. To measure language, the researchers looked at both expressive and receptive skills.
Expressive language included abilities like speaking single words, asking questions, and telling a story. Receptive language involved understanding instructions, pointing to objects, and recognizing the beginning sounds of words. The statistical models accounted for both the age and sex of the children.
The results showed that autistic children from households with a higher socioeconomic status tended to have higher expressive and receptive language skills. These children were also read to more often and spent less time using screens. The researchers found a direct association between reading frequency and communication abilities. Autistic children who experienced more shared book reading at home demonstrated better language skills across the board.
When analyzing the connections between these variables, the researchers found that shared book reading partially explained the link between socioeconomic status and language skills. This suggests that children from higher-income families experience more frequent shared reading, which in turn helps build their communication abilities. The daily habit of reading acts as a bridge connecting a family’s broader resources to a child’s specific developmental gains.
“Effect sizes are small, meaning that the environment has a small yet significant impact on language development in autism,” Pecukonis said. “Parents raising children in lower SES households may have less time and energy to devote to shared book reading if they are working multiple jobs to pay their bills. Lower SES households may also have reduced access to books in the home.”
“If we want to support autistic children’s language development, we need to acknowledge that children are shaped by various aspects of their environments,” she continued. While some aspects can be addressed through direct family interventions, she noted that others “will likely require systemic change through public policy (e.g., providing greater financial support and services to lower SES families).”
The study found that screen time was not statistically associated with expressive or receptive language skills in autistic children. This means that the amount of time these children spent on devices did not predict better or worse communication abilities. This lack of an association stood out to the researchers, as previous studies of neurotypical children frequently link heavy screen use to developmental delays.
“We were really surprised that the association between amount of screen time and children’s language abilities was non-significant,” Pecukonis said. “This contradicts with what has been reported in the literature on neurotypical children.”
“The non-significant association between screen time and language abilities doesn’t suggest that screen time is ‘good’ or ‘bad’ for autistic children… it just shows that there is no association,” she added.
The results are in tension with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which found that replacing shared reading with screen time was linked to lower developmental scores. However, that earlier study looked at neurotypical preschoolers, whereas the new study focused exclusively on autistic children. Similarly, a 2024 study linked higher screen time to poorer language skills in the general population, which contrasts with the neutral effect observed here for autistic children.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study relied on parent surveys, which can sometimes be subject to reporting biases, such as overestimating reading time or underestimating screen use. The data also captured a single snapshot in time rather than tracking the children over many years. Because of this, it is not possible to declare that reading directly causes better language skills in this group.
“We only looked at two household activities (shared book reading and screen time) as our measures of the environment when in reality there are probably hundreds, if not thousands, of other aspects of the environment that are shaping language development in autism that we just didn’t measure here,” Pecukonis explained.
“The purpose of this work isn’t to ‘blame’ parents for their children’s language delays, but rather to document trends, show that the environment does matter for language development, and find ways to support autistic children through modifications to their environment,” she emphasized. “Our hope is that these findings will ultimately help autistic children and their families by showing that there is a need for greater support for those from lower SES households.”
The study also measured the sheer quantity of screen time and reading without looking at the quality of those activities. It is entirely possible that autistic children with stronger language skills are more likely to request story time, leading to more frequent reading sessions. Future studies could use direct observation to see how the types of digital media and the specific reading strategies parents use shape language development.
“We just applied for funding to run a longitudinal study to see how screen time measured early in development relates to language abilities measured later in development,” Pecukonis noted. “This study will also measure both the quantity and quality of screen time.”
The study, “Socioeconomic Status and Quantity of Shared Book Reading, But Not Screen Time, are Positively Associated With Language Skills in a Nationally Representative Sample of Autistic Children,” was authored by M. Pecukonis and A. Geffin.

🔴 Greenland, Denmark say they expect to sign deal with the US on the sidelines of UN General Assembly
Unknown

Trump says US, Denmark reach deal to expand military presence in Greenland
US President Donald Trump said on Friday he had reached a deal with Denmark to expand the US military presence in Greenland, while respecting Danish and Greenlandic sovereignty. Denmark said the agreement would be signed next week during the UN General Assembly but still requires parliamentary approval.
President Donald Trump said Friday he has a deal with Denmark to bolster the US military presence in Greenland after months of threatening to take island by force from the NATO ally.
Trump in a social media post announcing the deal said the agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns.”
He added that with the agreement his administration would “immediately” begin the process of developing a larger military presence on the mineral-rich Danish territory.
The office of Denmark's prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said the deal will be signed by three governments next week during the United Nations General Assembly, but parliamentary action is still needed by the Danish and Greenland governments before it can be enforced.
In a statement she said “the agreement recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity” of Greenland and Denmark and upholds both people's right "to self-determination.”
Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the emerging deal benefits all three governments and “recognizes Greenland’s interests and our place in the international cooperation.”
With his return to the White House last year, Trump called on Denmark to sell the island to the United States, while insisting that Greenland is crucial for US security. He pointedly wouldn't rule out taking the island by military force, even though Denmark is a NATO ally of the US.
Denmark and Greenland repeatedly said the island is not for sale and condemned reports of the US gathering intelligence there. The US push for Greenland is also opposed by Russia and much of Europe.
Read moreLeaders urge EU to expand Arctic presence amid Russia 'threat'
But Trump in his social media post Friday suggested an understanding may been reached that could bring an end to what was viewed as an existential crisis by Denmark.
“We look forward to working with the wonderful people of Denmark and Greenland toward a magnificent future with respect to this large, and highly strategic, parcel of land,” Trump said in his post. “We will be very protective of it!”
Trump had raised concerns that Russia and China had become more active in the Arctic, making the need for the US to take control of Greenland necessary.
But the agreement bans any non-NATO base in Greenland, limits adversaries from being able to make investments in Greenland and guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, according to a State Department official who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio cheered the statement as a “historic deal” and “huge win” for the United States.
“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” Rubio said. “This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland.”
Despite Trump's repeated aggressive comments toward Denmark about Greenland, Danish officials had repeatedly made clear that they stood ready to work with the US to expand the American military presence and strengthen US commercial interests in Greenland.
Still, Trump’s repeated demands for Greenland and threats to take it by force rattled the NATO alliance and discomfited European allies, said Imran Bayoumi, an associate director at the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security.
“I think Americans really underestimate how damaging it was for the image of the United States in Europe,” he said. “I think Greenlanders, Danes, Europeans saw this as a real attack on their sovereignty, and it’s going to take a lot of work to repair.”
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

US warns allies of missile delivery delays due to shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:45:36 UTC
06:45:36 KST

US warns allies of missile delivery delays due to shortage
The US has warned allies to expect delays of as much as five years in key weapons deliveries as it rebuilds its own depleted munitions stocks.
Multiple European nations are expecting deliveries of key missile and air defence capabilities to be pushed back as a result of the US military exhausting its own arsenal in the Iran war, officials said.
Germany has asked the US to speed up delivery of the long-range Tomahawk cruise missile and the ground-based Typhon launcher, but depleted US stocks of the powerful weapon means its manufacturer, RTX Corp’s Raytheon, is unlikely to fulfil the order in the next five years.
Two other officials said some Eastern European nations also reliant on US weapons systems have experienced delays since soon after the US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb 28.
The Defense Department didn’t immediately return a call seeking comment.
The Pentagon’s decision to prioritise its own stockpiles is also straining Ukraine’s push for the US to send it more Patriot air defence interceptors ahead of what is expected to be a difficult winter for the war-torn nation. The issue of Ukraine’s badly needed air defense will be a key topic at next week’s United Nations meetings in New York.
President Donald Trump earlier this week told reporters that he’s talking to Ukraine about either sending them a “far less sophisticated version” of the Patriot system, or granting licences for Europeans to build the weapons.
The US is estimated to have used more than half of its most advanced Patriot missile variants, a third of its Tomahawk missiles and almost half of its precision strike missiles and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, interceptors in Iran. The Congressional Budget Office said the US had probably used as much as two-thirds of its inventory of missile defence interceptors since June 2025.
The military fired so many munitions at Iranian targets during the first few months of the war that it “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” Pentagon officials acknowledged to its inspector general.
Officials are now working to stockpile critical components and selected munitions, as well as streamline production lead times, the watchdog office said in a report released this week.
Defence firms are ramping up production, with Lockheed Martin Corp working to increase annual capacity from around 600 to 2,000 of the most advanced PAC-3 MSE, or Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement.
The stockpile shortages aren’t just impacting the US and Europe. In April the US told Japan its Tomahawk deliveries would be delayed by as much as two years. Saudi Arabia has also urged allies, including the US, to provide military support to help counter attacks from the Houthis in Yemen. Washington has not said if it will provide extra assistance.
Still, the US continues to deliver weapons bought by European allies for Ukraine through NATO and European Union initiatives, the people said.
Europe’s main concern is that the US continues to provide Ukraine with battlefield support.
European leaders plan to lobby Trump on providing Ukraine with more Patriots next week as world leaders attend United Nations meetings. EU officials also hope to push the US to grant European nations licences to build their own Patriots that could eventually be provided to Kyiv. BLOOMBERG

How a New Trump Administration Rule Could Restrict Access to Green Cards—and Confront Immigrants With a Tough Choice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:35:45 UTC
06:35:45 KST

President Donald Trump’s Administration is rolling out a new rule that experts predict will make it more difficult for immigrants to get green cards if they access public assistance programs, such as Medicaid and food stamps—and could deter those hoping to obtain the status from enrolling in public benefits.
The rule, which goes into effect on Friday, updates a policy dating back to the 19th century that the U.S. has long used to prohibit immigrants who are believed to be likely to become a “public charge” from getting green cards.
Trump’s Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has argued that the change “is restoring the basic principle that immigrants must be able to support themselves,” adding that it is “reaffirming the requirement of self-reliance, protecting public resources, and ending policies that encouraged dependency on hard-working American taxpayers.”
The rule marks the latest move in Trump’s efforts to sharply restrict both illegal and legal immigration. The President enacted a similar change during his first Administration, but the effort was subjected to court challenges and ultimately rescinded by his successor, Joe Biden.
The new rule has already been challenged in court by a coalition of more than a dozen states, including New York and California. It’s unclear at this point how the ongoing litigation will affect the rollout of the rule.
Here’s what to know about the new rule and how it could affect immigrants.
What is the “public charge” rule?
With its new policy, the Trump Administration is implementing a change to what’s known as the “public charge” rule, a policy first established under the Immigration Act of 1882. Since then, one factor that the U.S. government has considered when reviewing green card applications is whether the applicant is likely to become dependent on government assistance.
Historically, officials reviewing these types of applications have only taken into account cash benefit programs—for instance, Supplemental Security Income from Social Security—as “public benefits” that could lead to an immigrant being deemed a “public charge” and having their green card application denied. They have usually not deemed non-cash public benefits, such as Medicaid and food stamps, as programs that would disqualify an immigrant from obtaining permanent resident status.
During his first term in the White House, Trump tried to expand the programs that could result in an immigrant being deemed a “public charge,” but a federal judge ruled that the policy had to be vacated, saying it had “numerous unexplained flaws” that made it “arbitrary and capricious.”
When former President Joe Biden was in office, he officially rescinded Trump’s rule and stipulated that non-cash benefits would not result in an immigrant being considered a “public charge.”
How is the Trump Administration’s new policy different from the long-standing “public charge” rule?
In July, the Trump Administration revealed that it was revoking the Biden-era policy and was rolling out a change similar to the one that faced legal challeges during Trump’s first term. Under the new rule, officials reviewing green card applications are able to consider a broader scope of public benefit programs. The Trump Administration has noted that the new “public charge” rule does not apply to some immigrants—for instance, refugees.
The guidance, though, is vague—it doesn’t include a full list of the benefits that can be taken into consideration, saying only that immigration officers will be “using good judgment and discretion” and will be “making individualized, fact-specific public charge inadmissibility determinations, based on a totality of the alien’s circumstances.”
“Now, the officers who are reviewing and adjudicating these cases have much more discretion in how they make that determination—whether they believe the person is likely to become a public charge,” says Melissa Shepard, the legal services director at the Immigrant Defenders Law Center. “The difference now is that it’s a much broader analysis, whereas before it was a little more limited.”
Adriana Cadena, the executive director of the Protecting Immigrant Families Coalition, says she worries that, because the new policy is so broad, it “opens the door for abuses by immigration officials” during the green card application process.
“It’s going from having guidance and clarity and understanding to opening the door to any kinds of programs,” she says.
How could the Trump Administration’s new rule affect immigrants?
Immigration experts say that the new policy could result in more green card applications being rejected, as well as cause many immigrants to delay seeking permanent resident status.
Charles Kuck, an immigration lawyer and former national president of the American immigration Lawyers Association, says that he expects there will be “massive numbers of denials” of green card applications as this new policy is rolled out. He adds that he and his colleagues have heard from some of their clients that they plan to wait until after Trump leaves the White House before filing their green card applications.
People who do not have permanent resident status in the U.S. are not eligible for many public assistance programs, but experts also warn that the new rule could result in immigrants disenrolling from public benefit programs that they or their children are eligible for because they are afraid of potentially harming their chances of obtaining a green card in the future.
Experts are additionally concerned that the Trump Administration’s new rule opens the door to immigration officials taking into account whether a green card applicant’s family member used a public benefit. The new rule stipulates that “if there is evidence in the record the alien’s family members whom the alien is legally obligated to support receive means-tested public benefits based on the alien’s income falling below the designated threshold, DHS would consider that fact.”
Kuck says he fears that this could lead to a situation where, for example, if a green card applicant’s child who is a U.S. citizen receives a public benefit, such as a free school lunch program, that could lead to their parent’s application being denied.
According to Shepard, it’s not yet clear how exactly the new policy will be applied in practice because it is so broad and gives immigration officers “so much discretion.” But she says she believes the change will cause people to be “a lot more cautious” and potentially fearful to access public assistance programs.
Cadena says the new rule is “forcing families to choose between either being able to adjust their status in the future or be able to have access to essential programs like food and child care.”
“In the current environment that we are in, where immigrant family safety is constantly being threatened, immigrant families … want to be able to keep their families together,” Cadena says. “And if keeping their child enrolled in an important program like Medicaid is going to threaten that, then they would more than likely disenroll their children from these programs.”
DHS has previously estimated that the rollout of the “public charge” change could lead to more than 950,000 people disenrolling from or choosing not to enroll in public assistance programs.
The change is the latest action the Trump Administration has taken to restrict immigration, including ramping up efforts to limit several legal pathways to immigration and proposing raising the fees associated with applying for citizenship.
“This is just one small factor or small piece of the entire immigration system, I think, that is under attack,” Shepard says.

Saudi Arabia issues emergency alerts in 7 areas over unspecified threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:19:47 UTC
06:19:47 KST

Mohammad Sio
19 September 2026•Update: 19 September 2026
Saudi civil defense authorities issued emergency alerts Friday in seven areas, warning residents of an unspecified threat and urging them to follow instructions sent through the national early warning platform.
The alerts were issued in Jeddah, Taif, Yanbu, AlUla and Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Abha, according to separate civil defense posts on US social media platform X.
Authorities did not specify the nature of the threat that prompted the warnings or report any casualties or damage.
The civil defense authority later said the danger had passed in all five provinces.
The alerts came a day after Saudi authorities said one person was killed and two others were injured by falling debris from a Houthi drone intercepted over Taif province in the western part of the kingdom.
Saudi authorities have issued similar warnings in recent days in several areas, including Abha and Khamis Mushait, before later announcing that the danger had passed.
On July 20, Yemen’s Houthi group announced what it called a “maritime blockade” on Saudi Arabia before later claiming missile and drone attacks on Saudi vessels and sites.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition supporting neighboring Yemen’s internationally recognized government since March 2015 against the Houthis, who have controlled the capital Sanaa and several provinces since September 2014.
