US and Denmark reach deal on Greenland, Trump says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:18:38 UTC
06:18:38 KST

US and Denmark reach deal on Greenland, Trump says
WASHINGTON - The United States, Denmark and Greenland have entered into an agreement that will see the US develop a significant military presence on the island, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases there, US President Donald Trump said on Sept 18.
In a Truth Social post, the US leader wrote that no US enemies would be able to make sensitive investments on the island without the approval of the United States and that the agreement had no expiry date.
“At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America,” Trump wrote.
“Additionally, from now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.”
Earlier on Sept 18, Reuters exclusively reported that the US and Greenland were closing in on a deal for the island that would result in an increased US military presence, but would stop well short of Trump’s long-held dream of acquiring the island for the United States.
The US already has nearly total overflight and basing rights in Greenland due to a 1951 treaty.
Trump’s announcement suggests he was nonetheless pleased with the outcome of the negotiations, and that he may not revive his territorial claims, at least in the near future. 
He said, without elaborating, that the US would soon be rolling out a large military presence on the island, which already hosts one Space Force base in its remote north-west.
“This is a dream come true for the United States of America,” Trump wrote.
Extent of agreement remains unclear
The Danish prime minister’s office said on Sept 18 that the agreement would strengthen North Atlantic and Arctic security.
Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a statement that the agreement recognised Greenland’s interests and the Arctic island’s place in international cooperation.
“This benefits us all,” he said.
Much remained unclear late on Sept 18, including whether any new US bases would be constructed as a result of the agreement. Trump’s Truth Social posts about negotiations or agreements often lack context or specifics.
Imran Bayoumi, a former Pentagon official now with the Atlantic Council think tank, said it would be new if the US can build bases without the approval of Greenland or Denmark but that largely, “it seems that Washington could have achieved a lot of these objectives through diplomacy and dialogue without straining the broader US-NATO relationship”.
It was also unclear how the agreement would be received in Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark. The island’s residents aspire to independence and have bristled at US attempts to assert hegemony.
In a separate statement, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the deal “permanently and completely” addressed Washington’s national security concerns with respect to the island.
“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defence area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” he wrote.
A State Department official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss specific terms, said the deal prohibits non-NATO countries from building a base in Greenland, and will allow only the US and its allies to make unspecified “sensitive investments”. 
The official said the agreement grants the US permanent access, basing and overflight rights, and would continue to apply even if Greenland becomes independent. REUTERS

Why the Outcome of Russia's First Parliamentary Elections in Years Is All But Assured
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:18:06 UTC
06:18:06 KST

Russia is just one day into three-day elections that will determine the makeup of the lower house of the country’s parliament, the State Duma. But the outcome of the vote has been all but guaranteed since before the first ballots were cast.
The elections, the first parliamentary vote the country has held since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, are widely expected to result in the Kremlin-aligned United Russia party maintaining its overwhelming dominance in the Duma.
The party currently holds 310 of the 450 seats in the chamber, giving it a supermajority and the power to make major legislative decisions without the input of other parties. It needs to keep at least 300 seats to retain that supermajority.
Four other political parties are also expected to be represented in the Duma following the election, all of which generally vote in line with United Russia and support the war in Ukraine. They are the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia, the A Just Russia party, and the New People party.
Democracy watchdogs and foreign governments have denounced Russia’s elections as being neither free nor fair. Russian officials have rejected such claims in the past, saying that the country carries out its voting process in line with the law.
But experts tell TIME that the Russian government exerts its influence in ways that all but predetermine the results of elections and ensure that President Vladimir Putin and United Russia maintain control.
And this year’s vote, says David Szakonyi, an expert on Russia and election fraud who is professor at George Washington University, is “occurring in the most repressive political environment in Russia's post-Soviet history.”
Here's what experts have to say about how the Kremlin ensures elections result in its desired outcome—and why it continues to hold them.
Restricting opposition
The Kremlin uses multiple levers to influence elections on the government level, at the polls, and in daily civilian life, according to Szakonyi.
“Without a doubt, the most powerful tool” in the Kremlin’s arsenal, Szakonyi says, is limiting which candidates appear on the ballot in the first place.
In the case of the ongoing parliamentary vote, the one anti-war party that was registered by the Central Election Commission, the Yabloko party, was prohibited from participating in the election by Russia’s Supreme Court. The high court ordered that the party be removed from the ballot last month in response to a lawsuit from the pro-Kremlin Rodina party that accused the Yabloko party, which has garnered support from young Russians and those opposed to the war in Ukraine, of copyright infringement, receiving foreign funding, and extremism.
Szakoni says that the Kremlin has the ability to “harness the judicial system to pass rulings” such as the Supreme Court’s decision against the Yabloko party, which it uses as a “legal veneer” that shields the influence of Putin’s government over the ballot.
This screening of anti-war and other opposition parties, he says, comes months in advance of elections, creating a list of candidates that includes little or no meaningful opposition at all.
The Kremlin has also labeled opposition figures who oppose the war as “foreign agents,” a designation that prevents them from holding public office. In other instances, opposition leaders and activists such as Alexei Navalny have been prosecuted and imprisoned. Still others have fled the country.
The vote count
Experts tell TIME that the Russian government has also exercised its influence more directly on vote counts to achieve its desired election results.
“Historically,” Szakonyi says, Russian electoral officials have “intervened regularly to deliver votes to the ruling party and take them away from competitors.”
In the past, this was done via “crude ballot box stuffing,” he says; now, he asserts it is also performed by altering the results of online votes.
Online voting is used in more than a third of Russia’s regions, which Szakonyi asserts puts more power in the government’s hands since it eliminates the physical tally represented by paper ballots.
“The way that the electronic votes are being counted is almost completely a black box for the rest of society,” he says.
Regina Smyth, an expert on Russia and authoritarian regimes who is a professor at Indiana University, says that “falsification,” or the practice of altering the number of votes that are counted, occurs at precinct election commissions, of which there are over 90,000, all across Russia, that she says are “mostly staffed by loyalists, and they will simply report false numbers.”
There is also fraud, Smyth alleges, in “mobile voting,” when officials deliver and pick up ballots from people in their homes who are, for example, disabled or ill and unable to vote otherwise.
‘Implicit threat’
On a deeper level, an “implicit threat” stemming from the Russian government sways countless votes each election cycle, Szakonyi contends.
“Many Russian voters do not have the autonomy to cast an independent vote. They work for the state,” he says. He argues that many university students, healthcare workers, and teachers, whose livelihoods depend on state-run organizations, belong to a “block of captive, vulnerable voters” who fear prosecution by the Kremlin more than they value the influence of their ballot.
Voting is also taking place this year in Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine: in Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014, and in the Luhansk, Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
“In the occupied territories of Ukraine, where the elections are being held in these illegally occupied territories, soldiers, heavily armed soldiers, travel from house to house coercing people to vote,” Smyth tells TIME.
A lack of independent election oversight
On top of the various methods the Kremlin allegedly uses to achieve the voting results it wants, there are slim to no oversight mechanisms in place to document election interference in the country.
Golos, which was the only independent election watchdog within Russia, shuttered in 2025 following years of governmental pressure after its chairman was found guilty of working with an "undesirable organization" and imprisoned in a penal colony.
Szakonyi describes Golos’ loss as the “biggest blow toward any type of accountability” for the Kremlin, saying it was “the biggest tool that civil society had to identify, uncover, and publicize the fraud that was basically happening in every single electoral cycle.”
Russia has also refused to invite international election monitors from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), the world’s largest regional security organization, to observe this year’s elections.
Maria Telalian, director of the OSCE’s election-monitoring office, the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, said in a statement last month that the decision not to invite any OSCE monitors was “deeply regrettable, particularly as it continues a pattern of not implementing the commitments that every OSCE participating State has undertaken towards its own citizens and the international community.”
The ongoing vote marks the third nationwide election in Russia to take place without OSCE observation. Russia previously imposed severe limits on OSCE election observation in 2021 that the organization said made monitoring that year’s parliamentary elections in the country impossible. It did not invite the group’s monitors to the 2024 presidential election at all.
So why is Russia holding elections at all?
Despite the results of the parliamentary elections being all but determined, they carry a symbolic weight crucial to Putin’s legitimacy in the public eye and his desire to continue the war against Ukraine, experts tell TIME.
“There's lots of reasons to have elections. First and foremost, the Russian population expects elections,” Szakonyi says. “Putin's legitimacy depends on his ability to win election votes to the presidency and have his ruling party win on a regular interval, and demonstrate that they're popular and that their policies are in demand from the citizenry.”
During an address in which Putin urged Russians to vote days before the elections began, the leader said that “your choice and resolve will show once again that millions of people stand behind our fighters” and that “participating in the elections is our shared contribution to Russia’s victory.”
“This is a way for him to theoretically show that the Russian population is united behind his war and wants to continue fighting, and that Russia has had this referendum and will continue to push harder,” Szakonyi says.

Where thinking beats mugging up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:06:54 UTC
06:06:54 KST

(Top row, R-L): AM/NS India CSR head Vikas Yadvendu, Uttar Pradesh deputy CM Brajesh Pathak, Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka, and DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar with some of the winners of Times Critical Thinking Championship in Delhi
(Top row, R-L): AM/NS India CSR head Vikas Yadvendu, Uttar Pradesh deputy CM Brajesh Pathak, Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka, and DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar with some of the winners of Times Critical Thinking Championship in Delhi
(Top row, R-L): AM/NS India CSR head Vikas Yadvendu, Uttar Pradesh deputy CM Brajesh Pathak, Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka, and DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar with some of the winners of Times Critical Thinking Championship in Delhi
NEW DELHI: Hands hovered over buzzers as students listened intently to each question, ready to hit the button before their competitors. Every few moments, a buzzer broke the silence and another answer was put to the test. But points were not won through recall alone, as the questions pushed students to reason, judge, analyse and think beyond the obvious.The questions came thick and fast. "If a meteor crashes on the Moon and an astronaut is 1,000km away, when will they hear the sound?" A student quickly buzzed in with the answer: they wouldn't - sound cannot travel through the vacuum of space.Then came a word puzzle: "Which word becomes shorter when you add two letters to it?" Buzzers went off again. The answer was "short" - add "er" and it becomes "shorter".That was the scene at the auditorium of DPS RK Puram on Friday as students went head to head in the semi-final and final rounds of the AM/NS India Times Critical Thinking Championship 2026, conceived and conducted by Times Foundation. The Nav Ratna prize distribution ceremony was held soon after, during which chief guest Brajesh Pathak, deputy chief minister of Uttar Pradesh, handed over certificates to the winners.
Pathak, who spoke of the "immense effort" involved in reaching so many schools and students, urged participants to never stop asking questions. "Human beings are not machines meant to follow the same routine. We have the ability to think, understand and show the world a new direction," he said.The championship has been designed to encourage students to move beyond rote memorisation and develop the ability to question, analyse information and arrive at conclusions independently. The students who reached Friday's rounds had already made their way through a much larger field. From thousands of participants, 140 were shortlisted for written and oral assessments. The field was then narrowed to 36 students for the buzzer rounds, with nine winners emerging. The gathering included their parents, DPS teachers and other representatives."Critical thinking is very important for the younger generation because students need to learn to ask questions, reason and analyse before reaching conclusions. We see this initiative not as a one-off event but as a long-term process," said Vikas Yadvendu, head, CSR, AM/NS India.Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka said, "Critical thinking is the need of the hour. With young people exposed to so much information through social media, they can sometimes lose sight of their own judgement or be misled. So, such initiatives are important."DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar said, "This initiative encourages children to think, reason and analyse. Over 10 lakh students have participated across languages, and next year, we aim to reach one crore."Over the past six months, TCTC reached more than one million students from over 20,000 schools, spanning Grades III to XII across 28 states and eight Union Territories, with the programme conducted in 14 languages.
But amid those numbers were students from different corners of the country, each with their own interpretation of what it meant to think critically.Bhanvi, a Class V student from Kerala, summed it up simply: "Critical thinking is not agreeing with something just because everyone thinks it is right. Don't always listen to others. Use your own mind." Aaryahi Hazarika, a Class IV student from Assam, said it helped people find solutions carefully, while Sarah from Kashmir described it as the ability to "think out of the box". Divisha, a Class IV student of DPS East of Kailash, described it as "finding solutions by thinking with our own minds" rather than blindly following others.
Meghna Dhulia is an Assistant News Editor at The Times of India, bringing over a decade of experience in journalism. She specialises in education reporting, covering both foundational and higher education with a clear, insightful lens. Her work sheds light on critical issues shaping the future—ranging from policy impact and systemic challenges to compelling human stories from the field. Her experience also extends to the news desk, where she has overseen editorial workflows, ensuring readers receive balanced, reliable and impactful news.

Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story Has Nothing New to Say About Female Rage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:06:45 UTC
06:06:45 KST

This article discusses the full season of Netflix’s Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story
Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story is about female rage and repression. That isn’t my personal interpretation of the latest installment of Ian Brennan and Ryan Murphy’s Netflix true-crime anthology. It’s the talking point that the show’s makers have been leading with, in publicity materials and in multiple interviews. These are fine themes for the first season of Monster with a female subject, even if they’re not exactly unique within a post-Big-Little-Lies, #MeToo-informed TV landscape where so many dramas aimed at women double as amplifiers for gendered frustrations. The well of misogyny isn’t in danger of running dry anytime soon. But if we must keep diving into it, each descent should at least leave us with some new insight or nuance.
Lizzie Borden, now streaming, fails to clear even that bar. Perhaps the least historically accurate Monster yet—and that’s saying something—the season uses the infamous tale of a Fall River, Mass. woman who probably hacked her wealthy father and stepmother to death with an axe in 1892 as a conduit to just about every plague on womankind you can imagine, past, present, and perennial. Rape. Domestic violence. Pregnancy and childbirth. Housework. Menstrual maladies. Pressure to marry. The premium put on physical beauty. The perils of sex work. Confinement in the home and subjugation to male relatives. By tying together Lizzie’s story with the legends of supposed forerunner Elizabeth Báthory and descendent Aileen Wuornos, Brennan, who wrote every episode, suggests a simplistic kinship between all female killers.
There’s no use fretting over the extremely purposeful anachronisms and inaccuracies in this retelling, which plays as fast and loose with the Borden family as that classic nursery rhyme. With 26-year-old Ella Beatty starring as a dreamy, blank-screen Lizzie, who ages from 32 to her 60s by the end of the season, and Charlie Hunnam and Rebecca Hall cast as parents who were really a couple of decades the actors’ seniors, everyone is much younger and prettier than their real-life counterparts. And more shocking, in some ways, than the hyperspeed double murder reenactment that opens the premiere, is what immediately follows it: a flashback to four months earlier, when Lizzie scares off a suitor by passing a bucket of menstrual blood on the white sofa where they’re sitting. As it turns out, what the fictionalized Bordens refer to as her “lady time” had some relevance to the actual case. But Lizzie Borden is such a massive remix, mingling facts with half-truths and rumors and fabrications, it barely matters which detail is which.
Because its source material is not especially extensive—one double homicide, as opposed to the lengthy and lurid sagas of most past Monster subjects—the show is forced to stretch. The series is padded with Fall River horror scenes that either never happened (the oyster poisoning that leads to so much operatic barfing) or didn’t transpire remotely the way they’re shown (the murder of Bertha Manchester, played by Linda Reiter). Brennan also adds queer love to Lizzie’s life, in the form of the family’s maid, Bridget Sullivan, who they really did call Maggie, after a former servant. He is far from the first to investigate this angle; the 2018 film Lizzie, to take just one example, is also built around a romance, between Chloë Sevigny’s Lizzie and Kristen Stewart’s Bridget.
Monster is, however, the first dramatization to make such imaginative use of the character. Phantom Thread breakout Vicky Krieps, who played ‘Bitch of Buchenwald’ Ilse Koch in Monster’s Ed Gein season, is a conspicuously Germanic Irish maid, with an ahistorical shag haircut dyed a series of shades reminiscent of, by turns, Wuornos and Ziggy Stardust. She has picked up skills in everything from cooking and cleaning to pharmacology in the course of her global travels. It’s no mystery why the awkward, sheltered Lizzie, who craves a bigger life, is enchanted by this glamorous, androgynous outsider. Maggie is easily the best part of the season, thanks in no small part to Krieps’ at once humane and otherworldly performance.
She’s also the unstuck-in-time character who first connects Lizzie to murderesses from other eras. As Maggie reads from a French book about Báthory, a 16th century Hungarian noblewoman said to have killed hundreds of young women and bathed in their blood in pursuit of eternal youth, we see Krieps—with hair and makeup straight out of the goth club—as the so-called Blood Countess. The Runaways’ anthem of teen-girl rebellion “Cherry Bomb” blares. And Lizzie is electrified by the story. She feels a kinship with Báthory. Never mind that killing your cruel parents to free yourself and massacring a village’s worth of peasant girls because La Mer has yet to be invented are about as different as murder motives get. The fact that each woman is acting in response to some form of sexism is, I guess, supposed to bridge that gulf.
It takes almost half the season for the third member of the deadly trio, played by Murphyverse MVP Sarah Paulson, to show up. Often framed as America’s first female serial killer, Wuornos, a Florida sex worker who killed seven johns between 1989 and 1990, is, in this telling, as inspired by Lizzie as Lizzie is by Báthory. Her presence, and her unsuccessful attempt to claim in court that she acted in self-defense against rape, allows the show to take on—and force us to watch—sexual violence. I’m not sure it needed to be shoehorned into the rare true-crime drama where it doesn’t have an obvious place. Brennan also connects Aileen’s well-documented queerness with the speculative relationship between Lizzie and Maggie. On a pilgrimage to the Borden home, now a bed and breakfast, Aileen and her girlfriend (Jessie Lee) have public sex. A fantasy sequence has the two couples dancing side-by-side in Lizzie’s sacred garden shed. But it’s never clear what Monster is trying to say about lesbians and murder, and this is a case where ambiguity leaves space to insert some pretty dark assumptions.
The outcomes for each of the three female killers are as different as their motivations. Lizzie is acquitted and buys a mansion with her inheritance, presumably because sexist men can’t conceive of a woman committing such physical murders—and because she learns to correctly perform femininity, crying and fainting at appropriate moments, during the trial. Despite wrenching testimony, coarse, unfeminine Aileen is convicted and executed. This might lead you to conclude that privilege and falling in line with patriarchal expectations are what it takes for a woman to get away with murder. But then there’s the rich, powerful, and apparently quite appearance-obsessed Báthory. Our last glimpse of the countess is as a rotting corpse, bricked up in her castle for her sins. So what is really being said here?
Not much, as far as I can tell. Lizzie Borden certainly makes a strong case that women have always been repressed, that rage is the obvious product of that repression, and that liberation is the only antidote. (Of course we get a scene in the finale where Lizzie celebrates suffrage.) But if you didn’t know that, it’s probably also news to you that water is wet and the pope is Catholic. The show’s obsession with women’s bodies as the sites of unending horrors reminds me of House of the Dragon’s repeated depictions of traumatic childbirth. It’s as though viewers are expected to go in completely ignorant of basic hardships afflicting half the human population and must see them reproduced over and over again in gory detail to be enlightened, much less empathetic. And in that case, I suppose it’s also necessary to render interchangeable three notorious women defined by actions rooted in a near-universal form of rage.
But theirs are old stories, already told and retold in every conceivable media, and often, effectively, by women. Wuornos was, of course, most famously portrayed by Charlize Theron, in writer-director Patty Jenkins’ career-making, Oscar-winning 2003 film also titled Monster. Isabelle Huppert stars as Báthory in The Blood Countess, a new feature by German experimental cinema legend Ulrike Ottinger, which is earning praise on the festival circuit for its strangeness and sense of humor. Meanwhile, on TV, creator Liz Meriwether just gave us Furious—another story of female rage, female repression, and yes, even a (fictional) female serial killer. While Krieps is mesmerizing in Monster and frequent Murphy production designer Matthew Flood Ferguson has outdone himself with lavishly suffocating Gilded Age interiors, Furious is the superior show because it takes “being a woman is hard” as the given it is rather than as the endpoint of many repetitive episodes. It has dark, lived-in comedy and real stakes, posing the question of what can realistically be done about systemic misogyny and the anger over it that stains women’s lives.
“All your books are written by men,” Maggie scolds Lizzie in Monster’s season premiere. When you consider how heavily male the creative team behind Lizzie Borden is (executive producer Max Winkler directed six episodes and Sarah Adina Smith, two), this kind of has to be a self-aware line. But whether it’s intended as a wry apology or a small joke, I couldn’t tell you.

Farmers warn of food security impact from visa changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:06:38 UTC
06:06:38 KST

Farmers fear Working Holiday Maker visa changes will cause worker shortages and food insecurity
In short:
The federal government has outlined an overhaul of the Working Holiday Maker visa system, capping the number of renewed applications after one year in the country.
The agricultural industry warns this could limit production and negatively impact Australia's food security.
Farmers fear the changes could lead to worker shortages during peak harvest seasons.
Agricultural industries warn changes to working holiday visa migration policy could threaten crops and Australia's food security.
On Thursday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke outlined Labor's migration policy, including an overhaul of the Working Holiday Maker visa system.
Farmers are coming into the Christmas harvest of popular fruits such as mangoes, lychees, berries and cherries, as well as the summer grain season.
While the industry is concerned they will not be able to find enough workers to pick crops to get them to market, the "one bright light" is that agriculture will be added to the skilled worker visa list.
Less incentive to go bush
Across the country, agriculture employs more than 250,000 workers each year according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Figures from the 2021 census showed people from cultural and linguistically diverse backgrounds made up 13 per cent of the agricultural workforce.
Backpackers on Working Holiday Maker visas wanting to stay for another year need to work 88 days in regional or remote parts of Australia.
Under the changes, visa holders would also have to enter a ballot, with the number of places capped at 45,000 — down from the 57,000 who qualified this year.
The number of places will be capped further to 5,000 for those seeking a third year, down from 31,000 this year.
Queensland Farmers' Federation chief executive Kylie Porter feared a lottery-type system would not be attractive to visa holders.
"What we're doing is we're placing at risk Australia's food security over an issue which could be resolved in a way that's far more amenable to those regional and rural communities across Australia," she said.
"Christmas harvest periods are intense, and we absolutely rely on that workforce to be able to complete those harvests."
Kaya Barry is a senior lecturer at Griffith University who received an Australian Research Council fellowship to explore the contributions of seasonal migrants in Queensland's agricultural industry.
Dr Barry said larger farms secured most of their workers through the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme and Labor's policy change would have a greater impact on smaller operations.
"For smaller farms, particularly the family-run stuff … they can't guarantee the seasonal work is there year-round, and that's where the backpackers have filled those shortages," she said.
Dr Barry said PALM workers would not be able to replace backpacker labour on farms.
"It's really important to have highly mobile workers who are willing to just come and do two or three weeks and then move on to the next place and follow that harvest trail around the country," she said.
Dr Barry said it was also not feasible to rely on an Australian workforce.
"We don't have enough people living in regional and rural Australia to do all that work."
Industry needs workers now
Prior to Labor's policy announcement, the federal government had paused working holiday visa applications coming from 24 out of 29 countries.
Mr Burke said the time frame for processing these visas would now take three months; previously, it had taken days.
Head of Citrus Australia, Nathan Hancock, said the current backlog of processing applications is putting pressure on all industries.
"People have been waiting three to four months for their applications to be approved. In many of these industries, harvest is about to start in two weeks," he said.
"This just creates more angst and more concern for all of those industries that would normally rely on workers at this time."
With berry harvest underway in New South Wales and gearing up in Victoria and Tasmania, Berries Australia CEO Rachel Mackenzie warned workforce shortages could lead to wasted crops.
"You may have periods where you need quite a lot more workers than other periods … we need those backpackers to assist with surge capacity and be a complement to the existing PALM workers," she said.
"For some growers [fewer workers] might mean that they have to finish their season early, it may mean that they can't get their crops picked in time."
'One bright light'
The industry has welcomed the addition of agriculture to the skilled worker visa, with Mr Hancock calling it the "one bright light in all of this".
"It is positive to see that agriculture will be added to the [skilled worker] visa," he said.
But Mr Hancock is calling for more clarity on these changes, including specifically which types of workers will be added to the skilled worker visa.
"Hopefully that does, in my case, go down to horticulture … fingers crossed."

Germany receives first F-35 jet from US as NATO boosts military spending
Germany received the first of nearly three dozen F-35 stealth warplanes it ordered four years ago from Lockheed Martin.
Germany has received its first F-35A Lightning II fighter jet, as the country accelerates a major military buildup and increases defence spending amid a broader push by European NATO members to strengthen their armed forces.
The delivery on Friday is part of Germany’s effort to fulfil NATO nuclear-sharing duties and modernise its military after decades of relatively low defence spending.
Lockheed Martin formally presented the aircraft to the German government during a ceremony at its production facility in Fort Worth, Texas, attended by German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius.
“This is the beginning of a new era for the German Air Force: the new F-35A fighter jet is the world’s most advanced combat aircraft,” Pistorius said in a statement. “It is characterised by its stealth capabilities, close integration with other platforms, and exceptionally powerful sensor technology.”
Germany ordered 35 F-35As in 2022, the year Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. The aircraft are intended to replace Germany’s ageing Tornado fleet.
The Trump administration has long pressured Europe to spend more on defence, allowing Washington to focus on other challenges such as countering China.
European countries, including Germany, are ramping up military budgets as a result, agreeing in 2025 to Trump’s demand to devote five percent of GDP to security-related spending by 2035.

US Treasury’s Bessent plans to discuss AI and rare earths with China’s He, source says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:59:25 UTC
05:59:25 KST

US Treasury’s Bessent plans to discuss AI and rare earths with China’s He: Source
- US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will discuss AI, trade, rare earths, and economic issues with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng ahead of the Trump-Xi summit.
- The talks will address AI safety, tariff truce extension, and improving rare-earth mineral flows amid ongoing US-China trade tensions.
- Expectations for major deals are low; discussions focus on managing relations and ensuring commitments from the tariff truce are upheld.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent plans to discuss AI, trade, rare earths and economic issues when he meets with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York City this weekend, according to a source familiar with his plans.
The discussions are significant because the US and China are the two major forces driving development of advanced AI tools and the global adoption of the technology. Rare earths play a crucial role in the manufacturing of technology.
Bessent and He will meet ahead of a summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sept 24 in Washington.
The Associated Press first reported the US plans.
Bessent said in a statement that he expects the discussions to cover “both open- and closed-weight models.” Open-weight models are AI systems with publicly accessible core elements. Users can download and fine-tune them for specific tasks.
Chinese open-weight models are becoming more popular with US companies because they can be cheaper than so-called closed-weight AI tools, such as those developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and other US companies.
Chinese AI models have even been used by the US government. Reuters reported on Sept 17 that a US government website employed an AI model from a Chinese company to allow users to search proposed federal regulations even though the FBI accused the model’s developer, Alibaba, of “malicious” copying of Anthropic’s technology.
“The United States remains the leader in AI. And we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems,” Bessent said in his statement regarding the China talks.
The Treasury secretary has recently called for the US and China to agree on AI “guardrails” aimed at keeping powerful models out of the hands of malign non-state actors.
Questioned on AI safety at a House of Representatives Financial Services Committee hearing on Sept 15, he said it was up to US AI firms to decide whether to slow down their development, but argued they should be held liable for what they build and generate as a safety measure.
Broad range of discussions
Details about the meetings in New York, which are expected to explore possible areas for Trump and Xi to agree on, have been scant.
The source said that the meetings could extend to Sept 21 on a technical or “working” level, and that the agenda would stay flexible “to allow for substantive discussion across the range of relevant issues”.
Other key topics for Bessent and He to discuss include potential extension of a tariff truce that expires on Nov 10, and improving flows of Chinese-produced rare-earth magnets and critical minerals that China had severely curtailed in 2025.
The truce capped tariffs imposed during Trump’s second term in office at about 20 per cent. The Supreme Court later struck down Trump’s tariffs invoked under a national emergencies law, but his administration has been rebuilding them under new authorities.
The US has restored a 12.5 per cent tariff on Chinese goods over forced labour allegations and is finalising a separate tariff investigation aimed at curbing excess industrial capacity that it says is rampant in China.
At a Trump-Xi meeting in May, China pledged to increase purchases of US agriculture products and at least 200 Boeing aircraft, but details on those transactions have yet to emerge.
With only short preparation time, expectations for Bessent and He to arrange major new deals from the Trump-Xi summit are low, said Wendy Cutler, policy director for the Asia Society in Washington, adding that both sides have an interest in keeping trade tensions from flaring up again.
“If anything, it’s an exercise in kind of managing the relationship and ensuring that the elements in the truce are actually being lived up to,” Cutler said.
Also in May, the US and China agreed to launch discussions to reduce tariffs for non-strategic goods under a so-called “Board of Trade” mechanism along with a similar forum to deal with specific investment issues.
While the Trump administration has tightened restrictions on American companies investing in some industries in China, Reuters reported on Sept 18 that it is working on rules that would likely allow US pharmaceutical firms to invest in promising Chinese drugs and strike licensing deals for them. “We are here with great responsibility to give the Venezuelan people a consolidation of a path toward democracy,” opposition negotiator Dinorah Figuera said ahead of the talks.

UK court clears woman of voicing support for Hamas in university speech

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18

UK court clears woman of voicing support for Hamas in university speech
Sarah Cotte said her comments were not in support of Hamas, but in support of Palestinians’ right to resist.
A London court has cleared a British woman of supporting Palestinian group Hamas in a speech she gave outside her university in 2023.
The jury at the Central Criminal Court, more commonly known as the Old Bailey, on Friday found Sarah Cotte, 22, not guilty of expressing support for the group that’s designated a “terrorist” organisation under UK law.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Andy Burnham apology for Labour stance on Gaza: Is UK’s position shifting?
- list 2 of 3The British state has recast protest as terrorism
- list 3 of 3UK charities, protest groups: Israeli ban threat ‘will not intimidate us’
Public prosecutors had alleged that Cotte voiced support for Hamas two days after the group led the deadly attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023.
During a speech she gave outside the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) in London at the time, she expressed “unconditional solidarity” with the Palestinian resistance, the court was told. Prosecutors claimed this was a “thinly veiled reference” to Hamas.
Cotte repeatedly rejected attempts to equate the two, telling the court: “I don’t support Hamas and I have never supported Hamas. I was supporting the right to resist.”
Speaking to Al Jazeera after the verdict on Friday, Cotte said the court’s decision was a “testament to how people are feeling about British support for Zionism”.
“I never condemned the right to armed struggle in Palestine,” Cotte said. “I didn’t let them corner me and make this a conversation about what Zionists want to talk about.”
Instead, she said, “I used it as a platform to talk about what I thought was important, which was the Palestinian struggle, British support for Zionism and our rights as people of conscience.”
Hamas was officially proscribed in its entirety by the UK government in late 2021, when its political wing was also banned. Its military wing, the Qassam Brigades, has been proscribed since 2001. Those found guilty of supporting such groups can face up to 14 years in prison.
On the final day of the week-long trial on Friday, Cotte again denied expressing support for Hamas during her speech at SOAS while she was a student there and argued that she had only expressed support for Palestinians’ “right to resist”.
“I think that the killing of civilians is always a tragedy. At the same time, I don’t think it is a surprise,” she told jurors about her comments regarding Hamas’s October 7 attack.
“I think saying it is understandable and agreeing with it is two different things, so I think it is understandable and could be justified,” she explained.
“I don’t think it’s my role to impose conditions on the Palestinian people and their struggle,” Cotte added.
In comments to Al Jazeera after the verdict, she said: “This victory will re-energise the whole of the solidarity movement … We stand with the Palestinian people and their right to be agents in their struggle for freedom.”
Responding to the not guilty verdict, Anas Mustapha, head of Public Advocacy at CAGE International, said the ruling showed that “ordinary people will not accept the criminalisation of speech in support of the Palestinian right to resist occupation.”
“Sarah Cotte has been found not guilty, and we are delighted for her, her family, and everyone who stood alongside her through more than two and a half years of investigation and court proceedings,” Mustapha said.
Cotte gave the speech on October 9, 2023. She was arrested over it on January 31, 2024. An earlier trial found her not guilty of a second charge of expressing support for Hamas in a WhatsApp group chat.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Friday that his country needs to expand and update its aircraft fleet, as well as domestic airport infrastructure.
Speaking via videoconference at a signing ceremony for an agreement between Russian flag carrier Aeroflot and state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec for 90 MC-21 aircraft, Putin said projects to build new terminal buildings and upgrade airfield and border infrastructure have been successfully completed in several regions.
Putin said a developed aviation network is crucial for Russia to connect its territories and ensure accessibility to remote regions, including those in the Arctic, Siberia, and the Far East.
“Naturally, modern airports also provide a boost to regional economies, fostering growth in trade, business activity, and, of course, tourism. They also ensure higher service quality and faster passenger processing.

Putin further said that new terminals have been opened in a number of cities, including Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, Khabarovsk, Magadan, Novosibirsk, and Cheboksary, stating this work is being carried out through a combination of state funding and private sector investment.
“We will continue to provide all necessary support to investors,” Putin went on to say, adding that at least 75 airports in the country are slated for modernization by 2030, or over a third of Russia’s entire airport network.
The president also underlined the need to expand and renew Russia’s aircraft fleet, describing the issue as one of “fundamental importance.”
He called the contract for supplying the 90 MC-21 aircraft to Aeroflot a “highly significant step in this direction,” saying that it will provide a substantial workload for aircraft manufacturers, as well as their suppliers and contractors.
“I expect the contract to be executed strictly in line with the established schedule, without delays or disruptions,” Putin added.
According to Rostec, the delivery of the 90 MC-21 aircraft to Aeroflot is scheduled for the years 2029-2032 and is the largest such contract in the history of Russian civil aviation.
"The agreement includes not only the delivery of the aircraft, but also flight simulators, training for pilots and ground personnel, as well as technical support for the aircraft," it noted.

The US has warned its allies to expect delays of up to five years in deliveries of key weapons as Washington works to replenish munitions stocks depleted during its war with Iran, Bloomberg reported Friday.
Several European countries are facing delays in receiving missile and air defense systems, while Germany has asked Washington to accelerate deliveries of Tomahawk cruise missiles and Typhon launchers. Pentagon officials have acknowledged that heavy weapons use has created strategic inventory shortfalls and exposed production bottlenecks. Defense companies are now increasing output, including Lockheed Martin, which plans to raise annual production of PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors from about 600 to 2,000.
European leaders are expected to press Trump next week for additional Patriot support for Ukraine during meetings at the UN in New York. EU officials also hope to secure US licenses allowing European countries to produce Patriots for Kyiv.

OpenAI’s Sam Altman to brief UN Security Council next week
UNITED NATIONS – OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman will brief the United Nations Security Council next week during the annual gathering of world leaders in New York for the UN General Assembly, an OpenAI spokesperson said on Sept 18.
The 15-member Security Council is due to meet on Sept 23 on artificial intelligence and international security, just weeks after several AI industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the increasingly powerful technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and slip beyond human control.
“Sam Altman will brief an open UN Security Council meeting in person next week,” an OpenAI spokesperson told Reuters.
Altman’s remarks were expected to focus on the need for international coordination and shared safety standards, as well as steps OpenAI is taking to ensure people globally benefit, the spokesperson said.
Diplomats said they also expected high-level presence at the meeting from Anthropic, but that it was yet to be confirmed. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Security Council meeting has been convened by France, which is the president of the body for September, and will be chaired by French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noel Barrot.
In a concept note for the meeting circulated to council members by France and seen by Reuters, it said: “In light of the risk of misuse of this technology for malicious purposes, and drawing on the Council’s existing engagement in this field, France wishes to underline the urgency of action to foster safe and responsible development of artificial intelligence for the benefit of the international community as a whole.”
The UN Security Council, which is charged with maintaining international peace and security, met for the first time on the risks of artificial intelligence in 2023, when China said the technology should not become a “runaway horse” and the United States warned against its use to censor or repress people.
Altman has been warning about the risks well before the current AI boom.
In a 2015 essay titled Machine Intelligence, part 1, he said the “development of superhuman machine intelligence is probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity”.
France, in its concept note, said the meeting aimed to allow participants to “present their analysis of the risks linked to loss of control or the use of the latest AI models to develop, facilitate and conduct actions with an impact on international security and peace”. REUTERS

Russia seizes assets of Nestle, French firms over West’s Ukraine support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:35:45 UTC
05:35:45 KST

Russia seizes assets of Nestle, French firms over West’s Ukraine support
WARSAW - The Russian authorities have seized the businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestle and three French groups, a move the Kremlin defended on Sept 18 as a justified measure against firms representing “unfriendly countries” that back Ukraine.
A decree signed by President Vladimir Putin transferred the Russian operations of Nestle, French retailer Auchan and the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain, now known as Lemana Pro, to a company called LEV Management.
The decree, issued late Sept 17, also covers the Russian subsidiaries of French logistics group FM Logistic.
France late Sept 18 called on the Russian authorities to “reverse this decision”.
Investigative outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe reported that LEV Management was created only at the end of 2025, and is headed by a Russian interior ministry general. It had no known business activity.
It was the latest move by Russia against Western firms in response to a barrage of sanctions over its war against Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
Most Western companies quickly sold their Russian operations and holdings after the Ukraine invasion, or at least isolated them, as sanctions have made trading in most goods difficult.
Others remained, citing concerns for their employees or citizen’s well-being, but often sharply scaling back their operations.
Russia has since made it difficult for firms to leave, requiring presidential authorisation for deals, or seizing the assets outright.
Assets at risk
In a short statement, Nestle said it was “committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees”.
“The company is assessing the situation and its options,” it added.
Nestle has six factories and Russia and employs around 7,000 people, mainly for coffee, pet care, infant nutrition and confectionary products, a spokesperson said.
Jean-Philippe Bertschy of the Swiss investment bank Vontobel said he expected the financial impact to Nestle would be small “given Russia’s limited contribution to group sales”.
He said Russia now accounted for just over one percent of the group’s sales, down from around two percent before the Ukraine war.
It has suspended “the vast majority of sales, non-essential imports, advertising and capital investment”, he said, while continuing to supply essential food items.
“This practice has historically often been a precursor to a forced sale or effective expropriation of operations in the market,” said analysts at the brokerage Jeffries.
“This was the case already for Danone and Carlsberg for example in 2023,” they wrote, estimating that a write-off of Nestle’s Russia business, including money it had not been able to repatriate, could cost the Swiss firm around one billion francs (S$1.5 billion).
Nestle shares dropped 2.6 per cent on the Zurich stock exchange on Sept 18.
Auchan and Leroy Merlin are both controlled by France’s Mulliez family, which also owns the Decathlon sports retailer.
Auchan’s Russian subsidiary said on Sept 18 that it had requested “clarifications” from the authorities over Putin’s decree.
The French foreign and economy ministries said in a joint statement late on Sept 17 that France “condemns” the move, and urged Moscow to go back on its decision.
Auchan’s subsidiary is one of Russia’s main retailers, with 241 stores in the country, including 62 hypermarkets, and over 33,000 employees according to its website.
“Once the corresponding information has been received, we will be able to provide more detailed comments,” Auchan Retail Russia said a statement to Russian news agencies.
The latest seizure echoes a string of other forced asset transfers, including Moscow’s 2023 takeover of Danone’s Russian business, which was later sold to a nephew of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov. AFP

The exhibition brings together six medium- and large-scale paintings made between 2021 and 2026, alongside a screening of the short film ‘Natura Fugit,’ created by Lazkano in collaboration with production companies Dibulitoon and Art Frame. The 22-minute film premiered in 2025 at the San Sebastián International Film Festival. Developed over four years, the project involved nearly 3,000 drawings by Lazkano depicting the melting of the Alpine glacier Mer de Glace. The drawings were assembled into an animated short that extends the artist’s pictorial approach into moving image.
At Basque Luxury Studio, the film is presented alongside six works from ‘The Last Ice,’ a body of work focused on Lazkano’s representation of nature. Five of the works are acrylic paintings on canvas, while the sixth is a pastel and colored-pencil drawing on paper. Together, the pieces examine the landscape as a changing physical environment and question the ways in which nature is approached and used. The paintings depict landscape, reality, and the surrounding environment as spaces undergoing significant change. The works consider a future in which familiar landscapes may no longer exist in their current form, connecting Lazkano’s visual language with wider discussions around human impact on the environment.
‘Azken Natura’ uses visual art to frame environmental change
From the perspective of visual art, ‘Azken Natura’ addresses the relationship between environmental change and the sustainability of human actions. While these issues are commonly discussed through scientific, political, and social frameworks, the exhibition focuses on the communicative and emotional dimensions of the subject. Painting and animation become tools for translating environmental data and physical change into visual forms that can enter public and cultural discussion. The exhibition also considers the role of visual culture during periods of broader change. As new environmental concerns reshape social and cultural perspectives, artists contribute images and visual references through which these shifts can be understood and represented. ‘Azken Natura’ establishes this visual framework through a combination of large-scale painting, drawing, and animation.
‘Azken Natura’ is the eighth exhibition organized by Basque Luxury over the past decade. As part of its program promoting local culture, the company has previously organized solo exhibitions dedicated to Alfredo Bikondoa, Iñigo Manterola, Víctor Goikoetxea, Miguel Balliache, José Zugasti, and Jose Luis Zumeta. The current exhibition presents the work of Jesus Mari Lazkano, one of the prominent contemporary artists on the Basque cultural scene. ‘Azken Natura’ remains open to the public through September 2028.

US appeals court rejects Trump policy allowing swift deportations to third countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:33:26 UTC
05:33:26 KST

US appeals court rejects Trump policy allowing swift deportations to third countries
BOSTON, Massachusetts – A US federal appeals court rejected on Sept 18 a policy adopted by US President Donald Trump’s administration that allows the authorities to rapidly deport migrants to countries other than their own without giving them a chance to raise safety concerns.
Ruling in a case that is likely headed to the Supreme Court, a three-judge panel of the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld a February decision by a lower-court judge that declared the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) policy unlawful.
The ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by migrants subject to deportation orders that has become a key test of what due process protections the government must provide before removing people to countries with which they have no connection.
“This decision confirms that due process and the protections Congress enacted against persecution and torture cannot be circumvented by putting someone on a plane to a country that was never part of their removal proceedings,” Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said
Under Trump, the administration has entered into a series of agreements that have allowed it to send more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, in many cases Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.
The Trump administration is expected to appeal. Earlier in the same case, the administration twice convinced the Supreme Court to lift a preliminary injunction protecting migrants’ due process rights, clearing the way for eight men to be deported to South Sudan.
DHS had no immediate comment.
Under the third-country deportation programme, DHS adopted a policy in March 2025 that would allow migrants to be sent to such countries if immigration authorities have credible diplomatic assurances they will not be persecuted or tortured there.
The policy called for only minimal notice before a migrant could be sent to a third country that had not given the State Department such assurances.
Third country deportations
US District Judge Brian Murphy, an appointee of former US Democratic president Joe Biden, set aside the policy and concluded that it failed to protect migrants’ due process rights and could lead to their swift deportation to unfamiliar and potentially dangerous countries, without notice.
On appeal, the Trump administration contended that Murphy’s order if left intact would usurp its authority to execute potentially thousands of valid orders of deportation to third countries.
But US Circuit Judge Seth Aframe, writing for the panel on Sept 18, said Murphy adopted a “sensible” interpretation of the immigration law requiring migrants be given a “meaningful” chance to raise any concerns before they are deported.
“DHS’s proposed interpretation would deny access to that protection to a substantial swath of noncitizens who are sent to third countries with no notice of their destination,” Aframe wrote. “We decline to adopt such an interpretation.”
The panel included two Biden appointees, including Aframe, and a judge appointed by a Republican president.
However, the 1st Circuit overturned one part of Murphy’s ruling on procedural grounds. That part of the ruling concerned whether the government must first try to deport migrants to countries they have ties to before sending them to third countries. REUTERS

Air Force Set Up a Depot in UK During Epic Fury for Faster Battle Repairs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:33:06 UTC
05:33:06 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Air Force depots are not typically meant for quick repair jobs—aircraft can stay in depot for weeks and months getting repairs—but during Operation Epic Fury, the service moved some of its stateside heavy maintenance capability forward to fix battle-damaged aircraft closer to the fight.
As the war with Iran stretched from its projected timeline of weeks into several months, Air Force leaders were forced to adapt its aircraft maintenance strategy for a prolonged conflict.
The service relies on three maintenance depots at Hill Air Force Base, Utah; Robins Air Force Base, Ga.; and Tinker Air Force Base, Okla.—to conduct major maintenance overhauls and inspections on fighters, bombers, airlifters, and other aircraft.
During Epic Fury, barrages of Iranian missile and drone attacks on U.S. forces operating out of Middle East resulted in levels of battle damage that normally would have required the aircraft to be transported back stateside for repairs.
Instead, Air Force Materiel Command temporarily surged a depot capability to RAF Mildenhall in the United Kingdom so damaged aircraft could be patched up and sent back into combat, AFMC Commander Lt. Gen. Linda Hurry told an audience this week at AFA’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber conference.
“Most people think of depots as Tinker, Robbins, and Hill; well, it doesn’t need to be just there,” Hurry said. “We knew you needed a capability out at Mildenhall … what if we push that forward?”
“That’s what we’ve been asking all of our Airmen—how do we do things smarter? How do we deliver capability faster? It doesn’t have to be 7,000 miles away.”
Air Mobility Command’s new boss, Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley, said Hurry’s move paid off, describing how the depot operation quickly repaired damaged aerial refueling booms on KC-135 Stratotankers.
“I think we turned 30 [booms] instead of bringing them all the way back to the states,” Tulley said, adding it was a great example of “generating readiness in contact.”
Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink and Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach made readiness a defining priority soon after taking their jobs last year. The intense pace of operations against Iran will stress that focus, with much of the fleet likely to need heavy maintenance overhauls to reset.
The Air Force’s proposed 2027 budget includes $4.2 billion for the Consolidated Sustainment Activity Group, which is responsible for managing spare parts.
“We absolutely need additional funding for spares,” Hurry said, adding “right now, we have a $14 billion hole in supply.”
“I know we’re not going to get it all at once, … but once we get even a penny, we have to be ready to execute it,” Hurry said. That will mean securing long-term contracts to inject stability into the supply chain.
“The other thing is, we’re looking for is multiple sources of supply; gone are the days of monopolies. We can’t just have one person producing the one critical part,” Hurry said. “I need five of you producing them because if we get down to the crunch, we’re going to have to have a healthy shelf so that we can fight globally.”
Meanwhile, Hurry said AFMC has started using artificial intelligence tools to improve forecasting accuracy. “We’re using all sorts of things to try to make sure we better understand where the needs are and where we can position those critical assets globally around the world,” she said.
Additive manufacturing is another tool AFMC has started to use to “reverse engineer some of the parts that we need,” she added.
But technology alone isn’t enough, she said, adding that “process improvement” can solve a lot of challenges.
“Quite frankly, if we can understand the process and break it down into constraint and mitigate that constrain, the collective throughput of the entire system goes so much better,” Hurry said. “That’s exactly what’s going on in the depot. That’s exactly what we did when we surged operations for [Epic Fury].”

18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Sensitive F-35 fighter jet technology was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong this summer, prompting a congressional inquiry and concerns that China could gain access to components of the highly classified weapons system, Politico reported Friday.
A shipment of F-35 parts being sent from Australia to the US for repairs was rerouted while crossing the Pacific, according to the report. The Pentagon reportedly confirmed that some components had gone missing.
Anadolu separately contacted the Pentagon seeking confirmation and further details about the incident but had not received a response at the time of publication.
According to Politico, the parts were being transported by an intermediary for F-35 manufacturer Lockheed Martin but ultimately arrived in Hong Kong. It remains unclear why they were diverted or who currently possesses them, the report said.
The incident prompted ongoing briefings for congressional staff serving on key national security committees. State Department and Pentagon officials began briefing staff in June, with further briefings expected, it added.
Among the shipment’s contents was an F-35 canopy, which covers the cockpit and incorporates stealth technology available only to the US and its allies, according to the report. If obtained by an adversary, the components could potentially be studied and reverse-engineered.
The Pentagon’s F-35 Joint Program Office said it was “aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 Lightning II components.”
The office said it is working with US authorities and industry partners “to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence.”
Because Hong Kong is a Chinese special administrative region, the diversion potentially placed the equipment within Beijing’s sphere of influence, according to the report.
China has also conducted espionage targeting classified Pentagon programs, including the F-35, the report said.
“It’s no secret that China has been aggressively trying to get F-35 data through electronic espionage, among other means,” J.J. Gertler, a former House Armed Services Committee staff member, was quoted as saying.
“But even if they already had specifications or other data about the part, possessing a real one can give them even more to go on and can verify or refine whatever they already had learned.”

Bathla's books show company was $736m out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:28:56 UTC
05:28:56 KST

Inside the mammoth task that could keep Bathla in administration for another year
In short:
Administrators of the Bathla Group have been given up to another year to run the voluntary administration.
The ABC understands the company bank accounts had not been reconciled for some time and may contain about $736 million of overstated inter-company receivables and payables.
What's next?
Administrator Teneo has secured $4.7 million in initial funding and is continuing talks with lenders about longer-term support.
Administrators of the Bathla Group have been given up to another year to run the voluntary administration, as they try to secure longer-term funding and work through a sprawling portfolio of property projects and creditor claims.
The NSW Supreme Court on Friday extended the convening period for the administration until September 13, 2027.
But the order does not mean the administration, or Bathla's construction operations, are funded for another 12 months.
Rather, it gives administrators Teneo more time before they are required to convene the second meeting of creditors, where creditors would ultimately be asked to decide the future of the companies.
Why administrators sought another year
The ABC understands the administrators sought the 12-month period because they considered anything shorter inadequate, given the scale of the task ahead.
That includes assessing hundreds of individual projects, working through the group's financial records and, ultimately, providing creditors with enough information to make decisions about the future of the companies.
“We have taken a cautious approach to the time frame to ensure there is sufficient time to progress and complete projects in an orderly way,” Teneo's head of financial advisory Stephen Longley said.
But the ability to keep construction projects moving remains dependent on funding.
"The extension gives us the time needed to progress projects towards completion but that outcome remains dependent on securing further lender support to maintain critical central functions at Bathla," Mr Longley said.
"Locking in this funding is therefore an immediate priority and discussions are continuing."
Longer-term funding still not secured
Teneo has secured $4.7 million in initial funding and is continuing talks with lenders over longer-term support for active construction projects and the shared costs of keeping Bathla's operations running.
Six lenders are currently providing the initial funding, while discussions are ongoing with other financiers that could potentially join the arrangement.
The funding talks come as administrators continue to work out the financial position of the group.
There are about $3.4 billion in currently known consolidated creditor claims.
That includes approximately $3.08 billion claimed by secured lenders and $145 million owed to the Australian Taxation Office.
It is also understood it includes about $48 million to private lenders and $110 million to other unsecured creditors, subject to ongoing reconciliation.
Untangling Bathla's financial records
The ABC understands Teneo's review to date has found the group's bank accounts had not been reconciled for some time, while its records may contain about $736 million in overstated inter-company receivables and payables, subject to reconciliation.
Key planning, design and construction information is also understood to be spread across different systems, staff email accounts, network drives and hard-copy records, rather than held in a single central repository, and reviewing these books could take many months.
A preliminary review has identified about 219 current projects carrying approximately $3.13 billion in debt, against a preliminary total value of about $4.87 billion, with figures subject to ongoing review.
Hundreds of properties face different outcomes
The ABC understands about $400 million worth of completed property is currently for sale or under contract.
It is expected that sale proceeds would initially be applied against secured lending, with any further amounts available to the individual Bathla companies, dependent on the outcome of those sales.
Across projects under construction, about a quarter of the lots are already subject to pre-sale contracts, while three-quarters remain available for sale.
It is understood administrators' preliminary assessment also identified about 167 undeveloped sites forming part of Bathla's land bank.
About 30 per cent are expected to be marketed for sale in their existing condition, while the strategy for the remaining 70 per cent is yet to be determined.

Poland to receive 18 more South Korean K2 tanks, defence minister says
Poland's 16th Mechanised Division is to receive a further 18 South Korean-made K2 tanks to bolster its combat capabilities, Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz announced on Wednesday.
The delivery is part of an executive agreement signed on August 1, 2025, at the Bumar-Labedy plant in Gliwice, southern Poland, in the presence of the Polish and South Korean defence ministers. The deal covers the acquisition of 180 additional K2 main battle tanks, which will partially feature Polish components.
"Another important delivery of armaments for our troops," Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on X. "Eighteen Korean tanks will reinforce the combat capabilities of the 16th Mechanised Division - this is the result of our contract from August 2025." He added that subsequent batches would include tanks manufactured using Polish-made subassemblies.
The announcement follows the arrival of an initial batch of 28 Hyundai Rotem-manufactured tanks late last month, which were also assigned to the 16th Mechanised Division.
Under the August 2025 contract, 116 K2GF variant tanks are due to arrive between 2026 and 2028, followed by 64 K2PL variant tanks between 2028 and 2030. The agreement includes an extensive technology transfer enabling 61 of the 64 Polonised K2PL tanks to be built domestically at the Bumar-Labedy plant, after the first three are assembled in South Korea.
Additionally, the contract includes 81 Polish-produced support vehicles, consisting of 31 armoured recovery vehicles, 25 combat engineering vehicles, and 25 joint-assault bridges.
This follows an initial July 2022 agreement under the previous government for 180 South Korean-built K2 tanks, alongside a broader framework agreement for a total of 1,000 tanks, with the remaining 820 intended for deep Polonisation and eventual local production.
In late April this year, the state-owned Polish Armaments Group (PGZ) signed a subcontracting agreement with South Korea’s Hyundai Rotem for the domestic manufacturing and servicing of the K2 fleet. This deal integrated Bumar-Labedy with state-backed electronics firms PCO and Wojskowe Zakłady Elektroniczne to facilitate the integration of Polish technology into the final assembly line. (PAP)

Trump Announces Ban of CNN, Politico and MS Now From White House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:26:12 UTC
05:26:12 KST

President Donald Trump announced on Friday he was banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House, setting up a new test of the First Amendment’s protection of a free press as his Administration moves to punish news organizations whose coverage he dislikes.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump accused the three outlets of repeatedly publishing “FAKE NEWS” and warned that other news organizations could face similar restrictions.
“Effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW... and Politico... from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” Trump wrote. “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.”
Taking questions from reporters in the Oval Office later, Trump said there were no particular stories that prompted the decision. “It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years, you get sick of it,” he said. “They purposely write negative news, and they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration.”
It was not immediately clear whether the White House would enforce the prohibition. Despite Trump’s announcement that the ban was effective immediately, CNN reported that its team remained at the White House and continued to cover the Administration on Friday afternoon. No evictions had been observed in the press briefing room as of 5 p.m., although the mood among reporters there was tense.
“CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” the network said in a statement. “We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right.”
When asked by a reporter what exactly the ban would entail, Trump said, "I don't want them in my office. I don't want them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can." The White House Press Office did not respond to questions about the ban.
Last year, Trump barred reporters from The Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One, and other events with limited space after the news organization declined to update their widely used stylebook to adopt his preferred name, “Gulf of America,” for the body of water long known as the Gulf of Mexico. The Associated Press sued, and the case remains ongoing.
The uncertainty could set up another legal confrontation over the boundaries of presidential control over access to the White House and the First Amendment’s protection of freedom of the press. The First Amendment protects freedom of the press, a principle intended to allow news organizations to scrutinize those in power without government retaliation for their reporting.
Asked about the likelihood of his latest media ban being struck down in court, Trump responded, “I think it's good to point it out whether it survives or doesn't.” He added, “I don't think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day.”
The White House has historically maintained regular access for journalists representing a broad range of news organizations, allowing them to question the President, attend briefings, and document the activities of the executive branch. The press corps also serves a practical function in providing independent accounts of presidential movements and events to the public. CNN, in particular, has been part of the traditional five-network television pool that follows the President and provides ongoing coverage of presidential appearances.
Trump has tried before to use access to the White House and presidential events as leverage against news organizations whose coverage he disliked. During his first term, he revoked the White House press credentials of Jim Acosta, then a CNN correspondent, after a contentious exchange during a news conference. CNN challenged the decision in court, and the restriction was overturned.
The dispute over access has become part of a broader pattern in Trump’s relationship with the news media. Since returning to office, he has pursued legal action against news organizations including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC after reports he objected to. The cases against the Times and Journal were subsequently dismissed, while the BBC has sought to have the case dismissed.
The Trump Administration has repeatedly called itself the “most transparent Administration in history,” pointing to the President’s frequent gaggles with reporters.
—With reporting by Philip Wang

Alibaba has open-sourced an artificial intelligence (AI) model capable of identifying nearly 150 abdominal conditions, including cancers, from computed tomography (CT) scans.
The vision-language model, called Damo Radar, was developed by Alibaba's research arm, Damo Academy, the institute said Friday, according to the Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post.
The model analyzes contrast-enhanced CT scans covering 18 abdominal organs and can identify a broad range of diseases and abnormalities, including malignant tumors.
Damo Radar achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) score of 0.913 across 146 clinical findings in nearly 40,000 real-world examinations, approaching the maximum score of 1.0.
The research team described it as "the world's first expert-level generalist medical imaging model," adding that it could eventually be expanded to other types of medical imaging.
In a study involving 26 radiologists from multiple hospitals, the model outperformed 23 participants on average.
With the model's assistance, radiologists also reduced missed diagnoses by 10% and cut diagnosis time by more than 30%.
