313,000  “Janfada” for Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:37:20 UTC
02:37:20 KST

313,000 “Janfada” for Iran
Tehran stages a defiant display of sacrifice and unity
TEHRAN — From Imam Hussein Square to Enghelab Square, Tehran’s streets on Friday became the setting for one of the largest public mobilizations seen in Iran since the war began in February. Hundreds of thousands of people took part in the “Janfada-ye Iran” — Devoted to Iran — campaign, with women, young people, veterans and other sections of society joining a 313,000-strong parade, according to Iranian organizers.
The scale of the gathering was matched by the symbolism surrounding it. Participants marched under Iranian flags, military banners and images associated with the country’s wartime resistance. Iranian drones and other military equipment were displayed along the route, while veterans of the Sacred Defense and volunteers in military-style formations took part in the parade. Some participants wore white burial shrouds — a stark traditional symbol of readiness to give one's life for the country.
The photographs from Tehran captured the atmosphere from different angles. In one image, a woman in camouflage and a green headband is seen positioned beside a vehicle, looking through the sight of a rifle. In another, a woman with her face partially covered by a patterned scarf holds an assault rifle while other women stand behind her amid Iranian and other flags. The images offer a striking visual of the campaign's central message: that the call to defend the country is being presented not solely through conventional military formations, but also through the participation of civilians, including women.
313,000: A number loaded with history
The choice of 313,000 is not simply a numerical designation.
In Islamic tradition, 313 is associated with the companions of the Prophet Muhammad at the Battle of Badr in 624 CE and, in Shiite tradition, with the number of devoted companions associated with the Imam of the Age. For the organizers of Friday's event, the number therefore carries a religious and historical meaning of steadfastness, loyalty and readiness to stand with a cause at a moment of crisis.
That symbolism was visible throughout the rally. The parade was not presented merely as a military exercise but as a public declaration of readiness, with participants repeatedly invoking the ideas of homeland, independence, national unity and sacrifice.
According to Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, commander of the Greater Tehran Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), around 500,000 people had registered in Tehran for the initiative. Iranian organizers have separately said that more than 31 million people have registered nationwide, while other Iranian reports put the cumulative figure above 32 million.
A rally born in wartime
What gives the Janfada campaign its particular character is the circumstances in which it has developed.
The campaign began on March 29, following the US-Israeli attack on Iran on February 28, and has since evolved from a registration drive into a nationwide mobilization involving public gatherings, volunteer organization and preparations for training. Iranian officials say the volunteers are being organized into formations capable of contributing to national defense and other emergency tasks.
Friday's rally therefore came against the backdrop not of a distant or concluded war, but of an ongoing conflict, economic pressure and severe restrictions on Iran's trade and access to international markets. Recent reporting has also documented the effects of the US blockade and sanctions on Iran's economy and commercial routes.
This is an important distinction when placing the gathering in historical perspective. Across history, societies have mobilized around the idea of sacrifice when confronted by an existential military threat — from the Greek defenders at Thermopylae and the Soviet defense of Stalingrad to the French Resistance during World War II and Iran's own mass mobilization during the 1980–88 Iran-Iraq War.
But Janfada is being organized under a different set of circumstances. It combines a modern state-wide registration campaign, social-media mobilization, religious symbolism, and military-style public exercises while the conflict itself is still unfolding and while the country is simultaneously confronting economic pressure.
It is this combination that has given the campaign much of its political and social significance inside Iran.
Women, youth and veterans in the same formation
The Friday parade also sought to project an image of participation across generations.
Women appeared prominently in the event, including women in military-style uniforms and others carrying rifles. Young people took part alongside veterans of the Sacred Defense. Newly engaged couples were also reported among the participants, while a Jewish rabbi and a Yemeni delegation wearing traditional clothing were present, according to Iranian media reports.
President Masoud Pezeshkian, who attended the gathering, emphasized this diversity in his remarks. He described the turnout as a manifestation of the bond between the Iranian people and their homeland and stressed that “Iran belongs to all Iranians.” He called for unity and broad public participation in preserving 'the country's dignity, independence and territorial integrity.'
The message was significant: the campaign was being presented not simply as a gathering of members of Iran's military or paramilitary organizations, but as a national mobilization cutting across different sections of society.
From the 'Sacred Defense' to a new generation
Iran's modern experience of mass mobilization is inseparable from the Iran-Iraq War, known in Iran as the Sacred Defense.
During that eight-year conflict, Iran mobilized large numbers of volunteers through the Basij and other wartime structures. For an entire generation, the experience created a cultural vocabulary in which sacrifice, martyrdom, national defense and civilian participation became closely intertwined.
The Janfada campaign draws on that historical memory while speaking to a new generation.
The images from Tehran are particularly revealing in this respect. The rifles, uniforms and military vehicles evoke the visual language of wartime mobilization, while the presence of young people and women gives the event a distinctly contemporary character. The burial shrouds worn by some participants add another layer: rather than presenting sacrifice as an abstract concept, the participants were visually associating themselves with the possibility of death in defense of their country.
A message beyond Tehran
The significance of Friday's gathering also extends beyond the capital.
Iranian officials have said that Janfada gatherings are taking place in cities across the country and that the campaign is moving toward the organization and training of volunteer units. Basij chief Hossein Taeb said the volunteers were being prepared for “full-fledged defense,” while Iranian reports said training programs were being developed across ground, air and naval domains.
The campaign has consequently become both a domestic mobilization and an international signal.
For Tehran, the message is that the country's capacity to organize people around national defense has not disappeared under the weight of war, sanctions and economic pressure. The government is presenting the turnout as evidence of national resilience and social cohesion.
When a nation says it is ready
The most powerful element of Friday's scenes may not have been the military hardware displayed along Tehran's streets. It was the human presence surrounding it.
A woman holding a rifle. A veteran marches beside younger volunteers. Families moving through the crowd. Participants wearing burial shrouds. Flags rising above a sea of people stretching through one of Tehran's historic arteries.
For Iran, the language of Janfada reaches deep into a historical memory in which the survival of the homeland has repeatedly been associated with endurance and sacrifice.
Yet this time the setting is different. The pledge is being made while war is still being fought, while economic pressure is intensifying.
That is what makes the September 18 rally more than a single day's parade. It is the latest chapter in a campaign that seeks to transform the idea of sacrifice into an organized form of public participation — and to demonstrate, in the heart of Tehran, that the war has not removed the country's ability to mobilize large numbers of people around the defense of Iran.

TEHRAN — Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi has said the United States cannot avoid responsibility for war crimes in Iran simply by withdrawing from the UN Human Rights Council.
In a post on X on Friday, Gharibabadi referred to a recent report by a UN-backed fact-finding mission that examined two deadly US strikes on civilian sites in Iran. He said the attacks on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd were now being recognized as “clear war crimes,” rather than being dismissed as operational errors.
“History will not forget,” Gharibabadi wrote, referring to the February 28 attack on Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab, in southern Hormozgan Province. Iranian authorities have said 168 people were killed in the strike, many of them children.
He also referred to the US attack on a sports complex in Lamerd, Fars Province, which the UN investigation said killed 22 civilians.
“The United States cannot escape responsibility by withdrawing from the Human Rights Council,” Gharibabadi said.
UN mission examines two US strikes
Gharibabadi’s comments followed the release of a report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, which was established by the UN Human Rights Council.
The mission said it had “reasonable grounds” to believe that US forces were responsible for two attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure that amounted to war crimes under international law.
One of the cases concerned the strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab. Investigators said the school was clearly identifiable as a civilian facility and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes when it was hit.
The investigators pointed to features including school signs; murals designed for children and playground areas as evidence of the site's civilian character. They said the United States had failed to take all feasible measures to determine whether the school was a military objective before carrying out the attack.
The second case involved a US strike on a sports complex and nearby residential areas in Lamerd.
Investigators said the weapons used in the attack dispersed tungsten pellets over a wide area. Based on the evidence examined, the mission concluded that the attack was indiscriminate and amounted to a war crime.
The report is due to be presented to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva.
US withdraw from Human Rights Council
The UN findings came shortly before Washington announced its formal withdrawal from the Human Rights Council.
The US State Department said on Thursday that Washington had ended its membership and participation in the council, accusing the body of promoting what it described as “anti-American rhetoric” and of taking an overly accommodating approach toward governments, as the US says, accused of repressing their populations.
The United States had already announced that it would not seek future membership of the council as part of a broader policy of reducing its participation in several UN bodies.
Washington's decision came as the council was holding its 63rd regular session in Geneva, which began on September 7 and is scheduled to continue through October 7.
For Iranian officials, however, leaving the council does not settle the question raised by the UN investigation.
 
 Gharibabadi argued that withdrawal from an international institution cannot remove a state's responsibility for conduct that may violate international law. His comments also reflect Tehran's broader criticism of 'the selective application of international law and human rights standards.'
Minab school strike draws int'l scrutiny
The Minab school attack has become a particularly sensitive issue in Iran because of the high number of children reported to have been among those killed.
The UN investigation claimed the school was near a military installation but was physically separate from it. Investigators said the characteristics of the site should have made its civilian status apparent.
The mission reviewed satellite imagery, video footage, witness accounts and other material as part of its investigation. It also said it had sought information from the United States.
The US position has differed from the conclusions of the UN mission. American officials have previously claimed the school was not deliberately targeted and have attributed the incident to an intelligence failure concerning the nearby military site.
The UN investigators, however, said the circumstances raised questions beyond a simple targeting error, particularly over whether sufficient measures had been taken to verify the nature of the site before the strike.
Iran seeks accountability
Tehran has repeatedly called for international investigations into attacks on civilian sites during the war and has urged that those responsible be held accountable under international law.
Iranian officials have also argued that attacks on schools, residential areas and other civilian infrastructure cannot be justified without evidence that such locations were being used for military purposes.
Against this backdrop, the UN fact-finding mission's report has added a new legal and diplomatic dimension to Iran's calls for accountability.
The dispute also highlights a wider issue for the international system: whether states can be held accountable for alleged violations of international law regardless of their political weight or participation in international institutions.
Gharibabadi's message was unequivocal: withdrawing from the Human Rights Council, in Tehran's view, does not erase allegations already documented by an international investigation or remove the obligations imposed by international law.

Palestinians are responding to Israel’s stranglehold on the West Bank’s economy by forgiving each other’s debts en masse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:35:00 UTC
02:35:00 KST

On September 4, at 7:00 a.m., Palestinian journalist Alaa Rimawi posted a simple call on his Facebook page: forgive the debts owed to you. By 8:00 a.m., responses forgiving half a million shekels had already come in. By Tuesday, the total had reached 75 million shekels — approximately $24 million.
The campaign, which Rimawi named “Forgive for the Sake of God,” spread rapidly across the West Bank, drawing thousands of responses from individuals, business owners, and companies. A clothing store owner in Silet al-Daher, north of Jenin, filmed himself burning a registry notebook containing 47,000 shekels in customer debts. A chicken business in Silwad, east of Ramallah, published a photo of a debt ledger totaling 250,000 shekels, with a note stating that all of it was forgiven. A lawyer shared that his client had dropped two court cases against debtors over bounced bank checks. A sidewalk vendor who sells corn forgave a cleaning worker who owed him 36 shekels.
“They might not be much,” Rimawi told Mondoweiss, “but 36 shekels is a big difference both for a sidewalk vendor and for a cleaning worker.”
The campaign’s scale reflects the depth of an economic crisis that has been building in the West Bank for years — one that Israel’s policies have systematically deepened, and that has left hundreds of thousands of Palestinians surviving on debt, reduced salaries, and depleted savings with no public safety net to fall back on.
The making of a crisis
The economic crisis in the West Bank had started before October 2023. Since 2019, Israel has withheld parts of Palestinian customs revenue – money it collects on behalf of the Palestinian Authority (PA) through its control of the borders. That withholding intensified after October 7, 2023, while Israel simultaneously revoked nearly all working permits for approximately 200,000 Palestinian workers who had previously been employed inside Israel. These two sectors — customs revenue and labor income from Israel — are the single largest sources of income for the Palestinian economy in the West Bank.
The consequences have compounded over three years. The PA, the largest employer in the Palestinian labor market, has been forced to pay half-salaries for more than three years. Workers who previously held Israeli permits to work across the Green Line have depleted most of their savings and rely on irregular, unstable jobs.
According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, the cost of living rose by 53.67 percent across the Palestinian territories in 2024, while purchasing power fell by 34.93 percent in the same period, with a further 12 percent accumulation in 2026.
The result has been a widespread turn to debt. Many working Palestinians have been buying goods with borrowed money, promissory notes, or postdated checks, particularly from small wholesale distributors. For families doing their weekly grocery shopping, it comes down to a name and a number written in the store owner’s notebook.
While the economic hardship increases for Palestinians in the West Bank, Palestinians have resorted to cross-community solidarity to help each other face the effects of the economic strangulation. The success of the campaign is partly due to its tackling one of the most pressing economic problems for Palestinians.
The idea
The campaign began with a phone call. A schoolteacher contacted Rimawi to say she had a bank check for 2,000 shekels coming due, with insufficient funds in her account. In the West Bank, a bounced check can turn into a criminal offense — she was afraid of arrest.
Rimawi reached out to the check’s recipient, who agreed to pardon the debt. “I then thought, why not expand this call and launch a campaign?” he told Mondoweiss. “At the time, I thought it would solve a dozen cases like the teacher’s case, with a maximum of 100,000 shekels.”
With 166,000 followers on Facebook, he launched the call on the morning of September 4. Within an hour, a staggering half a million shekels (about $165,000) had been forgiven.
The geographic spread of the responses has been as striking as the total. In Qabalan, a town of 9,000 people southeast of Nablus, forgiven debts reached one million shekels ($330,000). In Qibya, west of Ramallah, with a population of 6,000, they reached 800,000 shekels ($264,000). In Sa’ir, northeast of Hebron, with 20,000 residents, the total hit two million shekels ($659,000).
One of the messages Rimawi published came from a man in Dahriyyah, Hebron, who identified himself as a former worker in Israel who lost his work permit and is himself wanted by Palestinian courts for unpaid bank checks. He wrote that he was forgiving six people who owed him 5,500 shekels ($1,800), for the sake of his dead brother’s soul.
A Palestinian from Jabaa, north of Jerusalem, announced the forgiveness of 7,500 shekels ($2,470) in promissory notes. Another, a lawyer, shared that his client asked him to drop two cases against debtors over bank checks in court.
“I also didn’t expect the participation to be so diverse,” Rimawi went on. “There are companies pardoning merchants for big amounts of money, but there is, for example, a sidewalk stall owner who sells corn, who pardoned a cleaning worker who owed him 36 shekels [$12].”
‘We have nobody to support us but each other’
The scale of the response, Rimawi says, exposes a gap between the legal framework of government debt in the West Bank and the reality of life under economic siege.
“This shows the disconnect between people’s circumstances in the West Bank and the requirements of the legal system: either you pay or you go to jail, as if we’re in a normal situation,” Rimawi explained. “We are living in the midst of a tragedy, and the economic situation is just one dimension of it.”
“In times of tragedy, we need to revive our human spirit, even at the expense of legal rights,” he went on. “Because, if we learned something in the past three years, it is that as Palestinians, we have nobody to support us but each other.”

Pentagon Picks 2 Companies for Reconnaissance Satellite Demo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:30:12 UTC
02:30:12 KST

The Space Force and the Defense Innovation Unit have chosen two firms to demonstrate the ability of small satellites built with low-cost, commercial technology to track both friendly and adversary satellites in geosynchronous orbit.
Northrop Grumman and True Anomaly will build prototype satellites for DIU’s GEO High-Resolution Optical Space-Based Tactical Reconnaissance, or GHOST-R, program, the Pentagon technology accelerator announced Sept. 18 in a LinkedIn post. The work will feed into a broader, multibillion dollar Space Force initiative called RG-XX, with the goal to begin fielding a fleet of reconnaissance satellites by the end of the decade.
Col. Bryon McClain, acting portfolio acquisition executive for space combat power, said the Space Force is trying to “push the envelope” when it comes to both speed and affordability.
“This approach burns down technical risk, drives down lifecycle costs, and gets vital capability to the warfighter faster to ensure a more resilient architecture,” McClain said. “Successful prototypes will have a direct transition into the program of record.”
The Space Force in 2024 started talking about a lower-cost, commercial-based capability to augment its current fleet of Geosynchronous Space Situational Awareness Program, or GSSAP, satellites. At the time, then-acting space acquisition executive Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy said the approach was partly motivated by a push from U.S. Space Command for more unclassified opportunities to partner with allies and industry.
It also aims to address two other SPACECOM needs: more maneuverable satellites and better space domain awareness to close gaps in its ability to characterize and track objects of concern in space. As recently as Sept. 16, Space Command Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting called for improved on-orbit targeting and tracking capabilities—and highlighted the fundamental role space domain awareness plays in the counterspace mission.
“To be able to negate threats in space, we must be able to find, fix, track, and target those threats,” Whiting said at the AMOS Conference in Maui, Hawaii. “Targeting in the space domain is maturing, but it still has a long way to go.”
In April, the Space Force chose 14 companies to be part of an industry consortium called Andromeda, where they’ll compete for task orders worth up to $6.2 billion. That contract will include work for both the maneuverable RG-XX reconnaissance satellites and a separate fleet of surveillance satellites called SG-XX.
As part of GHOST-R, Northrop and True Anomaly’s satellites are expected to launch in 2028 and then perform a series of demonstrations to prove they can collect high-resolution imagery and conduct weekly observations of target satellites. If successful, those spacecraft would become operational RG-XX platforms by 2029.
In parallel, the firms must provide a plan for scaling their satellites to a full constellation that can track all publicly catalogued objects in GEO.
Northrop, the incumbent prime contractor for GSSAP, said in a press release that its design will incorporate its ESPASat-L platform—a high-rate production bus—as well as optical payloads built by a company called TRL 11 based in Irvine, Calif.
“This award expands the company’s role in commercial, low-cost, proliferated space systems and builds on the success of the Northrop Grumman-built Geosynchronous Space Situational Awareness Program,” the company said.
In its own statement, True Anomaly said it will leverage is Jackal spacecraft as well as its Mosaic ground system for GHOST-R.
“Jackal and Mosaic were purpose-built for this mission, delivering superior maneuverability, sensing, and autonomy at a price point that enables scale without compromising performance,” CEO Even Rogers said.
True Anomaly recently showcased its maneuverable Jackal spacecraft as part of the Space Force’s Victus Haze responsive space mission. During the mission, Jackal has demonstrated the ability to approach a target—in this case a satellite built by Rocket Lab—capture an image of it, characterize it, and “engage in a space-to-space pursuit” of the vehicle, the company said in a July statement.
Meanwhile, DIU recently posted another space-related solicitation, this time focused on fostering AI tools that can help distinguish between friendly objects and threats. The project, perhaps complementary to GHOST-R, seeks software that can “ingest and fuse massive streams of multi-source data,” like satellite imagery, geospatial data, and live video.
“By automating advanced cross-data correlation, the architecture aims to uncover hidden patterns, complex operational relationships, and predictive threat behaviors far beyond the capabilities of human analysis alone,” the solicitation states.

15 nations call for ban on attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:28:57 UTC
02:28:57 KST

15 nations call for ban on attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities
TEHRAN — Fifteen countries, including Iran, China and Russia, have called for a clear and unequivocal prohibition on attacks or threats of attack against peaceful nuclear facilities operating under International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) safeguards, warning that silence over such actions could undermine international law and erode the credibility of the global nuclear safeguards regime.
In a joint statement issued on Thursday during the 70th General Conference of the IAEA in Vienna, the 15 countries stressed that nuclear facilities devoted to peaceful purposes and subject to international safeguards must never be targeted or threatened with attack.
They called on all IAEA member states to adopt a firm and unified position against such actions and to protect peaceful nuclear activities while safeguarding the credibility and integrity of the Agency's safeguards system.
The statement was endorsed by Belarus, Brazil, Burkina Faso, China, Cuba, Indonesia, Iran, Iraq, Nicaragua, Niger, Pakistan, Russia, South Africa, Tajikistan and Zimbabwe.
The countries warned that failure to respond to attacks against safeguarded nuclear facilities would undermine established international norms and weaken the international legal order. They further cautioned that silence could contribute to the normalization of actions that pose serious risks to nuclear safety and security, as well as to human life and the environment.
Iran pushes for 'zero-tolerance' policy
The joint statement came as Iran stepped up calls at the IAEA General Conference for the international community to adopt a “zero-tolerance policy” toward attacks on peaceful nuclear installations.
Reza Najafi, Iran's ambassador and permanent representative to international organizations in Vienna, said on Thursday that no political or military justification should be accepted for attacks against nuclear facilities.
“The international community must adopt a zero-tolerance policy toward any attack or threat against peaceful nuclear facilities,” Najafi said, stressing that no attack on nuclear installations should be tolerated.
Iran has made the protection of safeguarded nuclear facilities a major issue in international forums following attacks on its nuclear infrastructure.
The statement carries particular significance for Iran following military strikes against several of the country's nuclear facilities.
According to IAEA documents, Israeli attacks between June 13 and 24, 2025 affected several Iranian nuclear facilities, while the United States subsequently carried out strikes on three Iranian nuclear sites on June 22. The attacks led the IAEA to suspend its field verification and monitoring activities in Iran and withdraw its inspectors for safety reasons.
The 15-country statement places the protection of nuclear facilities within the broader debate over the future of the international safeguards regime.
Safeguards intend to provide assurances that nuclear material and activities covered by agreements with the IAEA are not diverted from peaceful purposes. Any military attack that damages safeguarded facilities, disrupts inspections or creates conditions in which inspectors cannot safely operate can therefore have consequences extending beyond the targeted country.
Iran maintains that its nuclear program is exclusively peaceful and has called for disputes over its nuclear activities to be addressed through diplomatic and legal mechanisms rather than military action.
The joint statement by the 15 countries also comes as the IAEA's 70th General Conference concludes in Vienna amid heightened international concern over attacks involving nuclear facilities. UN Secretary-General António Guterres, in his message to the conference, warned that attacks on nuclear facilities were increasing and stressed the need for member states to uphold international law and strengthen the safeguards system.
For Tehran, the statement represents a call for a broader international consensus that the protection of peaceful nuclear installations must remain a fundamental principle regardless of political disputes between states.
The 15 countries' warning that silence could normalize attacks against safeguarded facilities also places the issue beyond Iran's nuclear dispute with Western countries, framing the protection of nuclear installations as a wider question of international law, nuclear safety and the credibility of the global non-proliferation architecture.

US prosecutors accuse Huawei of ‘far-reaching criminal scheme’ spanning decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:28:45 UTC
02:28:45 KST

CHINA CAPITAL
US prosecutors accuse Huawei of ‘far-reaching criminal scheme’ spanning decades
The Chinese tech giant is on trial in New York for allegedly violating U.S. sanctions on Iran and stealing trade secrets as it built its global telecommunications empire.
The U.S. government has long warned, in sweeping terms, that the Chinese tech giant Huawei is effectively an arm of the Chinese state that acts with impunity on the global stage, including allegedly violating U.S. sanctions. Over the last two weeks, U.S. prosecutors have begun to make that case, labeling Huawei a “criminal enterprise,” in what could be a lengthy trial in a New York federal court.
Huawei enacted “a far-reaching criminal scheme extending over twenty years,” according to Department of Justice prosecutor Taylor Stout. “Crime was an important business strategy.”
Nearly eight years after the U.S. Department of Justice unsealed its indictment against Huawei, the company is facing 12 felony charges, including that it conspired to steal technologies from U.S. competitors and business partners. The federal government also alleges that Huawei lied to its Western banking partners about doing business in Iran in violation of U.S. sanctions. No individuals have been charged.
Huawei’s lawyers rejected the government’s characterization, with Brian Heberlig, one of at least a dozen attorneys working for the defense, arguing that the charges concerned “disconnected incidents.”
“It’s about competition, not conspiracy,” Heberlig said.
In December 2018, Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Vancouver at the request of U.S. officials and charged with fraud. After a lengthy period of house arrest, Meng reached a deferred prosecution agreement with U.S. authorities in 2021 in which she admitted to lying to HSBC and other banks about a Huawei subsidiary’s business in Iran. That admission will likely be introduced during the trial.
As reported in China Capital, ICIJ’s recent investigation into Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, Huawei had leaned on its close relations with the state-owned bank to insulate itself from the fallout of Meng’s arrest. After the Justice Department unveiled its indictment, the company’s bankers at ICBC’s London branch facilitated a transfer of $1.3 billion in “emergency cash” from London to a branch in China without informing compliance staff.
The federal government’s investigations of Huawei go back to at least the Obama administration. Some of the alleged crimes occurred around the turn of the century. The allegations include that Huawei stole technology from U.S. companies like the cell service provider T-Mobile and the networking giant Cisco. Prosecutors have claimed that Huawei paid bounties to employees for recruiting workers to leave rivals, bringing their trade secrets to Huawei, which employs about 210,000 people in more than 170 countries and regions. In one incident raised at trial, a Huawei employee allegedly snuck into a booth at a trade show to take photos of Fujitsu network equipment and was spotted by a security guard.
For years, U.S. intelligence and government officials have expressed concern that, along with being a dominant player in global telecommunications, Huawei is a tool of Chinese statecraft, enabling espionage and repression in autocratic countries like North Korea. Huawei’s global expansion, officials warned, might allow the Chinese government to eavesdrop on numerous countries.
In the first days of the current trial, Parham Baheshti, a former engineer at Mobinet, an Iranian telecommunications firm, testified that Huawei, working with Iranian intelligence, built a domestic surveillance system that could spy on users of Mobinet’s wireless network. “They help a dictatorship to rule and suppress people,” Baheshti said.
Huawei’s defense lawyers argued that the company furnished a so-called lawful interception program similar to the ones found in many other countries, both democratic and otherwise, which sometimes run on equipment from Western tech companies.
Judge Ann Donnelly told jurors last week China and the Chinese Communist Party “are not on trial.” But the backdrop of great power competition, especially in a trial that began with a focus on Huawei’s business in Iran in alleged violation of U.S. sanctions, is hard to ignore. Jurors were asked if they had any family ties to China and scrutinized for their opinions on the tech industry.
The trial is one of the biggest in the history of the Eastern District of New York, with hundreds of pieces of evidence expected to be introduced, along with numerous witnesses who have worked for or with Huawei in the U.S., Iran, and other countries. Judge Donnelly said she hopes that proceedings will conclude by Christmas, but the trial may run into next year.
“What is so remarkable is that the case is going to trial,” Duke University Law Professor Brandon Garrett said in an email to ICIJ. “The vast bulk of criminal cases, including corporate cases, are resolved through negotiated settlements. Here, the company has already been sanctioned and may have had little incentive to settle.”
Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to meet with President Donald Trump on Sept. 24 in Washington, D.C., where they will discuss issues such as AI safety and American citizens imprisoned in China. President Xi has championed Huawei, which just last month reached a potential agreement with the Egyptian government to build AI data centers. The State Department, hoping to stymie a potential victory for China’s tech industry, has reportedly encouraged U.S. companies to outbid Huawei’s offer.
If the world’s largest telecoms firm is eventually found guilty, it’s not clear what the Justice Department, or the Trump administration, may want as restitution.
“Should the government prevail, what consequences can be imposed on top of existing sanctions?” Garrett, the law professor, said. “What assets are available to pay fines, for example, if the company is found liable?”

Pentagon mandates testosterone tests for male troops over 30
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:28:36 UTC
02:28:36 KST

The Pentagon is reinstating mandatory screening for testosterone deficiency among male U.S. service members age 30 and older, reviving a program that some medical experts have warned could lead to unnecessary treatment and potentially harmful consequences.
The updated clinical guidance, announced Thursday, applies only to male service members and establishes standardized screening and treatment procedures across the military. Separate guidance covering female service members is expected at a later date.
Under the policy, testosterone testing will become part of periodic health assessments and annual physical examinations for men 30 and older. Younger service members may also be tested if they request it or if screening is considered clinically appropriate.
“Effective immediately, this guidance addresses male testosterone deficiency, establishing uniform screening and treatment pathways,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has publicly promoted testosterone as a way to improve military readiness, first announced the mandatory screening initiative in July.
The Pentagon temporarily withdrew an earlier version of the guidance in early September “to allow for updates.” Officials did not immediately specify what had been changed before the policy was reinstated.
Medical professionals have raised concerns about broad testosterone screening, particularly when treatment is prescribed without clear medical need. Testosterone therapy can affect fertility and may carry other health risks.
The previous version of the Pentagon policy also included women, who were to be screened through a questionnaire and could then be referred for treatment of conditions linked to hormonal imbalance. The revised guidance separates the two groups and says recommendations for women will be issued later.
The policy comes as federal regulators have also revised their approach to testosterone therapy for men.
Last year, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration removed its boxed warning about an increased risk of cardiovascular problems from testosterone products for men after reviewing post-marketing studies. The treatments still carry warnings that they can increase blood pressure.
In June, the FDA also asked manufacturers to remove labeling stating that the safety and effectiveness of testosterone replacement had not been established for men with age-related hypogonadism, following a review of newer evidence.
Testosterone products remain FDA-approved for men whose low testosterone is associated with an underlying medical condition.
There is currently no FDA-approved testosterone product specifically for women. Medical organizations generally recommend testosterone for women mainly in cases of persistently low sexual desire associated with menopause, while saying evidence remains insufficient to support broader use for purposes such as improving energy, cognition or muscle mass.

The Irish Finance Minister hit back against claims made by the US that Ukraine is causing the global energy crisis, saying de-escalation in the Middle East is the only solution.
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Trump's war with Iran are causes behind the turmoil in the energy markets, not Ukraine's attacks on Russian diesel refineries. That is the message Irish Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister (Tánaiste), Simon Harris, shared with Euronews in an exclusive interview
Harris pushed back against recent remarks made by US President Donald Trump, who blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russian diesel refineries for creating a shortage. Oil prices are hovering around $108 per barrel.
"The reason there's a major energy crisis in the world right now is because the Strait of Hormuz is closed," Harris said on Euronews' interview programme 12 Minutes With. "I always make the point, and I would make it again today, that the greatest economic intervention we could see is de-escalation in the Middle East," he added.
He noted that this became evident during the summer, when there was a brief moment of respite in the conflict. "We saw a very rapid fall in the commodity markets and therefore a benefit at the pump."
Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil and gas facilities are squeezing Moscow’s oil output and having an impact globally, as Russia is one of the world’s largest oil producers, but experts agree the current energy crisis is primarily caused by the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz – the transit route for 20% of the world's oil and gas supplies.
The situation has escalated after Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline, also known as Petroline, following drone attacks earlier this month from Iran-backed allied Houthis and Iraq.
"From an economic perspective, I'm very concerned [after] what we've seen on oil markets in recent days," Harris said. "I'm also very concerned about the fact that we aren't seeing de-escalation; we're actually seeing an escalation and indeed more fronts in terms of complications opening up regarding energy."
Windfall tax on the table
It is against the backdrop of mounting energy costs that finance ministers from eurozone countries gathered in Dublin on Friday, rushing to mitigate the rising prices and discussing measures to mitigate the impact on citizens.
One of the ideas circulating among EU ministers at the meeting is a windfall tax for firms profiting from energy price volatility, following calls from several member states to consider this measure.
"Some energy companies are making extraordinarily large profits on the back of this energy crisis," Harris said, noting that they are not doing so by "being innovative," but "because of the chaos that we're seeing in the energy markets as a result of the Strait of Hormuz being closed."
Without pre-empting possible outcomes of the talks, Harris said he would be having an initial conversation on such a tax with ministers in Dublin. Ireland currently holds the rotating EU Council presidency, allowing it to set the work programme and Council meeting agenda.
"It's likely that we will ask the European Commission to further examine this and that we would formally discuss it in Brussels at the next formal [Economic and Finance Council] meeting in October."
World 'cannot become numb to loss of life'
Harris stressed that, aside from the economic importance of ending the Middle East conflict, the world can not turn a blind eye to the human toll either.
"I think while I'm obviously speaking in the capacity of a finance minister, we should never become numb to the loss of life in war, whether that's the loss of life in Ukraine, whether it's the horrific genocide we've seen in Gaza, whether it's a situation in the Middle East more broadly," he said. "We need to see a de-escalation of conflict more broadly in the world."
On settler violence seen in the West Bank against Palestinians, the Tánaiste argued in favour of a tougher stance on Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law.
"I'm massively pro-European, but I think when it comes to Gaza, it's been disappointing, to put it mildly, that more hasn't been done at that coordinated level," Harris said.
Several European countries, including Ireland and more recently the United Kingdom, have announced national bans on the import of all goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
"Member states are listening to their public and are moving ahead, but we would always rather see action at an EU level because we think it's more impactful."
The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, recently put forward an EU-wide ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements as a "principled stance" for the bloc, comparing illegal settlements in the West Bank to Russia’s occupation of Crimea.

From Symbolism to Strategy: The Expanding Operational Role of Women in Baloch Militancy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:23:00 UTC
02:23:00 KST

On May 22, the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), one of the principal armed groups in Pakistan’s Baloch insurgency, announced the formation of a dedicated women’s wing and named Shaynaz Baloch as its commander. The announcement was significant not simply because it placed a woman in a more visible position within the organization, but because it appeared to formalize a trend that has been developing since 2022: the expansion of women’s participation in Baloch militancy from largely symbolic and support roles into direct operational activity.
The development raises a broader question: Why are Baloch militant organizations expanding women’s roles now, and what does this mean for an insurgency historically dominated by men?
The shift can be traced most clearly to April 2022, when Shari Baloch carried out a suicide attack at the Confucius Institute at the University of Karachi, killing three Chinese teachers and their Pakistani driver. The BLA claimed responsibility and presented her as its first female suicide operative. Since then, several other women have been linked to suicide operations attributed to BLA factions. In June 2023, Sumaiya Qalandrani Baloch carried out a suicide attack targeting a military convoy in Turbat. In August 2024, a woman identified by the BLA as Mahal Baloch conducted a vehicle-borne attack against a Frontier Corps facility in Bela. In March 2025, Mahikhan Baloch carried out another suicide attack against a paramilitary convoy in Kalat.
In November 2025, the trend extended to another major Baloch armed group, the Baloch Liberation Front (BLF), when Zareena Rafiq carried out a vehicle-borne attack against a Frontier Corps facility in Nokundi. The pattern suggests that the use of women is no longer confined to an isolated form of militant propaganda. It is becoming part of how some Baloch armed groups recruit, operate, and present themselves.
The development became even more visible during the BLA’s January-February 2026 offensive, which the organization called Operation Herof 2.0. The BLA publicized the participation of several women in the coordinated attacks, including female suicide operatives.
Balochistan, Pakistan’s largest province by area and one of its least densely populated, has experienced successive waves of Baloch nationalist insurgency, with the current conflict emerging in the early 2000s. The BLA and BLF are among the principal separatist organizations involved. They frame their campaigns around grievances including political marginalization, resource distribution, and alleged abuses by the Pakistani state. Pakistani authorities classify the groups as terrorist organizations and have attributed aspects of the insurgency to external support. The conflict has also acquired a significant international dimension. Balochistan hosts Gwadar Port and other major infrastructure associated with the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), making Chinese nationals and projects recurring targets for Baloch militants.
For much of the current insurgency, however, women associated with Baloch nationalism were more visible in political activism, advocacy, and community mobilization than in armed operations. Organizations such as the Baloch Students Organization-Azad (BSO-A) and the Baloch Yakjehti Committee have provided platforms for campaigns concerning enforced disappearances, alleged extrajudicial killings, and other grievances involving the Pakistani state. Women such as Mahrang Baloch and Sammi Deen Baloch have subsequently become prominent advocates on these issues. Karima Mehrab Baloch, who became the first woman to chair BSO-A, was another prominent figure in Baloch nationalist activism before she died in Toronto in December 2020.
This established a largely political role for women within the broader Baloch nationalist movement. But the emergence of women in militant operations since 2022 marks a departure from that pattern. The May announcement of a dedicated women’s wing in the BLA represents a potential further step in this evolution, from individual female participation in militant operations toward a more formal organizational role.
The motivations of individual women who join militant organizations cannot be reduced to a single explanation. Political grievances, personal experiences, family or social networks, ideological commitment, trauma, and the search for purpose can all influence recruitment. These factors differ from one individual to another.
The organizational incentives are easier to identify. Women can provide militant groups with additional operational flexibility. Gendered assumptions about who constitutes a security threat can affect how individuals are screened, monitored, or approached by security personnel. This does not make women inherently better operatives. Rather, it gives organizations another category of personnel through which they can attempt to exploit gaps in security practices. Female participation can also broaden the pool from which militant organizations recruit. It allows groups to portray their struggle as extending beyond young male fighters and into families and communities.
The propaganda value may be even more important. A female militant challenges the conventional image of an insurgent as a young man carrying a weapon. Baloch militant groups have used photographs, videos, and biographies of female operatives to portray their participation as evidence that the conflict has reached across gender and social boundaries.
However, reducing female militants to passive victims of manipulation obscures their agency and the possibility that some make deliberate ideological or political choices. At the same time, focusing exclusively on agency can obscure the organizational structures that recruit, train, indoctrinate, and deploy them. The analytical challenge is to account for both.
The Baloch case is part of a much broader history of women’s participation in political violence. Research on female suicide bombers has documented substantial participation by women in conflicts ranging from the Middle East to South Asia and Southeast Asia. Secular separatist organizations such as the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) were among the groups that developed significant roles for women in their military structures. The LTTE incorporated women into combat units and became particularly associated with female suicide operations. The PKK likewise developed extensive female military and organizational structures.
Later, jihadist organizations including Boko Haram, al-Shabaab, and the Islamic State expanded women’s roles in different ways, including recruitment, propaganda, logistics, and, in some cases, direct participation in attacks. The comparison should not be overstated, however. These organizations differ substantially in ideology, structure, social environment, and strategic objectives. Baloch armed groups are primarily ethno-nationalist and separatist organizations rather than transnational jihadist movements.
The expansion of women’s participation comes amid a broader deterioration in Pakistan’s security environment. The Baloch insurgency is only one component of that deterioration; the resurgence of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), particularly along the Afghan border, has also contributed substantially to the country’s terrorism burden.
The Global Terrorism Index 2026 ranked Pakistan as the country most affected by terrorism in 2025, recording 1,139 terrorism-related deaths and 1,045 incidents. Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa together accounted for more than 74 percent of terrorist attacks and 67 percent of terrorism-related deaths recorded in Pakistan that year. This wider context matters because the emergence of female militants could tempt security institutions toward an overly broad response.
The answer is not simply increased surveillance of women. A poorly designed response could stigmatize women participating in legitimate political activity and further blur the distinction between peaceful activism and militancy. Instead, intelligence assessments should account for women as potential participants across the spectrum of militant activity, including recruitment, propaganda, financing, logistics, and direct operations. At the same time, investigators must distinguish genuine indicators of militant involvement from political dissent, human rights activism, and ordinary civic activity.
That distinction is particularly important in Balochistan, where a significant political and human rights movement exists alongside an armed insurgency. Conflating the two would not only threaten civil liberties; it could also make counterterrorism less effective by expanding the pool of people who feel alienated from the state. The strategic challenge is therefore twofold: prevent militant organizations from turning women’s visibility into an operational advantage, while ensuring that the state’s response does not itself deepen the alienation that those organizations seek to capitalize on. That means combining intelligence-led counterterrorism with community engagement, strategic communication, and efforts to address the grievances that militant organizations seek to exploit.
The shift from symbolic female participation to a more structured operational role is still developing, but the direction is increasingly difficult to ignore.

This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myself | Jonathan Freedland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:20:45 UTC
02:20:45 KST

Candidates always say it, but this time it’s true. When Israel goes to the polls on 27 October, it really will be the most important election in the country’s history – and not just for Israelis. I saw that for myself this last week, in a visit that served as a sharp reminder of both what is at stake – and the role of those watching from afar.
More than one voter I spoke to voiced the fear that, if the coalition headed by Benjamin Netanyahu is returned to power next month, 27 October will not merely be Israel’s most important election: it will be its last. They were not referring to the absence of democracy in the occupied territory of the West Bank – which we’ll come to – but rather to Israel’s internationally recognised, pre-1967 borders: what you might call Israel-proper. There, the last four years have seen a sustained assault on the machinery of liberal democracy by the most rightwing government since Israel’s establishment in 1948 – a committed, focused attempt to remove the checks and restraints on its own power, installing instead a kind of elective dictatorship.
Democratic norms are breaking down all the time. While I was there, Netanyahu joined calls to strip two Israeli film-makers of their citizenship, as a livid mob surrounded the home of the parents of one of the two directors. The film in question is NAZA, produced by the Guardian, which features interviews with two dozen Israeli military insiders, their identities disguised, and which is named for the acronym euphemistically used by the Israeli military when calculating the number of civilians it expects to die in an airstrike. Unlike everyone protesting against it, I have actually seen the film: I have some misgivings about specific choices it makes, but that is irrelevant. A country true to its self-designation as the only democracy in the Middle East would not threaten with expulsion or violence those who say what its rulers do not want to hear.
But such egregious behaviour is becoming commonplace. Last month, Netanyahu’s wife, Sara, implied, without evidence, that Yair Golan, leader of the left-leaning Democrats party, had inside knowledge of the 7 October 2023 attacks that saw the massacre of 1,200 Israelis and the abduction of 251 hostages – the trauma of which still touches every aspect of Israeli life and looms over this election campaign. It’s part of a baseless conspiracy theory pushed by Netanyahu and his “poison machine” of acolytes and media allies to shift the blame for the PM’s own 7 October failures, but it’s especially despicable when directed against Golan. A former general, he leapt into his car on 7 October, drove south and personally rescued six of those who had come under fire. He is a hero of that dark day – and has threatened to sue Sara Netanyahu. As it happens, soon after her intervention, it was reported that someone high up in Israel had indeed been explicitly warned before 7 October that a devastating Hamas attack was on the way. That someone was Benjamin Netanyahu and the warning came from the president of the United Arab Emirates. Netanyahu vehemently denied the allegation.
It is a dirty campaign, filled with disinformation and lies, utterly in keeping with the degraded state of Israeli politics in the age of late-stage Netanyahu. Thanks to Israel’s unwritten constitution, there now remains only one serious obstacle in his way: the courts. He has had the judiciary in his sights since he returned to office nearly four years ago, not least because he wants to halt the ongoing corruption trial that could send him to jail. He tried to gut the supreme court once already, in early 2023, and, if he wins next month, most observers are clear: the court will be gone.
That matters for Israelis, who will find themselves in a Turkey- or Russia-style autocracy poorly disguised as a democracy. But it also matters for Palestinians. Yehuda Shaul, an Israeli anti-occupation activist fully aware of the court’s inadequate record as a defender of Palestinian rights, told me that Israel has been on the wrong road for a long time: “But so long as the courts and basic democratic institutions are standing, we can still turn back. If they’re gone, we’re heading off a cliff.”
I was with Shaul driving around the West Bank, seeing the changing reality there up close. I stood in the burnt-out and broken mosque of what had been the small Bedouin village of Mu’arrajat, its population chased out by settler terrorists – to use the formulation favoured, remarkably, by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee. Through harassment and violence, they made the lives of the inhabitants there so unbearable that the villagers could hold on no longer. It was the same story in Ras ‘Ein al ‘Auja, where I stood among similar ruins, including a small, abandoned school, and where a herd of settler-owned goats now grazes. Shaul points out the vast swathe of land, more than 100 sq miles, in the east of the West Bank, close enough to see Jordan, where now next to no Palestinians live. Small wonder that former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert speaks of ethnic cleansing, or that UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband does the same.
I saw, too, in what the settlers call northern Samaria, the four settlements that Ariel Sharon dismantled in 2005, now returned and rebuilt along with 14 others either built or approved for construction. Their arrival sees roadside buildings demolished and olive trees uprooted, in the name of safety for settlers as they travel. And dotted, seemingly on every ridge and hilltop, the distinct, bright white caravans that mark a new officially “unauthorised” outpost, popping up with such frequency that Shaul can barely name them all – he estimates 250 new settlements and outposts have gone up since 2023 – and which are steadily encircling the major Palestinian cities, reducing them to isolated enclaves, thereby preventing the territorial contiguity that would be essential for a viable Palestinian state.
Netanyahu’s coalition, with radical settler Bezalel Smotrich in de facto charge of the West Bank, has directed this settlement expansion and turned a blind eye to the pogroms staged by the movement’s most aggressive wing. The best chance to stop it going farther and further comes on 27 October.
Those outside the country appalled by what they see in Gaza or the West Bank sometimes struggle to know what they can do to help. The temptation is to rally around, say, the rapper Macklemore, calling out “Free Palestine” from Ed Sheeran’s stage – but that temptation fades a little when you see that the same Macklemore once performed dressed up as what looked unmistakably like an antisemitic caricature of a Jew, complete with a false, giant nose. He later apologised, saying a “Jewish stereotype” had never crossed his mind.
Or you might want to get fully behind Miliband’s sanctions package, which at long last signals that the settlement enterprise will not be allowed to continue with impunity – until you hear from those involved who say that the immediate impact will fall not on settlers but on Palestinians. That’s because the Netanyahu government’s predictable and predicted response – which included the closure of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem – has robbed Britain of its main mechanism to aid Palestinians through delivering development programmes and the like.
The truth is that, for those desperate to see change, the best hope is the ejection from office of what has been a vile, cruel, bigoted and lethally dangerous government. Be under no illusion: even if Netanyahu is toppled, he will not be replaced by a peacenik who will instantly lead the country in the opposite direction. It doesn’t work like that. But there is a bloc, unofficially led by former general Gadi Eisenkot, which is defined by its opposition to the man who has ruled Israel on and off for much of the last 30 years and there are campaigners and activists, such as Shaul, who are fighting every hour of every day to avert further disaster. They are branded as traitors at home and shunned simply for being Israeli by too many supposed progressives abroad. They need allies and friends, because right now they are all that stands between this moment and the abyss.
- 
  Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

China Coast Guard rams Philippine ship near Palawan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:16:59 UTC
02:16:59 KST

- A China Coast Guard vessel rammed the Philippine ship BRP Datu Magat Salamat on Sept. 18 during a fuel subsidy mission for Filipino fishermen.
- The Philippine Coast Guard said the collision caused structural damage but no injuries, while China blamed the Philippine vessel for the incident.
A Philippine government ship carrying fuel to Filipino fishermen was struck by a Chinese Coast Guard vessel on Friday, the latest collision in a South China Sea dispute that has grown more dangerous and more frequent throughout 2026.
The Philippine ship, BRP Datu Magat Salamat, belongs to the country’s Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources. It was on what the Philippine Coast Guard called a humanitarian and livelihood mission: bringing fuel subsidies to Filipino fishing boats so they could keep working in waters the Philippines considers its own. The ship was about 54 nautical miles, roughly 100 kilometers, off the coast of Palawan province when the encounter happened, well within the country’s exclusive economic zone.
According to the Philippine Coast Guard, the Chinese vessel, identified as CCG-21585, first cut across the stern of the Filipino ship at around 11:04 a.m. local time, passing within about 10 meters, or 33 feet. Nine minutes later, it repeated the maneuver, this time making contact. Video released by the Philippine Coast Guard captured the moments before impact, with crew members shouting “brace for impact.” The collision left the ship’s starboard side damaged: railings bent and torn loose, metal support structures deformed, and equipment and debris scattered across the deck. No one was hurt, but Philippine Coast Guard Commandant Adm. Ronnie Gil Gavan ordered additional ships and aircraft to the area to check on the crew and make sure the vessel could continue safely.
The Philippine Coast Guard did not mince words in its account, calling the incident a deliberate strike on a civilian government ship and accusing China of violating international rules for avoiding collisions at sea, a 2016 international tribunal ruling on the South China Sea, and the broader United Nations treaty that governs the world’s oceans.
China’s version of events looks very different. Its coast guard said it was carrying out routine law enforcement work near Sabina Shoal, an area both countries claim, when the Philippine vessel ignored repeated warnings, suddenly changed course, and sped up in a way that put it in the path of the Chinese ship. Beijing said its own crew acted professionally throughout and that responsibility for the collision rests with the Philippine side.
It is a familiar back-and-forth for anyone who has followed the increasingly tense standoff in these waters. China claims sovereignty over nearly the entire South China Sea, a claim so broad that it overlaps with waters the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, and other countries consider their own. In 2016, an international tribunal ruled that China’s claim had no basis under the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea, but Beijing has never accepted that decision and has continued to assert control through its coast guard and, at times, its navy.
This year alone has brought several similar flashpoints. In July, the Philippines accused Chinese ships of firing water cannons at government vessels near Scarborough Shoal on back-to-back days, and separately said a Philippine Navy crew member was struck on the head with a wooden baton during a tense encounter at Second Thomas Shoal. In March, a Chinese navy frigate closed in dangerously on a Philippine landing ship near Thitu Island in the Spratly Islands, coming close enough that the two vessels nearly collided. And in August 2025, a Chinese coast guard cutter and a Chinese navy destroyer actually collided with each other while chasing a Philippine patrol boat near Scarborough Shoal, a mishap that Manila said badly damaged the Chinese cutter.
What makes Friday’s incident notable isn’t that it’s unprecedented. It’s that the pattern keeps repeating, almost predictably, even as both sides know the world is watching. Fishing boats and government resupply vessels have become the recurring flashpoint, because they represent the practical, everyday reality of who actually controls these waters, regardless of what treaties or tribunals say on paper. Every time a fuel delivery mission turns into a shoving match at sea, it becomes another data point in a dispute that has resisted years of diplomacy.
For now, neither country has signaled a change in approach. The Philippines has continued sending its fisheries and coast guard vessels into the disputed areas as a way of asserting its rights, even knowing confrontations are likely. China has continued treating those missions as intrusions into its own waters. Friday’s collision caused property damage but no injuries, and the Philippine vessel was still able to receive help from other ships sent to the scene. Whether the next encounter ends the same way is, as always in these waters, an open question.

Shipki La and the Battle Over the History of China-India Trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:14:00 UTC
02:14:00 KST

After a six-year hiatus, the China-India border trade via Shipki Pass, a 3,930-meter pass in Himachal Pradesh’s Kinnaur district, resumed on August 1, 2026. After the 2020 Galwan military standoff, the border trade from this pass, often called the “Gateway to Tibet,” was suspended. With limited operations and economic scope but significant political symbolism, the resumption of border trade has also rejuvenated interest in the competing legitimacy narratives over the Tibet question.
According to China’s state-affiliated think tanks and media, border trade via the Shipki L Pass dates to the 7th to 9th centuries when the Tubo Empire reigned over the plateau. China frames trade along this route as a sub-set of the Silk Road. Between the 14th and early 20th centuries, Chinese tellings claim Tibet as a commercial bridge between China and South Asia, while in the late 18th century, the Qing Dynasty of China took measures to standardize trade activities between Tibet and its neighboring countries, for “better management” of Tibet.
As per the Chinese accounts, the “peaceful liberation” of Tibet in 1951 and the signing of the Panchsheel Pact led to the abolishment of India’s trade “privileges” in Tibet and the formalization of a new paradigm for Indo-Tibetan trade.
China claims to have set Sino-Indian border trade free from unequal terms set by colonial rule, ushering in an era of normalized development. Cut to the present: the reopening of Shipki La Pass, despite the minuscule trade volume, is received by Chinese media as a welcome move toward improving China-India strategic ties.
Every aspect of the Chinese reading of history sidelines the Tibetan side of the story. For starters, what the Chinese narrative misses is the independent agency Tibet exercised before 1951.
By contrast, Tibetan scholars characterize Shipki Pass as a major route for trade and cultural exchange between Indian territories and Tibet, independent of Chinese involvement. Consistent with Tibet’s claim to political and commercial autonomy, historical records describe Shipki Pass as a crucial route connecting Tibet with the Kingdom of Bushahar, Ladakh, and Kashmir. The exchange across the regions, involving a variety of products, was governed by gamgya, a traditional informal oath of mutual trust that was respected and maintained across generations.
However, with the development of modern state infrastructure on either side of Shipki Pass and growing geopolitical disputes culminating in the Sino-Indian War in 1962, the centuries-old trade system was fractured.
The Tibetan accounts also challenge the Chinese manipulation of history to appropriate the Shipki Pass trade route into a meta-narrative of the Silk Road. The commentaries consistent with the Tibetan narrative challenge the engulfing of Tibet in Chinese historical narratives as a simple commercial bridge, stripping it of its agency and independent existence.
Tibetan scholars argue that it was the PRC’s administrative and military consolidation post 1951 that led to the dismantling of traditional trade and transit networks, not the British colonial disruption. The PRC’s normalization with India involved the isolation of Tibet and the enforcement of new restrictions on previously autonomous trade practices between India and Tibet
This is not a dispute over mere historical fact-checking. It leads to the question of who holds legitimacy over Tibet, and the framing of the India-China-Tibet relationship since the 1950s.
The re-opening of Shipki Pass – often framed in terms of the overall China-India relationship – is seeing one version of history eclipse the other. Popular media crowds out the complicated, contesting narratives and historical claims by constructing a more attractive narrative around boosting local trade, development, and restoration of ancient ties. Given the meager economic value of this barter-driven border trade, the Chinese media has woven the narrative around regional livelihood, the possibility of infrastructure development, and building mutual trust. The Chinese commentary construes the opening as a “revival” of ancient Sino-Indian border trade, with Tibet as a commercial bridge, and part of efforts to eliminate the colonial inequalities after the “liberation of Tibet.”
Over the last few years, the construction of border village resettlement projects, combining civilian housing with military and surveillance infrastructure, in the Tibet Autonomous Region near the Shipki Pass has gained momentum. These villages help give physical form to China’s version of the story, elevating ancient Sino-Indian trade ties over India-Tibet exchanges. Expanding beyond academic and journalistic narratives, Beijing is consolidating its rendition of Tibet as a commercial bridge through trade resumption and border infrastructure.
The reopening of Shipki Pass matters for reasons beyond trade resumption and China-India diplomacy. It highlights the disputes over sovereignty, history, and measures to consolidate control over the border. As it turns out, the trade diplomacy along the Sino-Indian border is less about trade and more about whose history triumphs.

Auto industry urges Trump to bar Chinese automakers in U.S. ahead of Xi visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:11:39 UTC
02:11:39 KST

The American automotive industry wants President Donald Trump to maintain policies that make it difficult for Chinese automakers to operate in the U.S. — or even ban them altogether.
In a letter to Trump dated Thursday and viewed by CNBC, groups representing major facets of the U.S. automotive industry — from franchised dealers and suppliers to domestic and foreign automakers — urged the president to "maintain policies that keep the door firmly shut to Chinese automakers seeking to sell, import or manufacture vehicles inside the U.S."
"The automotive sector is foundational to our advanced manufacturing and defense base, with the capacity and workforce to respond during a national emergency. Once that base is hollowed out, it can't be rebuilt overnight," the letter reads.
The letter comes ahead of Trump's expected visit next week with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, as well as Trump last week saying he would permit Chinese automakers to move manufacturing to the U.S.
"If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I'd be OK with it," Trump said Sept. 11 on Fox News' "The Ingraham Angle."
The letter argues that allowing Chinese automakers to manufacture in the U.S. would "undermine fair competition and jeopardize the progress" the administration has made in preventing "Chinese dominance in key industries." Chinese automakers are heavily subsidized by their government and are rapidly expanding outside of China to other countries.
The letter is the latest in a string of messages from the automotive industry to the Trump administration, but this time represented a more unified coalition.
It was signed by leaders of six trade associations that represent every major automaker operating in the U.S., including Tesla and foreign automakers, as well as the nation's roughly 17,000 franchised dealers.

Brazil’s Lula announces higher welfare payments and free weight-loss jabs ahead of election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:10:37 UTC
02:10:37 KST

Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced a 15% increase in the country’s main cash-transfer programme for poor families, as well as free weight-loss jabs, prompting criticism from opponents who say the moves are electorally motivated just two weeks before the presidential election.
On 4 October, the leftwing incumbent will face the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who has been gaining ground in recent weeks.
The rise in the monthly payment, from about £98 to £113, that he announced on Thursday is due to take effect on 19 October, just before the likely runoff vote on 25 October.
The increase is expected to benefit between 15% and 20% of voters in what promises to be one of the closest ever presidential races in Latin America’s largest country.
Lula said it was not really an increase, but an adjustment in line with inflation to “protect the purchasing power of the most vulnerable families”, but his opponents have criticised its timing so close to the election.
Flávio Bolsonaro called it an “act of desperation” after polls showed him gaining ground – although the most recent survey, released on Thursday night, still showed Lula numerically ahead despite the technical tie. The senator added that Lula was trying to “buy the votes of the poor”.
Created in 2003 during his first term as president, the programme, called Bolsa Família, was a flagship cash-transfer policy that helped lift millions of families out of poverty during his first two terms.
Currently, families with an income of up to £32 per person are eligible, covering about 50 million people, or roughly 27 million of voting age.
The programme has long been fiercely criticised by rightwing politicians, including by Jair Bolsonaro, although he kept it in place during his presidency.
On the eve of the 2022 election, Bolsonaro announced a 50% increase in the monthly payment, prompting Lula’s campaign to file a case with the electoral court alleging abuse of political power and electoral use of the state machinery.
The similarities have sparked a debate between those who say Lula is doing the same thing Bolsonaro did four years ago, and others who argue that the two cases are different.
The journalist Miriam Leitão wrote for O Globo that although both Bolsonaro and Lula made the adjustments “out of electoral interest”, the current incumbent’s increase is in fact limited to inflation over the past four years, during which there had been no adjustment.
She also noted that Bolsonaro’s increase had an expiry date – precisely at the end of the electoral period – while Lula’s is permanent.
Victor Escobar, a researcher at the Laboratory of Parties, Elections and Comparative Politics, agreed. He said that although Lula, like his predecessor, is also being criticised for unveiling a package of benefits on the eve of the election – including a promise to distribute weight-loss jabs free of charge through the public health system – Bolsonaro’s measures were “even more irresponsible from a budgetary point of view”.
In addition to increasing benefits for poor families, Bolsonaro introduced temporary monthly payments of up to £727 for two groups that broadly formed part of his support base, taxi drivers and truck drivers, along with a series of other social benefits whose projected impact on the budget was so large that critics dubbed them the “kamikaze” package.
Escobar acknowledged that Lula’s intention was also electoral, but said that, as long as the measures comply with the law, “it’s something entirely expected when we’re talking about an incumbent running for re-election, who will try to use the legal mechanisms available to improve their voting numbers”.
Some electoral law experts have said that an inflation adjustment is not, in principle, prohibited, but another far-right candidate, the influencer Renan Santos, filed a case with the electoral court seeking to suspend the increase until the president-elect takes office. Although critical of the measure, Flávio Bolsonaro has not done the same, reportedly because of concern about the impact such a move could have among voters who benefit from the programme.

Need to state policy intent clearly while notifying rules, guidelines: Official
