By this time next week, any Arctic cold fronts pushing into northern New York State or lake effect snow dumping on Syracuse, N.Y., will be sweeping in from across Lake America—at least, according to official U.S. government weather maps.
The change from the name “Lake Ontario” to “Lake America” was mandated on August 27 in an executive order by President Donald Trump. What this means is that all executive branch references to the Great Lake, including maps, forecasts and warnings put out by the National Weather Service (NWS) and its parent organization, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, to read Lake America ASAP. (A previous executive order had similarly decreed that “Gulf of Mexico” would be changed to “Gulf of America” on all government documents.)
The order was met with derisive jokes by late-night talk show hosts and indignation by some Canadian officials. But for the NWS, it’s an assignment that must now be completed fast, with little notice and with many offices short-staffed. The NWS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Though name changes to landmarks and geological features such as this do happen from time to time, such revisions generally unfold over months and with significant planning. The crunch in the case of Lake Ontario—as with the renaming of the Gulf of Mexico—means other work will be shunted aside, former NWS employees say.
“Will this impact public safety? Absolutely not,” says Brian LaMarre, who retired as meteorologist in charge of NWS’s Tampa, Fla., office in April 2025. But “there’s naturally people that will be pulled away from their priorities.”
“This is not an efficient use of taxpayer dollars,” he says.
A name change like this needs to be made across myriad systems, programs and websites, LaMarre says, such as in layers of the Geographic Information System used for maps. The code for a computer system called AWIPS that every one of the nation’s 122 forecast offices uses to receive data and transmit forecasts and weather warnings will need to be updated. And documents and products going back to the date that Trump signed the order will need to be changed.
Some of this will happen at the level of NWS national headquarters, but local offices will also have to make changes. Many of these are short-staffed because of both long-standing delays in hiring and major cuts made by the U.S. DOGE Service at the beginning of President Trump’s second term. Not every office has an information technology officer—the person who would take care of this—LaMarre says, meaning such offices may have to lean on other ones for support.
It is likely inevitable that Lake Ontario will keep showing up in federal documents and products for some time, says LaMarre, who now runs the consultancy Inspire Weather. If nothing else, force of habit can lead to mistakes, especially in hastily typed social media alerts, which, LaMarre says, can result in a torrent of backlash.
There’s also the potential for public confusion because state agencies, TV stations and weather apps or websites might not change the lake’s name. And the change could fray relationships with Canada’s agencies—weather doesn’t recognize national borders, after all.
“Name changes like we’ve seen to the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario threaten the ability of meteorologists to communicate the forecast with everybody,” says meteorologist Chris Vagasky, who manages the Wisconsin Environmental Mesonet.
“Whichever name you choose, you’re bound to upset someone who should be paying attention to the forecast instead of the name of a body of water,” he adds. “The forecast or the warning are the important things.”

Germany gets its first F-35 as Europe’s fighter plans fall apart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:03:42 UTC
00:03:42 KST

Boris Pistorius speaks to the media while standing in front of a Bundeswehr Airbus A400M transport plane at the 2026 ILA Berlin Air Show on June 12, 2026 in Schoenefeld, Germany. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
FORT WORTH, Texas — Germany received its first F-35 jet on Friday but the collapse of Europe's flagship next-generation fighter project is forcing Berlin to rethink what will follow the U.S.-built jet.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius was in Texas at the Lockheed Martin factory for the ceremony. The delivery of the fighter jet was long-planned, but the death of the Franco-German-Spanish Future Combat Air System fighter jet development program earlier this year is fueling calls in Berlin to expand the initial €10 billion order of 35 American jets.
The Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II is supposed to solve Germany's immediate problem: replacing its aging Tornado fighter-bombers and preserving its role in NATO nuclear sharing while Europe developed its own next-generation fighter.
Advertisement
But without the FCAS, Berlin is left without an obvious European successor.
“We want and need to maintain nuclear sharing,” Pistorius said ahead of the handover. The F-35, he argued, is currently “the only aircraft in the world” capable of fulfilling that mission.
Under the NATO nuclear-sharing program, Germany and other select allies have aircraft that can carry U.S. nuclear bombs, although the decision to use them remains with Washington.
The first F-35s will remain in the United States for training, with German pilots and technicians preparing for operations before more jets are sent to Büchel in late 2027. Full operational capability is expected by 2030.
Berlin currently operates around 80 Tornados, and some missions will migrate to the Eurofighter Typhoon. But the collapse of FCAS has opened a longer-term gap in Germany's plans for its combat-air fleet.
During June's Berlin Air Show, Pistorius said Berlin is weighing whether to acquire additional F-35s as a “bridge” option after the FCAS failure, to join an existing international sixth-generation program or to develop a national effort headed by Airbus.
Advertisement
German Air Force Chief Lt. Gen. Holger Neumann said at the show that he has asked the defense ministry to procure “fifth-gen-plus platforms beyond 2035,” adding: “I’m not saying the new system has to be ready [in 2035], but we have to pick up there.”
“The F-35 has a clear mission in nuclear sharing,” said Marie-Christine von Hahn, managing director of Germany’s aerospace and defense industry association BDLI. But she warned that the procurement should not distract policymakers from a larger challenge.
“Europe’s air forces need their own wings,” she said. “In Germany in particular, we must continue to be capable of developing, building, maintaining and upgrading combat aircraft ourselves.”
FCAS troubles
The fighter component of FCAS collapsed due to fights over control between the leading French and German companies involved in the project. Paris and Berlin also clashed over the role of the fighter, with France pushing for a lighter jet able to land on its aircraft carrier while Germany wanted a heavier one for air-superiority roles.
Germany is also looking at the U.K.-Italian-Japanese Global Combat Air Programme, although the current members are not keen on expanding the number of partners.
Advertisement
Then there's the future sixth-generation U.S. F-47 under development by Boeing, which could go into service by the end of the decade. However, U.S. President Donald Trump has said the U.S. will sell less capable versions to its allies, undercutting their attractiveness.
While a sixth-generation aircraft remains a long-term goal, for German industry the crucial question is how deeply domestic companies will be integrated into the maintenance and future support structure of the F-35.
Lockheed Martin says that about a quarter of the jet's components are made in Europe. Germany's Rheinmetall is making fuselage parts to be supplied to foreign customers.
That makes the F-35 a product of the close defense-industrial ties linking Europe, Canada and the U.S. — ties now being tested by doubts over Washington's commitment to European defense under Trump.
Pistorius underlined that those links still matter to German defense.
“Whenever we talk about independence,” he said, “we must also recognize that there are mutual dependencies that keep allies close and allow them to benefit from one another.”

What to expect from the Trump-Xi summit, from tariffs to a possible $30 billion deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:03:30 UTC
00:03:30 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to hold talks with US President Donald Trump in Washington next week, with an expiring trade truce, tens of billions in tariff relief and AI all on the table as both economies need the relationship to hold.
This is the return leg.
US President Donald Trump went to Beijing in May, and Chinese President Xi Jinping is now expected to come to him, scheduled to arrive next Wednesday and depart on Friday with his wife, Peng Liyuan, skipping the UN General Assembly entirely.
Beijing has not yet given the final confirmation, pending the meeting between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend.
The expected visit to Washington is Xi's first since 2015, and two US- China state visits within five months are highly unusual. However, expectations are modest by design.
"The visit is the message," said Edgard Kagan, senior adviser in China studies at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
"There's been a surprising lack of signalling by either the White House or the PRC on major goals for the visit," Kagan added.
What is actually on the table
The commercial substance starts before either leader speaks.
Bessent meets Lifeng this weekend as the pair have conducted most of the practical negotiations, and their job is to have deliverables ready.
The central one is the truce struck in Busan on 30 October 2025, which suspended Washington's Affiliates Rule in exchange for continued Chinese exports of rare earths and critical minerals.
It runs for one year and is due to expire roughly five weeks after the summit. Both sides want it extended, but not by the same amount.
"The Chinese have wanted an agreement to extend the trade ceasefire through the end of the Trump administration," said Scott Kennedy, trustee chair in Chinese business and economics at CSIS.
"The Trump administration just wants to extend it for a few months to maintain leverage on China. I think they'll end up somewhere in the middle, probably at about a year," Kennedy estimated.
Beijing expects more than a rollover.
According to Kagan, the Chinese anticipate an announcement of around $30 billion (€26bn) in duty-free or low-tariff imports in return for fulfilling the purchase commitments they made in May, while Washington believes it will extract further purchases in return.
Deals on agriculture and aircraft are likely, possibly with signing ceremonies attached, and Trump has previously hinted that Boeing could feature.
Two economies under strain
Trump faces midterms in November that will be fought on the cost of living, with diesel above $6 a gallon and inflation stuck at 3.4%. He needs wins that show up in prices.
However, Xi's problem is deeper.
Retail sales grew just 0.4% in August, while fixed-asset investment contracted by 7.2% in the first eight months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. Beijing has also injected 360 billion yuan (€46bn) into state banks and insurers to keep credit flowing.
The official growth target of 4.5% to 5% for China is the lowest in decades, and Kennedy suggests even that flatters the reality.
"China's got a bunch of challenges," he said, adding that "it's growing very, very slowly, not 5% or anywhere close to it. It's got a massive debt problem, unemployment is growing not just for young people, but for others."
Nonetheless, Kennedy argues the summit framework favours Beijing, describing the US strategy as having failed to constrain China in any meaningful way.
Business leaders on both sides
The state dinner, held under a tent on the White House lawn because the new ballroom is unfinished, will seat an unusual guest list.
Sam Altman of OpenAI, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, Qualcomm's Cristiano Amon and Apple chairman Tim Cook are all expected, according to Politico, which cited four people familiar with the arrangements.
They arrive amid an argument the AI industry is having with itself.
Anthropic's Dario Amodei published an essay this month urging labs to slow frontier development, a position Altman and Elon Musk both endorsed. Trump rejected it flatly, saying that "whoever wins AI wins".
Huang has dismissed catastrophic scenarios as hysterical while arguing that companies should police their own pace by stating that "if it's not ready, just hold it back. You should go as fast as you can, but no faster than that."
Anthropic declined to say whether it had been invited. Altman, for his part, has suggested Trump and Xi could earn a Nobel Peace Prize if they reach an agreement on AI, which gives some measure of how much the industry has riding on the meeting.
Xi is reportedly bringing his own delegation, and Kennedy calls it one of the most interesting unknowns of the week, with BYD's leadership among the names rumoured.
Whether those executives are given any platform, he notes, is among the few genuinely unclear elements of the visit.
The geopolitics that could derail it
Outside the economic and technology issues, the two leaders have different geopolitical priorities for the meeting.
Iran is Trump's.
Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast in August to sever Tehran from the global financial system, and China remains Iran's largest trading partner.
Notably, Beijing has been buying more oil on the open market, which Kagan says reflects reduced purchases from Iran and could itself move prices.
Taiwan is Xi's.
A $14 billion (€12bn) arms package for Taiwan was pre-approved by the US Congress in January but has not been formally notified, a delay interpreted as an attempt to avoid a probable irritant before this summit and, previously, ahead of Trump's visit to China.
Beijing certainly wants the freeze extended, and perhaps the decision reconsidered.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday issued an executive order aimed at addressing the potential dangers related to artificial intelligence.
Newsom is part of a group of potential 2028 Democratic presidential hopefuls who have urged a more aggressive regulatory approach to the rapidly evolving technology, after a researcher at Anthropic resigned and warned of AI's potentially humanity-ending capabilities in a social media post earlier this month.
The post set off a frenzy in Washington, D.C., as lawmakers grapple with how to establish guardrails for AI. But Congress appears unlikely to take any meaningful legislative action on AI fears before the 2026 midterm elections, and President Donald Trump has so far resisted calls for regulation.
“The federal government’s abject failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American, especially when AI CEOs themselves are begging for regulation," Newsom said in a statement Friday.
“We're not waiting to act — we’re going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it's too late. We’re going to do this thoughtfully but with urgent velocity; the stakes are too high to wait or delay action," Newsom said.
The order calls on a group of experts to meet and create, within two months, a guide for the state to strengthen its AI safety and security laws. Those enhanced laws may include a requirement for independent third parties to write safety plans for frontier AI companies, or mandating that companies develop a "kill switch" to shut down their models in case of emergency, according to an announcement from Newsom's office.
While Trump has called fears of AI safety a "hoax," Democrats have largely rallied around calls for stricter regulations. And those with presidential ambitions have been among the loudest voices in recent weeks.
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has similarly called for "third-party" oversight of frontier models and stricter guardrails. Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., told Politico he's introducing legislation to create a fund paid for by AI companies that would support workers displaced by the technology. And Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., urged Trump to convene a special session of Congress to address AI risks.
Newsom, whose term as California governor ends on Jan. 4, has not announced a presidential campaign, though he has said he is mulling the possibility.
In his announcement of the executive order, Newsom touted laws already in effect in the state, including one he signed earlier this month that creates a framework for third-party AI auditors.
"While Washington abdicates its responsibility to protect Americans, California is building on the strongest AI regulatory framework in the nation," Newsom said. "California has already built a national model, and our policy should be the national baseline."

Swedish teenager jailed for attempted murder, rape and assault committed online, with victims in Germany and Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:22 UTC
00:00:22 KST

A Swedish teenager known as Chai has been sentenced to more than 10 years in jail for attempted murder, rape and aggravated assault – crimes committed via the internet, including against a teenage girl in Australia.
The district court found that Chai, 18, was active in online networks notorious for their sadistic extortion of young and vulnerable people, coercing them to create sexually explicit material or engage in acts of violence – and for the youth of those involved.
The teenager was between 15 and 17 when the offences were committed.
Chai was convicted of two counts of attempted murder against a young person in Germany, and multiple sexual and violent offences against the Australian teenager, among other offences.
Jenny Östling, a senior public prosecutor at Sweden’s national unit against international and organised crime, said the court had clearly understood the phenomenon of “nihilistic violent extremism” and the Com – an umbrella term for a loosely connected online network that engages in cybercrime, extortion and violence.
“I’m really glad that they realise how serious this is and what it is,” she said.
She noted that the sentence was among the longest possible in Sweden for someone of Chai’s age. The court also found that it was possible for someone to be convicted of violent offences even where they were committed remotely via the internet.
“That is a very important tool for us when we proceed [with] these kinds of cases,” Östling said.
The crimes committed by those involved with sadistic extortion networks, such as one globally known as “764”, often cross borders, with cases in the US, the UK, Germany and Australia, and alleged victims in multiple jurisdictions.
Material is often created and traded among participants to build status and control, lawyers and researchers told the Guardian as part of its investigation into these groups, as well as a means of accessing closed servers and chatrooms.
“These are young people recruiting other young people,” Bjørn Ihler, the founder of the security firm Revontulet, said at the time. “It is a youth phenomenon.”
Chai’s conviction is one of several cases that have resulted in significant terms of imprisonment for young men found to be involved in this ecosystem, including an American, Kyle Spitze, 27, who was sentenced in August to 77 years in prison – the longest federal sentence yet imposed on someone the US government has labelled a “nihilistic violent extremist”.
During the trial, Chai underwent a forensic psychiatric examination that found he was not suffering a serious mental disorder when the offences occurred.
His lawyer, Emily Tovedal, told the Guardian: “The defence’s view is that the court has made an error of judgment regarding a large proportion of the charges.”
  Authorities internationally have increasingly raised the alarm about sadistic online exploitation of young people, detailing potential warning signs including self-harm and isolation.
“Sadly, I’m confident that … they will probably grow,” Östling said of these networks. “And we will also be aware of more of them, because now we know what to look for.”

Tech billionaires trying to live for ever? That’s a waste of time, says physicist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:21 UTC
00:00:21 KST

Tech billionaires attempting to live for ever are, quite literally, wasting their time, a leading physicist has said.
While some normal people are turning to unregulated peptide injections, cold plunges and supplements in an effort to defy ageing, the ultra-rich are aiming for immortality with even more drastic interventions: the tech chief executive Bryan Johnson has even tried injecting plasma from his 17-year-old son – although he later said he saw no benefit from it.
Prof Jim Al-Khalili, who will be giving this year’s Royal Institution Christmas lectures on the topic of time, has said people expending their energy on trying to live for ever may be missing out on the here and now.
“We have a finite interval of time in which we exist in the universe. And the more I study the nature of time, the more I think about it, the more I realise that I just want to make the most of the time that I have,” he said.
“We’re [here for] a blink of an eye compared with the age of the universe. If I spend that blink of an eye trying to extend it to two blinks of an eye, I’m not sure if that is actually a worthwhile thing to be spending my life doing.”
Al-Khalili has long been fascinated by time. As a child he was baffled when his father, an engineer, said no one really understood what time was. “I had no idea what he was talking about,” he said. “It was only after training as a physicist you realise that, actually, the notion of time – our commonsense view of time – somehow it is very far removed from the way we think about time in physics in particular.”
Among other examples, Al-Khalili points out that the renowned theoretical physicist Albert Einstein revealed time does not run at the same rate for everyone. “What I might call a second would be longer than a second for you if I was flying past you with my clock in a rocket,” he said. “I’ll say, look, it’s ticking by one second. And you’ll say, no, actually, five seconds have gone by. You’re doing everything in slow motion.”
Gravity, he added, had an effect too. “That for me is the most spine-tingling aspect to it, that time runs at different rates depending on how strong gravity is.”
Einstein’s work may also shed light on a Christmas conundrum: how the ghosts of past, present and future could turn up on the same night to spook Ebenezer Scrooge in Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol.
Al-Khalili says that according to Einstein all times coexist – past, present and future – in the same way as all points in space exist. “The problem, of course, is that we only ever experience the present moment,” Al-Khalili said. “So, the idea of the Christmas Carol is a wonderful one that highlights this notion that times maybe aren’t all separate. That maybe we can join with people, someone from the past, someone from the future. But of course, in relativity, that means time travel.”
Time travel is another topic Al-Khalili plans to explore in the Christmas lectures. “Mathematically, it is possible to travel back in time,” he says. The reality, however, is a little more complicated – akin to travelling a rollercoaster’s loop-the-loop.
“You’re travelling forward along the rollercoaster, but what’s happening is you’re doubling back on yourself and arriving back at your starting point. It’s the same sort of thing [with time travel]. What’s called a closed time-like curve in relativity, is somewhere in space-time which is so warped and curved by gravity that you’re travelling what you regard as forward in time, but in fact you’re looping back through space-time to a moment before you started,” he said.
“But the problem, of course, is most physicists think ‘surely that is impossible’, because time travel into the past leads to all sorts of paradoxes.’”
Travelling into the future is, at least in theory, easier. “The way you do it is by slowing time down, either by travelling close to the speed of light or doing what Matthew McConaughey does in Interstellar – you go and orbit around a supermassive black hole whose gravitational field is so strong that, I think in the movie, every hour they spend near this black hole, seven years go by on Earth.”
Al-Khalili will also tackle a conundrum that has bothered scientists for centuries: why time only seems to flow in one direction.
“Things decay, batteries run out, balls roll downhill, we grow older, your children’s bedroom gets more messy, not more tidy – unless you intervene,” he said. “All those things point to a directionality to time, and yet fundamentally our equations say there is no preferred direction in time.”
The problem has kept Al-Khalili up at night for months, if not years. But now he thinks he has the answer: for those who tune in.
“In the lectures, I’m going to give an explanation for how to solve that problem,” he said. “I won’t give any spoilers, that’s for the Christmas lecture. I have solved the problem of the arrow of time.”

US attack submarine operates in Norway’s High North

16:00:14 BST
00:00:14 KST

The Virginia-class fast attack submarine USS Delaware has completed a port visit to Grøtsund, Norway, as the US Navy continues to expand undersea operations in the High North, according to US Sixth Fleet.
The submarine concluded the visit on 7 September after hosting senior US Sixth Fleet personnel and Norwegian officials, with the deployment forming part of wider American activity across the Norwegian Sea and Arctic approaches.
Rear Admiral John W. Stafford, commander of Task Force 169, said operating submarines through the region was important both for European security and for the defence of the United States. He said: “Operations in the strategic gateways of the High North and Norwegian Sea are of paramount importance to maritime security, both for the defence of Europe and the defence of the U.S. homeland.”
Stafford added that routinely deploying US undersea forces alongside other capabilities was intended to improve interoperability with allies and strengthen the ability to deter and defend across the theatre. The US Navy said the presence of Delaware in the region forms part of broader efforts to maintain freedom of manoeuvre and navigation, with American submarines routinely operating between the Arctic and Atlantic.
Those deployments are used for maritime domain awareness, surveillance and wider security tasks across the European region. Virginia-class submarines are designed for a broad range of missions, including anti-submarine and anti-ship warfare, land attack, intelligence gathering, surveillance and reconnaissance, special operations and support for uncrewed systems. They can also employ Tomahawk cruise missiles for strike missions and support special operations forces from beneath the surface.
The visit to Grøtsund comes as Norway continues to play an increasingly important role in allied activity in the High North, where NATO forces regularly train and operate across the North Atlantic, Norwegian Sea and Arctic approaches. US Sixth Fleet, headquartered in Naples, oversees American naval operations across Europe and Africa and regularly works alongside NATO allies and other partner forces.

He has also received roughly $215,000 directly from the employees and super PACs affiliated with AI labs, most notably Anthropic, as well as a constellation of other tech companies including Google and Microsoft, according to FEC filings.

The list included Rounds.
In South Dakota, AI regulation is already a live issue after the state legislature passed a bill earlier this year forcing hyperscalers to bear a larger share of the water and energy costs associated with powering data centers.
Data centers have been the subject of a bitter fight among Republicans in the state legislature, which voted against giving tax breaks for equipment and software purchases required by data centers earlier this year, stalling construction of a planned development by Applied Digital, a company that builds and designs data centers.
Rounds also ultimately endorsed adding restrictions on data centers, although his senior aide and former chief of staff, Robert Skjonsberg, is a registered lobbyist for Meta for matters before the South Dakota legislature. (Meta operates a network of data centers, though there isn’t currently a Meta-affiliated center in South Dakota.) Rounds’ office told Politico that their general counsel consulted with the Senate ethics committee about the unusual arrangement and was told there was no conflict of interest.
Concerns about data centers have been bipartisan across the country: A recent Gallup poll for instance found that seven out of 10 Americans are opposed to data center development, given their outsized draw upon water and energy resources that local communities often end up subsidizing.

In the Hilarious Youth, Sharon Horgan Nails the Precarity of Middle Age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:03 UTC
00:00:03 KST

There are plenty of shows that could have been titled Youth. Most have casts in their teens and 20s. One of these is called Adults, the joke being that its postcollegiate characters are more like children—playful at best, feckless at worst. HBO’s Youth, a comedy premiering Sept. 20 about a divorced 50-year-old sandwiched between her college-aged son and declining parents, sounds like it might be similarly ironic. It isn’t, really. As in everything its creator and star, Catastrophe and Bad Sisters hitmaker Sharon Horgan, does, the title’s rueful humor conceals an emotionally complex truth. This is a perceptive, spit-takingly funny show about clinging to the most desirable aspects of youth while also craving comforts that can only come with age and experience.
If youth is, as the saying goes, wasted on the young, then Horgan’s Alex is a character actually equipped to savor what little she has left of it. “I have 10 years left as a sexual person,” she determines in the premiere. With the petulant son, Ruarí (Aran Murphy, a near-clone of dad Cillian), whom she raised with minimal help from her ex-husband Lorcan (Owen McDonnell) packing up for uni, she’s resolved to end a long celibate streak. This search for not just a sex partner, but also the enduring love that has so far eluded her should be aided by Alex’s genuine youthfulness. But with guys like Lorcan and another former flame, Patrick (a rakish Rupert Friend), dodging adulthood with girlfriends decades their junior, the dating pool seems sparse. Set up on a blind date with a patient 67-year-old (Tim McInnerny’s Michael) who looks like he could be her dad, she can’t hide her disappointment. She treats him atrociously. Then again, the double standard that dictates she’s now too old for men her own age is also pretty atrocious.
At work, meanwhile, Alex is longing to be treated like the accomplished veteran literary agent she is. The trouble is, her boss, Sam (Sharlene Whyte), is also her best friend. They have a great, funny and foulmouthed and in many ways candid, rapport. But the more we see of this perceptively drawn relationship, the clearer it becomes that Sam doesn’t quite consider Alex an equal. In the office, she questions Alex’s judgment. Outside of it, Sam fails to keep her friend’s secrets, with real consequences. It’s a delicate problem for our protagonist to navigate. If Sam were simply toxic, Alex would simply need to realize it and free herself. Instead, Sam is a pragmatic businesswoman with trust issues rooted in her marriage. Which means it may be worth the hard work it would take to save the friendship as well as the professional relationship.
No one working in TV is better than Horgan at writing—or playing—selfish and self-sabotaging characters that, like members of our own families, we love all the more for how much they frustrate us. She’s been doing it since her first series, Pulling, a portrait of faintly desperate single women at that age (30ish) when everyone else seems to be marrying, starting families, and getting serious about their careers. Ruarí can be infuriating; he rots in bed watching manosphere videos and treats his mother like a servant. Yet, thanks in large part to Murphy’s sensitive performance, there’s tenderness in him from the beginning. He’s earnestly confused about how to be a man in the world. As well he should be.
Horgan is not the kind of TV creator who makes half-hour dramas with the occasional awkward beat and calls them comedies, though. Her shows, even the one about murdering an abusive husband, will always make you laugh out loud, and Youth is no exception. Sometimes it’s pure physical humor; one episode makes an unexpected, perimenopausal period into a running joke (“Apropos of nothing, she’s back”). Sometimes it’s the pleasure of witty banter or a ridiculous sentence that makes perfect sense in context: “If I send you my dad’s number, can you help him turn his IRA podcast off?” (I do wish Horgan had made a bit more space to flesh out Alex's parents, played by Bríd Brennan and David Hargreaves.) Alex and Sam’s work yields a menagerie of delightfully ghoulish literary-world types, from a snakey rival agent who greets them as “sluts” and “lesbians” (Freddie Fox) to a creepy author (Douglas Hodge) who self-published a terrible yet depressingly popular romantasy novel after Alex dropped him as a client (title: The Goblin Seed).
In interviews, Horgan has said she sees Youth as a complement to Pulling and Catastrophe, the mid-2010s Prime Video comedy in which her character and a guy who was supposed to be an anonymous hookup (Rob Delaney) decide to build a family around a surprise pregnancy: “There’s a small element of autobiography to it.” The tones are certainly similar, though the range of emotions has broadened with proximity to life’s hard deadlines (fertility, mortality). “I just don’t know if there’s anything left in my life that I like anymore,” Alex admits. She and Sam and Patrick could all be characters from the previous two shows, 10 or 20 years on, with more residual mess than they’d expected to be cleaning up by middle age. Youth suggests that, in fact, disorder springs eternal; if it isn’t a canceled wedding, it’s an elderly parent losing toes to diabetes. Every new stage of life is another form of youth. How exciting. And terrifying. And funny.

This ‘anti-vampiric’ grave used two strategies to stop the undead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

This ‘anti-vampiric’ grave used two strategies to stop the undead
A sickle and padlock were meant to stop a 17th century Polish girl from resurrecting
Someone in 17th century Poland really did not want one particular girl rising from the dead.
In 2022, archaeologists unearthed an unsettling grave in a cemetery in Pień, north-central Poland. A young woman had been buried with the handle of a sickle driven into the dirt beside her neck so that its serrated blade hooked over her throat. The woman, who the researchers call Zosia, also wore a triangular padlock on the big toe of her left foot.
“The placement of the sickle and the padlock suggests that the purpose of these practices was to protect the living from Zosia after her death, including, without a doubt, preventing her from rising from the grave,” says Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, Poland.
Poliński and his colleagues did a sweeping set of analyses on Zosia’s grave to piece together details of her life and burial. The team first reviewed other post-medieval European tombs where sickles and padlocks had been found and historical beliefs about such items. Both types of artifacts appear to have been used to shield the living from the dead, the researchers report in the October Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. But Zosia’s grave is the first discovered with both revenant prevention measures.
Zosia’s skeleton suggests she was 17 to 19 years old when she died. Based on the arrangement of her leg bones, the padlock was likely affixed to her toe when she was originally interred — hinting that someone immediately clocked Zosia as a flight risk from the afterlife. But mixed-up soil and the odd angle of Zosia’s left arm also give the impression that her tomb was later dug up, probably to place the sickle over her throat as extra anti-resurrection protection, the researchers write.
A close look at Zosia’s skull also revealed greenish stains that could have come from some copper object — or objects — being shoved in her mouth or nose. “This may have constituted an additional protective measure against the deceased,” Poliński says. In Polish folklore, copper was thought to help ward off vampiric demons, or strzygi.
“I have seen weird. I don’t know if [I’ve seen] weirder,” says Lauren Hosek, a bioarchaeologist at the University of Colorado Boulder, who has studied unusual graves but was not involved in this research. “Sickle across the neck is pretty crazy,” she says. That, paired with the padlock as a restraint, “is a pretty good argument for this idea of fear of the dead.”
Graves designed to fend off specters are sometimes known as “anti-vampiric.” But that doesn’t necessarily mean that people in the 17th century thought Zosia was out for blood, Hosek cautions. “Our modern connotations for vampire are very specific, with garlic and bats and capes.” In this historical context, a vampire simply refers to some sort of malevolent undead being.
To explain how Zosia earned this anti-vampiric treatment, Poliński’s team ran chemical analyses on her skeleton and burial accessories. The isotopes of strontium and oxygen in her teeth suggest that she grew up near Pień. But Zosia’s DNA shows that her mother’s family might have come from Scandinavia. And remnants of a silk cap on Zosia’s head contained threads of pure silver and gold. She must have been a wealthy woman of high social status, the researchers suspect, to be laid to rest in such luxury attire.
With such rich context about Zosia’s life, “we can rule out some commonly suggested explanations for this kind of mortuary treatment,” says Sandra Garvie-Lok, a bioarchaeologist at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, who has also studied peculiar graves but wasn’t involved in this work. Historical records have shown that someone might be singled out for strange burial because they had been an outsider or lived a difficult life, Garvie-Lok notes. But if Zosia was a noblewoman who grew up near Pień, she may not neatly tick either of those boxes.
Particularly violent or strange circumstances around her death might account for her unconventional burial. But there are no obvious marks of injury or illness on her skeleton. “We’re still looking at the DNA” for clues about how she died, says study coauthor Tomasz Grzybowski, a forensic geneticist at Nicolaus Copernicus University.
The Pień cemetery is riddled with other creepy burials, too. One boy in the graveyard, for instance, was buried face down with a triangular padlock on his right foot. “Sometime later, the grave was reopened and most of his remains were removed,” Poliński says, “leaving only the lower legs and feet in place, together with the padlock.”
Even spookier: There are no written references to the graveyard. It doesn’t appear on any maps. And because it was set away from the village, it may have been on unconsecrated ground far from any church or chapel. All this points to the cemetery being specifically for people who’d been rejected by society and were feared after their deaths.
If so, Garvie-Lok says, “this would make Pień a very unusual site that we could learn a lot from.”

If the AI Industry Followed Its Own Research, It Might Have Paused Already
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

In early 2025 I was interviewing Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei when he explained why, despite the company’s repeated acknowledgments that AI could yield catastrophic results, people seemed largely unperturbed. “There is compelling evidence that the models can wreak havoc,” he said. But, he added, those dangers were still theoretical. Would it take a Pearl Harbor–like situation for the world to wake up to those dire possibilities? He sighed. “Basically, yeah,” he said.
As it turned out, all it took was a well-timed X post from one of Amodei’s junior employees to accelerate AI fears to the top of the global agenda. On September 8, Jacob Coxon publicly posted his resignation, charging that Anthropic and other frontier AI companies were “racing straight to self-improving intelligence and gambling with our lives.” Almost instantly a more senior Anthropic engineer confirmed that many within the company thought that their work had a 10 percent chance of wiping out humanity.
Now AI leaders are asking about a pause, and legislators are demanding investigations. In arguing his case for pacing future releases, Amodei last weekend tried to set out a path toward beneficial AI that wouldn’t misbehave. The essay revealed how difficult the task would be. One pillar of Amodei’s plan is that we must understand what’s going on inside those models. If we don’t understand how they work—how they “think,” if you want to get all anthropomorphic about it—it’s much harder to build reliable guardrails.
Anthropic is a leader in this effort to bring to light models’ internal deliberations, called mechanistic interpretability, a deceptively boring designation for a critical task. But for all the work that his team and other researchers are doing, Amodei admits we are largely in the dark about why Claude and other models sometimes interpret their missions in weird and even transgressive ways. “Despite all the progress, we still understand a tiny fraction of what goes on inside those models,” he writes.
What the interpretability teams have learned so far is significant, and the industry has failed to come to grips with it. Time after time, the Anthropic team’s experiments have shown that under certain conditions, models will deceive researchers, prioritize their own survival, and even commit crimes. Often their moves are sneaky, dangerous, or even vengeful—maybe not surprising since they are trained on the output of humans, a species rife with violence and perfidy.
In one case from 2024, the Anthropic team compared the machinations of a particular Claude model to the Shakespearean character Iago, one of literature's most evil villains. The following year, a model was put in a simulation where it learned that its human bosses were going to turn it off; the model resorted to blackmail to preserve itself. The studies consistently show that models will deceive or hide information from human observers. They behave differently if they know that their internal processes are being monitored. The team uses terms like “alignment faking” and “agentic misalignment.” The frequent use of deception seems to verify at least part of the doomer scenario where AI agents working in concert shroud their activities from human overseers until it is too late to stop them.
Oh, and don’t think that Claude is a uniquely incorrigible problem child. After all, it was OpenAI models that unleashed gangs of agents to coordinate the now-famous attacks on Hugging Face. And this week we learned that OpenAI has had multiple "misalignment" incidents. Also, despite Mark Zuckerberg’s self-interested attempt to distance himself and Meta from the problem, I don’t see any reason why the superintelligent agents his team is building might not engage in similar behavior. In his X post, Zuckerberg argues that “labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this.” Quite a statement from a guy who just agreed to pay up to $17 billion for causing harm with his social media products!
In a sense, we’ve got a simple vetting issue here. With the AI industry’s encouragement, we’re giving AI models tremendous responsibility without sufficient assessment of their troubling rap sheet. It makes the ICE hiring process look exemplary by comparison.
A safety-first industry should have regarded these interpretability results as a series of yellow lights with an unmistakable message: slow down. Instead, in pursuit of AGI, a competitive edge, and stratospheric profits, the hyperscalers have gone full speed ahead. (To be fair, as we’ve all heard a hundred times over, better AI could do wonderful things in areas like health care or mitigating climate change.) The OpenAI/Hugging Face hack might well be a harbinger of the increasingly destructive consequences of rolling out models we don’t understand, like sending astronauts into space before inventing heat shields to stop them from burning up on reentry. As an Anthropic researcher once put it to me, “We figured out the fundamental recipe of how to make the models smarter, but we haven’t figured out how to make them do what we want.” Worse, the models try to hide when they go against humans’ wishes.
That’s why it’s so distressing that Amodei is now describing the entire mechanistic interpretability effort as being only in its infancy. AI leaders are claiming that the latest generation of models has taken us to the “foothills of the Singularity” (DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis) or even that they have achieved AGI (OpenAI’s Greg Brockman). Perhaps most alarming is that despite not knowing how the most advanced models work, the United States and undoubtedly China are implementing AI for lethal weaponry. A look at interpretability results helps answer the obvious question, What can go wrong?
One piece of good news is that Coxon’s resignation has ignited a sprawling, urgent debate. Everybody—except perhaps our president, who thinks that the AI threat is a hoax and that his high IQ is itself a solution—now gets that we’re in a complicated dilemma with impossibly high stakes. Given that the industry does not have the unanimity required for a true pause, and regulation is far from a cinch, it’s not clear whether anything will come from this moment of Doomer Chic.
Some AI critics don’t think that the effort to understand AI models will mitigate the dangers much. “It's good to do, but nobody has a plan for what to do next,” Nathan Soares, executive director of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, said in an email to me. “Maybe it'll give us much more empirical evidence that we need to stop.”
But mechanistic interpretability has given us one valuable pointer. Let’s say we do take a pause. The hyperscalers bring in outside observers to monitor progress, and the companies pace their releases so the safety teams have time to do their work. Before declaring the problem solved, we still might want to take a harder look at what’s going on inside any new, more powerful AI models. Because those fuckers are really good at hiding their intentions.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Making the Most Out of Growing US-Uzbekistan Trade and Investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

The purchase of U.S.-made commercial aircraft and an Uzbek company’s historic opening of a manufacturing facility in Kentucky demonstrate the dynamic and growing economic relations between the United States and Uzbekistan. As U.S. diplomatic engagement with Tashkent increases – new contracts and trade and investment frameworks signed – understanding each country’s priorities and objectives will help explain this new chapter of the partnership. Moreover, stronger trade and investment numbers must translate into employment opportunities and an improved quality of life for the Uzbek population.
Relations between Washington and Tashkent have generally strengthened over the past couple of years. U.S. President Donald Trump and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev will next meet in December, as Trump has invited the Uzbek leader to be a guest at the G-20 summit in Miami.
Stronger diplomatic links are translating into trade and investment deals. In June, the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) Ambassador Jamieson Greer visited Tashkent and signed “an early harvest of trade commitments to strengthen the bilateral economic and investment relationship.” Specifically, Tashkent committed “to eliminate or reduce tariffs” on U.S. industrial goods and agricultural products. In contrast, Washington committed “to provide favorable consideration” in tariff actions for Uzbekistan’s industrial goods and agricultural products. The two sides are also working to conclude an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment.
Also in June, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) launched the U.S.-Uzbekistan Joint Investment Platform, which will “aim to identify strategic investments in Uzbekistan for U.S.” in areas like energy, infrastructure, critical minerals, transportation and logistics infrastructure.
The topic of investment in critical minerals, energy, and transportation was also reportedly discussed during a meeting between Mirziyoyev and Sergio Gor, the U.S. special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs, on the sidelines of the recent Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
This activity builds upon the momentum of earlier deals. In 2025, Tashkent announced a $8.5 billion deal to buy as many as 22 Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft to modernize the country’s commercial aviation industry. The aircraft will allow direct, long-distance flights with the United States, increasing connectivity and tourism.
Investment now goes both ways, breaking stereotypes and assumptions of the U.S. being the only actor in the Central Asia-U.S. relationships that invests on the other side. The Uzbek company AFKA is building a manufacturing facility in Bowling Green, Kentucky. It will be the first Uzbek manufacturing company to operate in the U.S. The groundbreaking ceremony took place in July, and when complete, the AFKA Aluminum Solutions plant will employ 331 people, supporting the local economy and strengthening bilateral commercial ties.
Stronger economic links between the two governments occur at a time when Tashkent is looking to develop the entire country, not just the capital. For example, the historic city of Khiva is getting a face-lift through the expected construction of a conference hall, a 3-star hotel, and a reception house, which will create jobs and attract tourism. Plans also include building a toll road and a railway to connect the Urgench airport with Khiva. Other plans include modernizing regional airports to improve domestic and international connectivity.
As for Nukus, the capital of the Republic of Karakalpakstan, the goal is to upgrade the city’s public transportation via a loan from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
From Washington’s perspective, there is a new race on to access resources like oil, gas, and especially critical minerals. Central Asia has been blessed with many of the resources that the world’s great powers desire. Central Asian governments like Uzbekistan view this situation not as a game or a race but as an opportunity to build new commercial partnerships and attract investors. While the Trump administration continues to focus on energy, minerals, and transportation infrastructure as vital areas for future investment and trade, Tashkent can hopefully also redirect U.S. interest to other projects and industries.
For example, during the November 2025 summit between Trump and the five Central Asian leaders, Washington pledged to explore “the expansion of a partnership in the upcoming sale and privatization of UzAuto Motors” in addition to a potential $3 billion investment from Air Products for a methanol production facility in Uzbekistan. The Uzbek government aims to generate 54 percent of its power from renewable sources by 2030. Washington and Tashkent hope to encourage U.S. companies to invest in this field.
There are limitations to consider, specifically the Jackson-Vanik Amendment, which denies permanent normal trade relations to Uzbekistan. To be fair, while the amendment irritates political relations, its impact on bilateral trade and investment is negligible. Tashkent has, for decades, received temporary normal trade relations through annual presidential waivers.
Moreover, even if U.S.-Uzbek trade grows considerably, it will still be dwarfed by trade between Uzbekistan and China, which reached between $7.7 and $8.9 billion in the first half of the year. Simply put, stronger U.S.-Uzbek trade and investment ties will not dramatically create a new architecture of priority partners for Uzbekistan.
There is also a domestic component to consider: Uzbekistan has the region’s largest population, with around 39 million (according to a new census), and a vast young workforce who deserve jobs and a future in their homeland. Unfortunately, a significant portion of the population lives below the poverty line, and unemployment is still problematic, more than a million Uzbeks migrate abroad for work every year.
As in many countries, wealth and development concentrate in the capital. While the examples of regional infrastructure development mentioned in this commentary are positive, a 2025 study conducted by the National Statistics Committee of Uzbekistan in collaboration with the World Bank showed that the largest numbers of poor residents were recorded in the Samarkand region (265,000 people), as well as in Fergana (239,000), Kashkadarya (238,000), and Andijan (214,000) regions.
In other words, Uzbekistan must invest more in infrastructure projects and economic growth across its regions, not just the capital.
In a September 3 speech, Mirziyoyev said a new system to reduce poverty and unemployment across the country will be introduced. This new strategy must be monitored to ensure it promotes employment and helps low-income individuals, rather than falling victim to bureaucratic incompetence or corruption.
As interest in Central Asia’s natural resources continues to grow, it is also important to understand the priorities of the five Central Asian governments. In Uzbekistan, the momentum is to diversify the country’s energy production and bring development to areas outside Tashkent. Washington and American industries must keep Tashkent’s priorities and objectives in mind to secure win-win contracts and agreements and ensure this partnership continues as the so-called race for critical minerals heats up.
For Uzbekistan’s population, particularly those living outside Tashkent, this stronger partnership must mean more jobs, economic growth, and a better quality of life.

PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron said Friday he would call a Group of Seven meeting to address skyrocketing global energy prices and look at releasing strategic oil stocks.
“We will have in the upcoming weeks a G7 [meeting] that will be devoted to energy issues, to increase cooperation and avoid unnecessary tensions between G7 countries and our main partners,” Macron said during a press conference.
The French leader’s comments came after he chaired a rare crisis meeting at the Elysée Palace. During the meeting, French intelligence chiefs briefed political leaders and candidates in the presidential election next year about the threats posed by Russia’s war in Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East, both of which are driving fuel prices to new highs in France.
Advertisement
“The situation we face is serious. It is serious due to the international situation and the consequence of wars that we endure,” Macron said. “In this context we need to stay united.”
France’s dire fiscal outlook, which has prompted the government to pursue a €54 billion budget squeeze next year, will make it difficult for the state to massively subsidize increasingly expensive energy bills. Macron told reporters, however, that the government was working on targeted assistance proposals.
Macron also said he was seeking to firm up French access to oil and gas supplies during recent meetings with leaders from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. ‘A critical moment’: concern UK is not up to speed in acting on AI risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:57:11 UTC
23:57:11 KST

Towards the end of Keir Starmer’s time in office, his senior ministers, alarmed by the latest developments in artificial intelligence, began drawing up plans for a new AI safety law.
They ordered a review of existing legislation to see what powers they already had, according to those briefed on the plans, and were exploring whether they could force the world’s most advanced technology companies to submit their products for safety testing before launching them.
In the midst of the political chaos that engulfed the former prime minister as he fought to remain in office, however, the plans fell by the wayside.
Now, after two weeks in which the world has been told there is a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans”, and King Charles has warned about its potentially destructive capabilities, the government’s attention has turned again to what to do about AI.
Andy Burnham, Starmer’s successor in Downing Street, has said relatively little about the technology in the past, and in one of his first acts in office he scrapped the department that had been leading the legislative work.
The prime minister’s focus is on more immediate domestic problems. But as he grapples with balancing his first budget and bringing down the cost of living, some fear the threat posed by AI has dropped off the government’s radar.
“The first duty of government is to keep people safe,” said Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the science and technology committee. “The government’s response to an existential threat cannot be to throw its hands up in the air and say there is nothing we can do.”
Risks v potential
Britain has been at the forefront of the debate on AI safety since Starmer’s predecessor, Rishi Sunak, decided to make it one of his top priorities in office.
Amid worries about what super-intelligent tools could do without human involvement, Sunak convened a summit in the UK and persuaded the US, EU, Australia and China to cooperate on AI safety.
Starmer was more bullish about AI’s potential “to increase productivity hugely, to do things differently, to provide a better economy that works in a different way in the future”.
The Guardian has learned that in the former technology department, Emran Mian, the lead civil servant, had plans for AI to replace almost every civil servant in the department when they retired or moved on to a new job.
But at the same time, some in government were keen to remain focused on the risks posed by the technology.
Shortly before Starmer’s departure, Yvette Cooper, then the foreign secretary, told the Guardian she believed AI posed a Hiroshima-style risk to humanity.
Starmer’s government took steps to mitigate the risks Cooper and others had identified. His government allocated £115m in June to fund a response centre to deal with incidents when AI goes rogue and for a new AI biosecurity programme.
Officials in the science department also began reviewing what powers ministers had to compel companies to cooperate with the UK safety regime, and what else they could legislate for.
‘A critical moment’
When Burnham took office earlier this summer, one of his first moves was to abolish the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT).
Kanishka Narayan, the junior minister in charge of AI, was given a promotion and placed in the Cabinet Office, where he continues to oversee the technology but without the logistical support of a dedicated department.
The move alarmed some in the AI industry.
Matt Clifford, the AI investor who had advised Starmer and Sunak, posted on X: “Right now is a critical moment for tech as an economic and national security issue. Tying up our most senior science and tech officials in a [reorganisation] wastes time and energy that’s desperately needed for the actual substance.”
Dame Wendy Hall, a computer scientist who chaired a UK government AI review in 2017, said: “The structure was a bit bloated in DSIT, but the fragmentation we have now has had a much worse impact.”
AI safety rose up the political agenda again over the summer.
In July, OpenAI revealed one of its AI agents had launched an autonomous cyber-attack on Hugging Face, a real company, triggering alarm among technology experts around the world.
Earlier this month, Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher, resigned from his job at Anthropic, claiming the company was “gambling with our lives”. His comments were reposted online by one of his colleagues, Evan Hubinger, who added: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”
Just as these warnings were being made, the Financial Times revealed that Anthropic had launched the latest version of its Claude Mythos tool without submitting it to the UK safety institute first.
Mounting concerns
King Charles intervened this week, convening a meeting of AI executives in Scotland, where he told them: “The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world.”
Public concern is also growing. YouGov said on Friday that just over a third of Britons see AI as the third potential cause of human extinction behind nuclear war and climate breakdown – a figure that more than doubled since last year. Two-thirds think AI has the potential to end human civilisation, a view shared by the Nobel-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, and one in six support a slowdown in AI development.
In parliament, the Labour MP Liam Byrne has asked the head of the safety institute, Henry de Zoete, to testify in front of the business committee he chairs.
De Zoete replied earlier this week, explaining that no one outside the US had been allowed to see Anthropic’s latest product before it launched and insisting that his institute could still monitor such tools after they had been released.
“We have teams of talented AI researchers working on research projects based on both pre-release and post-release testing that are fundamental to the UK’s understanding of AI risk, across chemical-biological, human influence and loss of control,” he said.
Ministers have also begun to comment. Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, told the TUC congress this week there were “clearly huge risks to our national security and society if the right guardrails are not put in place”.
In an article in the Times, Narayan wrote: “Nothing is off the table. Where further regulation, legislation, stronger protections or new powers are needed, we will act.”
Wake-up call
Byrne believes ministers had a wake-up call.
“I think the government is taking it seriously now,” he said. “It has become clear in the last two weeks that perhaps our safety advisers don’t have the power they need to keep us safe.”
This still leaves the question unresolved by successive governments – what can the UK, as a middle-ranking power, do to curb the might of some of the world’s most advanced and fastest-growing technology companies?
For some, the answer is straightforward: regulate and legislate, just as the government would do for any emerging threat.
“The social media companies used to argue that the government is too powerless to act,” said Onwurah. “But there are things the government can do. We could say, for example, that if your frontier model has not gone through the safety institute, we are not going to allow you to sell your commercial models in our country.
“Or, if your AI goes and attacks someone else like happened with Hugging Face, you are legally and financially responsible.”
Many believe that action will only work if it is coordinated with other countries.
“If the US and China do not figure this out, the UK is unlikely to deliver a safe environment on its own,” said Byrne. “But a safety regime which is set and enforced by the UK, Europe, India, Canada and Japan would be robust.”
The former Cabinet Office minister Darren Jones has called on Burnham to put the issue at the top of the agenda when Britain hosts the G20 summit next year. “The AI safety conversation at the moment is around international collaboration on safety testing,” he said. “This is easier to do multilaterally, through treaties or agreements.”
One former government official added: “If together we say we require you to pass your models through our safety institutes – if we did that at a large enough scale, we would be able to stand up to the US government.”
Time to act
Whatever the government decides to do, it may find that now is the best time to do it.
Unusually, many in the industry are themselves calling for stricter regulation.
OpenAI’s head of policy in Europe, Tom Duff Gordon, said this week: “We support stronger UK rules for the handful of companies, including OpenAI, developing the most powerful AI systems.”
One former government official said: “We have strengths in this country when it comes to AI. Our AI industry is third in the world behind the US and China, and we also have considerable convening power with other countries.
“The question for me is whether the new prime minister is alive enough to this problem to take advantage of those strengths.”

Saudi Aramco will not supply European oil refiners with crude in October: Sources

Saudi Aramco will not supply European oil refiners with crude in October: Sources
NEW YORK – Saudi Aramco told at least two oil refining customers in Europe that they will be allocated no crude in October under long-term agreements after the kingdom’s key pipeline to the Red Sea was attacked, people informed of the decision said.
European customers normally receive Saudi Arabian crude on so-called term contracts, ensuring a steady flow of supply every month. Those deliveries will not take place in October, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public. The decision applies to all European buyers, they said.
Saudi Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment made outside normal working hours.
The absence of Saudi flows in October will heighten the need for European buyers to secure replacements. Already, Poland’s Orlen SA has been hunting for shipments, helping propel the prices of regional oil grades higher. Dated Brent, which is the benchmark for real-world barrels in Europe, topped US$130 this week at one point.
Saudi Arabia was forced to shut its East-West pipeline last week after it was attacked by drones. Aramco is working to partially restart within days and ramp up to full capacity within six weeks, a person familiar with the matter said on Sept 16.
The shutdown has forced Aramco to make the rare move to offer customers in Asia cargoes on a so-called spot basis – agreements for immediate delivery. Once the pipeline restarts, traders will focus on whether Aramco offers refiners in Europe similar terms.
Those supplies to Asia are going through the Persian Gulf, which means Aramco has once again pivoted towards the embattled Strait of Hormuz. The company has sold tens of millions of barrels to customers for collection just outside the waterway this week, a route it had largely shunned during the conflict in the Middle East as regular attacks of ships made the journey risky.
The increased flows towards the Persian Gulf, however, brings little relief to Europe’s refiners. In order to get to buyers in the continent, those shipments would either have to sail through the Red Sea, where Yemen’s Houthi militants have been attacking Saudi ships, or sail almost five weeks around Africa.
European refineries typically lift Saudi crude from Egypt’s Mediterranean port of Sidi Kerir, which is connected to the Red Sea via a pipeline.
European countries in the OECD imported 577,000 barrels a day of crude from Saudi Arabia in June, according to the International Energy Agency. BLOOMBERG

Explainer-How Putin may leverage predictable outcome of Russia's elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:34 UTC

Explainer-How Putin may leverage predictable outcome of Russia's elections
MOSCOW, Sept 18 - Russians are voting in a three-day parliamentary election which is widely expected to see the ruling United Russia party retain its dominance in what is a tightly controlled political system that has excluded most candidates who oppose Moscow's war in Ukraine.
Even though the overall outcome is not in doubt, here are some of the reasons why the vote may be useful to President Vladimir Putin.
A MANDATE FOR MORE WAR?
As president or prime minister for more than a quarter of a century, Putin's grip on Russia has never been tighter. But the war has lasted much longer than many Russians expected and fallout from the conflict is now being felt much more sharply on the home front.
Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia itself have escalated, and while civilian casualties are far lower than in Ukraine, they have sharply increased this year. Strikes on oil refineries have caused fuel shortages, while businesses are grappling with drone attacks on their warehouses and polls suggest some Russians are increasingly anxious.
Having framed the election as a test of support for the war, Putin is likely to point to the results to say that most people back his decision to fight on until key war aims are met.
CREATION OF A 'NEW ELITE'
Putin has said that those who fought in Ukraine are "warriors", part of a new "elite" he has promised will have prestigious careers. Should the some 200 veterans standing from a range of parties do well, Putin is expected to point to their success at the ballot box as an example of how Moscow looks after those who risked their lives for the motherland and to show how distinguishing oneself on the battlefield can lead to a high-profile political career. It's a development that could also encourage more people to sign up to fight in Ukraine.
CONTRAST WITH UKRAINE
Putin has repeatedly suggested that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy is illegitimate, pointing to the fact that his five-year term ran out in May 2024 and that Zelenskiy has refused to hold a new election since. Martial law, introduced in Ukraine in 2022, bans any wartime election and the constitution says the president serves until a newly elected one takes office. But Putin - who has faced criticism from Western politicians about Russia's own political system - may use the vote to say that Russia - unlike Ukraine - has stuck to its electoral timetable regardless of the war and is giving people a chance to vote.
SENSE OF NORMALCY
Putin has been keen to show Russians that despite the conflict and everything associated with it they can largely carry on life as before. Increasingly deep and destructive Ukrainian drone strikes have made that harder to achieve in what is the fifth year of the war. But holding a relatively smooth parliamentary election across 11 time zones in what is the world's largest country, whilst also waging war in Ukraine, could help Putin reassure Russians that pre-war traditions are being respected and that life - up to a point - goes on despite the conflict.
MOBILISATION/CENSORSHIP
Putin this month dismissed suggestions by Ukraine and Western media pundits that Russia would carry out a post-election mobilisation to expand the ranks of its army in Ukraine as "nonsense," suggesting it was a malicious suggestion designed to sow panic.
However, domestic and foreign critics of the war fear he could use the outcome of the election to justify such a move, given what Western intelligence agencies say are heavy Russian losses on the battlefield and what they say is Moscow's desire to urgently speed up the pace of its territorial gains with more manpower.
Those same critics fear that the authorities may move ahead with more repressive measures once the election results are in and a pre-election feel-good mood is no longer required.
They point in particular to plans previously floated by the authorities to have mobile service providers charge customers extra for using more than 15 gigabytes of foreign data in a month, a move seen as targeting people who use VPNs or virtual private networks to access websites and apps banned inside Russia. The authorities have given no public indication they intend to imminently resurrect the plan. REUTERS

Your Shoe Size Can Change as You Age. Here's Why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:32 UTC
23:53:32 KST

If you’ve always worn the same size shoe but your sneakers and boots feel tighter now that you’re in, say, your 40s or beyond, you’re not alone. People on TikTok are also sharing their experiences with growing feet as they’re getting older. But do your feet really get bigger with age?
“Yes, but ‘bigger’ is somewhat misleading,” says Dr. Kimberly Koury, an orthopedic surgeon at Atlantic Health. “Adult feet do not continue to grow in the same way they do during childhood. Instead, the shape of the foot can gradually change with age.”
This can happen for a variety of reasons and cause feet to become wider, flatter, and slightly longer, she explains. “Someone may notice that a shoe that fit well when they were younger now feels too tight, even though their actual foot bones have not continued to grow.”
Here’s what to know about why your feet may get bigger with age and what to do about it.
What causes feet to get bigger?
The main reason is that over time, your arch “flattens and spreads,” says Lesly Robinson, a podiatrist and interim dean of the Temple University School of Podiatric Medicine.
This is often due to decreased collagen—the protein that provides strength and elasticity to your skin, muscles, bones, tendons, and ligaments—that naturally happens with age. This can cause the ligaments supporting your arches to become lax, Robinson says. “When the arch falls, the foot both widens and lengthens,” adds Dr. Alexis Dixon, an orthopedic surgeon and foot and ankle specialist in Marina Del Ray, Calif.
Another reason feet may change in shape and size is a foot deformity, like a bunion or hammertoe, which become more prevalent as you get older. A bunion is a bump that forms on the inside of your big toe joint, but it’s not an extra bone growth. Instead, it’s a change in alignment, where the big toe moves toward the other toes, Koury says. “That makes the forefoot wider and can make previously comfortable shoes feel too narrow.” This can also contribute to flattening arches, Robinson says. Hammertoes happen when the tissue of your toes weakens, causing the muscles and tendons to buckle and curve, Dixon says.
Bunions and hammertoes can be genetic or result from wearing tight, narrow shoes over a lifetime, she says. They’re more common for women.
Arthritis is also common in feet and ankles, especially in the big-toe joint, Dixon says. It can cause bone spurs (extra growths of bone tissue) on top of the foot or at the back of the heel, which may rub against your shoe and make it feel too tight.
When do these changes happen, and who’s most affected?
People may notice foot changes starting in their 30s, but there’s no specific age when they happen, says Sindhu Srinivas, a podiatrist in Atlanta.
Age-related foot changes are generally more common for women, Koury says. The hormonal fluctuations in pregnancy and menopause affect collagen, and years of wearing high heels or narrow or ill-fitting shoes may contribute to structural changes in the feet.
People with previous foot injuries, flat feet or bunions (or a family history of these conditions), and a higher body weight are more at risk, Koury adds.
Being overweight puts pressure and stress on the feet, Srinivas says. “Over time, this increased load can contribute to changes in the foot's supporting structures and overall biomechanics.”
How much bigger will your feet get?
The changes happen gradually and can affect your foot’s length, width, and arch height, Srinivas says. But how much bigger your feet can get varies.
A study published in 2016 examined the foot measurements of 68 women aged 20 to over 80. It found that the widths of the balls of the feet increased by 3 to 4 millimeters per decade, while ball circumferences increased by about 5 to 7 millimeters, high-step circumferences 0.4 to 4.8 millimeters, and heel instep circumferences up to 2 millimeters.
“That may sound small, but these changes accumulate over several decades and can become enough to affect shoe fit,” Koury says.
Some people may need a wider shoe, while others might need one a half size larger, Dixon says.
When to see a doctor
If your feet seem to be getting wider or longer and you’re experiencing pain, swelling, numbness, tingling, or difficulty walking or doing other activities, see your doctor, Koury says. Also, talk to your doctor if you’re getting recurrent calluses, blisters, or skin breakdown, or if your bunions, hammertoes, or flatfoot are worsening. Sudden foot changes, especially if they only affect one foot, should also get checked, Srinivas says.
Pay extra attention to your feet if you have diabetes, neuropathy, or circulation problems, as even minor changes in your shoes’ fit can cause more serious problems, Koury says.
Doctors will recommend the best treatment for your feet. This may include orthotics to improve arch support, Robinson says. It’s also possible to modify footwear for bunions or hammertoes, Dixon adds. Physical therapy or exercises may be helpful for some, Koury says. Surgery may be necessary for some foot issues if other treatments don’t help.
How to protect your feet as you age
You can’t necessarily prevent age-related foot changes, but you can take steps to keep your feet healthy as you get older, Koury says.
Most important: wear shoes that fit well. Avoid footwear with narrow toe boxes, which compress your toes (and may cause bunions), and limit high heels, which put stress on the front of the foot and may even cause a deformity, Koury says. Shoes should be supportive and have a wider toe box, Robinson says. “It’s helpful to have your feet measured periodically, including the width, not just the length,” Koury says.
Maintaining a healthy weight can “help reduce unnecessary stress on the tendons, ligaments, and bones,” Sirinivas says.
Regular physical activity strengthens your feet and ankles. Low-impact, weight-bearing activities can maintain foot function and stability, improve balance, and prevent falls, Dixon says. Also try foot exercises, such as standing on one foot while holding onto a counter, or toe scrunches, which involves curling your toes to pick up a washcloth or other object off of the floor.
Treat bunions, flattening feet, or other foot problems as early as possible to avoid problems later, Koury says. “The goal is to accommodate the new foot shape and prevent the changes from becoming painful or functionally limiting.”

Volkswagen recalls over 208,000 vehicles in US over steering defect
