Apex Europe targets defence’s biggest challenges
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:43:56 BST
22:43:56 KST

Apex Europe will bring defence leaders, industry and experts together in London this October to tackle some of the most urgent operational challenges facing allied forces, from autonomous warfare and deep strike to air defence and protecting critical undersea infrastructure.
Allied defence forces across the globe now operate in an era where advantage is dependent on the ability to innovate at pace. Conventional conflicts as we’ve seen with Ukraine are increasingly being shaped by autonomy, mass, speed and connectivity. Armed forces across land, sea, air and cyber domains face the recurring challenge of how to adapt to a constantly shifting technological landscape.
An upcoming defence trade show attended by industry leaders and experts across the globe seeks to bring these pressing questions into sharp focus this autumn. Apex Europe, held in parallel with Apex Defense, is set to have its inaugural show on 7-8 October at the Magazine London, one of the city’s premier event spaces near The O2 area. At its core, the programme centres around identifying, assessing and solving the most pressing challenges facing the defence sector and collective allied armed forces in an increasingly complex geopolitical landscape.
The Mission Sets have been curated around the leading problems facing the sector, each inviting select industry, government, military, and academia to address them.
Operational Problem A: Interoperability and Integration of Uncrewed Systems Across European and NATO
The first problem brings into focus the large-scale challenge of integrating crewed and uncrewed forces across domains. Countries across the globe have highlighted this enormous challenge, particularly with regards to optimising the balance between high-end and low-cost capabilities, coordinating cross-domain command and control as well as building resilience against cyber and EW threats. In the UK we’ve seen great emphasis in the Defence Investment Plan on the Carrier’s Hybrid Air Wing, or equally the loyal wingman of the RAF. For this potential to be maximised, autonomous systems must be interoperable.
Operational Problem B: Delivering Warfare Advantage Through Autonomous Mass
Similarly, the event aims to invite discussion on how to utilise autonomy to gain decisive operational advantage. Autonomy changes the economics of warfare. The central question is moving from what a single exquisite platform can achieve to what a force can generate when hundreds or thousands of autonomous systems can be produced, deployed, replenished and replaced at speed. Mass, however, is not simply a matter of acquiring more platforms. It requires resilient supply chains, common architectures, software that can be updated rapidly, distributed command and control, and an industrial base capable of absorbing wartime demand. This will factor in sustaining autonomous operations under contested conditions as well as the adaptation and iteration at the speed of the frontline.
Operational Problem C: Generating Combat Power Through Deep Precision Effects
Long-range precision strike is becoming less about individual weapons and more about the ability to build a persistent, responsive system for generating effects at depth. Precision depends on the resilience of the wider architecture: radar, intelligence, communications, targeting and battle management must continue to function when the adversary is actively trying to disrupt them. The strategic opportunity is to think beyond inventories of missiles and strike platforms and towards an integrated deep-effects enterprise – one capable of creating dilemmas across an adversary’s system rather than simply hitting individual targets.
Operational Problem D: Countering Undersea Threats and Protecting Critical Infrastructure
Another mission set central to Apex Europe this year is countering undersea threats. As the seabed becomes a frontline, protecting energy pipelines, communications cables and other critical subsea infrastructure requires far greater awareness of what is happening below the waterline. The event will explore how to detect, track and neutralise undersea and hybrid threats, maintain persistent surveillance and deny access to critical infrastructure, and deploy layered sensing, precision effects and resilient architectures to sustain advantage in contested maritime environments.
Crucially, this challenge extends beyond traditional anti-submarine warfare, requiring closer integration between navies, governments, infrastructure owners, industry and autonomous systems. Later this year, Undersea Defence Technology (UDT) Australia is due to have its inaugural event in Adelaide, further reinforcing the importance of the subsea environment.
Operational Problem E: Countering Low-Cost, Rapidly Proliferating UxS Threats
Apex Europe will also address the growing challenge of low-cost, rapidly proliferating threats from uncrewed systems. The focus will be on detecting and discriminating small, low-signature threats, while balancing layered and cost-effective defeat mechanisms. Discussions will explore the role of attritable and mobile C-UxS capabilities, alongside greater integration of cross-domain and allied counter-UxS operations to deliver a scalable and sustainable defence against increasingly accessible autonomous threats.
Operational Problem F: Enhancing Layered and Integrated Air and Mission Defence Across Domains
Modern air and missile defence is increasingly a problem of integration rather than individual systems. The focus will be on 360-degree surveillance and real-time threat identification, cross-domain integration and adaptable, scalable engagement mechanisms across the threat spectrum. At the heart of this is resilient command and control – connecting sensors, effectors and decision-makers into a coherent architecture that can respond to complex, saturated attacks while preserving high-end capabilities for the threats that demand them.
Operational Problem G: Fighting in Denied, Degraded and Contested Battlespace
The final mission set addresses the growing reality of fighting in a denied, degraded and contested battlespace, where connectivity and access to information can no longer be taken for granted. The focus will be on spectrum management in an increasingly congested and contested electromagnetic environment, accelerating tactical EW adaptation, and building cyber and EW effects at scale. Alongside this, forces must be able to exploit and sustain access to space for command, control and targeting – maintaining decision advantage even when networks, data and communications are under constant pressure.
What this is all about
These Mission Sets represent Europe’s most pressing operational priorities and point to a broader shift in the character of warfare that must urgently be addressed. The issue is not simply acquiring more autonomous platforms, longer-range weapons or additional air-defence systems; it is building a force that can connect those capabilities, generate them at scale and continue operating when an adversary attacks the underlying architecture. Technological advances are key, but technology alone will not determine outcomes. Industrial capacity, interoperability, software, doctrine, data and operational experimentation are becoming inseparable parts of combat power and will be central to the discussions at Apex Europe’s inaugural event this October. The advantage will go to those able not only to field better systems, but to adapt, integrate and regenerate them faster than their adversaries.
Apex Europe forms part of a dynamic technology event series that puts near-term operational needs at the heart of the programme and exhibition; held in parallel with Apex Defense (January in Washington, D.C.)
Brought to you by the organisers of major international military and industry events such as DSEI Germany, DSEI Japan, and DSEI UK.

EXPLAINER – Why Reform UK is facing renewed scrutiny over its donations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:42:46 UTC
22:42:46 KST

Reform UK is facing renewed scrutiny over its finances as a police investigation into alleged breaches of political funding laws and government plans to tighten donation rules put the far-right party under pressure.
An undercover broadcast that appeared to show two senior Reform aides discussing ways to circumvent restrictions on foreign donations has widened the controversy, prompting their suspension and further police inquiries.
Meanwhile, large contributions from cryptocurrency billionaires have fueled debate over overseas funding as ministers seek restrictions that would apply retrospectively. Party leader Nigel Farage insists the donations comply with current law.
Farage also faces a separate parliamentary standards inquiry into an undeclared personal gift received before he became an MP in 2024. He has denied wrongdoing, while Reform says it will fully cooperate with the police investigation.
Here is a look at the donations, the proposed legal changes and the investigations.
Last week, Reform UK received two donations of £36 million ($48.5 million) each from cryptocurrency billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, totaling £72 million.
According to the BBC, the contributions are the largest individual donations to a UK political party since reporting requirements began in 2001.
Farage said the donations were “100% compliant with the law today,” but did not say whether they would be permissible under proposed rule changes.
In March, the government announced plans for a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, with retrospective effect from March 25. In July, ministers added that they wanted the cap to continue applying for at least 12 months after donors return to Britain.
The legislation is still working its way through parliament. Under current rules, British citizens living abroad can make unlimited donations to political parties, provided they are registered on a UK electoral register.
Farage has criticized the government’s attempts to retrospectively make some donations impermissible.
In April, Delo told The Telegraph that he was moving back to the UK to increase his support for Reform and “build a war chest” for Farage to fight the next election.
Harborne, a British businessman based in Thailand, matched Delo’s record contribution less than two days after it was announced.
Together, the donations exceed the amount either Labour or the Conservatives spent campaigning in the 2024 general election, according to Electoral Commission figures.
The latest controversy over foreign funding follows an investigation by Channel 4 News and Verbatim Investigations broadcast earlier this month.
The footage appeared to show Farage’s senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, discussing ways to circumvent electoral law to secure foreign funding.
Jukes met an undercover reporter posing as the UK-based son of a wealthy American financier. The reporter expressed concern that his father could not legally donate directly to Reform.
The discussions included a potential £500,000 contribution. Both officials stepped down following the broadcast.
Under UK electoral law, permissible donors include individuals registered on a UK electoral register and UK-registered companies that carry out business in the country.
Last week, the Metropolitan Police said they had widened a criminal investigation following the allegations.
Police said they had received “a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party,” according to the BBC.
A Reform spokesman said the party “denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation.”
In July, reports revealed that Farage’s aide George Cottrell and his mother, Fiona Cottrell, had also been interviewed under criminal caution by Metropolitan Police detectives last year over suspected evasion of restrictions involving donations made in May 2024.
That investigation followed a referral from the Electoral Commission.
Separate scrutiny of Farage’s finances intensified after it emerged that he had received a personal £5 million ($6.7 million) gift from Harborne in early 2024, shortly before announcing his intention to run in that year’s general election.
The Guardian first reported the gift in April. Farage later acknowledged receiving it but said he was under “no obligation” to declare it because it had been given before he became an MP.
In May, reports said the parliamentary standards commissioner had opened an inquiry into whether Farage breached Commons rules by failing to declare the gift.
According to the Institute for Government, lawmakers in the UK are allowed to accept gifts from donors, but they are meant to declare any gifts or benefits above £300 in value if they are received in their capacity as a lawmaker, as well as any other financial interests that "might reasonably be thought to influence their actions, speeches or votes in parliament."
They can only receive gifts worth more than £500 if it’s from a "permissible source," which includes individuals on a UK electoral register, local registered companies and some organizations.
Amid the scrutiny, Farage resigned as MP for Clacton in July and announced he would contest the resulting by-election.
In a video statement, he said the vote would become a “people vs establishment” election, calling on voters to judge his conduct.
“I repeat, I have done nothing wrong,” he said.
Farage regained his seat last month in the unusual by-election that other major political parties did not contest.
The parliamentary investigation into the gift resumed hours after his victory, according to the House of Commons website.

Who is Sufian Abu Zaida, the ex-PA official who says he carried Sinwar’s pre-Oct. 7 warning to Israel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:39:24 UTC
22:39:24 KST

Long before Sufian Abu Zaida identified himself as the Palestinian intermediary who says he carried Yahya Sinwar’s warning to Israel weeks before Oct. 7, he had built the kind of political résumé that made such a role possible. 
A former Palestinian Authority minister and senior Fatah figure who speaks fluent Hebrew, Abu Zaida spent about 12 years in Israeli prison before later working closely with Israeli officials. He also remained tied to Mohammed Dahlan’s camp and maintained contacts with figures inside Hamas.
That unusual network has now placed the 66-year-old at the center of renewed scrutiny over what Israel knew before Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack. Abu Zaida said Wednesday that he was the previously unidentified intermediary who received a message from Sinwar and passed it onward to the United Arab Emirates and Israel. According to an investigation by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval, Sinwar warned in September 2023 that he was preparing a major “surprise” if negotiations with Israel did not advance, repeatedly using the Arabic word “zilzal,” meaning “earthquake.”
Abu Zaida said in a video that he would reveal more “in the coming days” about the message and his role in indirect contacts between Israel and Hamas. His disclosure answered one of the central questions surrounding the story: Who was the Palestinian intermediary Sinwar allegedly trusted to carry such a warning?
From Israeli prison to the Palestinian Authority
Born in the Jabalia refugee camp in Gaza, Abu Zaida has been a familiar figure in Palestinian politics for decades. He spent about 12 years in Israeli prison for involvement in terrorist activity, then entered the institutions of the Palestinian Authority after his release and became closely involved in dealings with Israel.
He served in senior roles connected to Israeli-Palestinian relations, including as minister for prisoner affairs and later as minister for civil affairs, a portfolio dealing with coordination between Israel and the Palestinians. His fluent Hebrew and years of contact with Israeli officials gave him extensive familiarity with both the Israeli system and the politically sensitive issue of Palestinian prisoners.
Those connections later became relevant in negotiations involving Israelis held in Gaza and Palestinian prisoners held by Israel. During talks over the release of abducted Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit, Abu Zaida helped map out prisoners who could potentially be included in an exchange.
The Dahlan connection
Another central part of Abu Zaida’s political story is his close relationship with Mohammed Dahlan, the former Fatah security chief in Gaza and longtime political rival of Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas. Abu Zaida was for years considered one of the senior figures associated with Dahlan’s camp and was expelled from Fatah in 2014 along with other officials identified with him.
That relationship is particularly important because Dahlan has close ties to the United Arab Emirates. Abu Zaida remained associated with his camp even after losing his formal position in Fatah, creating another bridge between Gaza, Palestinian politics and Abu Dhabi.
In 2019, the Palestinian Authority seized Abu Zaida’s home in Ramallah, prompting him to return to Gaza. During the war, he moved to Egypt and continued appearing in Arab media as a political commentator.
Ties inside Hamas
Abu Zaida’s contacts were not limited to Fatah, the Palestinian Authority and Israel. Despite the bitter rivalry between Fatah and Hamas, he also maintained relationships with figures inside Hamas. In 2010, he met in Gaza with senior Hamas official Fathi Hamad, with the two described at the time as childhood friends.
Those ties did not shield him from the conflict between the factions. In 2006, Abu Zaida was briefly abducted by armed men identified with Hamas. The result was an unusual political position: a former Fatah official aligned with Dahlan, deeply familiar with Israel and the prisoner issue, yet also capable of communicating with Hamas figures.
According to Eldar and Yuval, it was that network that eventually brought Abu Zaida into indirect contacts with Sinwar.
The secret channel with Sinwar
For roughly a year and a half before the war, Abu Zaida was involved in a channel between Israel and Hamas aimed at advancing a prisoner and hostage deal, according to the investigation. The talks focused on the return of the bodies of IDF soldiers Hadar Goldin and Oron Shaul and the release of Israeli civilians Hisham al-Sayed and Avera Mengistu, who were being held in Gaza at the time, in exchange for Palestinian prisoners and measures easing conditions for residents of the Strip.
Eldar said the negotiations stalled in early September 2023. Sinwar then disappeared from the talks and later summoned Abu Zaida, telling him to warn the Israelis that if there was no progress he was preparing a “big surprise.” Sinwar used the word “zilzal,” or “earthquake.”
According to the investigation, Abu Zaida left the meeting alarmed and passed the message to a Palestinian associate who now serves as an adviser to UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. He initially did not pass it directly to the Shin Bet because he feared being accused of collaborating with Sinwar.
After the adviser informed bin Zayed, the Emirati president wanted clarification over whether Sinwar was threatening war. Abu Zaida was sent back to him. Eldar said Sinwar then told Abu Zaida: “Pass them a message that I am preparing a surprise from the land of surprises. A formidable operation. Something unusual.” He again used “zilzal” and asked that his words be conveyed to Israel verbatim.
Abu Zaida contacted the Emirati adviser again and, according to the investigation, passed the warning to the Shin Bet on Sept. 15. Then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar subsequently spoke with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and security discussions were held in which Bar recommended either acting to neutralize the threat or significantly strengthening defenses around Gaza.
The warning, however, was interpreted differently. According to the investigation, officials believed Sinwar might have been referring to an attempt involving Elizabeth Tsurkov, the Israeli researcher who had been abducted and was being held in Iraq.
The disputed Netanyahu warning
Eldar and Yuval’s investigation also alleges that bin Zayed later contacted Netanyahu personally after seeing no apparent Israeli response and wanting to make sure the warning had reached him. According to their account, the two spoke for about 45 minutes, with Netanyahu reassuring the Emirati leader that Israel was prepared in Gaza and suggesting that serious trouble was more likely to emerge in the West Bank.
The journalists further alleged that Netanyahu did not inform then-IDF chief of staff Lt. Gen. Herzi Halevi, Bar or Mossad director David Barnea about the purported conversation.
Netanyahu strongly denies that account. His office said no conversation between Netanyahu and bin Zayed took place from the beginning of September through Oct. 7, 2023, and said records held by the Prime Minister’s Office, National Security Council and military secretariat showed no such call. Netanyahu later threatened legal action over publication of the allegation.
Eldar has stood by the investigation, saying the journalists possess recordings, documentation and corroborating evidence. “People in the security establishment said, in the Shin Bet and the IDF, that if we had known about this conversation, it would have given us another assessment of the information that had already arrived on Sept. 15,” he said.
The investigation also examined an Oct. 1 security discussion, six days before the attack, concerning unrest along the Gaza border and intelligence indicating Hamas intended to carry out an attack in the West Bank. According to the journalists, Bar again recommended considering targeted killings of senior Hamas figures, including Sinwar. Netanyahu told security officials to prepare plans for his consideration.
A senior Shin Bet official quoted in the investigation said knowledge of the additional warning could have changed how the agency interpreted the information already in its possession. “If we had known about the warnings, there is a chance it would have given much greater weight to the first message we received from Sinwar,” the official said.
Abu Zaida has not yet publicly detailed the entire chain himself. But by identifying himself as the man who says he carried Sinwar’s pre-Oct. 7 warning toward Israel, he has put a name and political history to the mysterious intermediary at the center of the account. His decades moving between Fatah politics, Israeli officials, Dahlan’s camp and contacts inside Hamas help explain why Sinwar may have chosen him for that role, and why his testimony now matters to the continuing debate over what warnings reached Israel before Oct. 7.

Ceuta border crisis fuels EUs far right despite fall in migrant arrivals, commissioner says
BRUSSELS, Sept 18 - Images of migrants crossing into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta have fuelled support for far-right parties despite a sharp decline in irregular arrivals in Europe following tougher migration policies, EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner said on Friday.
More than 72,000 people surged into the enclave from Morocco at the end of July, although most later left. Spain estimates 12,000 migrants remain in the tiny territory, including minors.
"We have the decreasing numbers, but images from Ceuta, of course, overshadow the actual successes and the actual facts and figures," Brunner told Reuters in an interview.
He said these images "fuel the far right", which was why "it is so important to return those people as soon as possible to show that we have control."
Asked about Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal on Wednesday for an emergency framework to prevent "engineered and weaponised" mass movements of migrants, Brunner said the details would be discussed at the next EU Council meeting of member states. But "first of all, we have to implement the system we already agreed on," he added.
Anti-immigration sentiment has remained a potent political force across Europe since more than 1 million people, many of them Syrians fleeing war, arrived in the bloc in 2015. The surge has helped boost support for nationalist and far-right parties and pushed many governments towards tougher migration policies focused on deterrence and returns.
Brunner also defended the European Commission's decision to facilitate talks between EU member states and Taliban officials, as governments seek ways to return Afghans convicted of crimes in Europe. Rights groups criticised the move, saying it lent legitimacy to Afghanistan's Islamist rulers, put Afghans at risk and undermined core EU values.
"I think first and foremost, it's about European security and the security of the European citizens," Brunner said when asked how the bloc could ensure that deportees sent to Afghanistan would not face persecution or harm. REUTERS

Tamil Nadu govt to provide one-gram gold rings to newborns
NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay will launch the one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns on September 28, the state government said. The one-gram gold rings will be provided to babies born in government hospitals under the scheme.The rings will have a unique serial number and be packed in tamper-proof packaging, the government said. As many as 1.28 lakh one-gram gold rings have been procured for the first instalment of the scheme.
The government said beneficiaries must be permanent residents of Tamil Nadu to be eligible for the one-gram gold ring scheme.Vijay had announced the one-gram gold ring scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election as a symbolic gift to newborns, drawing on the Tamil tradition of ‘Thaimaaman Seer’. The scheme will have retrospective effect from June 22, Vijay’s birthday. A government order issued on June 23 described the initiative as a token celebrating the birth of a child, motherhood and the cultural tradition of ‘Thaimaaman’.The state has allocated around Rs 755.83 crore annually for the scheme, which will cover newborns delivered at government institutions. The Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation will procure the gold rings and supply them based on annual requirements, while a project and programme management unit will oversee the implementation and monitoring of the scheme.
Tamil Nadu records around 7.8 lakh deliveries annually, with institutional deliveries accounting for 99.9% of births, according to NFHS-6. Government health facilities account for nearly 4.2 lakh deliveries, or around 53% of the total.According to the state government, the average out-of-pocket expenditure for a delivery at a government hospital is Rs 1,364, compared with Rs 63,473 at a private hospital.The scheme is open to Tamil Nadu residents whose children are born at government institutions. Mothers will have to submit proof of residence, with documents including ration cards, voter identity cards, Aadhaar, Labour Welfare Board identity cards, Department of Posts address cards and nativity certificates accepted.The government said the initiative was aimed at combining cultural significance with public healthcare.

Istanbul Airport's fourth runway to boost global connectivity: Erdogan

The fourth runway at Istanbul Airport and additional investments will make major contributions to the major air hub's global connectivity, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said on Friday, addressing the runway’s opening ceremony.
Air passenger traffic across Türkiye in the first eight months of 2026 topped 167.5 million, nearly twice the country's population, he noted.
“In Istanbul alone, we have made a total of 2.12 trillion Turkish liras ($43.5 billion) in investments in transportation and infrastructure at current prices, including 604.4 billion Turkish liras ($12.4 billion) in air transport," Erdogan said.
The newly commissioned runway is 2,820 metres (1.75 miles) long and 45 metres (147.6 feet) wide, marking the airport’s first east-west runway.
Pointing to Türkiye's flight network, one of the world's most extensive, Erdogan said that in the last 24 years, under Justice and Development (AK) Party governance, the number of active airports more than doubled from 26 to 58.
"Together with our nation, we have made a Türkiye that is strong at home, influential in its region, and respected around the world into a reality," he added.
World’s most connected airport
His remarks came a day after Istanbul Airport was named the world’s most connected aviation hub by global travel intelligence company OAG, overtaking London Heathrow for the first time.
Istanbul Airport climbed from second place in 2025 to the top of the global ranking, with connections to 337 destinations worldwide.
Turkish Airlines operated 80 percent of flights at the airport, according to OAG’s Megahubs 2026 report. London Heathrow dropped to second place after potential connections on its busiest day fell 6 percent year-on-year, partly due to ongoing disruptions to Middle East flight schedules.
Amsterdam Schiphol ranked third, while Kuala Lumpur retained fourth place and remained the most connected airport in Asia. Chicago O’Hare climbed from seventh to fifth globally and remained the most connected airport in the Americas.

German leader under huge pressure as the far-right AfD gains steam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:32:17 UTC
22:32:17 KST

Germany's leader under huge pressure as far-right AfD gains steam, but could he be forced out?
Berlin — German leader Friedrich Merz's position is under threat as the far-right surges in popularity and support for his own center-right party tanks. The situation is so serious that he canceled a planned trip to New York next week to represent his country at the United Nations General Assembly.
Merz, a conservative, is facing tremendous pressure in the wake of the far-right AfD's landslide state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt last week.
Their success, fueled by frustration among many Germans about the impact of immigration, came at the expense of Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party. It has accelerated a monthslong trend that spells trouble for the center-right leader of Europe's biggest economy.
Merz's poll ratings have fallen sharply. His government is grappling with a weak economy, and many voters who had hoped the former corporate executive would fix that have become disillusioned with delays in implementing financial and tax reforms.
The pressure has raised a once-unthinkable question in Berlin: Could Merz be forced out as chancellor before the end of his term?
"A genuine crisis of authority and leadership"
The chancellor's crisis goes beyond poor polling, veteran journalist Kerstin Münstermann told CBS News.
"We are witnessing a genuine crisis of authority and leadership within the CDU," said Münstermann, who has covered Merz's career closely as a member of the regional Rheinische Post's editorial board and head of its Berlin parliamentary bureau.
When Merz became chancellor early last year, many Germans saw him, above all else, as someone who could help revive the flagging economy. The former corporate lawyer and board member had worked for years to position himself as a strong economic hand to take the reins from Angela Merkel and her successor Olaf Scholz.
But "the situation for people has not noticeably improved," Münstermann told CBS News. "If anything, it has gotten worse."
The economic upturn promised by Merz has, undeniably, not materialized. While Germany is again seeing moderate growth, the labor market deteriorated last year. In August, more than 3 million people were unemployed, an increase of 36,000 from the previous year. Demand for labor remains weak, according to the Federal Employment Agency.
AfD's rise fueled by immigration concerns
One of the key issues underlying Merz's political crisis is immigration.
Concerns about the number of and integration of migrants have shaped the political debate for years in Germany, like many European nations, and they were the key factor in the AfD's landslide state election victory this month in Saxony-Anhalt.
A resounding 91% of AfD supporters in the state voiced fear of a potential new influx of foreigners, according to an analysis by the Konrad Adenauer Foundation, while 85% said they were concerned about immigration causing too much change within German society.
Merz has attempted to tighten Germany's migration policies. Just this week the federal government adopted a new 10-point plan to combat Islamist terrorism. Among other things, it provides for stricter surveillance of certain individuals deemed to pose a threat, tougher penalties for spreading terrorist propaganda and amendments to criminal law.
But the pressure on Merz and his party, as the far-right gains ground by focusing almost entirely on the issue, keeps rising, exacerbated by recent acts of violence.
With the new measures, the government is trying to show it can and is taking concrete action on the issue. Whether it will be enough to win back voters who have turned to the AfD will become clearer with every new local and state election.
"Now he's fighting"
Merz plans to convene his party's leadership Sunday in Berlin. There are two more state elections that day, in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
If the results for the CDU are as disastrous as they were in Saxony-Anhalt, he will likely face some very tough questions about his leadership and the party's future.
The chancellor has realized how serious the situation is, Münstermann said, and "now he's fighting."
The CDU, which has run Germany's government off and on for the vast majority of its post-World War II history, is facing a major internal debate due to the AfD momentum.
The party has always ruled out any cooperation with the far-right — refusing to consider entering into a coalition government with the AfD or using votes from its lawmakers to get legislation passed.
That political red line, which all other major German parties also stand behind, is commonly referred to in the country as a "firewall." But as the AfD gains clout through regional elections, the debate within the CDU over exactly how impermeable that firewall should be is also intensifying.
Some CDU politicians remain adamantly against any cooperation with the AfD. Others now question whether the party should, at least on individual policy initiatives, accept a majority vote in the parliament that can only be achieved with AfD votes.
Münstermann said the issue could deeply divide the CDU, but she believes Merz himself is "very clear on this," and unlikely to change his position against working with the AfD. Doing so, she said, could lose him the support of moderate party figures who've continued to back him.
Could Merz be forced out?
Germany's constitution makes it difficult to remove a chancellor from office — they cannot simply be replaced by another politician from the same party, even if there is broad consensus within that party.
The parliament, or Bundestag, can oust Merz only through what is known as a constructive vote of no confidence. The bar is high, as it requires a majority of all members of the Bundestag to vote not only to reject the sitting leader, but also to agree on a single replacement at the same time. It has happened only once, in 1982.
Another possibility is a simple vote of confidence. Merz could ask the Bundestag to formally express its confidence in him. If he failed to win a majority, he could ask Germany's president to dissolve the parliament, which would potentially pave the way for new national elections.
Münstermann does not consider either scenario likely in the near future. She said, however, that calls for a confidence vote could start to rise later this year if Merz loses support of fellow CDU lawmakers on crucial votes, particularly on the budget and planned economic reforms.
Before that, there could be another way for the CDU to show it is heeding the headwinds.
The party could move to separate the office of chancellor from the CDU leadership role, which could then see Merz step down as his party's leader without automatically resigning as chancellor. It would be a way for the CDU to express its dissatisfaction with Merz without plunging Germany into a governmental crisis.
For now, Merz has appeared focused on trying to show he is still in charge. Eight CDU state leaders publicly backed him this week, temporarily cooling speculation about possible successors.
But it does nothing to resolve the underlying crisis.
"It has not ended the debate over the chancellor," Münstermann said. "That debate is still there, and it will probably remain after election night" in the two states — including the capital — on Sunday.

100-meter shroud in New York displays names of over 20,000 Palestinian children killed in Gaza

Khaled Yousef and Lina Altawell
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
The Israeli army is facing a “severe shortage” of troops and military equipment after three years of war and is preparing to suspend soldiers’ leave, Israeli newspaper Maariv reported Friday.
“As a result of the severe shortage in the number of soldiers in the Israeli army, it is prepared to violate their basic rights and deny them leave,” the newspaper said.
Despite the personnel shortage, Maariv noted the dismissal of Lt. Col. A., who served as the Gaza Division’s intelligence officer in October 2023, because he “bore command responsibility by virtue of his position.”
“The Israeli army does not have enough tanks and armored personnel carriers,” Maariv said, adding that three years of war had worn down the vehicles and that hundreds had been damaged.
“For political reasons, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich can cut funding to the Israeli army and busy himself with complaints, while the opposition is preoccupied with internal struggles like reckless children,” the newspaper said.
On Tuesday, Israel’s Channel 12 said the army had lost a planned purchase of 12 Apache attack helicopters from US manufacturer Boeing because of a shortage in its procurement budget.
The report came a day after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu failed during a routine meeting to persuade opposition leader Yair Lapid to cooperate on increasing the military procurement budget.
Channel 12 said the army was already warning that unless the requested funding increase arrives soon, efforts to return tanks and armored personnel carriers damaged during the war to service would stop, while some ammunition production lines would also be affected.
Over the past three years, the Israeli military has waged wars and carried out military operations across the region, including its war on the Gaza Strip, which began in October 2023 and continues in different forms.
Israel has also fought wars with Lebanon and Iran, alongside continuing military operations in the occupied West Bank and Syria.
The conflicts have imposed significant human and financial costs on the Israeli military, amid strict censorship by Israeli authorities over information concerning its losses.

The Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition on Thursday held its 4th planning meeting in Saudi Arabia, the Saudi Defense Ministry said Friday.
The meeting in Jeddah was part of the coalition’s "ongoing transition from the founding stage to the actual operational stage, having reached Initial Operational Capability," the ministry said in a statement on US social media platform X.

It reviewed developments in the coalition’s work, achievements during the previous phase, and progress in countries joining the coalition, according to the statement.
The discussions also discussed requirements for joint operations and the capability contributions of participating countries to support coordinated and integrated multinational defensive operations and enhance the coalition’s operational readiness, it said.
The meeting marks an "advanced stage" in the coalition’s development, focusing on operational readiness under a unified command ahead of deployment and the launch of missions in the area of responsibility, the ministry added.

Mamata gets 'footballer', but can she win TMC 'khela'? Maharashtra has a red-card warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:31:19 UTC
22:31:19 KST

Mamata Banerjee faction got 'football player' as its symbol.
For 28 years, TMC has been Mamata Banerjee and Mamata Banerjee has been TMC in West Bengal; the two are almost synonymous with each other. And for voters, the political shorthand for Mamata Banerjee has been almost absurdly simple: two flowers on grass.Now, that shorthand has been taken away.The Election Commission on Friday allotted Mamata's faction a new name - 'Mamata All India Trinamool Congress', with a football player as its symbol. The rival Arup Roy faction will contest as 'Democratic Trinamool Congress', with an 'envelope' as its symbol. The decision follows the commission's September 17 order freezing the original All India Trinamool Congress name and its reserved 'flowers and grass' symbol for the upcoming bypolls.
Mamata Banerjee is now fighting to save her own party name and symbol.
But the EC's interim arrangement is only the first chapter. The substantive question of who gets the original TMC name and symbol will have to be decided under Paragraph 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968.And here, the story might look familiar.The same movie was played out twice in Maharashtra in recent years, first with the Shiv Sena and then with the Nationalist Congress Party.
They do not know that I cannot leave TMC. It will always be with me until I leave this world. Absolutely dirty game, but we are also ready to fight it out. I want the BJP to go from India. We want solidarity in INDIA alliance.
Mamata Banerjee
What Shiv Sena and NCP cases tell us
When Shiv Sena split between Uddhav Thackeray and Eknath Shinde in 2022, the EC first froze the party's 'bow and arrow' symbol and allotted separate interim identities to the two factions.
In its February 2023 decision, the commission eventually recognised the Shinde faction as the Shiv Sena and allowed it to use the original name and symbol.The NCP followed a similar path. After Ajit Pawar's rebellion in July 2023, the EC decided in February 2024 that the faction led by Sharad Pawar had a weaker numerical claim, while Ajit Pawar's group had superior support in the organisational and legislative wings. It consequently recognised Ajit Pawar's faction as the NCP and allowed it to use the party's 'clock' symbol. The EC order specifically recorded that the Ajit Pawar group had "far superior numerical support" in the organisational and legislative wings.That is a crucial part of the precedent for the ongoing TMC dispute.The conclusion from the Maharashtra cases may be that the EC followed the majority of legislators. The legal position is more nuanced. Paragraph 15 allows the election commission to examine rival claims through the party's organisational structure as well as its legislative strength.In its May 11, 2023 Constitution Bench judgment in Subhash Desai vs Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court held that the EC need not determine a party's identity solely through the numerical strength of its MLAs or MPs while adjudicating a dispute under Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order. The court said the EC could consider the majority in the organisational wing, the party constitution and, where appropriate, "any other appropriate test", underlining that a split among legislators is not necessarily the same as a split in the political party itself.
The timeline of TMC split.
The observation is particularly relevant to the TMC case, where the eventual contest could involve competing claims over the party's organisational structure and not just a headcount of elected representatives. The Supreme Court, however, did not itself decide which faction should receive the Shiv Sena's name and symbol, leaving the merits of that EC decision to separate proceedings.That distinction could matter considerably in the TMC case.The Shiv Sena and NCP rebels who ultimately secured the original party identities had substantial support among sitting legislators. The TMC's internal arithmetic, however, has to be examined on its own terms.The 2026 assembly election setback changed the party's internal arithmetic sharply. Its tally fell from 215 of 294 seats in 2021 to 80, and within weeks, 58 MLAs backed expelled leader Ritabrata Banerjee as their legislature party leader. He was subsequently recognised as leader of the opposition, while the rebel camp rejected Mamata's nominee, Sobhandeb Chattopadhyay.The revolt then spread to Parliament, with 20 Lok Sabha MPs led by Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar joining the NCPI and backing the BJP-led NDA. The TMC challenged their move before the Lok Sabha speaker and sought their disqualification. What began as a post-election leadership challenge had thus expanded into a contest over control of the party's legislative and parliamentary wings.Mamata Banerjee, however, remains the founder and central political figure of the organisation, and her camp's claim is not based only on her position as party leader but also on its organisational and electoral support.
The 'new' Mamata party
The names allotted on Friday were revealing because neither faction chose to abandon the Trinamool identity. Mamata's camp was given 'Mamata All India Trinamool Congress', while the rival Arup Roy camp became 'Democratic Trinamool Congress'. Both were, in different ways, laying claim to continuity with the party Mamata Banerjee founded on January 1, 1998.The distinction lies in the source of legitimacy each side is emphasising. The rebels' use of 'Democratic' fits their argument that the TMC's organisational functioning should be more representative and less centred around one leader. Mamata's faction, meanwhile, has effectively put the founder's name where the old party identity used to be, making 'Mamata' part of its temporary electoral brand. That is particularly striking for a party whose political identity has been inseparable from its founder for almost three decades.
They had said beforehand, 'naam bhi rakhne doonga, nishaan bhi nahi rakhne doonga' (Neither let you keep the name nor the symbol). Who are these people? They are in power today; they might not be in power tomorrow. They should understand their limitations.
Mamata Banerjee
The football-player symbol allotted to Mamata's faction also carries its own political resonance in Bengal. Football has long had a deep cultural presence in the state, but there is also a direct connection to the TMC's campaign vocabulary: 'Khela Hobe', the slogan that became a defining part of Mamata's 2021 assembly campaign against the BJP.
The symbol does not automatically recreate that campaign, but it gives the Mamata faction a ready-made visual association at a time when it has lost the party symbol voters have known for nearly three decades.The test, however, has now changed in a rather dramatic way for the Mamata faction.
Nandigram changes the bypoll test
Mamata faction's candidate, Sanchita Pradhan Dey, withdrew her nomination from the Nandigram contest altogether, a day before the deadline. Her withdrawal came minutes after she met West Bengal chief minister and BJP leader Suvendu Adhikari, although the circumstances surrounding the meeting and her decision remain a matter of political speculation.Mamata Banerjee later announced in a press conference that her party will now back the Congress candidate in Nandigram, and mentioned that the decision was taken "for the greater interest of the nation" and to strengthen the INDIA bloc."Rahul Gandhi rang me up yesterday, Arvind Kejriwal also expressed solidarity; we will all fight together against BJP. We will support Congress in the Nandigram bypoll to strengthen the INDIA bloc," Mamata said. The Congress candidate, however, was also arrested by the cops late in the evening in a land-grab case.That makes the October 6 bypolls a very different test from the one that appeared possible 24 hours earlier. The Mamata faction will now not be testing its new 'football-player' identity in Nandigram, but instead, ask its supporters to transfer their support to a Congress candidate, even as the rival TMC faction contests the seat under its own new identity.The political significance is difficult to miss. At precisely the moment when the EC has stripped Mamata's faction of the old TMC name and symbol and given it a new identity, the faction is now out of a direct fight in Nandigram, a constituency that carries an unusually strong personal history for both Mamata and Suvendu Adhikari.
Nandigram was where Mamata lost to Adhikari in the 2021 assembly election, after making the constituency the centrepiece of her campaign. Adhikari, who had moved from the TMC to the BJP before that election, defeated her by a narrow margin in a contest that became one of the defining episodes of Bengal politics. He subsequently retained Nandigram while also winning Bhowanipore, which he vacated to retain Nandigram, necessitating the October 6 bypoll.The EC may eventually decide who owns the TMC name and symbol, but the October 6 bypolls will offer the first test of how much of the old Trinamool identity survives without 'flowers and grass'. In Rejinagar, the football player and envelope will face each other directly; in Nandigram, Mamata's decision to back Congress will test whether her political support can travel even when her own new party name and symbol are not on the ballot.

Adopt This Data Center Plushie and Hear Its Piercing Scream
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Uh oh, we got a cute alert! It’s Bezzy, your adorable, cuddly, anthropomorphized server-rack and stuffed-animal friend! Give this soft lil’ doll a squeeze, and it shall sing you its telltale song: the piercing, grinding ambient squeals emitted from a real US data center.
The Bezzy doll is a stuffed plushie made in a satirical collaboration between the New York–based creative studio Basura and Big Data, the musical project of producer Alan Wilkis, best known for the song “Dangerous,” a 2013 collaboration with the band Joywave. The joint project, which is coming out the same day as a new Big Data single, is called Adopt a Data Center. The goal is to present people with a “cuddly introduction to life with a real data center.”
Data Centers are very un-vogue right now. Built out by all the big AI companies to power their increasingly power-hungry AI tools, data centers have spread across thousands of acres of land in the US. They have been heavily criticized for their energy consumption and expansion of gas power. They have also proven to be audibly annoying, stirring up complaints about noise pollution from those nearby.
The Adopt a Data Center stunt aims to make people think differently about how services produced by data centers fit into their lives. That manifests as a plush stuffie that looks like a server rack in a data center, albeit with long arms and legs and googly eyes. It’s cute in the way Don’t Hug Me I’m Scared is cute. Squeeze Bezzy’s torso and the sound bursts out. It’s a screeching few seconds of a recording taken by a neighbor of a data center in Virginia. The tag on the Bezzy plushie reads, “Hug me for ear-piercing forever hum.”
“We picked this recording as it was the clearest and most suitably irritating,” wrote Rajeev Basu, the founder of Basura, in an email to WIRED. In an interview with the person who recorded the audio, Basu says they described the sound as “like a car alarm going off nonstop. It's high-pitched, and it's all you can focus on.”
Basura has worked on other projects like making luxury wear for dogs and a partnership with Yerba Madre that made dirt shoes designed to break apart during a walk to spread wildflower seeds.
Along with Bezzy, the data centers project includes a collection of stickers that say things like “Every data center deserves a forever home” and “Open your heart. And your power grid.” Basu says the project is the result of dozens of interviews with people who live near data centers in the US. The website itself reads, “Adopt a data center: All they ask for is everything.”
Wilkis, whose band Big Data has “It’s giving Black Mirror, but make it music” in its Spotify description, says that the one upside of the data center debate is that the backlash is genuinely bipartisan.
“AI is a proxy for decades of widening wealth inequality in America, and data centers are its physical embodiment,” Wilkis wrote to WIRED. “With roughly 40 percent of the stock market's value riding on a handful of tech companies, the US economy is already a bet on AI's success.”
Sadly, only 20 Bezzy dolls are available for $99 from the Adopt a Data Center website and the Big Data storefront. Basura designed the toys, which are handmade in the US. But the physical toy isn’t the real point. The satire is meant to hook people into looking at the facts for themselves. When you click “adopt now” on the website, you’re taken to a statement with links to research and stories about how data centers fit into the world.
“It’s not about whether AI data centers should exist,” Basu says. “It’s about who gets to decide where they go, what resources they consume, and whether the communities living beside them actually benefit.”

Flight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software error
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:28:16 UTC
22:28:16 KST

A software defect in part of the UK’s air traffic control system corrupted flight data “in the space of a millisecond”, leading to a six-hour outage and mass airline cancellations and delays across the UK last week, National Air Traffic Services has said.
But ministers said the Nats report into the incident still left questions unanswered, saying they needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”.
According to the report, the error first occurred at 10am and was notified to engineers who investigated – but the system appeared to be working again, until 12.30pm when a repeat occurred and a major incident was declared.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) industry regulator would now “check their findings” and investigate Nats more widely.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers had their travel disrupted after the Nats failure on Tuesday 8 September, which ended up delaying and cancelling flights across the UK and beyond late into the next day.
Airlines have called for compensation and a “credible plan”, with Ryanair demanding the dismissal of the Nats chief executive officer, Martin Rolfe, after the third major air traffic control failure in the UK since summer 2023.
A government source said the CAA review would be “a chance to fundamentally investigate” if Nats was fit for purpose.
Rolfe said the incident was unrelated to the previous failures. He said he could “confirm that it was a software issue and not caused by any incorrect actions by either military or civil operators”.
The preliminary report said the failure was a “legacy and previously unknown software defect and a combination of very specific events occurring simultaneously” in part of the National Airspace System (NAS), which allocates codes to individual aircraft to identify flights on radar.
Nats said the software error occurred at 10am, with engineers first notified at 10.02am that the link between the NAS and London area control system had dropped. The engineers reported at 10.06am that the system had apparently recovered with no operational impact, but continued to investigate.
The report said the fault presented when a manual request for an aircraft code was being processed but paused for another, unspecified “higher priority activity” request. It said: “When processing of the aircraft code request resumed, the software defect meant it did not resume correctly and the resulting output was corrupted, and affected some subsequent flight data updates. This happened in the space of a millisecond.”
At 12.32pm the link between the national and London airspace management dropped again and a major incident was declared, with controllers having to conduct some tasks manually. By 12.45pm, Nats was restricting flights as the system continued to glitch, before failing completely at 1.32pm.
At 1.40pm airlines were advised of restrictions, and between 2.50pm and 4.09pm Nats rebooted the system, eventually resuming full operations at 7.30pm – but leaving mass congestion, displaced aircraft and hundreds of thousands of delayed passengers in its wake.
It took more than two days for the backlog of passenger disruption to be cleared, with more than 2,000 flights cancelled in total and hundreds of thousands of people’s travel plans disrupted.
Rolfe said: “The issue has been identified and mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety tested and deployed.”
He added: “I would like to apologise again, very sincerely, to everyone who was affected last week. It’s our job to get people where they want to go, quickly and without delay and we are devastated when that goes wrong. However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question.”
The transport secretary said: “The disruption we saw last week was completely unacceptable and I know how frustrating it was for passengers, airlines and airports.”
Alexander said she had received Nats’ report, adding: “It’s clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos.
“I have therefore tasked the CAA with conducting an independent review to check Nats’ findings and investigate their investment plans to enhance resilience in the future, along with regulatory accountability.”
The CAA’s review will be published within six months.
Tim Alderslade, the chief executive of Airlines UK, a lobby group representing the industry, said: “The CAA’s review must mandate real investment in Nats’ resilience so a single fault can never again descend into nationwide disruption.”
He said his members were writing to Nats to “demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience”.
The EasyJet chief executive, Kenton Jarvis, said: “Passengers deserve more than just another promise that lessons will be learned. Firm actions must be taken … and there must be a fair solution to ensure that airlines are not left to pick up the bill.”
The Ryanair chief operations officer, Neil McMahon, said: “‘The software ate my homework’ is not an acceptable explanation … How many times must the UK ATC system collapse before Martin Rolfe accepts responsibility and resigns.”

South Sudanese migrant jailed in UK for piloting record Channel boat crossing

South Sudanese migrant jailed in UK for piloting record Channel boat crossing
LONDON, Sept 18 - A South Sudanese man was jailed for two years and three months in an English court on Friday after he admitted piloting a small boat across the Channel from France, which carried a then-record 165 people.
Chan Mathok Atak, 19, previously pleaded guilty to endangering another during a July crossing to Britain in an inflatable dinghy.
The record for most migrants travelling to Britain across the Channel by small boat was broken again last month, when 230 people made the journey.
Atak's sentencing comes as the numbers of those arriving in Britain across the Channel have fallen, but the crossings remain a prominent political issue which successive British governments have struggled to tackle.
Earlier this month, hundreds of black-clad protesters gathered twice in two days on Britain's south coast, blocking streets in response to arrivals of small boats, which a government minister described as "thuggish".
Right-wing opposition parties and anti-migration activists have called for more action, but greater cooperation with French authorities and even repeated deaths have not deterred many people from seeking to make the perilous journey.
OVERCROWDED DINGHY CARRIED 165 PEOPLE
Atak was sentenced to 27 months in prison at Canterbury Crown Court. Prosecutor James Harrison said Atak piloted the dinghy for at least 90 minutes while it carried 164 other people, including 31 children aged 14 to 17.
He said there was no navigational or first aid equipment on the boat, which had only one of its two engines working and was slowly deflating and taking on sea water before it was intercepted by Britain's Border Force.
Atak's lawyer Audrey Cherryl Mogan said Atak was a young asylum seeker from South Sudan who did not have anything to do with the number of people or the conditions on board.
Judge Sarah Counsell accepted there was no evidence Atak organised the journey, but said that "those who chose to steer such vessels assume responsibility for the safety of those on board".
"This undermines public confidence in the immigration system and places considerable strain on already stretched public resources," she added.
The National Crime Agency's senior investigating officer John Turner said in a statement: "Chan Atak was unimaginably reckless and his actions could have easily resulted in many deaths had this boat not been intercepted." REUTERS

Smooth take off: Pilot handles Punjab turbulence with ‘no CM face’ formula; but can he carry Congress beyond winning line?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:18:01 UTC
22:18:01 KST

Sachin Pilot with Charanjit Singh Channi and Amrinder Singh Raja Warring during a protest to demand justice for the late Gulzar Singh in Chandigarh on Tuesday.
NEW DELHI: The Congress in Punjab has finally hit the ground running. Sachin Pilot, who replaced Bhupesh Baghel as the party’s state in-charge, successfully navigated the state unit out of months of internal turmoil and ensured the party’s campaign for the 2027 assembly elections could finally take off.With arch-rivals - former chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi and state Congress chief Raja Warring - on board, Pilot led a mega protest demanding the resignation of Punjab finance minister Harpal Cheema, who faces charges of abetment of suicide of a Dalit, Gulzar Singh.The entire state leadership and thousands of party workers marched towards Cheema’s residence. Police used water cannons to stop the protesters’ march. But the point was made. The Congress was finally in action mode.Pilot ensured that Channi and Warring, whose open power tussle has derailed Congress’s Punjab campaign, not only shared the stage but also did a “tense” handshake.Putting up a huge show of unity during the protest, Channi said, "We will fight together." Warring reciprocated. The state Congress chief called Channi and other leaders his 'pagg da lar' (the fold of his turban).
Expressing gratitude to party workers for mobilising in such huge numbers at short notice, Pilot assured each one of them that the Congress will always stand by them. The Congress in-charge assured party workers that he was the representative of the high command and would not leave any stone unturned to restore the dignity and honour of every Congress worker.
But will Pilot’s truce hold?
That’s the big question. The Punjab Congress has seen a no-holds-barred battle between Channi and Warring ever since the high command announced on July 1 that Warring would continue as Punjab Congress chief, ignoring Channi’s claims.The announcement triggered immediate protests from Channi’s supporters. They demanded that Channi should be projected as the party’s CM face in the assembly elections. What followed left the Congress leadership red-faced. From war or words to slogan-shouting at party meetings, the wide split in the state unit was out in the open. The Congress sent Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhupesh Baghel to firefight, but he was also singed in the crossfire. Channi camp leaders accused him of siding with Warring.Pilot, who was then air-dashed to Punjab to set the house in order, has passed his maiden test. But assembly elections in the state are still at least 5 months away. Holding the rival factions together till then will indeed be a daunting challenge for the former Rajasthan deputy chief minister.
Well begun is half done
So, how did Pilot cross the first hurdle smoothly? What did he do differently, which Bhupesh Baghel couldn’t?Former Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhupesh Baghel was sent to Punjab in February this year. The Congress in Punjab then was a deeply divided house. Baghel worked hard on the ground to bridge differences between the state leaders. But on July 1, when the Congress high command announced to continue with Raja Warring as the state Congress president and made Channi the head of the campaign committee, the rebellion in the state unit came out in the open.Channi’s supporters openly opposed the decision. When Baghel reinforced the leadership structure and ruled out any change, the rebels openly protested and even raised slogans against him.Baghel tried to pacify the rebels by announcing that Punjab elections would be fought under the leadership of Rahul Gandhi and no state leader would be projected as CM face. But the rebels had lost his trust and refused to budge.With the rebels refusing to relent and their open infighting embarrassing the party leadership, the Congress high command decided to do a course correction to set its house in order.Baghel was shifted out, Pilot was brought in with a clear message: Congress would contest the 2027 assembly elections under collective leadership, and Rahul Gandhi would be the face of the campaign. This was a half-way compromise. The party leadership relented on Baghel but refused to budge on replacing Warring - at least for now.Warring was handpicked by the Congress high command to lead the Punjab unit after the party’s rout in the 2017 assembly elections - which saw the grand-old-party reduced to 17 assembly seats - its worst-ever performance in the state.
“No CM face” compromise
So, Pilot has crossed the first hurdle. But at what cost? Congress’s decision to fight the Punjab assembly elections under collective leadership, with Rahul Gandhi as the face of the campaign, may have at best delayed the inevitable power tussle.But it creates another challenge for the party. Much of the Congress’s success in the state till now has been driven by a strong local leadership - Captain Amarinder Singh, who is now with the BJP.The AAP has already announced to contest the upcoming assembly elections under the leadership of Bhagwant Singh Mann. Arvind Kejriwal, who is the face of AAP has largely worked from behind the scenes - planning and strategising for the Punjab challenge. For the Akalis, Sukhbir Singh Badal is the undisputed leader and the party’s campaign revolves around him.That leaves us with the BJP and the Congress.
PM Modi vs Rahul
The Congress decision to contest Punjab assembly elections with Rahul Gandhi as the party’s face makes the upcoming electoral contest interesting, and perhaps also challenging for the party.The BJP has already launched an aggressive campaign for Punjab with Prime Minister Narendra Modi leading the party’s campaign. PM Modi has already held two rallies in the poll-bound state and has announced a slew of development projects. As the campaign progresses, we will see the Prime Minister go all out against BJP’s political opponents. The BJP, which is in the process of building the party in the state, also has no visible local leadership. It has acquired quite a few prominent leaders from AAP and Congress, but it is unlikely any of them would be projected as the CM face. BJP’s campaigns in states are mostly centralised, with all top leaders campaigning for the party and PM Modi leading the charge. Punjab should be no exception.And that is what should worry the Congress. The fight to conquer Punjab could well become another PM Modi vs Rahul contest. In several such direct contests in the past, the Congress has struggled. However, Punjab could be different. The BJP, for a greater part of its existence in the state, has played second fiddle to the Akalis.
The BJP has announced a solo contest in 2027 elections.For the Congress, Punjab has been one of the happiest hunting grounds. Despite the haunting memories of Operation Blue Star and the anti-Sikh killings, Punjab has voted for the Congress. Now, it is over to Pilot to take the Congress beyond the winning line.

EU weighs windfall taxes on energy firms amid growing economic strain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:16:30 UTC
22:16:30 KST

EU ministers meeting in Dublin on Friday and Saturday are considering a windfall tax on energy companies, as price volatility continues to destabilise the economic outlook.
A windfall tax for firms profiting from energy price volatility is one of the ideas circulating among EU ministers meeting in Dublin on Friday and Saturday for the periodic meetings of the Eurogroup and Economic and Financial Council.
With the war in the Middle East continuing, Brent crude oil prices have surpassed $100 per barrel, and extreme volatility in energy prices is driving inflation higher across the bloc, which is not expected to return to the 2% target before the end of 2027.
While growth indicators are still performing well this year, the European Commission expects economic growth to slow down in 2027.
The EU is urging member states to pursue prudent fiscal policies and remain within the existing fiscal flexibility of 1.5% for defence spending, of which 0.3% can be used to contain energy prices.
Meanwhile, the European Central Bank (ECB) is gradually raising interest rates to contain inflation.
“There are several member states that put forward this initiative, it is part of our discussions," European Commissioner for Economy Valdis Dombrovskis said during a press conference on Friday, referring to the windfall tax.
"Member states can already implement windfall profit taxes at the national level if they decide to do so. From the Commission side, we are ready to support those member states by sharing best practices and finding a good way forward.”
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil is pressing the European Commission to present models for a windfall tax, asking to have something on the table by the next Economic and Finance Council meeting in October.
"You know that I have been fighting for this for a long time, together with other European finance ministers," Klingbeil said on the sidelines of Friday's meeting.
The Spanish Finance Minister Carlos Cuerpo also expressed his favour for the proposal on Friday.
“We are managing to lower the bill for homes, companies, industries, transport companies, and this at the expense of the taxpayer's money. We believe there may be fairer ways to distribute this cost,” Cuerpo said.
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure has been more cautious about the proposal.
“This [energy] shock can have a different impact on different countries. We do feel that whatever discussion we have, whatever work has been done, needs to take into account the specificities of each country," he said ahead of the meeting on Friday, specifying that France has a "bigger electricity mix".
To the direct question on whether he supports the proposal or not, Lescure said that he support any work that’s being done, but that "I can’t support something before I’ve seen it".
"I’ll see what the work comes out with, and then we’ll have a discussion.”
Energy taxes: the bulk of pricing
Although the energy crisis is affecting the bloc, not all member states are affected in the same way, with prices at the pump varying greatly.
Finland, Denmark and the Netherlands, the three EU countries currently paying the most for diesel, impose some of the highest fuel taxes in the world, pushing retail diesel prices much higher.
On the other hand, countries in Eastern Europe such as Bulgaria and Poland set excise duties far lower, keeping their pump prices down.
Yet according to EU official data published on Thursday, the EU country paying the least for diesel is Malta, with €1.20 per litre charged at the pump on 14 September.
The significant discrepancy in diesel prices across the EU is driven mainly by divergent national tax policies – excise duties and VAT – which make up the largest portion of the retail price of diesel.
However, the difference between diesel prices before and after taxes is staggering. Per the data released on Thursday, Finland’s diesel price stood €1.48 per litre before taxes and €2.50 after taxes.
Denmark also ranked high, with diesel at €1.43 before taxes and €2.50 per litre after taxes, while Dutch citizens would pay only €1.50 per litre of diesel without taxes and €2.49 with taxes.
France, which has the third-highest government debt in the EU, has chosen targeted to offer assistance for the sectors most exposed to the price shock rather than cutting fuel taxes.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asked ministers to extend support for sectors most exposed to higher energy costs until 31 December. Meanwhile, diesel prices at the French pump stood at €2.29 per litre on 14 September, against €1.30 before taxes.
Regional refining capacity also further amplifies energy pricing. All EU countries buy crude oil from the same volatile global markets, but the price motorists ultimately pay at the pump depends on whether there is sufficient refining capacity nearby, how easily fuel can be transported from other regions and how well local refineries can process the particular type of crude available.
During a supply shock like the one the EU is currently suffering, EU countries with spare refining capacity, diversified import routes and strong links to neighbouring fuel markets may be able to cushion the disruption more easily.

China Is Moving Toward a New Form of Coercion at Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
13:16:00 UTC
22:16:00 KST

Since Beijing announced special maritime operations on June 6, its forces have grown more assertive – pushing patrols into new waters, rotating formations to regularize presence, and deploying research vessels that can conduct military reconnaissance. This all points to a new form of coercion taking shape.
On July 4, the Global Times – a mouthpiece for the Chinese Communist Party – declared that China’s maritime patrols had entered “a new phase,” defined by a move towards “a more systematic, institutionalized, and long-term framework” and away from “isolated military exercises or patrols.”
Recent deployments bear this out. Between June 6 and June 10, China’s Ministry of Transport carried out its first special operation in waters east of Taiwan, halting commercial vessels and requesting information on their points of origin and destination.
While China has announced mandatory inspections during past exercises, it has never successfully enforced them. This time was different. Chinese Coast Guard ships conducted inspections en masse through radio communications with all transiting commercial vessels. Even foreign commercial vessels – including three vessels from Singapore, Benin, and Liberia – reported receiving radio messages from Chinese authorities to comply with requests.
According to Chinese state news agency Xinhua, across those four days, Chinese maritime authorities inspected 198 passing vessels, and even “rectified violations involving three ships.” The sheer quantity of reported inspections, followed by a public announcement of the results, demonstrates China’s ability to govern vessel traffic in Taiwan’s waters. Beijing uses that as grounds to assert jurisdiction over the island and to push the narrative that cross-strait dynamics are China’s internal affairs.
These operations may be testing grounds for an eventual quarantine, where China selectively permits commercial vessels to enter or leave, exerting immense pressure on Taiwan’s supply lines. If that is the case, the series of multi-day patrols serve two functions.
First, they test how foreign nations respond to maritime traffic controls. Knowing which nations elect to respond, and to what degree, gives Beijing some sense of what to expect. The United Kingdom, Germany, and France, for instance, issued a joint statement expressing alarm over the maritime activities. Australia raised concerns directly with Chinese officials. How forceful Beijing judges the pushback to be will affect the intensity of operations. In the event of an actual quarantine, though, responses are likely to be more pronounced.
Second, they normalize China’s vessel inspections, shortening the leap to a quarantine. In July, China’s Coast Guard began rotating its formations to regularize its law-enforcement presence. The Global Times has noted the advantages of maintaining a “constant presence” because “a normalized presence itself exerts pressure.” The longer Beijing can keep ships on station, the more quickly it can impose a quarantine.
The location of operations is unusual as well. Until June, China appeared to prioritize the Taiwan Strait, where conditions are most favorable for launching an amphibious invasion. Oddly enough, the maritime operations have been concentrated in waters opposite the strait, to the east of Taiwan. The island’s eastern coast has long been regarded as a low-priority zone as steep mountains make military landings difficult.
But choosing to operate in the east is not random. The move effectively shrinks the space that Taiwan can operate in, aligning with China’s broader boa-constrictor strategy to sever the island from international support. More telling is that these patrols, China claims, were initiated as a response to talks between Japan and the Philippines to delimit maritime boundaries east of Taiwan. Beijing hopes to deter strategic cooperation between two U.S. allies, one located north and the other to the south of the island, that may each play critical roles during a conflict over Taiwan.
A final novelty of the recent operations is the sharp increase in Chinese research vessels operating in waters around Taiwan. While Beijing maintains that these ships only conduct marine scientific research, their missions appear far less benign. Publicly available tracking data shows that these vessels could be systematically mapping the undersea terrain, presaging planning for naval operations. Since June 6, at least seven research vessels have been suspected of conducting research with military applications.
Taken together, these signs indicate that a more intrusive form of coercion is taking form. Regional nations would be unwise to dismiss this as more of the same.

Air passenger traffic across Türkiye in the first eight months of 2026 topped 167.5 million, nearly twice the country's population, he noted.
