Women and girls pay high price in DR Congo Ebola outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Women and girls pay high price in DR Congo Ebola outbreak
The deadly Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has taken a disproportionate toll on women and girls, many of whom are on the frontlines caring for patients as well as their own families despite the high risk of infection.
This is evident in the city of Bunia, epicentre of the crisis, said Dr. Setcheme Mongbo, UN Women Representative in the DRC, speaking on Friday following a recent visit to the city.
"Women are not only present in health facilities as attendants, but also in communities and homes where they care for the sick, provide them with food and water, and even participate in washing corpses as well as funeral activities," she said, speaking from Kinshasa to journalists in Geneva.
Statistics are clear
According to Dr. Mongbo, the division of care and responsibilities at home largely reflects the Ebola transmission chain. That situation, she said, is what puts women and girls at the greatest risk.
Official data shows that more than 54 percent of confirmed Ebola patients in the DRC are women. Girls make up 51 percent of those in the 10 to 17 age group.
Dr. Mongbo said the effects also spread to children, since when women get sick, dependent children are directly affected.
"Women and girls are the ones who take care of their children and siblings without protective equipment," she said, explaining that they often continue to provide care even when someone is seriously ill.
Journey of no return
Among the stories that touched Dr. Mongbo was that of a woman who shared her fear of going to an Ebola treatment centre.
The woman said entering the medical facility “felt like a one-way journey - being separated from her children and unsure of whether she was ever going to return home.”
That fear, according to Dr. Mongbo, is compounded by stigma, the possibility of abuse, exclusion from children as well as concerns about their own safety.
The women she met in Bunia also explained to her that they often put the health and safety of children and their families before their own lives.
Domestic deaths
Dr. Mongbo said there is also the possibility of community deaths that may not be included in the official Ebola statistics. “I heard stories of women who fell ill and died in their homes after some of them made statements calling for help but got no response,” she said.
Community members told her that “four women died at home in a single day with no official record. And we are not able to verify whether they had subsequently captured those figures.”
She cited latest data which show that two-thirds of the deaths reported in a 24-hour period occurred in communities, rather than medical facilities.
This situation, she said, increases the risk of cases and deaths not being handled properly as well as being absent from official outbreak response statistics.
Shut off from essential services
In addition to the risk of infection, the outbreak is affecting access to essential healthcare for women.
Dr. Mongbo said women are increasingly losing out on opportunities to access reproductive and maternal health services, when access to such services was already limited before the outbreak.
The problem is also compounded by decades of conflict, insecurity and poor road infrastructure which makes regular transport to some areas difficult or impossible.
Income and businesses hit
The outbreak has also affected women's livelihoods.
According to Dr. Mongbo, women make up a significant number of the traders in the affected areas. Travel restrictions and border closures – measures that could be crucial in controlling the outbreak – have deprived many women of their sources of income.
Women traders told her that their daily income had decreased by between 20 and 30 dollars.
While that amount may seem small, the reduction is “leaving them unable to feed their families and children, making them even more vulnerable to health infections.”
Dr. Mongbo said women-led organizations play an important role in the Ebola response because they have built trust within the community over the years.
However, she said a UN Women study shows that 86 per cent of the women-led organizations surveyed said they had not received any form of funding for Ebola response, with nine out of 10 not being involved in decision-making.
Boost women's participation
Dr. Mongbo said UN Women supports the Ebola response in the DRC by ensuring the needs, risks and special capacities of women and girls are taken into account in efforts to address the outbreak.
The measures include working with women leaders to raise awareness about Ebola and ways to protect themselves, increasing women's participation in the response and preventing gender-based violence.
She said UN Women is ready to launch a comprehensive gender response strategy against Ebola next Tuesday.
For Dr. Mongbo, the message from Bunia is clear: Women are not only Ebola survivors, but an important part of the solution, therefore, “women and their organizations are key to stopping the Ebola outbreak in the DRC.”

Sexual violence against civilians and POW’s in Ukraine widespread and ‘abhorrent’

Sexual violence against civilians and POW’s in Ukraine widespread and ‘abhorrent’
Over 1,000 cases of sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war (POWs) in Ukraine have been documented from the start of Russia’s invasion to the end of July this year.
That’s according to a new UN human rights office (OHCHR) report which details violations including gang rape, rape, genital mutilation, electric shocks and beatings to the genitals – together with other degrading acts of a sexual nature.
Violations were recorded on both sides of the frontline, but the pattern is very different “in scope and scale,” stressed Danielle Bell, the head of the Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, briefing journalists on Friday.
Russian authorities – including members of the armed forces, prison service and national security service – were responsible for 89 per cent of the documented cases.
Sexual violence was particularly widespread among detainees held by Russian authorities, with almost three-quarters of former prisoners of war and nearly half of all civilians detained experiencing sexual violence on more than one occasion, Ms. Bell reported.
The remaining 11 per cent of documented cases were attributed to Ukrainian authorities, and almost half of these exclusively comprised threats.
Ms. Bell also stressed that Ukraine provides the UN mission with “unfettered access” to the prisoner-of-war camps and to other detention facilities.
Most victims are men
Most of the victims of sexual violence were men, particularly in places of detention, and those interviewed for the report recounted deeply distressing experiences.
Many of the Ukrainian POWs and retained medical personnel suffering violations by Russian forces said they were tasered in the genitals using a Soviet-era military field telephone known as a “tapik”, with 155 (27 per cent) having endured this form at least once.
One Ukrainian POW described being raped with a baton, another being forcibly penetrated with cell door keys. One Ukrainian civilian said he had been raped with a shovel handle.
Women and children
Nonetheless, women and children were also affected, primarily in occupied territory of Ukraine.
The youngest documented rape survivor was a four-year-old-girl and the oldest an 82-year-old woman, with both cases perpetrated by Russian authorities.
One of the women interviewed recounted that a Russian soldier moved into her home in Zaporizhzhia and raped her several times a week for a month, promising that her detained husband would be treated better in exchange.
Another woman said a Russian soldier forced his way into her home in Kherson and raped her every night. He also repeatedly threatened her with gang rape.
In another case, a woman described how two Russian soldiers broke into a family home in the Kyiv region in 2022. After shooting and killing her husband, they gang raped her and threatened to shoot her in front of her four-year-old son if she resisted.
‘Almost certainly’ ongoing
“I am deeply alarmed by the prevalence of these abhorrent acts documented in our report, and fear that they are almost certainly continuing amid the unceasing violence we are witnessing every day in Ukraine,” said UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk.
“It must stop immediately, irrespective of the perpetrators,” he stressed.
“Given the high prevalence of cases attributed to its forces, however, the Russian Federation in particular must take concrete and discernible steps to protect civilians and prisoners of war from all forms of torture, including sexual violence,” he said.

‘Violence will only defer a problem’: UN Assembly President on trust, AI and lessons from the Rohingya crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘Violence will only defer a problem’: UN Assembly President on trust, AI and lessons from the Rohingya crisis
Khalilur Rahman took the gavel as President of the UN General Assembly's 81st session amid what he calls a crisis of confidence in the organization he has served – in one capacity or another – for 35 years.
The top Bangladeshi diplomat and sitting foreign minister has staked his one-year presidency on a single ambition: restoring trust.
It’s a theme he returns to often, tracing it back to the optimism of the UN’s founding in 1945 and the gap between what Member States expected then and what the organization has delivered since.
As High-Level Week gets underway – the busiest week of the UN calendar, the largest gathering of world leaders in one place anywhere on the planet – Mr. Rahman sat down with UN News to discuss what a “much needed transformation” would actually look like, why he believes artificial intelligence poses a test unlike anything the UN has faced before and what lessons from his work on the Rohingya crisis he is carrying into the role.
He also addressed critics who argue the assembly is toothless compared with a gridlocked Security Council, and reflected on the moment, more than four decades after serving his own foreign minister during a previous Bangladeshi presidency of the assembly, that brought him back to lead it himself.
UN News: High-level Week is underway. What are your expectations, and what do you hope world leaders will take away from it?
Khalilur Rahman: High-level Week is the most powerful manifestation of the convening power of the United Nations. It’s an opportunity to hear directly from those governing our societies – how they see the world, their regions, their own countries and what they expect from the UN.
One of the things I’m looking for most closely is what they say about reviving trust in the organization. That is the highlight of my presidency. I’ve made it my own theme, and I want to draw on their views as a guide for my work on this agenda.
UN News: Restoring trust is at the heart of your presidency. What does that look like in practice, and how will you know if you’re succeeding?
Khalilur Rahman: Go back to 1945 at the time of creation of this Organization. In Yalta that year, President Roosevelt, Stalin and Churchill met for about eight days. Alongside arrangements for ending the war, they conceived of a world organization whose primary purpose was to prevent a repeat of the conflicts we saw in the two world wars.
When the UN was formally created in San Francisco, delegations gave it a standing ovation and kept standing for a while. That represented the aspiration that the UN would be able to give peace.
And I’m happy to say that in the eight decades since, we’ve avoided a large-scale global conflagration. Countries that weren’t at the table then have emerged from colonial rule and built a robust development pillar within the UN.
But at the same time, we haven’t prevented many conflicts, and progress on development has often been sluggish. We have to work hard to ensure that the Security Council works more coherently and delivers as it was expected to.
Both pillars carry major unmet expectations, and that breeds frustration – a sense that the UN isn’t doing what people expected of it. That has fed declining trust.
I should also mention human rights, our third pillar: we spend only four per cent of our total spending on it. We’ve made major strides, but much remains to be done.
We have to work hard along all three pillars to bring back the confidence the organization had at its creation. It’s a major challenge, and it will require all member states and stakeholders to work together.
UN News: You’ve said this is not 1945, and the world has moved on. What’s one concrete change you’d point to?
Khalilur Rahman: Artificial Intelligence [AI]. It could be a great accelerator of human endeavour, but if you believe the doomsday predictions from some major figures, it could also pose serious dangers to humanity.
We shouldn’t do anything to slow innovation – that has to continue. But it’s vital that we put guardrails in place, so this innovation serves humanity rather than working against it.
That’s a job not only for governments but for everyone practically involved in developing and using the technology. We need all of these communities to be part of the discussions and decisions ahead, so we find a safe pathway toward AI genuinely serving humanity.
UN News: Critics say assembly resolutions carry moral weight but no teeth, and that real power still sits with a gridlocked Security Council. What do you say to that?
Khalilur Rahman: If the assembly were useless, there wouldn’t be a high-level week, and Heads of State wouldn’t come. There must be some utility. What I see is the great convening power of a body that represents the entire world — there’s no other place quite like it.
Diplomacy isn’t always done in the open. The assembly gives Heads of Government and Heads of State a safe environment to discuss serious issues together and find ways to resolve them. It’s also an authoritative way of hearing directly from those governing our societies.
I believe the assembly will continue to play an important role in setting norms and giving overall direction to the work of the international community.
UN News: You worked directly on the Rohingya crisis. What lessons are you carrying into the presidency?
Khalilur Rahman: It’s a grave human crisis – a population attacked, their homes bombed, their villages burned, chased out by their own countrymen. Pregnant mothers’ bellies cut open and the fetuses thrown into fire.
But I also saw their resilience, their ability to survive and their yearning to go home. When the Secretary-General visited Cox's Bazar last year, more than 100,000 refugees gathered on a Ramadan evening to share breakfast with him, each holding a placard reading: we want to go home.
The lesson I carry is this: violence will not solve any problem. It will only defer it and make it worse. Only through talks and negotiation, only by coming together, can we resolve these issues.
That’s why I see such value in the assembly – a place where people gather at the highest levels, in a safe environment, to work out the best way forward.
UN News: Looking ahead to the last day of your presidency, what would you hope to look back on with pride?
Khalilur Rahman: This is what I told my team today – I’m not looking at today. I am looking at the day when I’m handing over the gavel to my successor. If I can help Member States agree on necessary reform of the organization, agree to keep it financially solvent and agree to speed up delivery at the local level – if I have some movement on any of these, I’ll happily hand over my gavel to my successor.

How the Air Force Rigged F-15s in the Middle East with Drone-Busting Rockets in a Week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—As the threat of Iranian-made drones rose in recent conflicts, the Air Force rushed last year to equip F-15E Strike Eagles in the Middle East with a cheap, cost-effective way of defeating them.
The Air Force Test Center was able to field the new capability—laser-guided rockets—in roughly a week, the head of the center revealed at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference here Sept. 16.
It’s not the first time the Air Force has turned to this solution, known as the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, to neutralize enemy one-way attack drones and cruise missiles.
APKWS was originally designed as an air-to-ground capability, with a laser-guided kit added to Hydra-70 rockets to turn the system into a precision-guided munition.
The Air Force explored using the rockets in an air-to-air role in 2019, testing the system on the F-16 Fighting Falcon. For a few years, the experiment was considered nothing more than a proof of concept, not a real-world capability.
But as the use of Iranian drones was expanded, the program gained new urgency. The system was rushed first to F-16s in 2024 and then prioritized for F-15Es in 2025. Nine days after testing began in May of last year, the system was being equipped on Strike Eagles overseas, said Brig. Gen. Mark A. Massaro.
“At the end of the first week, we had demonstrated, both in a developmental and an operational sense, that it was a usable capability, and we deployed that capability at the end of the first week,” Massaro said. “We deployed that capability into theater. We deployed some of our maintainers and some of our testers into theater to help the first week.”
The initiative is an example of the Air Force Test Center’s ability to quickly “bridge between raw concept and decisive combat-credible power,” said Massaro. He was involved in tests of APKWS in his previous role as commander of the 96th Test Wing, which conducts developmental testing of weapons for the service, and worked alongside the 53rd Wing, which conducts operational tests.
The need for the system was clear. The Air Force had relied on expensive, radar-guided AIM-120 AMRAAM missiles and infrared-guided AIM-9 Sidewinders against Tehran’s relatively cheap Shahed one-way attack drones. AMRAAMs cost roughly $1 million each, and AIM-9s cost hundreds of thousands of dollars depending on the variant. The most capable model is the AIM-9X, which costs around $500,000.
The issue came to a head with a mass Iranian drone and ballistic missile attack aimed at Israel on April 13, 2024. Tehran, which sought to flood the zone, launched a barrage of drones, ballistic missiles, and cruise missiles to confuse and overwhelm Israel’s air defenses—some 300 projectiles in all.
The U.S. had anticipated the engagement, and F-15Es from the 335th Fighter Squadron and 494th Fighter Squadron carried up to eight air-to-air missiles each as they sought to intercept the drones over Iraq along with F-16s from the 121st Fighter Squadron. The Iranian drone barrage was so heavy that many fighters quickly exhausted their air-to-air missiles, and three F-15E crews attempted—unsuccessfully—to drop laser-guided JDAM bombs on drones.
While U.S. fighters had helped to defeat the barrage, it was an expensive proposition, which led to the effort to adapt APKWS rockets, which cost roughly $35,000 according to Air Force officials.
Dubbed the AGR-20F FALCO, the air-to-air APKWS rockets were first used in an air-to-air configuration on F-16s in 2024.
After that, work began at Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., to equip the system on F-15Es. That occurred in mid-2025, led by 96th Wing’s Air Force Seek Eagle Office, known as AFSEO, which had earlier integrated the system into F-16s.
“This was a very integrated test approach between operational and developmental,” Massaro said. “We were overlaying … missions on exactly the same day with each other and flying them together. That second week, where we have our maintainers and some pilots in theater, our operational testers are still refining some of the tactics, and we’re able to then through phone and digital means transmit the upgraded tactics. And then, so at the end of that second week, they had updated tactics, they had equipment, they had everything ready to go, and they were able to use it very quickly after that.”
Early last year, the team initially struggled to find a way to mount the rockets on the F-15E and connect them to the aircraft so they could be fired. In May 2025, a solution was found, and the integration became the top priority for the 96th Test Wing and 53rd Wing at the base, according to Air Force officials.
Aircrew from the 40th Flight Test Squadron and the 85th and 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadrons flew test missions and conducted live-fire tests at targets over land and water.
After the initial demonstrations, the 53rd Wing and 96th Test Wing deployed to deliver equipment and provide training to Airmen to use the new weapons. While the Air Force has declined to identify the location where the system was first fielded, U.S. officials confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine that air-to-air APKWS was first used in the Middle East, which is part of U.S. Central Command.
In 2024, Air Forces Central began to equip its F-16s to shoot down drones in the Middle East with APKWS rockets, which were employed to defeat threats from the Houthis in Yemen.
A U.S. F-16 scored its first rocket kill of a drone that year. In October 2024, the 480th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron from Spangdahlem Air Base, Germany, deployed to the Middle East with an advance but limited heads-up that they would be equipped with APKWS for air-to-air use against drones and cruise missiles.
“The first rocket kill was announced just prior to getting there. This was all new and innovative,” Lt. Col. William “Skate” Parks, the unit’s commander, recounted in a December 2025 interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “We have these rockets come online. It’s a brand new thing, and we’re the ones doing it. And it’s with guys who are now spending every minute of their day when they’re not flying actual combat missions, preparing and improving on this. It showed because that success rate just started really becoming amazing with these rockets as we’re defending partners and our own forces.”
The 480th scored dozens of kills using the rockets. It also used older AIM-9M Sidewinders, claiming the first air-to-air kill by an AIM-9M in over 30 years, and 108 total aerial kills of drones and cruise missiles during the deployment. News of the success quickly trickled across the Air Force.
By April 2025, U.S. Air Forces in Europe incorporated the APKWS into its air-to-air training for F-16s, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported. U.S. fighters based on the continent not only routinely deploy to the Middle East, but also increasingly must be wary of Russian drone incursions into NATO airspace. The F-16 experience helped speed up the use of the APKWS as a drone-buster on the F-15E, Massaro said.
“A lot of things had already occurred,” he said. “The F-16 had already integrated APKWS and was flying with that for about a year, so we knew how the system itself worked. We had that knowledge. The F-15E is a known quantity.”
APKWS rockets come in pods of seven, and multiple rocket pods can be fitted. F-15Es can carry up to 42 APKWS rockets. To guide an APKWS rocket, the target must be laser-designated or “lased,” unlike more expensive “fire-and-forget” missiles. This means air-to-air use of the rocket pods is best suited to defeating slow-flying targets such as one-way attack drones.
The work to put APKWS on the F-16 and F-15E would pay off in more than just cost savings for the Air Force. After the start of Operation Epic Fury on Feb. 28, Iran has fired more than 6,000 drones and 1,500 ballistic missiles, with numbers growing, U.S. officials said. What two years ago was an extreme outlier is now a routine threat.
F-16s flying in the area around the Strait of Hormuz, Persian Gulf, and Gulf of Oman, where Iran has repeatedly used drones and missiles to attack ships including U.S. Navy vessels, are flying with APKWS rocket pods to hunt down drones. U.S. Army Apache helicopters can also fire APKWS rockets in an air-to-air role, another recent capability fielded by the military. The U.S. also needs to protect its bases in the Middle East.
The former head of Air Forces Central, Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, said the use of APKWS was a key development during his tenure, which ended last month.
“From a technical aspect, it’s ‘Hey, I need more weapons on my jet,’ and that’s what the APKWS gives you: a pod of seven of those things versus a single AIM-9. You can shoot down a lot more drones when they’re coming in swarms,” France said in a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “From an operational perspective, there’s not just the magazine depth of an individual airplane, which I care about, but I care about the magazine depth of the theater and making sure that, across the theater, I’ve got wings with the right weapons in the right place and get them in the air where they can defend their bases. … There’s the cost curve, which is significant as well.”
And the proliferation of the drone threat is only increasing, U.S. military officials and experts say, making further advancements necessary.
“I would say that APKWS is a step in the right direction, but it can’t be the final step,” France said. “The two things that we need to focus on are air domain awareness at range: where are the drones coming from? How many are there? What’s their target? What do I know about them? And then magazine depth, both individual airplanes and theater-wise, to have enough to shoot them down in a layered defense kind of way. So both of those are important.”
“This drone problem is not going away. It’s accelerating in tactics, speed, advancements, and the numbers,” France added. “That’s the direction that we’re going.”

Police begin operation to move migrants from Ceuta beaches
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
12:59:42 BST
20:59:42 KST

Shots heard as police start moving migrants from Ceuta beaches
- Published
Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa.
Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air.
Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people.
Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned. Ceuta's authorities have estimated that 13,000 remain in the enclave, but the Spanish central government has said it is lower.
The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe.
During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control.
More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue.
The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined.
The chaotic scenes will do little to dampen opposition criticism in Spain of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has faced strong criticism over his handling of the crisis.
Since the migrant influx, residents of the 18.5 sq km (7.2 sq miles) territory have expressed safety concerns. Some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.
Ceuta's Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas told lawmakers in the European Parliament earlier this month that the migrants had turned Ceuta into a "pressure cooker".
"The city is completely different than it was before this event, Ceutans have lost their joy and their lifestyles have been completely shaken up," the conservative mayor said.
The opposition also accused Sánchez of knowing about the influx of migrants in advance. Sánchez has insisted that it was impossible to predict, but according to government documents, its intelligence services had warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before the events happened.
Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party said the government was "directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died".
Sanchez has blamed trafficking gangs and has also said the crisis was sparked by hoaxes and rumours spread by social media.
Ceuta was "a humanitarian crisis and also an administrative challenge within the city itself", the prime minister said.
The incident has also created diplomatic headaches for Sánchez.
The prime minister is at odds with Italy, with the two countries earlier this week extending temporary border controls imposed on each other. He is also trying to maintain his bilateral relationship with Morocco.
The influx of migrants in late July came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.
After the ruling, some social media accounts spread misinformation and offered to help migrants cross the Spanish border for hundreds of pounds.
Thousands of people then flooded across the border fence and swam around the ocean barriers. At least 100 people died during the crossing, according to local authorities.

Rubber bullets fired as Spain moves migrants from Ceuta beach camps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:58:28 UTC
20:58:28 KST

Spanish riot police fired rubber bullets into the air and struck people with batons on Friday as they began an operation to clear thousands of migrants off beaches in the North African enclave of Ceuta and move some of them into temporary housing.
Spain estimates 10,000 migrants remain in the tiny territory. More than 72,000 crossed into the enclave from Morocco at the end of July in an unprecedented border rush, although most later left.
The authorities have built new temporary housing inside the enclave's port to hold 1,700 people. NGOs say thousands remain unhoused and have been sleeping rough in camps.
Friday's operation to clear the beaches began shortly before 7 a.m. local time and involved both riot police and the Spanish military.
Migrants who had spent the night waiting on the beach in hope of a place in temporary shelter initially applauded as the march got under way, but tussles later broke out as they competed for the limited number of places available.
Footage from state broadcaster TVE showed crowding and jostling as people struggled to enter the designated route. Police fired rubber bullets into the air and struck several migrants with batons before the situation calmed down and the operation resumed.
Later footage showed mostly adult men carrying belongings, walking in small groups under police escort along a route of just over 1 km. (0.6 miles) from the El Trampolin beach to the port.
Most Ceuta migrants are men, boys
The vast majority of the migrants are men and boys. The temporary housing is built only for adult men, so minors are being separated and housed separately.
Three NGO leaders told Reuters that authorities had been too slow to provide migrants with the minimum shelter required under the European migration pact, and that reception centers opened so far could not accommodate those still sleeping on the streets.
One NGO estimated that about 4,000 migrants remained outdoors on Ceuta's beaches and pavements, meaning the new center would not be sufficient to clear makeshift camps in public areas. Two NGO leaders said officials probably expect most migrants to return voluntarily to Morocco.

Russians began voting on Friday in a three-day parliamentary election which President Vladimir Putin has said will show that millions of people back his army fighting in Ukraine, even though most anti-war candidates were not allowed to run.
The State Duma election, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, is widely expected to see the ruling pro-Putin United Russia party retain its dominance in Russia's tightly controlled political system.
The result is likely to be held up by the Kremlin as evidence of widespread public support for Putin's policies and, in particular, for his prosecution of Europe's deadliest conflict since World War Two, now in its fifth year.

In another move to boost morale and support for fighting on until victory, bone fragments from the sword hand of a medieval Russian prince who won a famous victory over the Mongols were sent to the front in Ukraine in the run-up to the vote.
Voting in Moscow, Anatoliy Simonenko, 76, said he was sanguine about what might happen after the election amid speculation, repeatedly denied by the authorities, that a new wave of mobilization may be announced.
"There are some very grim predictions, and others that are more optimistic. I expect the outcome will likely fall somewhere in the middle. War is war. It entails expenses, defense spending, and cuts to various social benefits. Well, it’s necessary; there’s no getting around it," he told Reuters.
Another voter, who declined to give his name, said he believed the results were easy to rig and raised doubts about an electronic voting system being used in some parts of the country. The electoral commission has rejected such suggestions as false.
State media showed Putin casting his own vote electronically from his Kremlin office.
Candidates against Ukraine-Russia War have been excluded from Moscow's Duma election ballot
Most anti-war candidates were excluded from the ballot before voting across Russia's 11 time zones got underway, after the Supreme Court ruled last month that the liberal Yabloko party, which wants a ceasefire in Ukraine, had breached electoral rules, something it denied.
Some candidates from Yabloko, which has traditionally only got single-digit support in opinion polls, are still running in individual constituencies that account for half the 450 seats in the lower house of parliament.
In the run-up to the vote, Lev Shlosberg, a senior figure in the Yabloko party, was jailed for 11 years for comments about the war. Its deputy leader, Maxim Kruglov, was jailed for seven years on similar charges in June.
Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news is punishable with long jail terms.
Some opinion polls show public support for peace talks has risen to over 60%, and the Kremlin has repeatedly said that it is ready to resume such talks.
However, it has also made clear, as its troops push to take control of the rest of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, that any settlement must leave it in full control of all of that territory and that it only wants a long-term deal, not a ceasefire.
Voting is taking place at a time when opinion polls show some Russians have become more anxious about how the conflict affects them.
The economy is also under strain, and the authorities are expected to use the vote to gauge the depth of society's war weariness as fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian drone strikes on oil refineries roil some parts of the country, and businesses grapple with drone attacks on their warehouses, high interest rates, a labor crunch and Western sanctions.
National unity vital amid Ukraine attempting to stir unrest, Kremlin claims
The Kremlin says national unity is vital because of what it says are increasingly dangerous efforts by Ukraine's intelligence services and other enemies to stir unrest inside Russia.
Initial and partial results are expected to begin trickling out on Sunday evening, and near-complete results to be available on Monday.

The Federation of Western Thrace Turks in Europe (ABTTF) has raised concerns at the U.N. Human Rights Council over the Western Thrace Turkish minority’s right to elect its own muftis and the state’s control over its religious institutions.
In a written statement submitted on Sept. 18 to the council’s 63rd regular session in Geneva, the federation said the minority’s religious rights and autonomy are protected under the 1913 Athens Treaty and the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne.
ABTTF said the minority had elected its own muftis until 1985, but that a legal change in 1991 led to the state appointing religious leaders, effectively ending the community’s right to elect its muftis. It also said a 2022 law placed mufti offices under the Ministry of Education, Religious Affairs and Sports.
According to the federation, the Greek government appointed a mufti in Didymoteicho in 2026, while similar appointment processes were underway in Xanthi and Komotini.
ABTTF said the state’s control over the minority’s religious institutions raises concerns over freedom of religion and equality, arguing that followers of other recognized faiths in Greece are able to choose their religious leaders.
Greece also appoints the administrative boards of minority-owned charitable foundations, a practice opposed by the Turkish minority, which has called for its elected muftis to be allowed to serve.
The Western Thrace region, near Greece’s northeastern border with Türkiye, is home to a long-established Muslim Turkish minority estimated at around 150,000 people.

Strait of Hormuz disruptions lead to worst threat to global trade in 80 years: WTO chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:53:47 UTC
20:53:47 KST

Nuran Erkul and Emir Yildirim
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Global trade is facing its worst disruption in 80 years as supply chain bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz threaten global food and fertilizer prices, the World Trade Organization's (WTO) director-general warned.
Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, speaking on the sidelines of the WTO’s Public Forum in Geneva, told Anadolu that the global trading system remains resilient, but the ongoing Middle East conflict presents a major test for the organization’s 166 member countries.
She noted that global trade in goods grew by an unexpectedly strong 4.6% this year despite geopolitical pressures, while 72% of all global commerce continued to operate under WTO rules.
The initial projection for overall goods trade growth was 1.9% for the entire year, but the first-quarter growth rate of 3.2% outpaced expectations.
Okonjo-Iweala stated that a significant portion of the momentum was driven by the surging trade in artificial intelligence, which it turn was driven by low- or zero-tariff agreements covering $3 trillion in global semiconductor and chip shipments.
She urged caution over the sustainability of the trend, while warning that the economic benefits of this booming trade remain concentrated in North America and East Asia, raising concerns about global market inclusivity.
Okonjo-Iweala said national reserves temporarily shielded markets from the shocks that the Strait of Hormuz disruptions have caused thus far, but prolonged blockades in the vital waterway will inevitably lead to higher agricultural costs.
The WTO’s previous estimates showed that crude oil prices reaching $90-a-barrel could drive down overall trade growth by 0.5 points, while current crude oil prices have exceeded that threshold.
Maritime shippers maintained trade volume by rerouting vessels via alternative routes, but these lengthy detours are adding steep premiums, calling into question the long-term stability of the current supply chain, Okonjo-Iweala warned.
Governments around the world are drafting contingency plans to protect their economies from future chokepoint failures, while the combination of supply chain instability and rapid shifts in technology has furthered internal WTO talks over the need to overhaul global trade rules for this century.
She noted that comprehensive institutional reform is key to equitable global development, and that the current framework of the WTO has frequently failed developing nations.
Okonjo-Iweala urged developing countries to participate in drafting modernized policies to ensure they can also seize economic opportunities, while the proposed reforms would target failing institutional mechanisms and help prevent these countries from being left behind.
A recent WTO report unveiled as part of its Public Forum estimated that a collapse in multilateral cooperation and a failure to modernize regulations could wipe out up to 10% of potential global economic growth by 2050.

Anduril wins deal to help design future aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:52:31 UTC
20:52:31 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Anduril Industries an $85 million ceiling contract to build digital design tools for aircraft and thermal management systems.
- The 10-year VOLARE contract runs through 2036, with only $50,000 obligated so far on its first task order.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Anduril Industries a contract worth up to $85 million to develop computer-based design tools for future aircraft, part of a push to design and test new systems digitally before building physical hardware.
The Air Force Research Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, made the award under a program called VOLARE, short for Digital System-Level Mission-Driven Integrated Design Methods for Aerospace Systems.
The contract is structured as an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity agreement, meaning the $85 million is a ceiling rather than a guaranteed payout, and the Air Force will issue individual task orders against it as work is needed. Eight companies competed for the award. Anduril will do the work in Dayton, Ohio, and the contract runs through Sept. 17, 2036, giving it a 10-year window.
The program covers two related goals: building a software product that can model an aircraft’s overall vehicle systems, and developing methods for designing thermal management systems, the cooling architecture that keeps an aircraft’s engines, electronics and sensors from overheating. Modern military aircraft pack increasing amounts of high-power radar, computing and directed-energy equipment into the same airframe, and managing the heat that equipment generates has become a design challenge in its own right rather than an afterthought.
No money has been obligated on the base contract itself. The Air Force has funded only the first task order, worth $50,000 in fiscal 2026 research money, with additional funding expected to follow as later task orders are issued.
The award adds to Anduril’s growing work in digital engineering for military aircraft and missiles. The company won a Naval Postgraduate School and Office of Naval Research prize in April 2026 for a proposal that combined digital modeling, simulation and flight testing into a single development process for tactical missiles, an approach the judges described as a credible way to speed up how new weapons move from concept to prototype. AFRL’s Aerospace Systems Directorate, based at Wright-Patterson, has pursued similar digital modeling tools for aircraft thermal systems for more than a decade, including earlier government-funded research into software for simulating aircraft cooling systems.

U.S. Navy advances first new nuke since Cold War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:47:14 UTC
20:47:14 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded JRC Integrated Systems a $47.4 million contract modification for engineering support of its SLCM-N nuclear cruise missile program.
- The missile is also planned for the new Trump-class battleships Trump announced in December 2025, reviving a surface nuclear strike role after decades.
The U.S. Navy has awarded JRC Integrated Systems a $47.4 million contract modification to provide engineering and technical support for the Nuclear-Armed Sea-Launched Cruise Missile, or SLCM-N, the service’s effort to field its first new nuclear weapon since the Cold War.
The modification adds to a contract Strategic Systems Programs, the Navy office overseeing the program, awarded earlier and covers work through Nov. 30, 2030. Tasks include systems engineering and integration, test and flight test engineering, modeling and simulation, oversight of prototype work, system design documentation, and configuration management. The contract also covers nuclear command, control and communications support and both executive and tactical subject matter expertise on nuclear weapons, along with broader program management and acquisition support.
The Navy is obligating $10.1 million in fiscal 2025 research funds now, with the rest tied to optional line items. The work was awarded without competition under a legal provision allowing sole-source nuclear weapons contracts, after being posted publicly on the government’s contract announcement portal.
Work will be split mostly between Washington, D.C., where 80 percent of the effort will take place, with 15 percent at Naval Base Kitsap-Bangor in Washington state, home to the Navy’s Trident submarine fleet, and the remaining 5 percent in Norfolk, Virginia.
The award follows a separate, larger contract The Defence Blog reported earlier, when the Navy gave General Dynamics Missions Systems $194.1 million for engineering support on SLCM-N’s Fire Control Subsystem, with work split between Pittsfield, Massachusetts, and Manassas, Virginia. Rear Adm. Randy Wolfe, director of Strategic Systems Programs, told Congress in May 2025 that the prior year had been spent defining the missile’s overall system architecture, spanning the missile itself, its fire control and launcher systems, platform and warhead integration, and support equipment and training materials.
The SLCM-N traces back to 2018, when the first Trump administration proposed it in that year’s Nuclear Posture Review as a way to restore a low-yield, sea-based nuclear cruise missile option the Navy had given up when it withdrew the nuclear-armed Tomahawk Land Attack Missile from service in 2010. The Biden administration tried to cancel the program in its 2022 Nuclear Posture Review, arguing it was redundant given the submarine-launched W76-2 warhead, but Congress overruled that decision in the fiscal 2024 defense policy act, establishing SLCM-N as a formal program of record. Wolfe has said the Navy expects to deliver the capability in 2034, and Sandia National Laboratories announced in January 2026 that the missile would use a new W80-5 warhead variant.
The program’s surface-ship role became clearer in December 2025, when President Trump announced approval to build an initial pair of nuclear-armed “Trump-class” battleships, with the Navy eventually aiming for a fleet of 20 to 25 of the roughly 30,000- to 40,000-ton ships. As The Defence Blog reported at the time, the design includes Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic missile launchers, more than 100 vertical launch cells, and is expected to carry the SLCM-N, restoring a surface-based nuclear strike role the Navy has not fielded in decades. Navy Secretary John Phelan said the lead ship, the future USS Defiant, would serve as the Navy’s flagship.

It said checks of telephone logs and entry records found no evidence of the alleged conversation or a visit by an Emirati representative carrying the secure telephone used for such calls.

Abu Zaida did not address the alleged UAE warning to Netanyahu in his video, The Times of Israel pointed out.
A former PA minister for prisoner affairs, Abu Zaida belongs to the Fatah faction aligned with Mohammed Dahlan, who broke with PA President Mahmoud Abbas and left the West Bank in 2011. Türkiye cracks down on Israel-linked int'l fraud network, detains 175 suspects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:44:31 UTC
20:44:31 KST

Fatma Zehra Solmaz
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Türkiye on Friday launched simultaneous operations against an Israel-linked international fraud network accused of defrauding foreign nationals through fake forex and cryptocurrency investment schemes.
Authorities detained 175 of 239 suspects in raids at 286 addresses in Istanbul and the western province of Mugla, Türkiye's Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said.
Four separate investigations conducted by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office in 2026 uncovered evidence that some companies operating as call centers had used social media and the internet to advertise forex and cryptocurrency investments, promising high returns to foreign nationals, Gurlek said on US social media company X.
The investigation was coordinated by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office’s Bureau for Investigating Terror Financing and Money Laundering Crimes, in cooperation with the Istanbul Regional Directorate of the National Intelligence Organization, the Department of Combating Organized Crime and the Istanbul Police Department’s Cybercrime Branch, he noted.
Analyses by Türkiye’s Financial Crimes Investigation Board, findings by intelligence and police units, and hundreds of victim complaints obtained through Interpol revealed that people linked to Israel were predominant in the ownership and ultimate beneficiary structures of the companies, Gurlek added.
The findings led authorities to uncover an organized fraud network targeting victims in multiple countries, he said.
The network allegedly used multilingual customer representatives to recruit victims and directed them to investment platforms controlled by suspects, where fabricated profit figures were displayed to encourage them to deposit more money.
When victims attempted to withdraw their funds, they were allegedly asked to make additional payments under pretexts such as “account blockage” and “taxes.” The money deposited by victims was then transferred to bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets abroad.
The network targeted many countries, particularly in Europe, the Far East, and Africa, and reached a transaction volume of approximately 13 billion Turkish liras ($266.4 million) over two years in transactions believed to have been related to office expenses and salary payments, he said.
Based on the findings, authorities launched simultaneous operations at 5 am local time against 28 companies, 42 call centers, and 239 suspects at 286 addresses in Istanbul and Mugla, with Interpol units also participating.
By 10 am, raids had been carried out at the call centers and 175 suspects had been detained, while operations to apprehend the remaining suspects were ongoing, Gurlek said.

EU to ban metal scrap exports to India, Egypt on environmental grounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:42:50 UTC
20:42:50 KST

BRUSSELS — The EU has proposed banning metal waste exports to India and Egypt after both countries failed to prove they manage the waste in an “environmentally sound” manner.
The two countries, which are among the top importers of Europe’s recyclable materials, did not show they were applying the correct pollution controls on how the waste is treated, a European Commission assessment found.
The Waste Shipment Regulation — the bloc’s rules that restrict exports of certain types of trash to third countries to curb pollution — bans the export of non-hazardous waste to non-OECD countries from May next year, unless they are granted specific exemptions.
Advertisement
The EU exported nearly 19 million tonnes of scrap metal in 2025, accounting for over half the bloc’s total recyclable raw materials exports.
Egypt and India respectively bought over 1.3 million and 850,000 tonnes of scrap metal.
Last-minute concerns over the EU’s trade deal with India led the European Commission to withdraw planned export duties on aluminum scrap earlier this month.
India is a major importer of aluminum scrap. The country last year exported over 350,000 tons of aluminum scrap alone.
The executive was due to present an instrument to slow exports of cheap aluminum scrap to buyers outside the single market, keeping prices down for aluminum producers and users within the bloc. The European aluminum sector has pushed for priority access to local scrap.
EU industry chief Stéphane Séjourné said, however, that the EU would scrap the measure after it became clear it would only cover around half of the bloc’s aluminum scrap exports and decided to pursue a solution “entirely independent” of trade policy instruments.
Egypt and India will still be able to export other scrap materials, including paper, wood, rubber, and textile waste.
The Commission will consult on the suggested country exemptions until October 16, before adopting the final list in November, as required under the regulation.

Bradley-Jones has served as representative of the British Office Taipei since February 2025. The British Office represents UK interests in Taiwan and works on areas including trade and bilateral cooperation.

INTERVIEW – EU ‘not afraid’ to confront tech giants over children’s online safety, commissioner says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:41:49 UTC
20:41:49 KST

The EU is ready to make technology giants take greater responsibility for children’s online safety through new legislation, European Commissioner Glenn Micallef told Anadolu.
Speaking in an exclusive interview, Micallef, the European commissioner for intergenerational fairness, youth, culture and sport, discussed the EU KIDS Act proposed this week.
“We're not afraid of sitting down around the table and making sure that they shoulder the responsibilities,” he said.
The proposed rules would place greater responsibility on platforms to make their services safer for minors, while introducing age-based restrictions, stronger age-assurance requirements and new obligations concerning potentially harmful or addictive design features.
Micallef said the shift represented a fundamental change in how responsibility for children's online safety is shared between parents, governments and technology companies.
"A parent can set a rule at home around the dinner table for their children, but you cannot expect parents to fight algorithms which are designed in a way to be addictive," he said.
"The biggest change is the shift towards greater responsibility for those companies, those corporations, those platforms that are designing spaces online where there are children.”
The commission's plans would establish a graduated system of access based on age.
"The younger you are, the stronger the protection,” Micallef said.
Under the proposal, children under 13 would not be allowed to access social media services.
For children aged 13 and 14, the proposal would introduce so-called "mini accounts," which would be linked to a parent's or legal guardian's account.
"This is age-based protection that we're talking about, with a responsibility on the platforms and on those designing these spaces to actually make sure that these spaces are designed in a way which is safe for who is using them," Micallef said.
Micallef pointed to enforcement of the Digital Services Act as evidence that the commission was already engaging with major technology companies over the safety of their services.
"We do this in a way where we converse, where we dialog, where we have an exchange with these platforms,” he said.
Under the commission's approach, platforms would be expected to demonstrate that services used by minors are safe by design, rather than simply responding after harm has occurred.
 
Micallef rejected the idea that the commission's proposals were simply an attempt to restrict children's freedom online.
"This is supporting parents. A lot of parents out there are concerned about their children and their children growing up with all the risks associated to online environments," he said.
He said that parents increasingly face a challenge that cannot be addressed through household rules alone because digital platforms are designed around highly sophisticated recommendation and engagement systems.
The responsibility, he said, must therefore be distributed among parents, educators, policymakers and the companies that build and operate online services.
"We acknowledge that the parents have a responsibility,” Micallef said. 
 
“Us as legislators and policymakers, we have a responsibility. We're shouldering that by putting these rules on the table. Educators have responsibility, but then we're also ensuring that the companies, the platforms, they also have the responsibility to make sure that these spaces are safe.”
The latest proposal still needs to go through the EU legislative process and is not yet law.
It will be examined by the European Parliament and the Council of the EU, with member states involved in the negotiations.
Micallef said he believed there was broad agreement on the need to strengthen protections for children.
"I trust and I have faith that there is a common understanding that we need to protect children and support parents," he said.
But he also warned that the EU could not afford to delay action.
"We are talking about safeguarding children, that's our responsibility. We have to show that, and we have to move fast on this."
Micallef stressed that tougher regulation of online platforms should be accompanied by greater investment in real-world opportunities for children.
"We need to make these online spaces safer and more secure, and this is the priority here," he said.
"But this is only half the youth and childhood policy that we need to work on, because we also need to make sure that there are healthy alternatives or interesting spaces for young people and children to be children in the real world."
He pointed to sports facilities, public parks, libraries and theaters as places where children can socialize and develop away from screens.
The commissioner also spoke about the ongoing debate over football governance and the role of FIFA.
Several European national football federations, including those of Sweden, Scotland, Italy, Belgium and France, have withdrawn their support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino amid growing disagreements over the governing body's leadership and direction since the 2026 World Cup.
One of the most controversial issues has been a FIFA proposal to establish a commercial company that would allow private investors to acquire a 20% stake in the management of World Cup commercial rights.
The proposal was reportedly developed without consultation with FIFA's member associations and drew strong opposition before Infantino abandoned it several days later.
"I think that sport governing bodies should be there to protect and to safeguard sport, not to make profit out of it or not to make money out of it," Micallef stressed.
He referred to what he described as a "very controversial idea" that had been strongly rejected by parts of the football community.
"There's a shared feeling that football should not be for sale," the commissioner said.
He acknowledged that competition policy could potentially provide another avenue for action against FIFA but stressed that any competition case would require evidence and jurisdiction.
His preference, however, is to resolve disputes through dialogue.
"My preference would also always be to address these cases through dialog rather than through competition lawyers," he said.
"We continue to support also on a political level those federations, those fans, or those people who have strong voices, strong concerns, and we'll continue to work with them.”

New 120mm turret passes tests on Turkish medium tank

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:40:04 UTC
20:40:04 KST

- Otokar and Leonardo completed live-fire testing of the Tulpar medium tank fitted with Leonardo's HITFACT MkII 120mm turret at Italy's UTTAT Nettuno range.
- The Tulpar is one of four finalists to replace Brazil's Leopard 1A5 BR tanks, alongside the CV90, ASCOD and Lynx.
Turkish manufacturer Otokar and Italy’s Leonardo have completed integration and live-fire testing of a 120mm turret mounted on Otokar’s Tulpar medium tank platform, a combination now being pitched as a potential replacement for Brazil’s aging Leopard 1A5 tanks.
The companies ran the tests at Italy’s UTTAT Nettuno test range near Rome, fitting the Tulpar with Leonardo’s HITFACT MkII turret. Before any live firing, engineering teams from both companies worked through an extensive integration program covering the mechanical, electrical, electronic and software interfaces between the tracked platform and the turret. Once that phase was complete, the combined system went through live-fire trials in both static and moving conditions, testing the weapon system, fire control, stabilization and overall functionality across a range of operational scenarios. According to the companies, the system met all of its planned test objectives.
“The successful completion of this program demonstrates TULPAR’s ability to integrate advanced large-caliber turret systems, while delivering the mobility, survivability and firepower required by modern armed forces,” said Sedef Vehbi, head of Otokar’s military division.
“We are pleased with the outcome and proud to demonstrate the technological excellence of our systems,” said Luca Perazzo, deputy general manager of Leonardo’s Defence Systems Business Unit. “The HITFACT turret is currently the only system in the world equipped with a 120mm smoothbore gun that offers the same firepower as a main battle tank system, while being able to integrate onto light or medium platforms and use the new Vulcano 120 guided ammunition for precision engagements.”
The HITFACT MkII carries an OTO-Melara 120mm, 45-caliber gun capable of firing all NATO-standard 120mm ammunition under the STANAG 4385 specification. The same turret already arms the Centauro II wheeled cavalry vehicle, which Brazil’s army recently ordered and plans to produce domestically. For now, the Centauro II and the Tulpar are the only two platforms qualified to carry the HITFACT MkII. The Tulpar itself belongs to a modern medium armored vehicle family Otokar designed with weights ranging from 28 to 45 tonnes, built around cross-terrain mobility and a modular architecture that can accept different mission equipment.
Brazil’s interest stems from a program to replace its Leopard 1A5 BR tanks, whose availability has suffered as spare parts from Germany have become harder to obtain. The Brazilian Army’s Armored Forces Strategic Program is working toward a new family of tracked vehicles that would share components between a future main battle tank and a new infantry fighting vehicle, reducing logistics complexity as the force modernizes. Four platforms have been shortlisted for the tank requirement: BAE Systems’ CV90, General Dynamics European Land Systems’ ASCOD, Rheinmetall’s Lynx, and Otokar’s Tulpar. Brazil has held government-to-government talks with the supplying countries as part of its evaluation.
Otokar’s pitch to Brazil goes beyond building the vehicle locally with Brazilian components. The company has offered full technology transfer and the possibility of handing intellectual property for Brazilian versions of the vehicle to the Brazilian army, along with a supply chain the company describes as free of U.S. and German export-control restrictions, which it says would give Brazil complete logistical independence.
Turkey’s armored vehicle industry, which began with licensed production and adapted foreign designs in the early 1980s, has since grown into a major exporter, led by the Otokar-developed Altay main battle tank, a roughly 65-tonne design influenced by South Korea’s K2 Black Panther. Turkish officials have said the country exported roughly 2,000 armored vehicles over the past five years. Otokar signed a contract worth about 857 million euros with Romania in late 2024 for 1,059 Cobra II vehicles, most of them built locally with full technology transfer, and the company is preparing to produce the Tulpar, including the HITFACT-armed version, at a plant in Kazakhstan. Turkey’s overall defense exports reached $11.2 billion between July 2025 and July 2026, according to trade publication TurDef.
Brazil’s Senate has already approved a defense industry cooperation agreement with Turkey, adding to Brazil’s existing defense industrial relationship with Italy. No decision has been announced on which platform will replace the Leopard 1A5 BR.

Royan Institute achieves global milestone in regenerative medicine with WhartoCell
TEHRAN – Iran has taken a major step forward in regenerative medicine with the approval of WhartoCell, an allogeneic stem cell therapy developed by researchers at Royan Institute to treat osteoarthritis.
The achievement was also highlighted by MedPath, an international platform specializing in medical information, clinical trials, and healthcare technologies, putting the spotlight on Royan Institute’s contribution to this scientific and technological breakthrough.
According to Mehdi Lotfipanah, Director of Public Relations and International Affairs at Royan Institute, the therapy is designed to reduce inflammation, support cartilage regeneration, and improve joint function in patients with osteoarthritis. “The introduction of innovative cell-based therapies requires a scientific and evidence-based approach to ensure their appropriate integration into clinical practice,” Lotfipanah said.
Technical Profile and Mechanism of Action
WhartoCell is derived from Wharton’s jelly of the neonatal umbilical cord, a rich source of mesenchymal stem cells. These cells possess anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties while supporting tissue repair and regeneration. A distinguishing feature of the product is that it does not require genetic matching, or human leukocyte antigen (HLA) matching, between donor and recipient.
This characteristic allows physicians to administer the treatment without lengthy preparation procedures, positioning WhartoCell as an off-the-shelf therapy expected to improve patient access to advanced regenerative treatments.
Manufacturing and Quality Standards
Royan Institute has emphasized that WhartoCell is manufactured under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, with quality and safety monitored throughout the production process. This adherence to internationally recognized manufacturing standards is intended to ensure consistent product quality and patient safety.
Broader Clinical Potential
Although WhartoCell was initially approved for osteoarthritis, researchers at Royan Institute suggest the technology may have broader applications in regenerative medicine. Potential future indications include cartilage repair, tendon and ligament injuries, bone fracture healing, avascular necrosis, and the management of inflammatory joint disorders.
Strategic Significance
Lotfipanah noted that the product represents an important achievement in developing indigenous biotechnology, reducing dependence on imported therapeutic products while expanding access for healthcare providers across the country. He added that greater awareness among physicians and healthcare providers would facilitate broader adoption of regenerative medicine technologies.
 
 Royan Institute plans to increase scientific communication around WhartoCell through specialized workshops, educational programs for physicians and patients, and scientific meetings, including activities tied to the upcoming 27th International Royan Congress. The institute, one of Iran’s leading centers for stem cell research and regenerative medicine, has developed several advanced cell-based therapeutic technologies over the past two decades as part of the country’s growing biotechnology sector.
Iran among top 10 countries in regenerative medicine
With the approval of six new advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs), Iran has showcased breakthroughs in regenerative medicine, improving the country’s global ranking from 12 to 7.
According to the latest global report, out of 148 ATMPs approved in 2025 under the supervision of 12 internationally recognized regulatory bodies, seven were made in Iran, placing it among the top 10 countries in the field, IRNA reported.
The number of licensed products in regenerative medicine has grown from one product in the Iranian year 1402 (March 2023-March 2024) to seven in Iranian year 1404 (March 2025 – March 2026.
These include cell therapy, tissue engineering, and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy products, which are used to treat different diseases such as vitiligo, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), cerebral palsy (CP), burns, diabetic foot ulcers, arthritis, and B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (B cell ALL). Some of these high-tech medical products have export potential.
In August 2026, the Royan Institute played host to the 17th International Summer School in Tehran to examine the growing role of the microbiome in regenerative medicine.
Bringing together researchers, physicians, faculty members and students, the event opened on August 15 and came to an end on 19.
Titled “The Symphony of Therapy: Unlocking Regenerative Potential through the Microbiome,” it focused on recent scientific advances and clinical applications of microbiome research, IRNA reported.
According to the Royan Institute, the program explored how the human microbiome influences immune regulation, chronic diseases, tissue repair and regeneration, while highlighting emerging therapeutic approaches and translational research.
The five-day event featured sessions on stem cells and the microbiome, intestinal stem cells and microbial ecology, reproductive health, inflammation and tissue repair, and microbiome-based therapies, including prebiotics and postbiotics.
Participants also discussed advanced research technologies such as organoids, omics platforms and co-culture systems, alongside the ethical and clinical challenges of translating laboratory discoveries into medical practice.

Luxembourg insists that if France is able to get a particular oligarch delisted, it should be able to do the same, raising fears of a domino effect among member states.
Luxembourg has deepened the deadlock over the EU's sanction list renewal, tying a French demand to delist Russian businessman Alisher Usmanov to the case of Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the Grand Duchy over his frozen assets.
Last week, Paris joined Slovakia in demanding the removal of Usmanov from the sanctions list pending renewal. Now Luxembourg says that if Usmanov comes off the list, Fridman should too.
"France risks setting off a race to the bottom, which is the absolute opposite of what the EU is signalling politically, given the Russian escalation in Ukraine but also against EU member states in recent weeks," an EU diplomat told Euronews on condition of anonymity.
Slovakia has long pushed to delist both Usmanov and Fridman, oligarchs whom Brussels placed on the sanctions list for being close to the Kremlin. Both men deny the allegations.
Under EU rules, the list of 1,600 sanctioned entities and individuals must be renewed with the unanimous support of the bloc's member states every six months. The deadline was set to expire on Tuesday, but was extended by one week to allow time for a diplomatic solution.
Earlier this week, it also emerged that France's request to delist Usmanov was intended as a trade for the release of French citizens detained in Azerbaijan, a revelation that caused frustration among other member states.
Luxembourg raised the stakes further on Friday, telling a meeting of EU ambassadors that if France succeeds in delisting Usmanov, Fridman should be delisted as well.
Fridman is locked in an ongoing legal battle with Luxembourg over its implementation of EU sanctions, seeking compensation for his frozen assets in the country, which are estimated to run to around $16bn. He has also sued the Council of the EU before the European General Court.
For other member states, Luxembourg's latest demand illustrates exactly why national interests should not be allowed to shape individual sanctions listings, since doing so risks a domino effect in which other capitals begin pushing their own agendas.
EU ambassadors will reconvene on Monday. A Luxembourg official did not reply to Euronews' request for comment.
"Putin only speaks the language of power. If Paris really wants to push this through, France risks making the EU look weak," the diplomat added.

The spokesman for the central African nation's government and its embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment.
VIDEO SHOWS ALTERCATION IN HOTEL

Video of the incident and news of Soliman's subsequent arrest spurred fresh criticism from rights groups of the so-called third-country deportation deals that the Trump administration has struck with several African countries.
The deals enable Washington to deport migrants who cannot legally be sent to their home countries because they obtained protection from US immigration judges.
Washington has defended the third-country deals as lawful and said deportations are carried out in accordance with US immigration law.
Soliman was in custody at La Luna gendarmerie station in Malabo, his lawyer said.
The facility has been used in the past to hold human rights activists, according to rights groups including Amnesty International.
DETAINEES ACCUSED OF BREAKING MIRROR, AMNESTY SAYS
Soliman had been accused of breaking a mirror in an elevator in the hotel, though that was a pretext for his arrest, the lawyer said.
"We are certain that it was a retaliation for Ahmed speaking out and the videos leaked," said the lawyer, referring to footage of security forces pulling guns on deportees.
Amnesty International said in a statement on Friday that Soliman was being held with another deportee, Samson Birhane, and that they were both accused of breaking the mirror.
"Police officers covered the two men’s heads with a bag and beat them in their heads, backs and ribs," Amnesty said, describing how they were allegedly taken into custody.
"The authorities must immediately release them, inform them of any charges against them and allow them unimpeded access to counsel."
Equatorial Guinea's government spokesman and its US embassy have not released any statements on Soliman's case.
In a statement on Wednesday, US Representative Adelita Grijalva, a Democrat from Arizona, where Soliman has spent much of his life, criticized the third-country deportations.
"Our country is responsible for sending people out this way, period," she told Reuters.
"And so we should make sure that where they're going is somewhere safe. Just because a country accepts somebody does not mean that that's a good placement." REUTERS

New species of wild cat discovered for first time in more than a century

New species of wild cat discovered for first time in more than a century, researcher says
Scientists have discovered a new species of wild cat for the first time in more than a century, a Bolivian researcher told AFP on Thursday.
The Tilcayo tiger cat, a small feline with a spotted, leopard-like coat, was identified in the mountainous Yungas region near the capital, La Paz.
Locals who saw the creature in the Bolivian Andes had mistaken it for an ordinary house cat, said biologist and National Geographic explorer Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who was part of the research team that studied them.
The nickname "tilcayo" given to the animal by locals inspired its new scientific designation: Leopardus tilcayo.
Nogales-Ascarrunz lauded the discovery as a "remarkable event, because a new wild cat species hasn't been described in 100 years."
The cat is the first feline discovered since the Uruguayan pampas cat in 1923.
The tilcayo is slightly smaller than a domestic cat, measuring around 18 inches, with rounded ears.
A pair of tilcayos -- the only such creatures found so far -- have undergone whole genome sequencing, Nogales-Ascarrunz said, referring to a type of in-depth genetic testing.
A male tilcayo is living at an animal shelter in Yungas after it was handed over by a family who had taken it in.
A female was rescued and released into the wild after being attacked by locals.
Research on the species was published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology, capping off research that scientists began in 2021.
"So far, it's only been detected in Bolivia" and not "anywhere else on the planet," Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
She said the creatures were classified as vulnerable to extinction, but their small numbers meant they could soon be considered "at much greater risk" of dying out.
