Scientists are about to test Einstein’s gravity with exotic matter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:07:25 UTC
20:07:25 KST

Scientists are about to test Einstein’s gravity with exotic matter
- Date:
- September 18, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- Scientists have found a new way to create a controlled beam of muonium, an exotic atom containing a heavier cousin of the electron. The advance could allow researchers to test for the first time whether gravity acts on second-generation particles exactly as Einstein’s theory predicts. Any unexpected difference would be a major surprise and could potentially point toward new physics, including a hypothetical fifth force.
- Share:
Does gravity affect every type of particle in exactly the same way? Researchers at ETH Zurich and the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen are preparing an experiment that could test that fundamental assumption using one of nature's more unusual particles.
"We have taken an important step towards carrying out an exciting experiment on this topic," says the professor of physics: "We want to measure the gravitational interaction of the muon."
The familiar matter that makes up people, planets, and nearly everything around us consists of protons, neutrons, and electrons. Physicists classify these particles as belonging to the first generation of matter. Two additional generations also exist, made up of heavier particles. One of them is the muon, a heavier relative of the electron that belongs to the second generation.
Researchers at PSI can create muons and their antiparticles using a large particle accelerator. When a positively charged antimuon combines with a negatively charged electron, the pair forms a neutral atom known as muonium.
Why Physicists Want to Test Muons
The Standard Model of particle physics describes these different generations of particles, but it does not explain why nature has multiple generations in the first place.
"But we physicists do not yet understand why these additional generations exist at all in the first place," says Soter. "And why are there three in total?"
That mystery raises another important question. Do the heavier particles of the second and third generations respond to gravity in exactly the same way as the lighter particles found in the first generation?
Testing Einstein's Equivalence Principle
For ordinary matter, objects at the same location in a gravitational field fall at the same rate. Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton recognized this universality of free fall centuries ago. It later became central to Albert Einstein's theory of gravity through the equivalence principle, which connects gravitational mass with inertial mass.
So far, however, researchers have demonstrated this principle only with ordinary matter or first-generation antimatter. Measuring how muonium behaves under gravity would provide the first test involving a second-generation particle.
"The exotic muonium is very well suited to this because it is a neutral atom," explains Soter: "After all, to make something fall, you need something neutral."
Neutrality is essential because gravity is extremely weak compared with electromagnetism. If researchers tried to perform the experiment with a charged particle, stray electromagnetic fields could overwhelm the gravitational effect they are attempting to detect.
Muonium presents another major obstacle. Muons survive for only about 2.2 microseconds before decaying. Earlier methods also produced muonium atoms traveling at different speeds and in many directions, making them poorly suited for extremely precise gravity measurements.
Researchers at PSI have now found a way around that problem.
"We have managed to produce the muonium atoms in a 'cold' state, which is what makes the gravity experiment possible in the first place," says Soter. "In this case, 'cold' means that the atoms propagate at similar speeds, almost parallel to one another."
Superfluid Helium Creates a Controlled Muonium Beam
The team describes its new method for producing muonium in Nature Physics.
"In order to achieve this, we used superfluid helium that had been cooled close to absolute zero at minus 273 degrees Celsius," explains Jesse Zhang, lead author of the study. "Superfluid helium is what is known as a quantum fluid, in which the individual helium atoms lose their identity, and which does not tolerate any impurities within it."
The process begins by directing antimuons from PSI's accelerator into a thin layer of superfluid helium. Inside the helium, the particles slow down. When an antimuon encounters a free electron, the two form a muonium atom with positive chemical potential.
That chemical potential effectively drives the newly formed atom out of the liquid. When it reaches the surface, the chemical potential is converted into kinetic energy, giving the muonium atom a boost that sends it vertically upward.
"So we're using the chemical potential as an atomic cannon," explains Zhang.
The muonium atoms must pass through the quantum liquid without collisions and at a predictable speed. Their lifetime is so short that any significant delay would prevent them from reaching the surface before they decay.
"For our experiments, we also rely on PSI's particle accelerator, which generates the world's most intense, continuous muon beams," says Soter. "Thanks to this high-quality source, a great many muonium atoms can be produced."
Watching Gravity Shift an Atomic Pattern
The researchers are now building an instrument known as an interferometer to measure how Earth's gravity affects the muonium beam.
The device takes advantage of the wave properties of atoms to produce an interference pattern. Earth's gravitational pull should cause an extremely small shift in that pattern. Measuring the displacement would allow the researchers to determine how gravity acts on the muon.
"We hope to be able to test the method for the first time with the atomic beam this year, and if all goes well, the actual gravity experiment should follow in two or three years' time," as Soter relates.
The new beam could also make much more precise laser spectroscopy experiments with muonium possible. Those measurements could improve scientists' understanding of the muon's mass and fundamental physical constants, another long-term goal of the research group.
Could the Experiment Reveal a Fifth Force?
If muonium responds to gravity differently from ordinary matter, the implications could be profound.
"That would indeed be surprising, and, in addition to other theories, it could point to the existence of a fifth force," as Soter outlines.
Modern physics recognizes four fundamental interactions: gravity, electromagnetism, the strong interaction, and the weak interaction. Scientists have repeatedly proposed the possibility of an additional fifth force, but no such force has ever been confirmed.
Discovering one is not the main objective of Soter's experiment. The immediate goal is more fundamental: determining whether one of Einstein's central principles also holds for a different generation of particles.
"I am completely open-minded," she says. "I simply want to measure, for the first time, whether the equivalence between gravitational and inertial mass also applies to the second generation of particles -- this alone is quite an inspiring piece of work."
This research is supported by the National Centre of Competence in Research Muoniverse.

Journal Reference:
- J. Zhang, A. Antognini, M. Bartkowiak, D. Goeldi, K. Kirch, A. Knecht, D. Taqqu, R. Waddy, F. Wauters, P. Wegmann, A. Soter. Generation of a high-intensity, superthermal muonium beam for gravity and laser spectroscopy experiments. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03433-x

Turkish archer Mete Gazoz has set his sights on winning two medals at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games after a successful 2026 season.
Gazoz, who won the individual Olympic title at Tokyo 2020 and helped Türkiye claim a team medal at Paris 2024, said he wanted to reach the podium in both events in Los Angeles.
“I feel completely ready for the Olympics. The 2028 Games will be better than Tokyo and Paris,” he told Anadolu while attending the Turkish national archery team’s training camp in Antalya.
“I won an individual medal in Tokyo, and we won a team medal in Paris. In Los Angeles, I want to win both medals.”
Gazoz said Türkiye’s international season concluded with the final stage of the 2026 Archery World Cup in Mexico.
The 2026 campaign was highly successful both for him personally and for the Turkish national team, he said, pointing to his seven World Cup medals as well as the team's strong performances at the European Championships and Mediterranean Games.
“We had a wonderful year as Turkish archery in 2026,” Gazoz said. “It was a year that gave us hope for 2027 and showed our rivals that they should be wary of us.”
The 2027 season will be particularly important as qualification for the Los Angeles Olympics gets underway.
Gazoz said his immediate objective was to earn an Olympic qualification spot by becoming world champion, while Türkiye’s men’s team would seek to complete what he described as “unfinished business.”

Gazoz said he then acted as though the shot had been intentional because his opponents were watching the match and studying his reaction.
“It became a message to them: ‘Whatever score I need, that is what I will shoot.’ But that really is how I feel,” he added.
Gazoz also welcomed archery’s growing popularity in Türkiye, saying major sponsorship agreements involving athletes could help raise the sport’s profile both domestically and internationally.

Who gets to decide how quickly AI moves?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:04:01 UTC
20:04:01 KST

Who gets to decide how quickly AI moves?
The biggest AI companies want to slow development together. The real question is what power they gain in return.
Artificial intelligence (AI) has stirred up more controversy than most things in the past five years. Ever since the introduction of accessible generative AI in 2022, institutions, universities, students, scholars, activists, cognitive specialists, public policymakers and members of the public have all been divided over the ethics of its use. As of the beginning of this month, even the founders of AI companies have taken the same stance. Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, released an essay calling on AI companies to slow the development of their most advanced models, as the safeguards currently in place are unable to keep up. Shortly after Amodei’s essay, his position was endorsed by Sam Altman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind, and Satya Nadella of Microsoft. In addition, Sam Altman said that OpenAI will not be going public in 2026, as further safety advances are still required. While on the surface this may seem like a development in the collective conscience, the problem is far more multifaceted and layered – leaving the industry and the intended audience divided.
The products
Take a look at the products that each AI giant sells. Amodei, Altman, Musk and Hassabis sell models, while Nadella sells the cloud those models run on. Both groups have advised slowing down. On the other hand, Jensen Huang, founder, president, and CEO of Nvidia, sells the chips that these companies buy before they can build anything. Huang does not advise a slowdown and has instead asserted that AI does not need new legislation because market forces can push companies towards safe innovation without the need for regulation. Mark Zuckerberg, whose company gives its models for free, warned that the proposal could expose companies to greater legal risks.
The common thread between these divisive recommendations is profit. Some companies will benefit from a slowdown, while others will earn greater profits by moving faster. Nvidia’s ability to charge high prices has benefitted from the intense competition between these AI companies, which fear falling behind their rivals. If this competitive pressure decreases, companies may be less willing to pay a premium for Nvidia’s chips. Hence, Huang’s opposition to the proposal may reflect both genuine concerns and Nvidia’s commercial interests.
The word the White House used
In the world of AI, antitrust law prevents these companies from holding private meetings to decide what they can and cannot do. This is intended to prevent them from coordinating the pace of development and engaging in unfair competition. However, some of these AI companies have now come forward arguing that they should be allowed to work outside antitrust law for the sake of technological safety. Huang and David Sacks, the White House AI lead, have been critical of this request, as it could reduce competition and increase the influence of these AI companies over their rivals. Sacks also questioned the independence of nonprofit evaluators tasked with evaluating AI safety “independently”. In essence, he asks: how is it fair for one company to inspect another?
The clause that travels badly
Amodei’s proposal would deny China access to the most powerful AI chips and advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and prevent smuggling and remote access to computing capacity abroad. China’s foreign ministry countered the proposal, saying that these warnings are a fearmongering tactic aimed at slowing down China’s technological advancement, echoing the Cold War. Amodei did admit that China poses the toughest predicament for his plan. Despite its alleged advantages, the proposal gives American firms leverage over Chinese ones.
A precedent, and why it does not fit
Supporters of AI coordination have compared it with the regulation of banks following the 2008 financial crisis. Basel III was introduced only after a major financial crisis had already occurred. Attempts to regulate AI before harm occurs can represent a genuine effort to prevent future risks, rather than reflecting the commercial interests of AI companies. However, there is an important difference between these two cases. Banking regulations were imposed by external regulators, whereas the proposed AI regulations would involve competing companies coordinating with one another.
What the debate is actually about
Before this debate began, researchers had already issued warnings about the capabilities of AI models. OpenAI slowed down the development of its leading systems after a security incident. Amodei and Altman have both claimed that Anthropic and OpenAI will aim to bring in independent evaluators – a practice not seen among “cartels”. Both concerns can coexist: companies may genuinely fear the risks associated with AI while also pursuing their own commercial interests. The more relevant question remains whether the proposed solution adequately addresses the problem it is intended to solve. An agreement between five major American companies, to be overseen by evaluators they fund, would not apply to international competitors such as those in China and would require an exemption from existing competition law. This solution appears to reflect the structure and interests of the AI industry more closely than the nature of the risk it is intended to address.
The seats nobody is sitting in
Much of the debate surrounding the pace and regulation of AI development has taken place without meaningful participation from other regions, including the Arab world. PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) estimates that $31.6 trillion will be invested in AI infrastructure worldwide by 2050. Countries that can provide large amounts of cheap, reliable and low-carbon electricity will be particularly well positioned to attract this investment. Hence, the significant energy, land and investment required for AI infrastructure may provide countries capable of supplying these resources with considerable bargaining power. These states could seek a greater role in determining the conditions under which AI companies operate within their jurisdiction. This could include negotiating who evaluates these AI systems, how the evaluations are to be conducted and who bears legal responsibility when autonomous systems cause harm. This means that the debate goes beyond whether AI development should be slowed to questions of who has the authority to make decisions about its development, and whether other countries should accept decisions made elsewhere.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Russians vote in elections with no party opposing Putin or war in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:03:48 UTC
20:03:48 KST

The three-day vote will fill 450 Duma seats and 11 regional governorships, with only parties backing Putin and Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine on the ballot. Despite official denials of a new draft, fears of mobilisation are overshadowing the vote.
Russians began voting Friday in a tightly controlled three-day election that will likely see President Vladimir Putin tighten his grip on power after 26 years at the helm, as Russia's all-out war in Ukraine continues well into its fifth year.
Only parties backing Putin and his war in Ukraine are on the ballot: the ruling United Russia, the Communist Party, A Just Russia, the nationalist LDPR and New People.
Yabloko, Russia's only publicly anti-war party still operating inside the country, was barred from participating. The party saw a surge in social media support, particularly among young people, after it was initially allowed to stand.
An unnamed European diplomat said the elections were "pretty much a sham" but described them as "a ritual the Kremlin considers necessary," adding that it would seek to ensure a high turnout.
Independent observers have previously documented the use of state resources to influence results, including bussing voters to polling stations, pressuring employees of state institutions to vote for the ruling party, and pushing online voting as it is easier to monitor and control.
"As in the Soviet era, elections must demonstrate the loyalty of citizens," Russian political scientist and Head of Analysis of Transformation Processes at the NEST Centre Nikolai Petrov said.
The election will fill 450 State Duma seats and the governorships of 11 federal regions, with the country's only remaining anti-war party excluded from the ballot and fears of mobilisation overshadowing the vote.
Running from 18 to 20 September, the election will also choose deputies to regional legislatures in 39 federal subjects.
Voters will choose eight of the 11 regional heads directly, while regional parliaments will elect the remaining three. Polling stations have been opened at Russian border crossings with Poland and the three Baltic states.
Half of the 450 Duma seats will be allocated through nationwide party lists and the other half through single-member constituencies.
Voting in Russian elections is also taking place in parts of Ukraine occupied by Moscow's troops, a move that neither Kyiv nor the West recognises as legitimate.
Kremlin pushes pro-army narrative
Almost 200 candidates in these elections have taken part in Russia's war in Ukraine, according to electoral commissions.
The Kremlin has promoted them as part of Russia's "true elite," but the initiative is primarily a recruitment tool to boost Moscow's troops on the front lines, with few standing any real chance of being elected.
Ahead of the vote, Putin urged Russians to vote to show troops that "behind our fighters stand millions of people" and to deliver an "answer to those who want to weaken Russia".
Meanwhile, Russians fear another wave of military mobilisation, despite Putin personally denying plans for a call-up twice in three days in September alone.
Independent Russian media have counted 17 official denials of an imminent mobilisation. Russia called up 300,000 reservists in the autumn of 2022 in a move that triggered significant public alarm and a mass departure of men of fighting age from the country.
Tatiana Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre, which is banned in Russia, said she considered a new draft unlikely.
"They have put so much effort into persuading Russians not to worry about this," she said. "I would be very, very surprised if it happened."
In the streets of Moscow today, few visible signs indicate an election is even under way.
Fears of mobilisation have been further compounded by Ukrainian long-range drone strikes on Russian infrastructure in a bid to defund its war machine, causing fuel shortages and economic losses running into billions of euros.
Many Russians feel the attacks break what Stanovaya described as the Kremlin's tacit bargain with the population over the war.
In prison, in exile, dead
All of Putin's main political opponents are in prison, in exile or dead. Alexei Navalny, his most prominent challenger, died in a Russian penal colony in 2024.
Putin's political opponents have mostly been driven into exile and his main opponent Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in 2024.
Russia's exiled opposition has urged anti-Kremlin Russians not to boycott the elections but instead vote "against Putin's party".
Navalny's widow Yulia Navalnaya also called on anti-war Russians to cast their ballots at noon on Sunday.
Yabloko — which critics say outlived its usefulness after the Kremlin allowed it to exist for many years to create a pretence of political plurality as a catch-all for liberal and discontented voters — disagreed, arguing that it was better not to vote.
"You are suggesting that we once again go, like sheep, dancing to their tune, and vote for those who have caused the deaths of people in Russia and Ukraine?" party chairman Nikolay Rybakov said this week.
'Mad printer'
Parliamentary elections were previously a source of significant political tension: in 2011, mass fraud during the Duma vote and Putin's return to the presidency from the post of prime minister triggered the largest street protests in Russia since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Putin has ruled Russia since 1999 and his United Russia party has dominated politics since the early 2000s.
Under Putin, the Duma's powers have been substantially curtailed, reducing it largely to approving legislation initiated by the Kremlin — a role that has earned it the popular nickname "the mad printer" to mock the speed at which it rubber-stamped highly restrictive and controversial laws.
Any criticism of the war is treated under Russian law as "discrediting the army" and can carry a prison sentence.
Older voters remain among Putin's strongest supporters, although many still complain about living standards.

An effective ban on disabled people leaving Britain? You read that right, and we will not settle for it | Frances Ryan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:00:25 UTC
20:00:25 KST

Disabled people are being barred from leaving the country. This isn’t the first line of a dystopian novel but a scandal quietly happening across swathes of England. For the past six months, myself and my colleague Patrick Butler have spoken to disabled people who have effectively been blocked from going abroad on a holiday or to a work event by their local care provider.
There’s 38-year-old Lucy from Oxfordshire who needs to travel internationally as the president of the European Spinal Cord Injury Federation. And Chelsea from Lancashire, a 25-year-old with cerebral palsy who dreams of swimming in Spain again. Then there’s 40-year-old Joel*, who has a muscle weakness and works for a global marketing brand but hasn’t been able to leave the UK for nine years.
Some have live-in personal assistants (PAs) via NHS continuing healthcare, the non-means-tested home support for people with high needs. Others have 24/7 social care through their local authority. But when they try to leave the country, all hit the same wall: they are told they are not allowed to use their care package abroad, sometimes even if they pay any extra costs themselves.
Here’s the plot twist. Some areas of the country are permitting care users to go on holiday or travel for work – while disabled people just a few miles down the road can be stopped. Others are told they can travel but have to pay any extra expenses – effectively still barring them financially from going – while some care boards offer to cover the cost. As there is limited to no national guidance on the issue, disabled people’s right to travel depends on a postcode lottery, with local care officials inspecting their plans for a trip away and having the power to rule “go” or “stay”.
This week, MPs and peers called for national guidelines to end this injustice. Figures such as the work and pensions select committee chair, Debbie Abrahams, the crossbench peer Jane Campbell and the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn told the Guardian that the government must guarantee the rights of disabled people to travel and ensure they have the support they need to do so.
You can practically hear the right preparing to oppose the move with a cry of “Free holidays on the NHS!” But care users going abroad doesn’t cost the taxpayer anything extra in care bills. Disabled people who need 24/7 support for everyday activities already have care funding in place, and in many cases use their own money to pay PAs’ travel expenses, such as accommodation and plane tickets (on top of the already extortionate price of accessible travel). When Lucy was told by her care board she couldn’t take her PAs to a spinal cord conference in Germany this spring, her employer had already offered to pay any additional costs.
The question, then, is why would authorities want to stop disabled people going abroad? If it’s not just about tight budgets, why should it matter to them how an adult chooses to use their care package? You could say that it’s about practicalities: it’s easier not to worry about insurance or visas (disabled people largely sort this themselves for their PAs anyway). But it seems naive not to think there’s some prejudice lurking under the bureaucracy. Blocking disabled people from going on holiday or working abroad goes to the heart of cultural assumptions about disability: that we don’t have careers or families or friends like other, “normal” people.
Sixty years after disabled people left institutions and were able to live independently, alongside the vast gains, the stain of paternalistic control still lurks in disability services. It’s the social worker who suggests you get a commode next to your sofa because it’s cheaper than an accessible bathroom. It’s the care worker who speaks very slowly to you and picks your clothes out on your behalf. It’s the occupational therapist who suggests you get a hospital-style bed that your husband can’t fit in (and is visibly surprised you have a husband).
We’re not supposed to talk about this stuff. There’s an unwritten rule that says disabled people should be just grateful for what they’re given by the state, lest we appear to be scroungers or burdens. I say “unwritten”. It’s written in some newspapers most weeks.
It is uncomfortable, I suppose, in part because it is so ordinary. This isn’t the sort of prejudice that comes with an ableist slur or a violent push. It is the gentle, everyday belief that certain kinds of lives – certain kinds of people – come with low expectations.
Just look at the way much of the political and media class discuss social care. In the rare instances that younger disabled people are mentioned alongside elderly people, social care is still solely spoken about in terms of personal care – say, help to wash or prepare a meal. As Andy Burnham has put reform of the care sector on the agenda in recent months, it’s notable there has been little talk of its role in supporting a disabled person’s family role or career: whether that’s help to drop the kids off at school on the way to the office or to get to the pub to celebrate a friend’s birthday.
That’s understandable. Under the current system, as many as 1.5 million disabled people in England are left without access to even the most basic help. If you are suffering the indignity of sitting in soiled clothes because a care worker hasn’t arrived to assist you to the bathroom, it can feel pointless – delusional, even – to mention you’ve not seen the sea in years.
But to settle for this state of affairs forces disabled people to accept a half-life, to be relieved to at least be clean and fed, and to try to forget the colour that defines being human. It diminishes not only our humanity but the principle that disability campaigners fought for decades for and underpins the modern care system: for disabled people to have choice and independence over our lives, just like everyone else.
When I recently spoke to Campbell, who has 24/7 PAs herself, about the care abroad scandal, she said something telling: “It’s as if those controlling [these decisions] believe disabled people don’t deserve the same experiences they enjoy.”
As pressure for national guidelines mounts, I can’t help but think that is a wise litmus test. Would you expect a non-disabled person to live like this? And if not, why do you think it’s OK for disabled people?
*Name has been changed
- 
  Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist

Disabled people need right to travel abroad, say UK MPs amid ‘ridiculous’ restrictions row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:00:17 UTC
20:00:17 KST

Disabled people must have a guaranteed right to travel abroad, MPs and peers have said, as further cases emerged of individuals barred from taking holidays as a result of “ridiculous” rules imposed by local NHS care boards and local councils.
Leading figures have called on the government to bring in clear national guidelines to ensure people who require full-time personal assistants (PAs) are not prevented from using funding for their 24/7 support team for breaks and work trips.
Wide variations in local rules governing foreign travel mean whether a disabled person can take their care team abroad can depend on where they live, the whim of local officials or whether they are prepared to mount a legal challenge.
The call came as it emerged two men with the same health condition and care packages, living 40 miles from each other, are subject to different rules regarding overseas travel with their PA support team.
While Joel, 40, a graduate who works in marketing for a global brand, is barred by his local health board from using his personal health budget to contribute to the travel costs of his PAs when going abroad, David, 25, who lives in a neighbouring health board area, receives a travel costs allocation.
While Joel (not his real name) has been effectively prevented from travelling overseas for the past eight years – he can afford his own travel costs but not those of his two PAs – David was free to take a trip to Europe this summer with his PA support team.
“This is really unfair and brazenly discriminatory,” Joel said. “It is a fundamental human right that individuals with disabilities should have the same freedoms, opportunities and choices to travel as any able-bodied person would.”
Jane Campbell, a leading disability rights campaigner, said: “These ridiculous care restrictions are against common sense. Stipulating where and when the person can use the support they’ve been assessed as needing is like tagging somebody, as if a prisoner out on parole.”
The Guardian previously revealed NHS care boards and local councils were refusing to allow disabled people to use their care funding outside the UK, even when they paid PA travel expenses themselves. Joel’s case suggests other care boards are indirectly barring disabled people from travelling: while overseas travel is in theory allowed, in practice it is unaffordable without NHS funding for PA expenses.
Lady Campbell said: “It’s as if those controlling the purse strings believe disabled people do not deserve the same experiences they enjoy. The government constantly says how important it is for disabled people to work and take responsibility for their lives and yet when we do, these kind of rules are imposed.
“We need national guidelines on using care abroad now to protect disabled people’s rights and end this nonsense once and for all.”
Debbie Abrahams, the chair of the Commons work and pensions select committee, said the restrictions potentially breached the UN convention on the rights of persons with disabilities, which the UK has ratified.
“Disabled people should have the same freedom as everyone else to travel for work, to visit family or simply to go on holiday,” said Abrahams.
Joel, who has spinal muscular atrophy, was initially allowed to use his health budget to pay for his PAs to travel with him and had two short breaks in Europe, at his own cost. Eight years ago, his NHS funder, now Cheshire and Merseyside NHS integrated care board, reversed its decision, ruling travel costs were valid for the UK only.
He challenged the ruling but was rebuffed, being told earlier this year by the care board that the period in 2017 when it permitted him to use his personal care budget for overseas PA travel costs was a “historical error in decision-making”.
Just 40 miles (64km) away David (not his real name) said his local care board made very different rulings. Greater Manchester integrated care partnership blocked his requests for holiday PA expenses for five years. Officials finally relented last year after he submitted detailed evidence suggesting its decision would breach NHS guidance and human rights law.
It allocated £2,370 annually to enable David to contribute to his PA team’s travel and accommodation costs. David, a graduate with a first-class degree, last year took his first trip abroad without his parents, paid for by himself.
He said: “It can feel like being in a prison for a person with my condition. I want to live how my peers live. I want independence. I want a change of scenery from time to time.”
The MP Marsha de Cordova, who is a former minister for disabled people, said local variations highlighted the urgent need for national guidelines: “Disabled people’s right to travel should not be decided by the mood of local officials.”
Cheshire and Merseyside’s most recent policy, approved last week [10 September] states that while disabled individuals can request holiday travel expenses for their PAs it would “not ordinarily” pay for them. It states it has an obligation to use NHS funds “in a way which is fair and equitable”.
NHS Greater Manchester said it had no ratified policy on holiday travel.
The Department of Health and Social Care’s (DHSC) position is that care boards should examine all requests for PA travel support and consider the health and wellbeing benefits for the applicant of overseas travel for the applicant.
A DHSC spokesperson said: “Personal health budgets work best where people have real flexibility over how they use their budgets and we expect integrated care boards to examine each proposal on a case-by-case basis, in line with national policy and legislation.”
NHS Cheshire and Merseyside and NHS Greater Manchester separately issued the following statement: “While we cannot comment on individual patient cases, all requests for personal health budget funding are assessed according to our personal health budget and integrated budget policy on a case-by-case basis according to patient need. This policy has been developed in line with national NHS guidance.”

From old railways to an oasis of art, food and nature: how an eco-park was born in Greater Manchester
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:00:17 UTC
20:00:17 KST

Standing in the open green space of Northern Roots, it is hard to imagine the landscape as it once was.
Two cotton mills, two coalmines and an industrial railway once occupied this 65-hectare (160-acre) site in Oldham, Greater Manchester. Later, about 24 hectares became a tip, with much of the space left to nature.
Over the past five years, Northern Roots, a charity, has been developing this once industrial land, running community programmes including a Natural Health Service.
On 19 September a new facility will open to the public, featuring a cafe, shop, production kitchen, performance space, forestry skills centre, outdoor play areas and an urban farm. The charity’s ambition is to turn what was once a “burden” into the UK’s largest urban farm and eco-park.
The idea began with Oldham council, which wanted to explore green space as an asset. Today the council works in a unique partnership with Northern Roots.
“We wanted to look at what this land could do for Oldham, rather than simply seeing it as land that needed maintaining,” said Anna da Silva, the founder and chief executive of Northern Roots.
The charity’s seven activity programmes, which include farming and food, arts and culture, sports, business and learning, have been designed to appeal widely.
“The hardest part is getting people … physically and psychologically out of their house, down to the site, meeting people where they are on that journey,” said da Silva.
Once they are through the doors, the aim is to encourage continued engagement so they can unlock the environmental, economic and social benefits – a challenge that led to the creation of “participation pathways”.
This philosophy is perhaps best demonstrated by Faiza Awan and Louise Gibbs, who both grew up in the area and became involved with Northern Roots as community champions. Awan said: “It’s really important to have something for everyone.”
Gibbs added: “There’s just so many doors to come in through Northern Roots, and then to continue development.”
Both now have roles as Natural Health Service guardians. Unlike green social prescribing programmes that are centred on exercise or gardening, Northern Roots’ Natural Health Service focuses on intentional connection with nature. In doing so, it embodies the wider aims of creating opportunities for people who might not otherwise come together.
The site sits between two different and historically divided communities, and its outdoor setting helps to make it a space where people feel able to participate. “It’s a very welcoming, inviting environment,” said Gibbs. “With it being outside, people automatically feel comfort.”
Awan said: “There’s something really levelling and very democratic about doing things outside in nature,” adding that it could create a sense of belonging that might be harder to achieve in other settings.
The importance of connection is reflected in the relationship between the community and the site. Gibbs said: “Because [people] are local they feel more connected to the space … it’s giving the ownership to the community.”
The Natural Health Service was commissioned through Northern Roots by NHS England. It launched in 2023 as a six-month pilot with patients from the Hill Top GP surgery in Fitton Hill. It now works with healthcare providers to support people experiencing mental health challenges.
A session may involve foraging, bushcraft, making something from natural materials or simply noticing what is around you. The principle is that being outside, in an environment without the clinical associations of a healthcare setting, can create room to slow down.
Gibbs said: “People might come in and they might be flustered from the morning, the school run or the next 10 things they need to do, but we really encourage people to slow down, to take that breath, to give themselves permission, to spend this time on themselves and to simply just be in this space.”
Independent NHS research published in 2025 found that participants in Northern Roots’ Natural Health Service improved their wellbeing scores by an average of 8.15 points on the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale, a seven-item questionnaire used to measure a person’s recent wellbeing. The project generated an estimated £4,940 in social value per participant.
However, the benefits extend beyond metrics. “You can’t put it in facts and figures, in black and white,” said Gibbs. “Seeing someone’s eyes light up when they’ve said they have not been out for years. They’re excited to come the next week.” The benefits were mutual, she added. “It makes me feel good within myself, seeing that person is happy in that moment.”
Northern Roots is intended to be a model for others. “There are bits of land like this all over the place,” said da Silva. “They’re seen as a problem. We have got an approach to evaluating the place where you are, the site that you have, the needs of the community, the opportunities within the site.”
Northern Roots aims to attract 300,000 visitors a year by 2030, dispense hundreds of Natural Health Service social prescriptions – connecting people to non-medical community-based services – and create employment and training opportunities.
The idea that land can be a resource is part of Northern Roots’ wider proposition: that urban green space should be treated as critical infrastructure in the same way as hospitals and schools. Da Silva said it should be seen as “part of an arsenal of tools that can be used to address issues and support communities”.
The challenge is not simply to demonstrate what the land can provide, but to build the case for investment to make that possible.
“We need commissioners to invest in these spaces in the same way they would built infrastructure,” said da Silva. The aim is to show that relatively modest investment in land can help to reduce pressure on other public services.
For da Silva, however, the value of the project is not only in what it can deliver for public services. It is also in how it changes people’s relationship with the land. The ambition is to change “the way people feel about a place, themselves and their place in that place”.

Drivers ignoring roadwork closures to skip queues ‘wilfully putting lives at risk’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
11:00:15 UTC
20:00:15 KST

Drivers ignoring roadwork closures to skip queues are putting lives at risk, National Highways has warned, after recording hundreds of incidents this year where cars were deliberately driven through cones or barriers.
The agency, which manages motorways and major roads, said there was increasing concern about incursions into closed-off roadworks and the danger they posed.
It said its works contractors had reported an increasing proportion of such incidents as deliberate. According to National Highways data, 53% of the 814 incursions reported nationwide in England between January and July this year involved drivers trying to avoid queues, closures or diversions.
Repeated dangerous driving around roadworks has led National Highways to close parts of motorways to protect workers rather than just closing lanes, causing significant delays for road users.
To highlight the issue, the agency released clips showing drivers entering closed-off roadworks areas, which led to successful prosecutions and driving bans. They included footage of the M1 motorway in Hertfordshire, where repeated incursions earlier this year led to it being closed completely to keep workers safe, creating a 10-mile diversion for drivers. There were no casualties in any of the incidents shown.
On average, about 30 incursions a week are recorded across England’s motorways and A-roads. While most are defined as “seeking benefit” – drivers deliberately entering restricted roadwork areas hoping for a short cut – factors including breakdowns or simple driver error also lead to dangerous incursions.
In the latter cases, however, most drivers quickly stop and seek assistance, according to Melanie Clarke, the director of health, safety and wellbeing at National Highways. She said the latest figures showed “a worrying number of drivers wilfully ignoring roadworks to save time, putting road workers and other people at risk”.
Clarke said: “This year alone there have been over 400 incidents of those ‘seeking benefits’ as we describe it. We are definitely seeing a rise. We really encourage our road workers to report these instances so we can understand the level of the risk that they are facing when they are simply just trying to do their jobs.”
She added: “Drivers who just come through to avoid the closure or diversion are often travelling at speed and not necessarily aware of the activities that are going on within the roadworks. Often there’s plant, there’s machinery, the surface may already been treated. Obviously our concern is for our road workers – but those drivers need to understand that they also put themselves at risk.”
At least one fatality had occurred because of incursions this year, Clarke said.
She added that, contrary to occasional driver perception, roads were never sealed off without some activity ongoing or imminent. “If you don’t see people working, that doesn’t mean that there aren’t people working nearby. Or maybe the road surface has been compromised in some way in order to complete the work. So it’s simply not safe for vehicles to travel through that road work session until the work is complete.”
Regardless of the risk, drivers attempting to take a shortcut would normally not make their journey quicker, she said. “It’s simply not worth it.”
Sinead Ryan, a lead traffic management operative for HW Martin, a contractor, said: “People don’t always realise how dangerous our job can be. We work close to live traffic and, while we can do everything possible to keep ourselves safe, we can’t control the actions of drivers.
“When someone ignores a closure or drives into a work area, it only takes a second for someone to get hurt.”

Seamless interoperability with our NATO partners is of particular importance to reinforcing the cohesion of the Alliance and a great deal of mutual learning has taken place with our Polish friends.”
Operating from grass strips and other temporary surfaces gives transport aircraft greater freedom to move troops, vehicles and supplies without being tied to a small number of permanent airfields. The capability can also complicate targeting for an adversary by allowing aircraft and supporting personnel to be dispersed across a larger number of locations.
The A400M is designed to combine strategic transport capacity with the ability to operate from shorter and less developed airfields than larger transport aircraft, allowing it to move personnel, vehicles and equipment closer to forward operating areas.

‘I crawled through a sea of flames’: remembering the fatal Sabena plane crash of 1946
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:52:06 UTC
19:52:06 KST

Eighty years ago, on the night of 18 September 1946, a plane operated by the Belgian airline Sabena crashed in forests in Newfoundland, today part of Canada. The crash killed 26 people, 20 of them Belgians. What followed was a historic rescue operation.
‘I crawled through a sea of flames’: remembering the fatal Sabena plane crash of 1946
Forty-four people were on board the Douglas DC-4 plane that night, which was travelling from Brussels to New York. Only 18 people survived. The rescue operation lasted two days and involved the use of a helicopter to evacuate the seriously injured – one of the first times this had ever been done. The wreckage still lies at the crash site, alongside a small cemetery for the victims.
“I and others spent the night in great fear, because the weather was exceptionally bad,” said Jef Deschuyffeleer. He was one of the survivors of the crash and spoke on the radio the day after he was evacuated to Belgium.
We heard a tremendous cracking sound; I think it was the plane first making contact with the treetops
“The descent was erratic, with sudden jolts. After a few minutes, everyone began to sense that something unusual had happened,” he said. “Then we heard a tremendous cracking sound; I think it was the aeroplane first making contact with the treetops. What followed was a whole series of explosions and noises.”
Deschuyffeleer describes how flames shot out of the plane from all sides after it came to a halt. “I crawled 15 to 20 metres away from the sea of flames and told people to crawl further away, because of the risk of explosions.”
This was one of the first transatlantic flights operated by Sabena, the predecessor of Brussels Airlines. Cynrik De Decker, author of the book Sabena: The Turbulent Story of an Aviation Pioneer, explains: “Before the Second World War, there were no transatlantic flights. But during the war, the Americans developed large bombers capable of covering great distances and carrying large payloads. After the war, transatlantic commercial air travel took off. Sabena was quick to jump on the bandwagon.”
Flights were carried out in several stages. From Brussels, they first flew to Shannon in Ireland to refuel. They then continued to Gander in Canada, where they refuelled again, before flying on to New York.
A small cemetery was laid out at the tail end of the aeroplane. The remains were never moved
That night 80 years ago, it took some time before people realised the plane had crashed. And once it was known, it took until midday the following day before the wreckage was spotted in the vast Canadian forests.
Water was gradually supplied via parachutes, a doctor arrived and the survivors were evacuated a day later. In total, the rescue lasted two days.
It was one of the first ever rescue operations to involve a helicopter. Men were dropped off and cleared a space where they laid planks so the helicopter could land. This enabled them to evacuate the seriously wounded by helicopter. They were then transported by seaplane via the nearest lake in what De Decker calls “a truly massive operation”.
The wreckage still lies where it crashed all those years ago. “A small cemetery was laid out at the tail end of the aeroplane. The remains were never moved,” De Decker says.
It was Sabena director Gilbert Périer who decided to bury the victims there. No one had been injured during the rescue operation, and he wanted to keep it that way. Among the graves are those of his ex-wife Marie Noblet and his daughter, also called Marie.
“It was a huge event at the time,” De Decker says. “The air disaster dominated the front pages for days on end, not only in Belgium but also abroad.”
National carrier
Sabena was Belgium’s national airline and was founded in 1923. Its first flight was from Belgium to the United Kingdom, but Sabena soon expanded its network, with the Congo – then a Belgian colony – also becoming an important destination.
In the decades that followed, Sabena grew into an internationally recognised brand. However, financial problems mounted and in 2001 the company went into administration.
Shortly after the bankruptcy, SN Brussels Airlines was established. It later merged with Virgin Express and continued as Brussels Airlines. Today, Brussels Airlines flight numbers begin with SN, in a nod to the company’s history.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — More than 450,000 listings for noncompliant machinery and equipment from e-commerce platforms have been removed as of the end of August, the Ministry of Labor said Friday.
Government agencies began working with major e-commerce platforms in 2025 to prevent unsafe products from entering workplaces. The parties established procedures to screen regulated machinery before listings go live, audit products after they are listed, and remove those that violate regulations.
Regulated items include grinders, circular saws, band saws, planers, power presses and forklifts. Authorities previously identified more than 520 violations a year, but the number has fallen to around 15 cases per month since the new system was introduced, according to Taisounds.
Major domestic e-commerce platforms, including Shopee, Momo and Pchome, are taking part. Before a product is listed, platforms use data matching and keyword searches to identify machinery that may fall under regulated categories.
Sellers are then required to provide relevant safety documents before the products can be put up for sale. The platforms also conduct random checks after products are listed.
Regulated machinery must be properly registered or type-certified and carry the required safety labels or certification marks before being listed for sale. Sellers who violate the regulations can face fines of up to NT$2 million (US$62,892).

Digested week: BuzzBallz signed by Tory leader builds excitement for conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18

19:51:20 KST

Monday
It’s funny, isn’t it, how many things we take for granted in life? How many things go wholly unmentioned, even wholly unconsidered in any even minutely conscious way – and yet, when they are suddenly kicked away you realise just how much of your internal organisation, your mental integrity, your structural soundness altogether, rested on these unexamined pillars.
One of mine, it turns out, is the belief – no, surely more than that? The sure and certain knowledge, in my bones if never alas vouchsafed by my mere mortal eyes – that Bruce Springsteen does not wear pyjamas.
This is fundamental, surely? The Boss sleeps naked. This is an eternal verity.
But no. According to what I can only describe as reports, he is a loyal customer of the venerable sleepwear shop Schostal in Rome, which was opened in 1870 by two brothers from Vienna. There’s a photo of Bruce hugging the manager, Shirley Braine – to whom he apparently sends regular postcards – and everything.
So. There you have it. The Boss sleeps in pyjamas. Acceptable province of 1950s boarding school boys, your worst boyfriend, and your dad. Please go carefully about your day and from the fragments of your shattered psyche may you rebuild better soon.
Tuesday
Party conference season is almost upon us – I know! Try to contain yourselves! – and the preparations for fun times are gathering pace. News breaks that Blue Beyond, a young Conservatives group (and I always like to know that they’ve found each other rather than roaming free and confused), is offering as a grand raffle prize a BuzzBallz signed by Kemi Badenoch! I said try to contain yourselves! And not only is it signed, but it is a large BuzzBallz! I SAID TRY TO CONTAIN YOURSELVES.
In case you are not as young as a youngster or as cool as a Conservative, I should explain: a BuzzBallz is a spherical plastic container that contains a cocktail, usually of a lurid hue and unsubtle flavour profile (the inscribed orb itself is Berry Cherry Limeade and whyever not?). They come in two sizes – small, which is a bit larger than a tennis ball, and large, which is a bit smaller than a football.
Tickets are available now. The winner will be drawn at the Tory conference and must be over 18 to collect. Rumours that Michael Heseltine will launch it at your head for a small further fee are popular but as yet unsubstantiated.
Wednesday
I find myself unaccountably drawn to the story of the Hyrox poo-er. Not because of any coprophiliac inclinations, you understand, but because the idea of exerting myself to the extent that I might lose control of my bowels is so out of my realm of personal possibility that I am increasingly intrigued by the question of whether Joanna Wietrzyk and I technically qualify as the same species at all.
Again, for the uninitiated/hitherto and possibly blissfully ignorant, a recap: Hyrox Beijing is an intense indoor fitness event and Wietrzyk one of its world record- holding contestants. About halfway through the insanely difficult competition, which comprises a series of horrendous things – I don’t know precisely what, I passed out after reading the word “burpees” – Wietrzyk suffered what was later termed “a severe faecal event”, which went down her leg but didn’t stop her progress round the course.
Cue a roar of outrage against her and the organisers, who didn’t disqualify her immediately before she touched any other equipment, and eventually an apology from Wietrzyk and a forfeit of her points.
To hell with the critics, say I. Biohazardry be damned! You push yourself so hard you crap yourself and keep on going, you’re a winner in my book. Now, someone unwrap this Mars bar for me. Typing is exhausting, you know.
Thursday
Not all heroes wear capes. Or a light coating of faeces down their legs. Some of them are headteachers who suspend 25 students in the first week back after the summer holidays, including one for the crime of zipping his bag too loudly. The head’s name is Dan Jeffries and, while he denies parents’ claims of suspension for minor infractions, it is clear that whatever measures he has indeed taken, he has no regrets about any of them.
Parents of some of those suspended from Frome college have compared the school to “a military base” and say the strictness demotivates pupils. Whatever, whatever. The world is made up of two types of people: those who want to hear the children’s side of things and those of us who just want Jeffries put in immediate charge of a new government department called The Whole of Modern Life, Starting With Quiet Coaches on the Train and After That I Have a List.
Friday
My mother summons me and my sister home. Apparently she needs to clear out the attic before she dies, but ideally before Sunday.
“What’s happening on Sunday?” I ask.
“Sunday,” she replies.
Deadlines by fiat were a mainstay of my childhood and so I ask no more.
My mother has lived in our house for 50 years. We brace ourselves for a hard 48 hours’ work and climb up into the loft.
Three small cardboard boxes of stuff await us.
“There are – there are just three small cardboard boxes of stuff up here.”
“Yes,” she says. “I can’t believe I’ve let it get this bad.”
We bring them down.
My wedding shoes and some papers – including my first book, The Story of Esmerelda, written when I was nine and some letters home from university – are in the first one. The second one contains my son’s baby clothes. The third has my sister’s childhood attempts at making a working model of Sizewell B and some postcards she wrote to Dad when he went on his first trip to America. “Come hom. Shez insane.” On reflection, she shouldn’t have given them to Mum to post.
“Excellent,” Mum says. “We can bin the lot.”
Ah, fiats. Ah, memories.

how the situationists turned spectators into participants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:50:44 UTC
19:50:44 KST

the city as a field of possibility
What if the city wasn’t something to consume but something to play? For the Situationists, this was a way of challenging the passive role assigned to people in modern society. Instead of simply following the routes, functions, images, and routines laid out for them, they imagined inhabitants who could wander, interfere, improvise, and collectively reshape the environments around them. The city, in other words, could become a field of possibility.
This ambition runs through the work of the Situationist International, the group of artists, writers, and theorists formed in Europe in 1957. Their critique extended from advertising and mass media to architecture, urban planning, art, and everyday life, all of which they saw as contributing to a culture in which people would experience the world as spectators. Guy Debord gave this condition its most influential name: the spectacle. But the Situationists’ response was not to produce better images. They wanted to change the relationship between people and the world those images represented, proposing wandering through cities without predetermined destinations, hijacking existing cultural material, constructing temporary situations, and imagining entirely new environments organized around play.
More than half a century later, their ideas have become strangely familiar. We move through immersive installations, interact with responsive architecture, participate in temporary urban interventions, and constantly produce and circulate our own images. Yet this raises a question the Situationists would probably have recognized immediately: when a space asks us to participate, are we actually given agency or are we being offered a more sophisticated way to perform within the spectacle?
New Babylon-Barcelona, 1963, original dimensions | image via @constant.101
the problem with being a spectator
The Situationist International emerged in postwar Europe amid economic growth, expanding consumer culture, mass media, and the reconstruction of cities. Everyday life was becoming more and more mediated by advertising and images of consumption. Urban space was being reorganized around specialized functions: housing here, work there, shopping somewhere else, with movement between them structured by roads, schedules, and infrastructure.
Guy Debord gave this condition its most influential formulation in The Society of the Spectacle, published in 1967. For Debord, the spectacle did not mean television, advertising, cinema, or visual entertainment, but it described a social condition in which relationships between people take place through representations and images. As he writes, the spectacle is ‘a social relation between people that is mediated by an accumulation of images that serve to alienate us from a genuinely lived life.’
The distinction matters because the Situationists were not simply opposed to images. Their criticism was directed at the relationship produced by the image, the distance between the person watching and the reality being watched.
Asger Jorn and Guy Debord, The Naked City, 1957, published in Guide psychogéographique de Paris
leave the map behind
One of the Situationists’ most concrete attempts to create that activity was the dérive, or drift. Instead of moving through the city according to practical objectives like going to work or buying something, the dérive asked participants to abandon their usual reasons for moving and allow the attractions of the terrain and unexpected encounters to influence their route. The practice grew out of psychogeography, which the Situationists used to describe the effects of geographical environments on emotions and behavior. A street could feel inviting or hostile. A familiar route could produce a completely different experience depending on the person moving through it. The city was psychological.
The Situationists responded by trying to read it differently. Their maps and diagrams did not describe streets according to geography but attempted to represent zones of attraction, movement, and atmosphere. Guy Debord’s The Naked City, produced in 1957, fragments a map of Paris into separate pieces connected by arrows, presenting the city through psychogeographical relationships. The dérive changes the relationship between an existing environment and the person moving through it, and architecture becomes more about the behaviors it permits, discourages, or makes imaginable.
If the dérive attempted to disrupt the way people moved through the city, détournement attempted to disrupt the way they read culture. The Situationists used détournement (rerouting) to describe the reuse of existing cultural material within a new context. Images, texts, advertisements, comics, films, and other familiar forms could be appropriated and reorganized so that their original meanings were altered or contradicted. The Situationists hijacked the language that already surrounded them. Asger Jorn’s Modifications, for example, intervened in existing paintings with new painted elements, transforming the source material. The gesture reflected a broader Situationist interest in taking existing cultural forms and putting them to different uses.
For design, the interesting part is the shift from making to using, as a cultural object is no longer understood as a finished message passed from an author to an audience, but as something whose meaning can change through the way it is picked up, reused, and reinterpreted by the people who encounter it. In this sense, the spectator is no longer just receiving meaning but interfering with the work and helping to shape what it becomes.
Untitled (unfinished dis-figuration), 1962, Oil on canvas, 122 × 97 cm, Museum Jorn Collection
build a situation, not an object
This idea comes into focus with the Situationist concept of the constructed situation, which treated everyday experience as something that could be deliberately set in motion. The Situationists were interested in creating temporary environments, events, and encounters that people could enter and influence, with the outcome left open to what happened between them.
The distinction becomes particularly interesting when we look at experience design today. An installation might invite visitors to move, touch, trigger sounds or lights, and follow different paths, while every possible response has already been anticipated by its designer. It can feel highly interactive while leaving the structure of the experience untouched. For the Situationists, participation depended on the possibility of changing what was happening and introducing something that had not been planned in advance. Play offered one way to make this possible. It loosened the fixed functions of everyday spaces and opened them to experimentation. A street could become a place to wander, a building could take on an unexpected use, and a gathering could develop according to the people involved.
These moments gave people a chance to test the limits of their surroundings and discover forms of activity that ordinary routines tended to suppress. The ambition was to bring that sense of possibility into everyday life, where people could have a greater hand in shaping the experiences and environments they moved through.
Espencat, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
constant imagines a city without fixed uses
No project brings this ambition into architecture more clearly than Constant Nieuwenhuys’ New Babylon, the vast urban vision he developed from the mid-1950s through 1974 around the idea of homo ludens, the playing human. Constant imagined a city made up of interconnected sectors where living, working, moving, and leisure could overlap, giving inhabitants the freedom to continually alter the spaces around them. Light, climate, color, and atmosphere could all become part of this changing environment, with the configuration of spaces responding to the activities taking place within them. Constant was interested in what might happen when a city could accommodate a society that was constantly changing, with its inhabitants shaping their surroundings through everyday use.
The project was deeply utopian, but its focus was less on what the perfect city might look like and more on how people might live within it. Constant gave considerable attention to models, drawings, maps, and other studies that allowed him to explore an environment without a fixed final form. The city remained open because its inhabitants were expected to give it meaning through the way they occupied it.
Freedom in New Babylon was never completely without structure. Constant was designing the spaces, systems, and conditions within which people would be able to change their surroundings, so the question of how much an architect could determine and how much could be left to the people living there was built into the project from the beginning. The architecture had to provide enough structure to hold the city together while leaving enough open for its inhabitants to take over, adapt it, and give it new uses.
Constant’s time with the Situationist International was relatively short. He joined in 1958 and left in 1960, after which New Babylon continued to develop as an independent project. He worked on it until 1974, producing an extensive body of models, drawings, maps, texts, and paintings around the idea of a city shaped by the people who inhabit it.
New Babylon-Paris, 1963 | image via @constant.101
when the ideas reached the street
By 1968, Situationist ideas about everyday life, participation, and the use of public space had begun to circulate beyond the group itself. When students and workers occupied universities, factories, and streets across France in May, the city became a place for collective action, with familiar spaces taken over and put to new uses.
The Situationists were not responsible for the uprising, but their criticism of institutions and passive social roles had already found an audience through texts such as On the Poverty of Student Life, published in Strasbourg in 1966 and principally written by Situationist member Mustapha Khayati. Two years later, the distinction between watching and taking part had become physical as people occupied the spaces around them and disrupted their usual functions.
The same period also exposed a problem that had always been present in the Situationist project: recuperation, the process through which radical ideas could be absorbed into the culture they were meant to challenge. Images, slogans, publications, and gestures could circulate as forms of resistance before eventually becoming things to reproduce, collect, exhibit, and consume. The Situationists’ own afterlife carries this contradiction, with their once-radical publications, maps, and images now preserved and displayed as cultural artifacts. Their critique was built around escaping the spectacle, but the spectacle proved capable of turning even that escape into an image.
Constant, Portfolio New Babylon, nr. 5, 1963, 37 x 36 cm, lithograph, multiple collections incl. Collection Kunstmuseen Krefeld, Germany and collection Boijmans van Beuningen, NL | image via @constant.101
are we participants now?
Today, participation is almost everywhere. We move through immersive installations, interact with responsive environments, occupy public spaces for temporary events, and spend much of our time making and sharing images online. The figure of the passive spectator seems, at first, to have disappeared. Look a little closer and the picture becomes less clear. A visitor can trigger a light, choose a route through an installation, or change something on a screen, while the experience remains tightly controlled. The visitor is active, but only within the limits of what has already been designed.
This is where the Situationists’ ideas feel current. They were interested in what people could do with a space once its usual rules were loosened: wandering without a destination, taking over an existing environment, giving a place an unexpected use, or seeing the city differently. Much of the pleasure came from not knowing exactly where the experience would lead. Contemporary interactive spaces often work in the opposite direction. They are carefully programmed to anticipate what a visitor might do, with every response, movement, sound, and image accounted for. Even the photograph taken at the end can become part of the experience, ready to be shared and circulated.
None of this makes these spaces uninteresting, and interactivity can certainly change how we experience architecture and art. The Situationists set the bar somewhere else, as for them, participation became meaningful when people could affect what happened around them, introduce their own uses, and leave the experience different from how they found it. That idea reaches beyond museums and installations, raising questions about public space, architecture, and the increasingly designed environments of everyday life: who decides what a place is for, how easily can people change it, and what happens when they use it in a way nobody anticipated?
We live with a different version of that problem now, surrounded by spaces that promise interaction and platforms that invite constant participation. The difference between taking part and having a say can be surprisingly small on the surface, and enormous underneath. When we enter a space designed to respond to us, how much of it can we actually change?
Eric Koch for Anefo, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away.
