No one was injured in the attack, which occurred Wednesday in the town in central Israel’s Sharon region.
Police said the investigation is part of a broader effort to combat violent feuds and organized crime in Israel’s Arab communities, as well as the flow of weapons stolen from Israeli military stockpiles into criminal hands.
The teenager was brought before the Kfar Saba Magistrate’s Court at the request of police. The court ordered him released under restrictive conditions.
As part of the investigation into organized crime figures and violent feuds in the area, officers from the Kafr Qasim police station, including detectives and intelligence investigators, carried out searches at several compounds in Jaljulia under court-issued warrants.
They were joined by members of the National Guard and Border Police.
During a search of one compound, officers found a Beretta handgun concealed inside a false wall in a kitchen and an FN handgun hidden in an attic, police said. Officers also seized a drum magazine, additional magazines and ammunition.
In a separate search at another compound in the town, officers using engineering equipment seized 14 surveillance cameras, including some positioned to monitor public areas.
The cameras were taken to the Kafr Qasim police station for further examination as part of the investigation.
Police said large numbers of officers were dispatched to the scene after the rocket was fired. They searched the surrounding area and collected evidence and other findings from the site.
Authorities allege the rocket had been stolen from the Israeli military. The investigation into the shooting and the broader criminal feud remains ongoing.

Türkiye’s net foreign liabilities fall to $398.7 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:10:24 UTC
19:10:24 KST

Türkiye’s net international investment position deficit narrowed to $398.7 billion in July from $407.2 billion in June, Central Bank data released on Sept. 18 showed.
The net position measures the difference between residents’ financial assets abroad and liabilities to non-residents. A deficit means liabilities exceed assets.
External assets rose 4.2 percent month-on-month to $419.6 billion, while liabilities to non-residents increased 1 percent to $818.3 billion.
The Central Bank’s reserve assets rose by $17 billion to $164.4 billion, from $147.4 billion in June.
Direct investment assets abroad increased 0.8 percent to $81.8 billion, while other investment assets fell 0.5 percent to $161.7 billion. Banks’ foreign currency deposits abroad declined 6.9 percent to $44.7 billion.
Financial derivative assets rose 0.7 percent to $2.5 billion.
On the liabilities side, portfolio investment rose 3.5 percent to $160.2 billion. This included $50.2 billion in equities and investment fund shares, up 1 percent from June.
Direct investment liabilities fell 0.3 percent to $232.5 billion, while other investment liabilities increased 1.6 percent to $421.6 billion.
Financial derivative liabilities declined 43 percent to $4 billion.

Yemen conflict displaces 112,000 people inside country, thousands flee to Djibouti, UN migration agency says
GENEVA, Sept 18 - At least 112,000 people have been displaced inside Yemen within the last two weeks as fighting continues along the country's west coast amid a renewed conflict, while nearly 3,000 have fled by sea to Djibouti, the United Nations migration agency said on Friday.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure while advancing along Yemen's Red Sea coast towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route. Responding to the Houthi offensive, the Saudi and Yemeni air forces have bombarded Houthi targets.
Nearly 3,000 people have crossed the Gulf of Aden to Djibouti in the Horn of Africa in less than a week as escalating violence have forced more families to flee, Sandrine Desamours, the representative for the UN’s refugee agency, UNHCR, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Djibouti.
The government of Djibouti is preparing for the arrival of up to 10,000 refugees - which will add acute pressure on the country’s health care and education services, she said.
The UN International Organization for Migration said people are fleeing on overcrowded boats and arriving with very limited food and water. Most fleeing are Yemeni families seeking refuge in Djibouti, but IOM is also beginning to see a small number of migrants, mainly from Ethiopia, heading in the same direction.
Additionally, authorities in Somaliland and Puntland have also reported increased arrivals from Yemen, including Yemeni refugees and Somali refugee returnees, though numbers remain in the hundreds for now, UNHCR said.
UN agencies described the latest fighting as being a crisis on top of multiple crises as the country’s health services and economy have been shattered amid a long civil war between forces of the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed administration and the Houthis created one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises.
The Houthi advance along Yemen's Red Sea coast is bolstering Tehran’s hand in its conflict with the US, as the group tightens its control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a strategic chokepoint for global oil and commodities shipping, more than six months after US and Israeli attacks on Iran. REUTERS

The China Coast Guard deliberately rammed a civilian government vessel on a humanitarian and livelihood mission, endangering the lives of its Filipino crew,” he said.

Notorious ex-Assad prison chief gets 60 years for torture in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:05:56 UTC
19:05:56 KST

Samir Ousman Alsheikh, a former senior official in the government of Syrian President Bashar Assad, was sentenced Thursday in the United States to 60 years in prison for torturing political prisoners at Syria’s notorious Adra prison and defrauding U.S. immigration authorities by concealing his past.
Alsheikh, 74, is the highest-ranking official from the Assad government to have been prosecuted and convicted outside Syria. Given his age, the sentence means he is likely to spend the rest of his life in prison.
“The message is clear: human rights violators who come to the United States will receive no safe harbor here,” the U.S. Justice Department said after the sentencing. “We will find them, and they will be prosecuted and punished for their heinous crimes.”
The federal judge in Los Angeles described Alsheikh’s conduct as “despicable,” unimaginably cruel and so violent that it was almost beyond description.
Prosecutors had sought a sentence of at least 80 years. Alsheikh’s attorneys asked for five years, citing his age and medical and cognitive condition. His lawyers said after the hearing that they planned to appeal.
A jury convicted Alsheikh on all six counts against him: conspiracy to commit torture, three counts of torture, one count of visa fraud and one count of attempted naturalization fraud. The trial lasted nine days, and jurors took only several hours to return guilty verdicts on every count.
Torture inside Adra prison
Alsheikh, a retired brigadier general, held a series of senior positions in Syria’s police and internal security apparatus and was affiliated with the ruling Baath Party.
From 2005 to 2008, he headed Damascus Central Prison, commonly known as Adra prison, one of Syria’s most notorious detention facilities.
The prison contained an underground punishment section known as “Wing 13,” which included cramped isolation cells and interrogation rooms. According to evidence presented at trial, Alsheikh ordered prisoners sent to the wing, monitored their torture from his office through surveillance cameras and at times personally participated in their abuse.
Three of his victims testified against him. Two said they were sent to Wing 13 after refusing to abuse political prisoners. A third was punished after guards intercepted a letter of support he had written to a political prisoner.
They described cold, damp cells infested with insects and prisoners being shackled to pipes in the ceiling and suspended by their arms for hours or even days. They said detainees were beaten with cables while hanging in the air. One witness testified that he felt as though his arms were about to be torn from his body.
A central focus of the trial was a torture device known as the “flying carpet” or “magic carpet.” It consisted of two hinged wooden boards onto which a prisoner was strapped on his back. Closing the boards folded the victim’s body at the waist, inflicting extreme pain and sometimes causing spinal fractures.
One witness testified that Alsheikh personally stepped on the device while it was being used.
Another prisoner said that after being tortured he was forced to put on a red jumpsuit reserved for prisoners facing execution, leaving him convinced he was about to be killed.
Other testimony described detainees being forced inside automobile tires and beaten while unable to move.
‘He still lives in my memory’
Alsheikh continued rising through the Assad government after leaving his prison post.
In 2011, as the uprising against Assad began and Syria descended into civil war, Assad appointed Alsheikh governor of Deir el-Zour and head of the province’s security committee.
Syrian documentation groups have accused forces operating under his authority during that period of firing on protesters, carrying out arbitrary arrests and committing torture. Those allegations were not part of the charges on which he was convicted in the United States.
Alsheikh applied for a U.S. immigrant visa in 2018 and entered the United States in March 2020. Prosecutors said he concealed his work at Adra prison, his ties to the Baath Party and his involvement in political persecution and violence on immigration documents.
He obtained permanent resident status, commonly known as a green card, and later applied for U.S. citizenship while continuing to conceal his past, according to prosecutors.
His presence in the United States came to light after a Syrian woman recognized him in a photograph circulated on social media in 2022 and contacted human rights activist Omar Alshogre, himself a survivor of detention and torture in Assad government prisons.
Syrian activists gathered testimony and passed information to U.S. authorities.
Alsheikh was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport in July 2024 as he prepared to board a one-way flight to Beirut.
He was initially charged only with immigration offenses. In December 2024, four days after the fall of Assad’s government, prosecutors filed a superseding indictment adding the torture charges.
Alsheikh became only the fifth person prosecuted under a U.S. law enacted in 1994 that allows authorities to prosecute people found in the United States for torture committed abroad.
German police assisted U.S. investigators in locating and interviewing Syrian witnesses living in Germany.
More than 50 relatives and acquaintances submitted letters to the court describing Alsheikh as generous and compassionate, while his children appealed to the judge for leniency.
His victims offered a starkly different account.
Sultan Abd al-Malik, who was tortured at Adra prison, said that even after 20 years, he still “lives in the prison of memory.”
His brother, Khaled, said he continues to suffer chronic back pain and restricted movement as a result of the abuse. When his son asks to ride on his back, Khaled said, he has to tell him, “I’m no longer strong enough to carry you.”
Assad sentenced to death in absentia
The sentencing comes about a month after a Syrian court sentenced former president Bashar Assad to death for war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by his forces during the country’s 13-year civil war, which began with the 2011 uprising.
Assad’s conviction and death sentence were handed down in absentia. He remains in Russia, where he fled as the collapse of his government became inevitable and where he has been granted asylum by the government of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The number of electric cars registered in Türkiye rose 53.2 percent year-on-year to 472,157 at the end of August 2026, according to Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) data compiled by Anadolu Agency.
Electric cars accounted for 2.62 percent of the country’s 18.04 million registered cars. Their number stood at 308,217 in August last year.
The electric car fleet numbered just 565 in 2015, reaching 183,776 at the end of 2024 and 370,591 by the end of 2025.
The net increase over the first eight months of 2026 was 101,566 cars.
An expanding charging network and changing consumer preferences have supported the increase.
Domestic carmaker Togg’s growing market share and new model launches have also contributed.
The number of registered hybrid cars reached 896,270 in August, up from 697,027 at the end of 2025 and 391,296 at the end of 2024.
Hybrids accounted for 4.97 percent of registered cars, up from 4 percent at the end of last year.
Hybrid cars first appeared in Türkiye’s registration statistics in 2011, when there were 23. Their number rose to 13,877 in 2019 and 222,328 by the end of 2023.
Together, electric and hybrid cars numbered about 1.37 million at the end of August, accounting for approximately 7.6 percent of the country’s registered car fleet.

Barcelona has a bold plan to protect its vulnerable coastline – and it could be prize-winning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:01:58 UTC
19:01:58 KST

The Spanish city has been selected as a finalist for The Earthshot Prize.
This summer, Barcelona recorded its highest temperature in more than a century.
It’s part of a worrying trend: the Mediterranean is warming around 20 per cent faster than the global average, while record-warm waters are fuelling stronger storms, sea level rise and coastal erosion.
The collapse of a stretch of a storm-hit promenade on Barcelona’s northeast coast in 2023 underlined the need for climate resilient infrastructure. Around 70 per cent of the artificial sand added in 2010 has since disappeared.
“Cities like ours must learn to live with climate change while protecting the places and communities that define them,” says Jaume Collboni, Mayor of Barcelona.
The Spanish city’s ambitious coastal resilience project is now in the running for a prestigious environmental award.
Barcelona is a finalist for The Earthshot Prize
Barcelona has been announced as a finalist for The Earthshot Prize in the Revive Our Oceans category. First launched in 2020 by Prince William, the awards recognise environmental solutions to “repair” the planet.
The Spanish city is pouring €150 million into restoring one of Europe’s most intensively used urban coastlines. The project will create 22 hectares – roughly the size of 31 football pitches – of climate- and heat-adapted public space along the Sant Martí seafront, integrating restored marine habitats, natural coastal protection and waterfront access.
It is hoped that it will become a blueprint for coastal cities around the world facing increasingly severe sea-level rise, stronger storms, flooding, biodiversity loss and extreme heat – something The Earthshot Prize will help with by boosting visibility and knowledge-sharing opportunities.
“Every year, our Finalists give me renewed optimism,” says Prince William, President and Founder of The Earthshot Prize. “They show us that, even as the environmental challenges remain urgent, extraordinary people around the world are already proving that progress is possible.”
‘Climate-resilient infrastructure designed for everyone to enjoy’
Instead of repeatedly rebuilding its vulnerable northeast shoreline, Barcelona is intentionally moving parts of the waterfront inland, including relocating a popular seafront football pitch, and moving the sea walls back.
This will allow for wider beaches that act as natural buffers, absorbing wave energy and creating more space for storms, erosion and rising sea levels, as well as providing a vital refuge during increasingly severe heatwaves.
Scheduled for completion in spring 2027, Passeig Marítim de la Mar Bella will encourage sustainable use of the coastline while boosting air quality and biodiversity with a 15,000-square-metre linear park.
Visitors will be able to stroll along a 12-metre-wide pedestrian path or cycle down bike lanes – stretching all the way to the Fòrum – resting at energy-producing solar pergolas along the way.
“The choice facing coastal cities is no longer whether to adapt, but how,” says María Buhigas, Chief City Architect of Barcelona. “This is not a defensive structure added to the edge of the city; it is a new piece of climate-resilient public infrastructure designed for everyone to enjoy.”
Who else is in the running for The Earthshot Prize 2026?
From nearly 7,000 nominations across 169 countries, 15 finalists have been selected for The Earthshot Prize.
Each is aligned with one of the five ‘Earthshots’: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate – with winners in each category poised to receive a £1 million (€1.17m) prize.
For the first time, positive tipping points were part of the selection process, rewarding innovations where progress builds on itself, costs fall with scale and recovery becomes self-propelling.
Other European finalists include Ørsted (Fix Our Climate) – the Danish renewable energy company behind some of the world’s largest offshore wind projects – and PFAS-Free France (Build a Waste-Free World), the policy and civil-society campaign that helped securing, and is now implementing, France’s ‘forever chemical’ phaseout in everyday products.
Further afield, Argentina’s Satellites on Fire is being recognised for its AI-powered wildfire detection and alert platform, alongside zero-emission shipping alliance ZEMBA, and India’s electric three-wheeler pioneer Mahindra Last Mile Mobility.
Reconnecting a vast mountain landscape across Canada and the US so wildlife can move freely once again, conservation collaboration Yellowstone to Yukon is among the contenders for the Protect and Restore Nature prize.
“Seeing solutions work gives us all confidence to act. When they succeed, they inspire others and accelerate change,” says Prince William.
The five winners of The Earthshot Prize 2026 will be announced at an awards night in Mumbai, India, on 17 November.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — US Representative Young Kim on Tuesday urged Washington to support Taiwan's bid to join the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

"This legislation directs the IMF representative to use the US voice and vote to support Taiwan's membership in the IMF," said Kim.

The ministry said it is consulting with relevant agencies, diplomatic allies, and like-minded countries, including the US, to develop a feasible strategy, and will provide updates on progress.
Taiwan was a founding IMF member, but its representation was transferred from Taipei to Beijing in 1980. Former IMF historian James M. Boughton said, “Its 1980 decision involved neither the admission of a new member nor the termination of an existing membership, but only the recognition of a different government to represent the member.”
Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research Director Liu Da-nien (劉大年) told UDN that Taiwan's biggest obstacle to joining the IMF would be recognition of its status as a state. He noted that Taiwan joined the World Trade Organization as the Separate Customs Territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen, and Matsu, a designation available to territories with autonomy over their external trade policies.
The IMF presents additional challenges because applicants must meet requirements concerning their financial systems and membership obligations, Liu said. Although the IMF operates independently of the UN, it could still draw on the UN's definition of statehood when assessing Taiwan's eligibility, he added.

19:00:55 KST

NATO has carried out a multinational air and missile defence exercise over Romania as the Alliance shifts from traditional air policing towards a broader system designed to counter aircraft, drones and cruise and ballistic missiles, according to Allied Air Command.
The Flexible Deterrent Option training on 9 September brought together fighter and tanker aircraft from France, Greece, Romania, Spain and Türkiye, alongside NATO Airborne Warning and Control System aircraft and a tanker from the Multinational MRTT Unit.
The main focus was Integrated Air and Missile Defence, with the participating forces also conducting Close Air Support training with Romanian ground forces. Aircraft taking part included French Rafales, Romanian and Greek F-16 Fighting Falcons, Spanish F/A-18 Hornets and Turkish F-16s. Spain also deployed an A400M Atlas tanker, while Turkey contributed a KC-135 Stratotanker.
NATO said the activity formed part of a wider move away from an Air Policing framework primarily concerned with safeguarding Alliance airspace against aircraft and uncrewed systems, towards a multi-layered air defence posture capable of dealing with a wider range of threats.
The new framework is intended to cover threats including conventional aircraft, uncrewed aerial systems, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, using sensors, command-and-control systems, fighters and other capabilities as parts of a single integrated network.
Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Alberto B. Calvo López, commander of the Spanish detachment conducting NATO Air Defence duties at Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base, said: “The evolving threat also reminds us of the importance of collective, layered air defence, in which sensors, command and control systems, fighters and other Allied capabilities must be able to operate as a single, integrated system.”
The exercise used a “Red” versus “Blue” scenario focused on Integrated Air and Missile Defence.
NATO AWACS aircraft acted as the principal command-and-control element for the “Red” force, directing tanker aircraft and coordinating with Romanian forces on the ground. The training was designed to test how airborne and ground-based systems could be brought together in real time, with information shared between participants and command procedures rehearsed against a simulated air threat.
NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre at Torrejón in Spain oversaw the activity, providing operational-level command and control while coordinating aircraft and supporting capabilities across the exercise. AIRCOM said the new Air Defence framework brings the Alliance’s air and missile defence activities under common rules, guidelines and command procedures regardless of the type of threat being faced.
The intention is to give NATO commanders greater flexibility to move and combine forces supplied by different member states, synchronising sensors, aircraft and other assets across several domains. The Romanian exercise was also intended to test how quickly allied forces could be assembled and integrated under a Flexible Deterrent Option, with those activities used to rehearse collective defence arrangements before they might be required during a crisis.

Taiwan must weigh military AI’s benefits against escalation risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:49 UTC
19:00:49 KST

Taiwan should carefully weigh its military AI applications as they offer opportunities to strengthen deterrence and national resilience, but their integration must account for escalation risks and vulnerabilities.
In recent months, Taiwan has accelerated efforts to integrate artificial intelligence into military systems. In October, President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) announced T-Dome, a multi-layered air-and-missile defense system that will use AI to improve real-time decision-making.
At the same time, the Ministry of National Defense established a pilot AI office within its Defense Innovation Division to explore military AI applications, starting with image recognition, cyber defense and anti-hacking. Yet while the government has identified militarized AI as a way to enhance national defense, it has not received attention comparable to that given to unmanned vehicles.
Military AI applications offer new opportunities to raise deterrence in the Taiwan Strait and enhance monitoring and data-gathering on Chinese operations, and therefore deserve serious consideration. At the same time, they carry risks of escalation, deception and exploitation.
As the environment evolves, Taiwan needs to evaluate military AI applications according to their military value, their reliability under disruption, and the degree of authority delegated to them.
Taiwan currently faces multi-sectoral threats, from disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks to blockade rehearsals. Growing tensions in the strait require Taipei to enhance both its military capabilities and defense resilience. In that context, the benefits of integrating autonomous weapon systems and AI-enabled decision support systems cannot be neglected.
Deterrence and preparedness
First, AI can help counter several aspects of China’s gray-zone tactics. China has leveraged its coast guard as a form of hybrid warfare to create uncertainty and normalize intrusions into Taiwan’s waters.
To raise deterrence and preparedness, Taiwan could integrate AI into maritime patrols. A fleet of autonomous unmanned surface vessels could provide constant, real-time monitoring and data-gathering on Chinese operations. AI systems could then digest that data to identify behavioral patterns, key zones of intrusion and timing characteristics.
The defense ministry has identified coastal surveillance drones as crucial systems to meet operational requirements for national defense, and new funds have been requested for the acquisition of such maritime drones in 2027. By reinforcing intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities, it can strengthen its decision-making and early-warning processes, accelerate vessel detection and reduce response times.
AI can also enhance unmanned vehicle operations through drone swarms and a faster kill chain, increasing deterrence in the strait.
Since February, the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology has partnered with Shield AI, a US defense-tech company, to integrate Hivemind, an end-to-end AI pilot, into Taiwan’s unmanned systems.
AI pilots
These AI pilots can decide and act autonomously, without human intervention, allowing Taiwan’s unmanned systems to remain effective in GPS- and GNSS-denied environments. Keeping unmanned systems operational under constant communications and GPS jamming would be essential should China invade.
Moreover, by allowing one operator to supervise multiple unmanned systems, AI could help Taiwan expand drone operations without a corresponding increase in the number of pilots. Overall, AI can accelerate the targeting cycle — identifying, selecting and engaging targets — reducing the time between detecting a threat and responding to it.
These developments would enhance Taiwan’s defense capabilities and support the island’s capacity to deny the People’s Liberation Army passage across the strait.
Beyond the military, AI’s contribution to Taiwan’s defense can extend to civilian capabilities that help society withstand coercion and information manipulation. The 2024 presidential election illustrated how China uses AI-generated content to shape narratives in its favor through disinformation.
This information warfare requires constant, high-quality fact-checking, which AI systems can support. Taiwan FactCheck Center and Cofacts, two key actors in Taiwan’s fact-checking environment, are using AI to collect and analyze data to ensure quicker and stronger fact-checking.
Together, these applications offer tangible benefits for Taiwan’s military capabilities and national resilience.
Escalation and exploitation
However, these benefits should not eclipse the risks that military AI applications carry. The Taiwan Strait is a tense, fast-paced environment in which one wrong decision could inflame the situation.
Taiwan’s armed forces and the Coast Guard Administration do a remarkable job protecting the nation — a task that requires judging when to respond, how strongly to respond and when to exercise restraint. In this environment, removing humans from the loop could drastically increase the risks of escalation. In 2025 alone, China’s air incursions across Taiwan’s median line amounted to 3,764 intrusions.
Because autonomous weapon systems do not possess the same contextual understanding as humans, each of those 3,764 events could have become a moment in which a deployed autonomous weapon system mistakenly decided that a PLA aircraft represented an imminent threat and opened fire without prior human approval.
Unintended escalation is not tied to strikes alone and can also arise from flying too close to an aircraft or crossing into China’s territory. Moreover, through their indications, predictions and recommendations, AI-enabled decision support systems can alter the process of making a decision to use force by influencing human judgment.
AI-enabled decision support systems could, for example, deceive commanders or wrongly assess a situation, prompting an escalatory response. Biases in the data and lack of transparency compound the risks.
Finally, integrating AI into military systems also carries risks related to cyberattacks and adversarial machine learning. Through data poisoning, an adversary could manipulate the data used to train these systems, undermining their reliability or causing them to misidentify threats.
In the strait, the consequences of a military AI failure could be used as justification for an invasion. Taiwan therefore needs a dedicated framework to assess these applications and establish the safeguards required before deployment.
Framework for AI adoption
Finding the right balance between military AI integration and AI safety is complex. Tensions in the strait push Taiwan to accelerate adoption of new technologies that could offer a military advantage. Conversely, adopting immature technologies too quickly could undermine its own military capabilities.
As Taiwan plans to deploy AI across military systems, it will need robust control architectures that ensure risk mitigation. Testing and evaluation will be key to establishing how systems behave under disruption and when human intervention is required.
Currently, Taiwan does not possess a clear framework to assess the inherent risks of military AI applications. The Ministry of Digital Affairs’ recent AI Risk Taxonomy and Assessment Framework excluded military uses from its classification.
The defense ministry could, for example, define clear conditions for military AI deployment, including which decisions must remain under human authority. The central objective should remain reinforcing Taiwan’s defense without increasing the risks of a conflict it seeks to prevent.
These safeguards should be developed alongside Taiwan’s military AI capabilities, as any failure would carry a cost Taiwan cannot afford to pay.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei’s interim Dongmen Market began a trial run on Wednesday and will officially open on Oct. 9, allowing vendors to continue operating while the century-old original market is redeveloped.
CNA reported that all 45 vendors from the original Dongmen Market have moved to the temporary site. Taipei’s Market Administration Office said the facility has air conditioning, improved lighting and ventilation, and wider walkways for shoppers.
Dongmen Market was established in 1928 during the Japanese colonial era (1895-1945) and later became known for its high-quality fresh food. Older generations of Taipei residents called it the “aristocratic market” because it was near government offices and official residences.
The city built the interim market to keep vendors in business during redevelopment. The temporary site also provides cleaner and more spacious shopping areas than the original market, per Liberty Times.
Some vendors said they are still adjusting to the new equipment and layout. They said longtime customers returned on the first day of the trial run, while residents welcomed the cooler and less humid environment.
The market is divided into three sections for prepared food, fresh produce and meat, and general merchandise. Vendors sell items including rice noodle soup, vegetables, meat, seafood, imported goods, religious supplies, hardware, and clothing, per FTV News.
The market office said the city plans to begin demolishing the original Dongmen Market on Feb. 1, 2027. It said that the interim market’s official opening on Oct. 9 will include promotional offers and other activities.

‘minimalism feels cold when empty of narrative’: how aarke shapes its brand identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:25 UTC
19:00:25 KST

AARKE TRANSFORMS HIDDEN APPLIANCES INTO COUNTERTOP ARTIFACTS
For the sixth feature of Navigators of Design, a 10-part interview series produced with Most Studios, designboom connects with Malin Gäfvert, Creative Director at premium kitchen appliance brand Aarke. Stepping into the digital and physical frontier of contemporary brand building, Malin explores how creative direction transforms everyday objects from functional utilities into elevated lifestyle artifacts. Rather than viewing kitchen appliances as disposable tools to conceal in cabinets, her approach injects worth into mundane daily moments, turning routine tasks into quiet rituals of understated design.
‘Kitchen appliances have traditionally been purely utilitarian and transactional. Aarke started with a simple insight: the kitchen category was overlooked by design, in both form and function,’ opens Malin Gäfvert in the interview. ‘Sparkling water makers used to be bulky plastic pieces you’d rather hide in a cabinet. Our mission was to replace the disposable with the desirable, by making things people really want to have visible in their kitchen — pieces that stand the test of time and withstand the wear and tear of the eye for many years to come.’
portrait of Malin Gäfvert, Creative Director at premium kitchen appliance brand Aarke | all images © Petter Bäcklund, Frida-M, Malin Gäfvert
INTERSECTION OF PRODUCT DESIGN, INTERIORS, AND FASHION
Founded in 2013 by industrial designers Carl Ljungh and Jonas Groth, Aarke — derived from the Southern Sami word for everyday — was built to refine forgotten home essentials. While the founding team leads the industrial design and product engineering, Malin Gäfvert shapes the intangible ecosystem surrounding the objects, establishing a distinct brand identity that bridges product design, interior space, and fashion imagery.
‘Our visual identity doesn’t have to look like a typical appliance brand. It shouldn’t. I think we are more at the intersection of product design, lifestyle, interior, and fashion,’ Gäfvert notes. ‘One defining decision was building a distinctive identity — an identity with a few cues, repeated consistently, that carry the brand and build recognition. In our storytelling, that shows up as Everyday Engineering: celebrating how Aarke integrates into daily life, not just talking about what the products do and perform, but how they improve your everyday, your lifestyle, your kitchen.’
founded in 2013, Aarke was built to refine forgotten home essentials
HOW AARKE BALANCES FORM, FUNCTION AND CULTURAL RESONANCE
Driven by a clear strategic vision, Aarke’s creative direction shifts focus from functionality to deeper meaning. Placing the emphasis on what objects represent rather than just what they do allows the brand to establish a consistent narrative across its entire product collection.
‘We treat the product like a piece of design from day one, rather than as an accessory that gets shoved in a cupboard between uses. In our branding, function became the entry point, not the whole story. We really emphasize how we can inject a sense of worth into the everyday, mundane tasks you do, turning those moments from ordinary to extraordinary by transforming them into small rituals,’ says Malin.
the brand’s identity bridges product design, interior space, and fashion imagery
Aarke’s visuals balance precise product close-ups that highlight materiality and form with dynamic lifestyle imagery. Physical evidence of human interaction brings warmth and context to the design narrative, allowing the brand to create a grounded visual identity free from cold minimalism.
‘Minimalism only feels cold when it’s empty of narrative. Our fix is to balance the more product-close visuals we do, where we focus on design and tactile material, and mix them with visuals that bring in the physical evidence that a human being is present and using the thing,’ declares the creative director. ‘In art direction, that means we favour authentic settings, capturing real moments, shot in ambient light, often on analogue film. It creates a nice contrast between the two visual worlds we’re in: from the precise product-focused engineering to the real everyday moments in the home. That tension, between the engineered and the everyday, is what makes the brand interesting and recognisable.’
Aarke’s creative direction shifts focus from functionality to deeper meaning
Focusing on daily routines, the brand creates products designed to eliminate minor frustrations and clutter. This user-centered perspective steps away from fast-moving trends, elevating everyday objects through thoughtful storytelling that adapts to seasonal shifts by relying on deliberate tone and timing rather than altering its core identity to fit brief fads. Beyond the physical objects themselves, internal filters ensure that packaging, unboxing, and retail environments mirror this exact design standard, establishing a unified identity across every brand touchpoint.
‘Moments that happen every day deserve better design, because those are the moments people actually live in, repeatedly. They should be free from mess, errors, and bumps,’ concludes Malin Gäfvert. ‘Aarke’s product philosophy: durability, longevity, quality materials, considered design – doesn’t move with trend cycles. But the way we talk about it can flex and adapt: seasonal content, cultural moments, platform-native formats, etc. We can jump on a craze if we think it’s interesting and has something to do with us. And if we do, it happens at the edges, never in the object or the core message.’

====================================================================================================

“Mankeeping” takes a toll on women’s mental health and relationship satisfaction, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:19 UTC
19:00:19 KST

A newly developed psychological survey provides a way to measure the unpaid, emotional labor that women perform to manage and maintain the social lives of their romantic partners. The research, published in Sex Roles, details the creation of a scale that captures how women experience the effects of men’s shrinking friendships. The tool offers a standardized way to study this dynamic and its impacts on relationship satisfaction and individual well-being.
The survey centers on a concept called mankeeping. This term describes the effort women exert to compensate for the decline in their male partners’ social networks. It involves behaviors like organizing social events, encouraging men to reconnect with friends, and serving as a primary or sole source of emotional support to prevent the men from becoming isolated.
The concept builds on a long history of sociological research into household and emotional labor. For instance, a 1985 study established the idea of kinkeeping, which refers to the everyday, invisible work that women typically perform to keep family members connected and preserve relational harmony.
At the same time, recent public health data indicates that men are facing a widespread decline in close friendships. A 2022 study observed that men generally face greater social isolation than women across most of their adult lives. This vulnerability is also reflected in a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, which showed that psychological distress tends to shrink men’s support networks much more severely than it does for women.
Recognizing the intersection of these two trends, researchers Angelica P. Ferrara and Dylan P. Vergara formally theorized mankeeping in a 2024 paper. They proposed that the ongoing decline in men’s friendships shifts a heavy, unreciprocated social burden onto their female partners, who act to shield the men and the relationship from the negative consequences of isolation.
“‘Mankeeping’ is something many women express that they have been doing for their partners for quite some time,” lead researcher Vincent Mancini told PsyPost. Mancini is an adjunct senior research fellow at the UWA Medical School and a senior research fellow at the UWA Centre for Child Health Research. “With loneliness being a population health crisis that has gendered features, the aim of this work was to better understand how women may engage in additional effort to help maintain their male partner’s social needs.”
Prior to this work, scientists lacked a validated survey to actually quantify the extent of mankeeping and its psychological toll. By developing a specialized scale, Mancini and his colleagues aimed to provide a reliable way to investigate how men’s loneliness reshapes the daily lives of the women who care for them. To build the scale, the researchers first drafted a large pool of questions based on the initial theory of mankeeping.
They recruited 402 women residing in the United States who had been in a heterosexual romantic relationship for at least six months. The participants rated their agreement with 62 potential scale items using a seven-point rating system. They also completed several established psychological questionnaires measuring depression, anxiety, stress, relationship burnout, relationship burden, and overall relationship satisfaction.
Through a statistical process that groups related questions together based on how participants respond, the researchers refined the survey down to 46 items spanning six distinct categories. These six factors include the actual behaviors women perform to manage their partner’s social life, the emotional impact of that labor, and a recognition that their emotional support is often unequal or unappreciated. The remaining three factors capture the woman’s appraisal of her partner’s social network status, a desire for her partner to expand his friendships, and the extent to which the partner depends on her for emotional support.
The results indicated that the survey accurately captured theoretical predictions about mankeeping. Higher scores across the mankeeping dimensions strongly correlated with lower relationship satisfaction and higher levels of relationship burden and burnout. In addition, five of the six dimensions positively correlated with women’s self-reported depression, anxiety, and stress.
“There is now a validated and useful measure that can help to assess how women engage in this effortful process to help address their partner’s unmet social needs,” Mancini said. “Women who engage in these behaviors more tended to show poorer relationship satisfaction, which may signal the importance of social connections outside the romantic relationship that can help to more widely distribute social needs.” He added that “these results, whilst preliminary, indicate fairly robust and strong effects.”
Interestingly, simply appraising that a partner lacked friends was not strongly linked to psychological distress; rather, it was the active behaviors and the resulting emotional impact that were associated with poorer mental health. The data also showed that women who held more traditional beliefs about gender roles were more likely to report engaging in mankeeping behaviors.
Next, the team sought to verify that their newly developed survey, titled the Mankeeping Scale – Partner Report, operated consistently across different populations. They administered the 46-item survey to a second group of 395 romantically partnered cisgender women living in the United Kingdom. Statistical analyses confirmed that the original six-category structure fit the UK data just as well as the US data. This suggests that the survey measures the same underlying concepts regardless of which of these two countries the women reside in, establishing what researchers call measurement invariance.
Recognizing that a 46-item questionnaire can be overly long for many research or clinical settings, the scientists combined the data from both the US and UK participants, totaling 797 women. They identified the three most mathematically and theoretically strong questions from each of the six categories to create an 18-item brief version. Testing showed that this shortened survey maintained excellent reliability and produced similar associations with relationship satisfaction and psychological distress as the full-length version, offering a practical alternative for future studies.
“It is incredibly useful to have validated measures of concepts such as mankeeping, so that research can move from theory to actually testing associations with possible outcomes,” said Sara B. Chadwick, an assistant professor of Gender and Women’s Studies and Psychology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. “Having a validated measure of mankeeping will allow researchers to better understand how women’s efforts to support and maintain their men partners’ social networks and emotional health are connected to a variety of outcomes for both women and men in these partnerships,” she told PsyPost.
“The development of this measure offers a clear extension of research theorizing ‘mankeeping,’ and builds on previous feminist scholarship that has aimed to conceptualize the many ways that gender norms shape women’s romantic relationships with men,” Chadwick added.
She noted that earlier research has highlighted how gender norms often position women as caregivers for their male partners in ways that mimic a parent-child dynamic. “Overall, I would say this offers an important contribution to feminist research by specifically naming the kinds of behaviors that women engage in for the sake of supporting their men partners and by creating a way for researchers to measure and thus further explore it.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind about these findings. The survey relies entirely on self-reported data from one partner, meaning it captures a woman’s perception of her partner’s social life rather than an objective measure of his actual friendships. A man might feel his social needs are adequately met, even if his partner appraises his network as lacking. Future studies would benefit from surveying both members of a couple simultaneously to get a complete picture of the relationship dynamics.
“It is absolutely crucial to recognize that these results at the population level might not apply in the same way to the individual/couple level,” Mancini cautioned. “Romantic couples are incredibly diverse, not every man is lonely, nor does every woman need to engage in this process. This paper should also not take away from the importance of understanding loneliness as a population health issue, that all genders can experience.”
Chadwick agreed that context is crucial, noting that emotionally supporting a partner or helping them maintain social networks can sometimes be a consensual arrangement or a necessity based on temporary life circumstances, such as moving to a new city or dealing with a period of depression.
“The behaviors listed are not in themselves problematic, even when they may be burdensome,” Chadwick explained. “The key here is consent and mutuality, or in other words, it is essential that women either have consented to an arrangement where they take on the majority of social networking and emotional labor, or that this labor is offered to women in their times of need from their men partners.”
The current data is also a single snapshot in time, which makes it impossible to determine a strict chain of cause and effect between mankeeping behaviors and declining mental health. In addition, women’s responses to the survey might be influenced by internalized societal expectations about how a romantic partner is supposed to act.
Because the study focused on populations in the US and the UK with similar cultural norms, the survey might perform differently in other cultures. Expanding the research to include non-Western populations, as well as developing a companion survey to capture how men experience and perceive this social labor, will help clarify the full scope of this dynamic.
The issue arises, she pointed out, when women are automatically expected to take on this labor. “Unfortunately of course, with the way that gender norms function, the majority of mankeeping is indeed likely to be nonconsensual and non-mutual and thus have a disproportionately negative impact on women,” Chadwick said. In future research, she hopes to see investigations into whether this support is reciprocated, noting that the labor might not have a negative impact “if women feel they are offered the same types of labor from their partner in their own time periods of loneliness or need.”
“Our team is looking to engage in some longitudinal work that can allow us to follow couples over time, so that we can better understand how the phenomenon of mankeeping unfolds over time,” Mancini explained. “Being able to also capture the experiences of male partners, and develop interventions that can bolster the relationship quality between partners are our key future priorities.” He noted that the researchers are “always happy to chat to clinicians, researchers, and communities who have thoughts and ideas about the utility of this work!”
The study, “Measuring Mankeeping: Development and Validation of a Scale Assessing How Women Experience the Impact of Men’s Declining Social Networks,” was authored by Vincent O. Mancini, Briana N. Guerrini, James J. Clarke, Dylan P. Vergara, Zac E. Seidler, and Angelica P. Ferrara.

Trump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation

19:00:16 KST

The Trump administration has started sending a majority of undocumented children who came to the US alone and have new immigration court cases to Texas, where government facilities for them are unlicensed, their chances of getting a lawyer are low and advocates fear that “a deportation churn-out factory” awaits them, the Guardian has learned.
Almost 80% of children in federal custody who arrived unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian and who were placed in immigration court proceedings in July – and over 90% in August – have been funneled into shelter networks somewhere in Texas, a dramatic upswing from the months prior, according to analysis shared exclusively with the Guardian from researchers at the immigration data insights platform bklg.org.
This is understood to amount to a total of 925 children in the care of the Health and Human Services (HHS) department’s office of refugee resettlement (ORR) and in open immigration court proceedings based in Texas, with 651 sent there in July and August alone.
Federal officials’ sudden shift toward ushering these vulnerable kids to the Republican-controlled, deeply conservative state for no publicly stated reason has alarmed immigrants’ rights advocates amid concerns about their treatment and access to due process under US laws.
Experts who spoke to the Guardian fear the advent of a mass apprehension campaign – forcing immigrant children from their communities within the country’s interior to gather them in Texas to ultimately pack them onto repatriation flights, which often leave from areas along the US’s southern border.
“We’re thinking about congregating children in facilities in Texas, where there are less attorneys, where it’s one of the harshest jurisdictions, you know, in the country with regard to immigration judges and how they handle cases. And it’s close to the border, where they can just get planes,” said Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu, deputy director at the Arizona-based legal service non-profit, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project.
She added that these facilities could be “a deportation churn out factory that has attorneys in name but not real representation”.
Unaccompanied immigrant kids, who often come to the US fleeing abuse, neglect, abandonment, trafficking or other harms, regularly cross the US-Mexico border and enter the custody of ORR, which is legally tasked with their welfare, not the Department of Homeland Security’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency.
There were more than 1,800 kids in ORR’s care nationally at the end of July, scattered among shelters, foster care and secure facilities across the country. Yet already, more than 60% of those still detained with ongoing immigration court proceedings are now believed to be living in Texas, compared with fewer than half in June.
ORR did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.
The processing to Texas is occurring despite the state’s GOP-dominated government refusing to provide state licensing for ORR care providers, a policy that hasn’t stopped the facilities from operating there, but has meant less child welfare oversight and protections for kids.
“Texas is very sympathetic to the Trump administration, at least the governor and the Republican legislature. And so I think the Trump administration knows that not only will there be no pushback from the state government and from the governor, but that people like Governor Greg Abbott are willing accomplices,” Veronica Escobar, a Democratic congresswoman from west Texas, told the Guardian in a phone interview this week.
Meanwhile, many of the kids – from toddlers to teenagers – are navigating the US’s byzantine immigration laws mostly without attorneys. Already, only 31.7% of children in ORR custody with active immigration court proceedings nationally have had a notice of legal representation filed in their cases. Kids held in Texas are faring even worse, with 17.2% in Houston, 18.6% in El Paso and just 8.7% in San Antonio having a legal representation form filed on their behalf, bklg.org’s research found.
“There needs to be far more oversight and representation, for children especially. These kids deserve lawyers,” Escobar said.
At the same time, ORR officials have alarmed advocates by seeking multiple contracts for “emergency influx facilities” of up to 3,000 beds – despite the fact that such facilities can only open when the agency’s operational capacity reaches 85% or higher for multiple days, and ORR’s shelter and foster care network, by its own count, is operating at about 27% capacity.
“Who are they planning to fill those facilities with?” Avila-Cimpeanu asked. “Our fear is huge mass internal apprehension of children.”
Plans for such facilities were first reported by the Independent last month.
At a recent roundtable presentation for roughly 120 stakeholders, ORR officials said the contracts would potentially give the administration “the capability to rapidly respond to any surges at the border of unaccompanied alien children”, according to a transcript of the meeting shared with the Guardian.
But encounters with unaccompanied children at the south-west border have been exceptionally low over the last year and a half. Still, officials pushed for an aggressive timeline, with only 90 days for a facility to become fully operational after a contract is awarded.
“That’s fast and you’re like: ‘I don’t know if I can do that.’ I think it’s very feasible. That is the intent of where we need to be,” said Tony Canales, a branch chief at ORR’s division of acquisition requirements, according to the transcript.
“We’re looking to see whatever you got. I mean, if it’s a permanent facility, if it’s temporary buildings, if it’s a site that is blank that you plan on building on, whatever the case may be. We will definitely look at it and take [it] into consideration,” Canales told the attendees.
The presentation specified that any shelter would require an 8-ft high perimeter fence.
Although officials did not specify a location for such emergency influx facilities, many of the stakeholders closed in on Texas while asking questions.
Officials also said the chosen contractors would be responsible for providing legal services, which could present a serious conflict of interest given that attorneys tasked with representing kids would now be dependent on ORR.
For critics of the second Trump administration, the emergency influx facilities raise the spectre of a worst case scenario, with large-scale detentions for immigrant children in communities across the country, given that there is no apparent current need for the massive shelters otherwise.
“The way that a country and a government treats its children and children in their custody is a direct representation of the level of morality or immorality of that government and those individuals,” Escobar said. “And so it is shameful the way that this administration has chosen to treat children.”
José Olivares contributed reporting

The Earthshot Prize Is Embracing the Idea of Positive Tipping Points
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

At a time when companies are racing to deliver commercial fusion energy and promising a new generation of geothermal wells across the U.S., three-wheel electric vehicles may not seem like the most exciting clean energy technology. But in India, three-wheel vehicles are an essential part of daily transportation and account for up to a quarter of motorized trips in many cities.
The majority of new full-size passenger auto rickshaws sold in India are now electric, according to registration data, a striking milestone given that 10 years ago they were barely off the ground. Initially, scaling took a mix of policy, infrastructure build out, and innovative financing; now, the market has taken on a life of its own. “Once you cross 50%, electric becomes the dominant technology,” says Suman Mishra, the CEO of Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a key player in the market.
The development underscores an idea that is gaining currency in some climate circles: sometimes technologies that matter most are not the futuristic breakthroughs waiting to scale but the familiar ones where adoption begins to reinforce itself.
That shift sits at the heart of a new framework the Earthshot Prize is using this year to evaluate climate solutions. Rather than simply picking the climate solution with the most impressive technology, the judges looked for ways to recognize and advance “positive tipping points” that will unlock transformative changes beyond any individual company or project. “We know exactly the things that we’re looking for to try to tip these global systems in the right direction,” says Jason Knauf, CEO of the Earthshot Prize.
The pattern is visible across the finalist list. Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, one of this year’s Earthshot finalists announced on Sept. 18, has not just built affordable electric three-wheelers but also helped facilitate the infrastructure and policy necessary for them to take off. Another finalist, the Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance, or ZEMBA for short, has sought to coordinate demand for low-carbon shipping fuel from customers that ship goods. And Yellowstone to Yukon restores habitat corridors across North America, which then unlocks feedbacks that restore the underlying ecological ecosystem.
The concept of climate tipping points entered the vernacular nearly two decades ago to describe some of the most alarming risks posed by climate change. At the time, tipping points referred to the thresholds that, when crossed, would trigger a chain reaction of often irreversible damage—think of Antarctic ice sheet collapse leading to sea level rise or the destruction of the Amazon releasing stored carbon dioxide.
More recently, scientists have sought to reframe tipping points, showing that positive developments can have tipping points, too. Cheap energy leads to a rewiring of economies. Social movements unlock widespread policy changes. “The tipping point is where you have strong amplification within the system,” says Tim Lenton, a professor of the University of Exeter who has written seminal papers on the tipping points concept.
The reframe comes at an important moment for the climate narrative. With increasingly bleak climate news, positive tipping points offer grounded optimism about how things may change. That was a key logic for Earthshot’s embrace of tipping points.
“We don’t think you can just leave people with the negatives and the warnings,” says Knauf. “We think we have a responsibility to show them” where positive action is possible.
But the positive tipping point framework is also useful from a capital allocation perspective. As companies cut costs and governments look for ways to trim public spending, tipping points offer a way to identify what Lenton describes as the best “bang for your buck” for climate investment dollars.
In some cases, that means supporting initiatives outside the typical wheelhouse of climate technology startups. ZEMBA, for example, works with the customers who would like to reduce their shipping footprint with low-carbon fuel but cannot afford to do so on their own, thereby helping create a demand signal. That’s a coordinated effort that competitors rarely engage in. “Once those markets are spinning, we will fade into the mist,” says Ingrid Irigoyen, the organization’s CEO.
Such an approach makes sense for governments evaluating how they spend their public dollars. It also makes sense for pension funds and institutional investors concerned with the long-term economic implications of climate change. With relatively few dollars, certain investments will generate a long-tail of positive climate outcomes.
In a future world where climate impact is an important investment metric, tipping points may be a useful tool. For those interested, the Earthshot finalists may offer a useful place to start.

Dolly Parton, Gloria Steinem, and Why Grieving a Celebrity Feels So Personal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Recently, the world has collectively mourned the unexpected losses of several well-known public figures, from Dolly Parton and Gloria Steinem to Bob Mackie and Tim Curry. Their deaths have hit fans, followers, and industry colleagues hard, and their tributes are going viral online.
Although these celebrities primarily appear to us on screen or on stage, many people feel as though they know them personally because of the meaningful impact they’ve had on their lives. These are known as parasocial relationships or “nonreciprocal social-emotional connections” with public figures and celebrities, per the journal of Current Opinion in Psychology.
When a public figure or celebrity dies, we grieve collectively. According to Gina Moffa, grief therapist and author of the book, Moving on Doesn’t Mean Letting Go, this happens when a large group of people mourns at the same time. “This can be felt even if they never knew the person or community, or weren’t directly affected by the event,” says Moffa. And it isn’t limited to the passing of public figures and celebrities. Many people also experienced shared loss after 9/11, Sandy Hook, COVID-19, and the Nepal floods.
In this current cultural moment, we’re seeing collective grief intersect with a psychological phenomenon called parasocial grief. According to psychotherapist and NYU adjunct professor Olivia Verhulst, this can occur when there’s a one-sided sense of familiarity with a public figure after they die. “Relationships don’t need to be reciprocal for feelings to be real,” Verhulst says. “Loss brings up a lot for all of us no matter what form it takes, whether it’s shock, disbelief, or confrontation with our own mortality.”
A small study in 2025 from the journal Acta Psychologica found that parasocial grief can negatively impact mental health and can lead to unhealthy coping mechanisms like substance use.
In comparison with individual grief, shared bereavement is more diffuse. “It doesn’t have the built-in rituals we rely on, like experiences of a funeral and traditional closure,” Moffa explains. Therefore, when celebrities or public figures die, it’s now common practice to post online and engage in comments sections with other grievers. In this way, the comment sections become public memorials.
After Steinem’s passing, people expressed their gratitude and heartbreak by leaving flowers and cards outside her home. When Parton died, fans held up their iPhones with the flashlight on during Harry Styles concert at Madison Square Garden while her song, “I Will Always Love You,” played. Both of these in-person tributes circulated on social media and were widely shared.
Verhulst argues that the most significant difference in mutual sorrow is its “being witnessed” and it can offer more validation than individualized grief. “Given that human beings are fundamentally wired for connection, this broader sense of communal loss can feel comforting in many ways,” she says.
Shared bereavement isn’t a new idea; it dates back for centuries. Some of the most visible representations in recent decades have been the outpouring of support after the deaths of President John F. Kennedy, the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., and Princess Diana. At her funeral, there were an estimated one million people in-person and roughly 2.5 billion viewers who watched it on television.
Society often pushes individual grievers to move on from their losses, rushing them to heal before they’re ready, which can lead to more people struggling alone. But in our current culture, shared bereavement has become more widely accepted. “Social media has become a kind of ‘modern funeral,’ a space where people can come together online, without the barriers of physical geography getting in the way,” Moffa says. “For a lot of people, it’s become the primary place mourning happens now.”
Research has found grieving together is more beneficial than doing it without help. A meta-review from 2022 in the journal Frontiers in Psychology discusses the theory of collective effervescence, a phrase coined by sociologist Émilie Durkheim, as it relates to mourning practices, public memorials, and communal storytelling like after the loss of a public figure. This “intense state of shared emotional activation and sense of unity” can help people feel connected in the long term to others who understand their pain.
“When Steinem and Parton passed within days of each other, comment sections turned into genuine gathering places, telling each other how these women shaped their lives. It made the feeling less isolating and more like something they were carrying alongside a whole community instead of alone,” Moffa says.
Working with a therapist, especially for cognitive behavioral therapy, can also be effective. Treatment can give people a safe space to talk about discomfort and divulge feelings of loss over someone they didn’t know personally, with validation and without shame. It can provide more insight into a person’s emotional state, to see if there’s any unresolved or prolonged grief.
Integration is another useful method. Moffa suggests creating a small ritual in honor of that person, like playing their music, reading their books, or rewatching a favorite video clip. Then, write down what that person meant to you, rather than what they meant to the world, and talk about it with someone. “This can provide validation and connection, instead of having to carry it alone,” she adds. In fact, a recent study from the Death Studies journal in 2026 found sharing emotions, ceremonies, and rituals offer “sense making, solidarity and healing” in shared mourning.
While these are effective ways to navigate the pain, they aren’t the only ones. It’s key to adapt them to meet your needs and determine what works for you.
Verhulst noted there’s an outdated idea that grief occurs in fixed stages which is somehow linear. But, she says, there are truly no universal stages to heal from loss and no right way to grieve.
Sometimes, the best way to mourn is together.

It Still Feels Like Summer in Parts of the US. Blame El Niño
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

A summer that started early across the US has no intention of quitting, even as the calendar turns to autumn.
The culprits? El Niño and climate change, which contributed to this summer’s record-breaking warmth and are delaying pumpkin spice season.
Forecasters with the US Climate Prediction Center continue to see increased odds for hotter-than-normal temperatures across much of the country through at least the end of September.
Computer models show a pronounced ridge pattern, an atmospheric arrangement that can lock in sustained spells of warmer-than-normal conditions. This setup will feature widespread unseasonable warmth throughout the country, a pattern consistent with a strong El Niño. The greatest odds of above-normal temperatures exist around the Upper Midwest and the Deep South. Some models suggest temperatures could run 5 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit above normal for the latter half of September.
The blast of unseasonably warm air comes after the hottest summer in US history in a year in which tens of thousands of heat records have fallen across the US. That includes nearly 44,000 record daytime highs and more than 53,000 record-high overnight minimum temperatures recorded at weather stations across the country. Thousands more monthly and all-time heat records have fallen since the start of 2026. Over the same period of time, only about 21,500 low-temperature records fell, or around one cold record for every four heat records.
Many of the busted records date back more than a century. Salt Lake City hit 109 degrees Fahrenheit on July 12, for example, marking its hottest-ever temperature since records began in 1874. Washington, DC, tied its all-time warmest overnight low of 84 degrees Fahrenheit on July 3, where daily observations date back to 1871.
The heat hasn’t relented, despite the calendar turning to September. Even areas that typically escape countrywide heat waves have suffered. Much of Southern California endured excessive heat warnings during the second week of September as hot conditions and soupy air made Rodeo Drive feel more like Bourbon Street.
Why Has Fall Started So Hot?
Climate change is far and away the primary driver of the extreme heat baking the US. Rising average temperatures raise the baseline for extreme heat, making very hot days even steamier now than they would’ve been just a few decades ago.
That trend has been especially notable at night: Many communities across the country have also seen a precipitous increase in overnight temperatures during the warm months as both temperatures and mugginess increase. The lack of relief is what makes heat waves particularly deadly; without beneficial overnight cooling, heat stress becomes too much for many people to withstand.
A warmer climate is also altering upper-level patterns in a way that’s more favorable to extreme heat events. Strong centers of high pressure aloft force air to sink toward the ground. This air heats up as it compresses, combining with intense sunshine and dry soils to ratchet the heat well above normal. These ridges, often called heat domes, are more common in a warming world.
When Will the Heat End?
While overall highs for the remainder of September won’t be as extreme as they are in July, many areas will continue to endure summer-like heat.
El Niño is also lurking in the background. This pattern of warmer-than-normal waters in the Pacific Ocean affects weather patterns around the world.
We typically feel El Niño’s greatest effects during the cold months as these abnormally warm ocean temperatures alter the jet stream, which are responsible for weather patterns during the autumn and winter months.
This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be a record-setting event. Each El Niño is different, but the patterns during previous strong El Niños suggest that a vast swath of the US is in for overall warmer-than-normal temperatures through the fall and winter. In other words, we’re likely not done breaking heat records yet this year.
