Arrests and Court Appearances Heighten Political Tensions in the Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:21:00 UTC
17:21:00 KST

Philippine politics was anything but dull in the past two weeks.
During this time, an arrest warrant was issued against Vice President Sara Duterte, who immediately posted bail and called for the resignation of her erstwhile ally, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez was arrested for plunder while recovering in a hospital before being transferred to a regular jail facility.
And lastly, former President Rodrigo Duterte made his first trial in-court appearance after more than a year of being under the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC).
These high-profile events will continue to unfold and affect not just the Marcos presidency but also the narratives of the 2028 elections.
Sara Duterte’s arrest warrant was issued in relation to the grave threats complaint filed against her after she said in an online video in late 2024 that she hired someone to kill Marcos and his wife. She posted bail to avoid arrest and called out Marcos for being ungrateful and betraying those who voted for him.
Duterte minced no words against Marcos in a speech delivered in front of her supporters outside a local court: “You’re a liar, abusive. He has no debt of gratitude to our people and everyone who went to the precincts to put him in power. He has no shame.”
The case is distinct from the current impeachment trial against Duterte, although the first article presented by the prosecution also related to the threats made by the vice president against the First Family.
After the drama surrounding Duterte’s posting of bail, an anti-graft court ordered the arrest of Romualdez in connection with his role in the flood control kickback scandal. The arrest was cited by Palace supporters as proof that Marcos is seriously pursuing accountability, since Romualdez is his close ally and first cousin. Romualdez spent a few days in the hospital before being placed in a regular prison cell.
The arrest was also seen as a move to counter the claim of Duterte’s camp that the vice president, her family, and allies were being unfairly targeted by the Marcos government.
It was also timed a few weeks before the first anniversary of the massive anti-corruption protests that demanded accountability against all those implicated in the flood control controversy.
Arresting Romualdez was therefore a political necessity for Marcos to dispute the allegations that he was persecuting the Dutertes, boost the credibility of his government’s anti-corruption drive, and assure the public that there’s no let-up in pursuing cases against corrupt officials.
As a former House speaker, Romualdez was the highest official tagged in the corruption scandal. It could ease the pressure on Marcos, who is also accused of masterminding the anomalous budget insertions. It could divert attention toward Romualdez and his accomplices in Congress, and weaken the clamor to scrutinize the culpability of Marcos and other Palace officials in the rollout of corruption-tainted pork barrel projects.
Meanwhile, Duterte’s appearance at the ICC coincided with the presentation of evidence concerning his daughter’s alleged unexplained wealth in the ongoing impeachment trial.
What are the political implications of Sara Duterte’s case, Romualdez’s arrest, and Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC appearance?
Sara Duterte’s fiery speech after posting bail may be intended to consolidate her base, portray herself and her family as victims of political persecution, and enhance the prospects of her presidential candidacy. On the other hand, the case reflects their eroded political influence and signals to senator-judges sitting in the impeachment trial that the Marcos government is mobilizing all remedies to remove the vice president from her position.
Romualdez appears to be the Marcos government’s sacrificial lamb amid the continuing uproar against the unresolved corruption mess. Public vigilance is crucial to reverse the impunity that has plagued the country’s political system. A former Cabinet member of Marcos who was also charged with plunder was recently released after agreeing to be a witness. Imelda Marcos, the president’s mother, was acquitted this month by the Supreme Court in a 1991 case involving a portion of their alleged ill-gotten wealth. This is the reason why Romualdez’s arrest could not totally appease the public, who have become skeptical about the real agenda behind the decision to finally charge the president’s first cousin with a non-bailable plunder complaint.
Rodrigo Duterte’s surprise appearance at the ICC, after months of waving his right to attend the trial, has agitated his loyal following and could strengthen his family’s clout. But it also made it clear that he is finally being held to account for the bloody “war on drugs” during his term.
The recent political developments should not be reduced to a mere maneuver among political factions competing for dominance ahead of the 2028 elections. Marcos is evading accountability and desperately denying his lame duck status. Sara Duterte wants to survive the crisis that she herself created, but could not muster enough political support to hit back at Marcos. It is the people speaking out against corruption and protesting in the flooded communities that could sway the political balance and determine how the Marcos presidency will end in 2028. This is the crowd that embodied the anger against the corrupt budget system and demanded an end to political dynasties. They are not easily swayed by spectacles staged by political parties, and they can certainly make Philippine politics more interesting in the lead-up to the 2028 elections and beyond.

Could the EU Kids Act unwittingly widen the transatlantic AI divide?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:19:10 UTC
17:19:10 KST

Europe must prepare for the potential consequences of implementing further digital rules that could make it more difficult for smaller European developers to compete, warns an industry insider.
Brussels wants to shield children from Big Tech. It may end up handing Silicon Valley an even bigger competitive edge.
The EU Kids Act, unveiled this week, promises age limits, parental controls and a crackdown on the "addictive" features baked into social media, video platforms and AI chatbots alike.
But as the bloc moves to police the tech giants, a harder question looms: can Europe regulate its way to child safety without regulating itself out of the AI race it is already losing?
The stakes could hardly be higher. Europe has just one significant AI company to speak of, Mistral, dwarfed by its US rivals OpenAI and Anthropic in both valuation and investment.
The bloc has never really left the starting blocks when it comes to scaling digital platforms to rival America's, relying instead on the strength of its single market and its power to regulate.
Now, as AI becomes the defining technology of the decade, that trade-off — rules versus growth — is seen as a "make or break" moment for the bloc.
What the Kids Act actually proposes
The legislation includes a number of measures aimed at protecting children online, including age restrictions, parental controls and limits on potentially addictive features.
The proposals have been welcomed by some in the tech industry, but Stanislas Marchand, a former mobile gaming lead at French unicorn Voodoo, says Europe must also consider the potential consequences for its own digital sector.
He argues that Europe "must prepare for the potential consequences by investing more urgently than ever in its homegrown AI capabilities".
The European Commission's proposals come amid growing pressure on governments to protect children from the risks posed by social media and other online platforms.
In the last couple of years, though, Big Tech has come under increasing scrutiny for its failure to protect children online, from cyberbullying, harassment and grooming to exploitation, extortion and misinformation.
Australia famously implemented the world's first social media ban for under-16s in December last year, a move that was watched keenly by governments around the world, prompting many to follow suit in implementing their own bans or exploring the possibility of doing so.
France, Greece, Austria, Denmark, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Germany, Poland and the Netherlands have all been considering or advancing national legislation on social media bans, piling pressure on Brussels to present an EU-wide measure and avoid fragmentation.
Meanwhile in the US this year, social media companies have faced and lost landmark liability cases, with many choosing to settle instead — such as Meta's recent $17bn (€14.9bn) deal to end a lawsuit brought by 47 US states.
Beyond social media
The EU Kids Act calls for a total, blanket social media ban for under-13s, while those up to 15 years old would be able to make "mini accounts" — limited, highly supervised profiles linked to a parent's profile.
Not only that, these accounts would also come with mandatory one-hour daily limits and a complete ban on "toxic or addictive features" like infinite scroll, endless autoplay and engagement rewards.
Marchand welcomed the proposed ban for under-13s, but said the proposal "should have been extended to everyone under 16" rather than permitting mini accounts for teens.
He argues the message from the Commission should have been that the platforms in question are "unsuitable for children" because they are "engineered to maximise attention".
The Kids Act goes well beyond social media.
It encompasses video-sharing platforms such as YouTube and Twitch, online video games like Roblox, Fortnite and Minecraft, and more recent entrants like AI chatbots and companions such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.
It would also require app stores and operating systems to integrate strict age-assurance filters to prevent underage users from downloading restricted apps and software in the first place.
And implementation, for Marchand, is where the problem lies, because the EU is asking platforms to "verify children's ages, operate parent-controlled accounts, enforce daily limits, restrict contacts and features, and prove that the resulting product is safe."
These requirements altogether could increase the cost and complexity of launching a product in Europe.
"Every one of those responsibilities creates another potential point of failure, and history gives us little reason to trust social media companies to execute them properly."
That concern is particularly relevant given that Europe's digital sector is dominated by American firms, and the continent has somewhat failed to make sure Big Tech follows the rules.
Meta has been fined twice for illegally transferring European user data to US servers, breaching GDPR in 2023 and the Digital Markets Act in 2025.
TikTok was fined €530m last year for failing to protect children's data and illegally transferring it to Chinese servers.
Elon Musk's X, which has had the most acrimonious relationship with EU lawmakers, was fined €120m last December over its deceptive "blue checkmark" verification and for denying researchers access to data.
Google, too, has been fined repeatedly for breaching antitrust rules, amounting to €10.38bn so far.
A patchy enforcement record
All of these fines are pocket change for Big Tech, and with the arrival of potentially even larger firms in the shape of AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic — again based in the US — it could become even more difficult for Europe to shape and enforce its own digital rules.
Marchand fears the Act could also make the EU a less attractive market to launch new products, while doing little to support European alternatives.
"If the Kids Act requires separate European products and costly ongoing assessments, US labs may delay launches here while smaller European developers struggle to compete," he warns.
He also points out that frontier AI companies already face enormous computing costs and uncertain paths to profitability, while some advanced Anthropic models have already been restricted outside the US and withheld from the UK's AI Security Institute.
For Marchand, the result could be an unintended consequence of the EU's attempt to protect children online.
"My feeling is this will further add to the transatlantic AI divide."

The body is in police custody, and the panchanama and post-mortem proceedings are underway," police told PTI videos.Koli's death comes less than a year after the Supreme Court acquitted him in the final case connected to the Nithari killings and ordered his immediate release in November 2025. He had spent nearly two decades in prison after being arrested in connection with the disappearance and killings of children and young women in Noida.Koli, who was 30 when arrested in 2006, had worked as a domestic help at the Noida home of businessman Moninder Singh Pandher. He was convicted in multiple cases and awarded several death sentences before the convictions were overturned in subsequent appeals.
The Supreme Court's final acquittal brought an end to the criminal cases against him related to Nithari.
What happened in Nithari
The Nithari killings came to light in December 2006 after human skeletal remains were found in a drain near bungalow D-5 in Sector 31, Noida, which belonged to Pandher. The discovery followed months of complaints over missing children and young women from the area.s in the 12 cases in 2025. In November that year, it also allowed his curative petition in the final pending cThe recovery of skulls and bones triggered nationwide outrage and led to the arrest of Koli and Pandher. The case was subsequently transferred from the Uttar Pradesh Police to the CBI amid criticism of the initial investigation. CBI searches around the bungalow and adjoining areas led to the recovery of further human remains.Koli was eventually convicted in 13 cases by the trial court. However, the legal case against him unravelled over the years. In October 2023, the Allahabad High Court acquitted Koli in 12 cases and Pandher in two, citing serious shortcomings in the investigation and questioning the reliability of crucial evidence, including Koli's confession.
The Supreme Court upheld Koli's acquittal, setting aside his conviction and ordering his release. The court held that the evidentiary basis for the conviction could not stand after the same evidence had been rejected in the other cases.Pandher, meanwhile, was released from prison in October 2023 after his acquittal.

Burnham urged by opposition parties to follow Macron and act with more urgency on Russian threat
The French president, Emmanuel Macron said today that the threat posed by Russia’s shadow operations was growing across Europe, and he had ordered measures to protect France’s critical infrastructure from increasing Russian “hybrid attacks”, AFP reports. AFP says:
“The Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified,” he said after a meeting with French political leaders, before he heads to the UN General Assembly next week.
France’s interior minister had met regional prefects to step up “vigilance in response to the Russian hybrid attacks”, Macron said after the meeting with presidential hopefuls and party leaders ahead of next year’s election.
He said he had ordered “the government to prepare a plan to protect our critical infrastructure” and the “most sensitive” defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyber-attacks.
The French president said that despite the Russian threats France would continue to support Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion of the pro-Western country in February 2022.
He also vowed that France would respond to Russia’s shadow attacks.
“This will not go unanswered,” Macron said, without elaborating.
“The intention behind it is to intimidate us and to derail the effort to support the Ukrainians. The consequence will be the opposite,” he added.

Social care review chief Louise Casey says she is opposed to 'profiteering' by privately-run homes
Louise Casey, the crossbench peer and former Whitehall official leading the government’s review of adult social care, has said she is opposed to what she calls “profiteering” in the case sector.
In an interview with ITV News, Casey said that she thought that allowing large parts of adult social care to be run by private companies for profit was a “mistake”.
She told ITV:
What I would just personally object to on behalf of the taxpayer is what I call profiteering.
You’ve got, in some cases, I would say profiteering on the back of taxpayers and specifically on the back of people with higher levels of need. Where I think people are making bag loads of money, I think that’s wrong.
If you look back to the history of what we now call social care, we saw a massive shift in the 1980s. Essentially, the sort of outsourcing of all of that [care] to the private sector, without it being organised and managed, I think was probably a mistake.
Casey suggested she was particularly opposed to foreign-based private equity companies making huge profits from the UK care sector. She said:
I’m a great believer in not letting other people take British taxpayers money, whoever they are. And I think if we could provide those services and those resources here, then we should do it …
If there’s a private provider that’s taking 12 or 15% profit out of running care services for people, is that a good use of how we would plan for the next decade, when actually lots of FTSE 100 companies are very happy to take 5% profit? So these are the things we need to look at.
But Casey also suggested she would be wary of sudden changes to the system.
I think at the moment though, I would say one ought to be a bit careful because a lot of those companies, if you pulled them, the lifeline for the people we’ve met the same afternoon would stop. So you’ve just got to be really measured.
Casey is due to present her final report to the government next year. Andy Burnham has said that, for him, reforming adult social care is a priority, and he is prepared to use a lot of poltical capital pushing through change.
Most of the public discussion about adult social care focuses on the needs of people with dementia. But it is also a lifeline for adults with learning disabilities and Casey focused on this in her interview with ITV News, which has run a series of investigations into how public services look after people in this category.
Casey said she thought the NHS was failing people with learning disabilities and hospitals and that was why people with a learning disability have a life expectancy more than 20 years shorter than the average.
She told ITV:
I think that the National Health Service, particularly hospitals, are unable to sufficiently treat and look after people with learning disabilities,.
[There was] a case very recently of a woman who was 70 and had a stroke.
She had profound learning disabilities, ended up at a general ward, and they wouldn’t let her carers come into the ward, and her carers were the only people that could probably fully understand what she was saying and thinking.
Now people watching this tonight on the news will think, well, that’s insane, isn’t it? It’s almost hard to explain how the system just does that.
It’s like it’s got a one-track mind: it’s a medical condition, if I can’t medically treat you, it’s game over, not our responsibility anymore.

Crypto millionaires would gain £500m over 5 years from Reform UK's crypto tax cuts, Labour analysis says
The Labour party has released an analysis suggesting that cryptocurrency millionaires could benefit to the tune of around £500m from Reform UK policies over the course of a parliament.
It is based on proposals in a bill published by Reform UK last year, and new figures published by HM Revenue and Customs about the number of Britons making large profits from cryptocurrency.
Last weekend it was announced that two cryptocurrency billionaires, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, have given £72m (£36m each) to Reform UK. These donations dwarf previous record donations to British political parties – although legislation going through parliament about residency requirements for donors may result in the donations being deemed impermissible.
Reform UK insists that Delo and Harborne have not asked for anything in return for their donations, and it says they are just contributing out of a sense of patriotic duty to a party they believe will rescue the UK.
But it has been noted that a sharp rise in crypto donations to the party in recent years has coincided with Nigel Farage and his colleagues showing increasing interest in policies that would help the sector grow.
One example came last year when the party published a cryptoassets and digital finance bill. At the time it was the only draft legislation published by the party, suggesting policy in this area was more advanced than in others.
The bill proposes cutting capital gains tax on crypto investments to 10%, and this has allowed Labour to calculate that crypto millionaires could gain a total of around £500m over the course of a parliament.
The calculation is based on figures released in August by HM Revenue and Customssaying that “240 people reported more than £1m in capital gains from cryptoassets in the 2024 to 2025 tax year … accounting for £717m of cryptoasset gains between them.”
Explaining its figures in a briefing, Labour said:
Reform’s policy on crypto includes cutting capital gains tax (CGT) on crypto assets from the current level of 24% (for higher-rate taxpayers) and 18% (for basic-rate taxpayers) to a flat 10%.
Analysis of this policy shows that most of Reform’s tax giveaways would go to a very small high-earning group, after official HMRC statistics published last month found that 240 people in 2024/25 reported more than £1m in capital gains from crypto assets.
The HMRC stats show that this tiny group of crypto millionaires made £717m of the total £1.38bn crypto asset gains – reported by 17,600 people – in 2024/25.
The high-earning group of crypto investors could save around £100m a year in total under Reform’s policy. That means a tax cut worth half a billion pounds going to just 240 millionaires over the course of the next parliament.
A Labour spokesperson said:
Farage and Reform are drowning in sleaze and scandal. They can’t buy their way out of the questions that the public need answers to. It’s clear Reform are on the side of a handful of crypto-billionaires, while Labour is delivering the change people across the country want to see.
In response, Reform UK said it was the only party with a plan for crypto. A Reform UK spokesperson said:
Reform UK are the only party calling for proper regulation of cryptocurrency and ensuring that consumers are protected. Labour and the Tories don’t even have a plan.

The two leaders began by reaffirming the close partnership between the UK and Ireland, as well as their shared commitment to upholding the Good Friday agreement.
They next discussed the importance of their joint commitments to addressing the legacy of the Troubles and working towards lasting reconciliation in Northern Ireland.
The prime minister then underlined the UK’s desire to work closely with Ireland during its presidency of the European Union as the UK seeks a closer relationship with Europe.

Reform UK says it would intensify immigration checks on coaches and trains travelling from Ireland into Northern Ireland
Tonight the DUP is starting its annual conference in Belfast. One speaker will be Danny Kruger, the Reform UK MP in charge of the party’s plans for government. He has announced that Reform UK would intensify immigration checks on coaches, buses and trains travelling from Ireland into Northern Ireland.
In his speech, Kruger is expected to say:
Illegal and unvetted dangerous criminals, who cross into Northern Ireland, are abusing the soft Irish border, using it as a backdoor route into the UK. The absence of checkpoints at the border does not remove the requirement to have a right to enter.
Almost all illegal movement from the Republic into Northern Ireland is by scheduled coach or train, arriving at a handful of terminals. We will impose a civil penalty of £10,000 per passenger on any bus or rail operator for each illegal immigrant transported into Northern Ireland.
Reform UK says the checks would be carried by immigration enforcement officers and they would happen at terminals, not at the border crossing. In his speech, Kruger will insist that what he is proposing is “not a border check”. Reform UK says the Irish government already carries out immigration checks on vehicles on north-south transit routes but it claims these are “grossly insufficient”.
Disabled people in UK need right to travel abroad, say MPs, after ‘ridiculous’ restrictions
Disabled people must have a guaranteed right to travel abroad, MPs and peers have said, as further cases emerged of individuals barred from taking holidays as a result of “ridiculous” rules imposed by local NHS care boards and local councils, Frances Ryan and Patrick Butler report.
Kemi Badenoch says the Tories might take the government to court to stop council tax in Wandsworth having to almost double. (See 10.16am.)
But why is it going up so much?
In part, it is because it has always been so low for a long time. Wandsworth currently has the lowest council tax in England, at £509.84 for a band D home, plus a £510.51 precept set by the Greater London Authority.
In a blog about its funding situation this week, Wandsworth Conservatives say “a major factor behind the financial pressure is the Labour government’s decision to cut Wandsworth’s government funding by 40%”. Other factors are relevant too. They illustrated them with this chart.
The review updated and replaced the formulas that are used to assess each local authority’s level of relative need for funding, and which had last been updated in 2012/13. The new formulas take into account various socio-economic indicators such as deprivation, numbers of benefits claimants, and population (both resident and daytime).
The level of need, as assessed by these formulas, was then adjusted to take account of two things:
-the cost of delivering services in each area (using things like the costs of labour and of property, and travel times) – this was called the area costs adjustment;
-the resources that local authorities had available in the form of council tax; councils which charged less than the average level of council tax had their assessed level of need adjusted downwards, on the theory that they could raise their council tax to compensate for reduced central government funding. This was called the resource adjustment.
Tories argue that this means Wandsworth is now being penalised for the fact that it has been fiscally prudent in the past. Labour argues that this is just a matter of the system becoming fairer.
One government figure pointed to Wandsworth’s £194m of reserves. “For too long, an outdated council funding system, based on decades-old data, has entrenched inequality, leaving councils on a cliff edge and communities in deprived areas facing service cuts and rising bills, while some councils in less deprived areas have benefited disproportionately, building up their reserves.”
Labour has long argued that Wandsworth’s low rates were enabled by the decision of John Major’s Conservative government to bake in higher central government grants when it created council tax in 1993 to allow them to continue to hold it up as an exemplar.
They also quote Kate Ogden of the Institute for Fiscal Studies as saying the previous council funding formula was “arbitrary and quite hard to defend”. Residents in areas like Wandsworth would now have to accept that lower council tax “comes with consequences for public services”, she said.
Although Badenoch has described the cuts to funding in Wandsworth as “outrageous”, she seems to have glossed over the fact that, even with council tax going up 94%, residents will still be paying less then their counterparts in other London boroughs.
The Wandsworth Conservatives admit this. In their blog post, they say:
Under the proposals, the average band D council tax charge would increase by £958, taking the average total bill, including the amount paid to the Mayor of London, to £1,978. This represents an increase of 94% on today’s total bill …
Wandsworth currently has the lowest council tax in the country, with a band D property paying £1,020. Even with the proposed increase, Wandsworth would remain significantly cheaper than neighbouring boroughs including Lambeth and Merton, where current Band D charges are £2,047.11 and £2,146.76 respectively.

17:14:24 KST

Alison Sargent is pleased to welcome Grégoire Roos, Director of the Europe and Russia and Eurasia Programmes at Chatham House. According to Roos, Russia’s parliamentary election is revealing because of what the electoral process can still tell us about the political system Vladimir Putin has constructed. In the absence of any meaningful competition, and anti-war opposition excluded, Roos argues that the most revealing signals may lie elsewhere: in turnout, the timing of voting, the performance of the remaining parties, and the Kremlin’s effort to frame participation itself as evidence of national unity.

Nvidia expects to double chip sales next year, CEO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:12:35 UTC
17:12:35 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
US chipmaker Nvidia expects to sell twice as many chips next year as it does this year, CEO Jensen Huang said Thursday, citing strong artificial intelligence demand across industries and economies.
“I expect Nvidia to sell twice as many chips next year as we do this year,” Huang told reporters ahead of an AI summit with Britain’s King Charles III in Scotland.
“The reason for that is because AI has so much contribution to the benefits of different industries, different economies, and you can see that in almost every single country that we’re in, people want to invest in AI,” he said.
The forecast signals continued rapid expansion at the semiconductor giant over the coming six quarters. Nvidia recently projected revenue growth of 70% for the fiscal year ending in January 2028, potentially bringing its annual revenue to about $673 billion.
The company does not disclose the total number of chips it sells. Its best-known products are data center graphics processing units, including its Blackwell and Rubin chips, which power the development and operation of advanced AI systems.
Huang said last year that Nvidia had shipped 6 million Blackwell GPUs over four quarters.
Beyond GPUs, Nvidia produces central processing units, networking switches, optical networking chips, laptop processors, Jetson systems for robots and vehicles, and the processor used in Nintendo’s Switch 2 console.
Huang attended the summit alongside representatives from Google DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic to discuss AI safety amid growing concerns about the risks posed by increasingly advanced models.
“When a product is not safe, we should hold it back and keep engineering it,” Huang said.

Prévot: Belgium preparing to be observer member of Arctic Council
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:12:20 UTC
17:12:20 KST

Belgium is preparing to become an observer of the Arctic Council, Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot said during a visit to Iceland with his Benelux counterparts.
The intergovernmental forum comprises eight countries with territory in the Arctic: Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden and the US. Belgium is finalising the administrative and diplomatic process to join as an observer state.
Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands, the UK and Japan are among the existing observers. They do not have voting rights but are invited to participate in working groups on issues such as climate and pollution monitoring, protection of the marine environment, biodiversity, emergencies and sustainable development.
What happens in the North Atlantic has a direct impact on European security
“Climate change is transforming this region. People here are the first to feel its effects, but the consequences affect us all,” says Prévot, of Les Engagés. “The same applies to our economy and security. Our ports depend on safe maritime routes. Europe needs secure energy and data connections and reliable access to critical raw materials. And what happens in the North Atlantic has a direct impact on European security.”
Topics on the agenda during Prévot’s visit to Norway and Iceland this week include energy, hybrid threats, defence, European strategic autonomy and relations with two of the EU’s closest partners.
Europe “has a great deal to learn from Iceland”, he said, and Belgium contributes through polar research, maritime expertise and technology. “We share fundamental interests: ensuring that international law and international cooperation remain central to the Arctic, now that its strategic importance is growing.”
He added that Iceland remained part of the European family, even though the country voted against resuming accession negotiations with the EU at the end of August.
“We respect that choice and we will continue to reach out a hand,” he said. “For us, the solution lies in investing further in our partnership: listening to sensitivities, explaining more clearly what we are doing together and demonstrating that our cooperation can deliver results.”

====================================================================================================

Portuguese prime minister outlines plan to tackle rising cost of living, keeps VAT unchanged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:12:09 UTC
17:12:09 KST

Luís Montenegro says the current situation could drag on for some time. But, unlike other European countries, he will not lower the consumption tax.
"Here I am, putting myself on the line," said the Portuguese prime minister, Luís Montenegro, in a televised address to the nation on Thursday night. Timed for the main evening news bulletins, the speech was used to set out the measures against the cost of living, in particular those triggered by rising fuel prices.
Some elements of the plan were already known. This is the case of the pension bonus and the cut to personal income tax (IRS) bands, announced last week in Parliament when the government survived a no-confidence motion. But they have now been formally approved by the Council of Ministers.
Montenegro explained how the pension bonus will be applied: 200 euros for pensions up to 537 euros; 150 euros for pensions up to 1,704 euros and 100 euros for pensions up to 1,611 euros. The amount will be paid in December.
The Council of Ministers also approved a reduction in six IRS bands, with the remaining bands also affected because of the tax’s progressive nature. According to Montenegro, this measure is aimed above all at "middle-class households".
At the same time, the government’s portal published the table of IRS withholdings, with simulations, (source in Portuguese) but this is still a draft law that must be approved by the Assembly of the Republic.
On fuel price increases, the main strategy will continue to be the discount on the tax on petroleum products (ISP). Montenegro says this discount will remain in place until the end of the year, amounting to a total reduction of around 1.3 billion euros.
The prime minister also said that this discount "will probably rise to 25 cents as early as next week", from the current 23 cents, in anticipation of further increases in fuel prices.
The government will also once again support the sectors most exposed to rising fuel costs, with a total package of 38 million euros. This support covers taxis, freight transport, social solidarity institutions, firefighters’ associations and farmers. The solidarity bottled gas scheme will also remain in place.
The package also includes extending the green rail pass to the urban areas of Lisbon and Porto. The pass, costing 20 euros a month, allows travel on all rail lines except the Alfa Pendular high-speed service.
Government steers clear of VAT
The speech also served for Luís Montenegro to spell out what he will not do: tamper with the consumption tax, VAT.
"I will not swap cutting VAT on some foodstuffs from 6% to zero for the 800 million euros we are returning to families through IRS and the pension supplement," said the Portuguese prime minister.
The measure has long been demanded by the Socialist Party (PS, centre-left) and by Chega (far right). This has also been the strategy in several European countries to tackle the rising cost of living.
"I have every respect for the choices of the opposition parties and for the choices of my fellow heads of government in the European Union," Montenegro said. "I will not trade our fiscal and financial policy for that of other countries, even those closest to us, such as Spain, France or Italy."
The Spanish case is particularly relevant for Portugal. Fuel is cheaper in Spain, prompting consumers in Portugal to cross the border to fill up.
To defend these choices, Montenegro repeatedly invoked the past during his address to the nation, referring to the international bailout programme the country was subjected to.
"Do not count on me, or on the government, for illusions today that come with a heavy price to pay tomorrow," he said.
Luís Montenegro also made it clear that "the situation may drag on". In the morning, at a conference, he had criticised what he called the "stupid" course of the conflict in the Middle East.

China, Philippines make conflicting claims over fresh vessel 'collision' in disputed South China Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:10:30 UTC
17:10:30 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Beijing and Manila on Friday issued conflicting claims over a fresh vessel "collision" in the disputed South China Sea, blaming each other, according to statements from the two sides.
The Chinese Coast Guard (CCG) said a Philippines vessel “ignored repeated warnings and suddenly cut across a CCG boat’s bow near Xianbin Jiao causing a collision,” Beijing-based daily Global Times reported.
Xianbin Jiao, also known as Escoda (Sabina) Shoal, is a disputed low-tide elevation atoll located in the Spratly Islands.
China accused the Philippines of being “fully responsible for the actions, which seriously violated international law and threatened the safety of CCG vessels.”
However, the Philippines Coast Guard (PCG) spokesperson Jay Tarriela said it was Chinese vessel CCG-21585 which “rammed BRP Datu Magat Salamat (MMOV 3015) … as it carried out its maritime patrol to deliver fuel subsidy to our fishermen.”
“Even after the collision, CCG-21585 conducted yet another dangerous maneuver, passing dead astern at a distance of only about 5 meters (16 feet),” he claimed in a statement posted on US social media company X.
Tarriela said the incident happened off the coast of the Philippine province of Palawan “well within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone.”
“Let us be clear about what this vessel was doing: it was bringing fuel to Filipino fishermen so they can keep fishing in our own waters and keep food on Filipino tables. The China Coast Guard deliberately rammed a civilian government vessel on a humanitarian and livelihood mission, endangering the lives of its Filipino crew,” he said.
However, the CCG urged the Philippine side to “stop all acts of infringement and provocation,” warning that Manila “would bear the consequences.”
The latest incident comes amid persistent tensions between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea, where the two countries have repeatedly confronted each other over competing territorial claims.

The latest attacks followed a broader Russian strike campaign that Ukrainian officials said killed and wounded civilians across the country on Thursday.
Moscow reports hundreds of Ukrainian drones
In Russia, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said more than 350 Ukrainian drones had headed towards the Moscow region, with most destroyed before reaching the capital and 64 intercepted as they approached Moscow.
Falling drone debris in the Rostov region damaged apartment buildings and private cars, regional Gov. Yury Slyusar said.
Russia’s defence ministry said its forces intercepted and destroyed 629 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over Russian territory, the Azov and Black Sea regions, and Ukraine’s Russian-occupied Crimea.
Claims from both sides could not be independently verified because of the ongoing war.

New Power Party Chair Claire Wang (王婉諭) suggested that the criminal record disclosure requirements for local council candidates could be expanded to include a new category, per Liberty Times.
TPP Chair Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) called on the legal system to remain even-handed, per Newtalk. He also suggested that reports involving figures aligned with the DPP appear to have received less attention at the prosecutors offices.
With Hsieh Tien-lin mired in legal trouble, his challenger for the speakership, Changhua County Council Deputy Speaker Hsu Yuan-lung (許原龍), confirmed that he would seek to replace Hsieh, per ETtoday. Hsu’s power base is in northern Changhua, where he has strong connections across party lines and a solid grassroots organization.
Political insiders also pointed out that with Hsieh Hsin-lung, widely considered the backbone of the family, detained, the political futures of Hsieh Tien-lin and his sister, KMT Legislator Hsieh Yi-fong (謝衣鳳), could also be affected, per Liberty Times. The DPP might also be able to challenge the KMT’s hold on the council’s speakership and deputy speakership, ending the party’s control of the two positions since the council’s establishment 75 years ago.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) said Friday that biotechnology could become another industry for which Taiwan is known globally, alongside semiconductors, CTEE reported.

She said part of a diplomat’s role is to promote the country’s achievements overseas. Those efforts depend on strong industries and competitive products supported by long-term strengths in technology and manufacturing, she said.
The vice president also said artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are changing drug development and healthcare. While debate continues over the benefits and risks of AI, Hsiao said innovation should ultimately lead to better treatments and improved quality of life for patients.
Hsiao said PharmaEssentia’s development reflected the broader progress of the biotechnology sector and expressed hope that more companies would continue to innovate and compete internationally.

====================================================================================================

How Looming US Sanctions Test India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:09:00 UTC
17:09:00 KST

On September 16, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act with a 262 to 159 vote. The U.S. Senate had passed the legislation on August 7 with an overwhelming majority, which means that the bill now awaits only presidential approval.
Named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine, who spearheaded negotiations on the bill with the White House, the bill effectively allows President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on exports to the U.S. from the top five purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas, making exceptions for countries that import less than 15 percent of their natural gas from Russia and are taking “significant” steps to reduce the imports. Additionally, the bill provides for a range of sanctions against Russian officials and Moscow’s shadow fleet of vessels.
Following the bill’s passage, Senator Richard Blumenthal publicly remarked that China and India “better clean up” their “act” and buy oil and gas “somewhere else.”
As of August 2026, India was the second largest buyer of Russian oil, behind only China, leaving the two Asian giants most exposed to potential U.S. tariffs. Between December 2022 and August 2026, China accounted for 50 percent of Russia’s total crude exports, while India accounted for 37 percent.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) was quick to issue a statement on the passage of the bill, stating that it had raised the issue with the U.S., highlighting its impact on “not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market.” It reiterated that New Delhi remains “committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people…..through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics.” It also reaffirmed India’s determination to take “all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests.”
The language and tone of India’s statement are notably different from its response last year, when Trump first announced “punitive” tariffs on Indian goods over Russian oil purchases on August 6, 2025. New Delhi had then explicitly called out Washington’s actions as “unjustified and unreasonable,” highlighting Western hypocrisy by pointing out that both the European Union and the U.S. continued trade with Russia. It also said that India would take all necessary measures to safeguard its “national interests and economic security,” linking the dispute with state sovereignty.
This time, the MEA dropped the word “national interest” entirely, focusing instead on “trade and economic interests.”
Rhetoric aside, the impact of Western scrutiny on New Delhi’s oil purchases is evident from the actions of major Indian refineries. By November 2025, India’s largest conglomerate, Reliance Industries, which owns the world’s largest and most complex oil refining hub in the world, announced that it would stop importing Russian crude oil for its exports. However, this proved to be short-lived as Reliance resumed buying Russian crude from December 2025.
State-controlled refineries such as Mangalore Refinery & Petrochemicals, Ltd., and HPCL-Mittal Energy Ltd also reportedly suspended Russian oil imports in the aftermath of the U.S. sanctions.
Meanwhile, in October 2025, India’s oil imports from the U.S. increased to 10.7 percent from around 3 percent earlier in 2025, while Russian oil imports decreased by 38 percent. By January 2026, India’s crude oil imports dropped to about 1.1 million barrels per day, down by 23.5 percent from December 2025 and by about a third compared to numbers from January 2025.
Correspondingly, the share of West Asian oil in India’s crude imports rose to 55 percent, its highest since late 2022, when India started buying Russian oil aggressively.
Such curbs proved to be short-lived as disruptions in West Asia, stemming from the U.S.-Israel war on Iran, created instability in energy supply chains in the region. Following a temporary U.S. waiver issued on March 5 this year — to allow the sale and delivery of sanctioned Russian oil which has already been loaded on vessels to India — India purchased around 30 million barrels of Russian crude. By July 2026, India’s imports of Russian crude reached a record high for the second consecutive month, rising by 2.1 percent month on month, 53 percent of which was transported by “shadow sanctions.” Global Trade Research Initiative data reveals that India bought $40.8 billion worth of Russian crude in FY 2026, accounting for 30.3 percent of its total crude imports.
In September 2026, amid the looming threat of U.S. tariffs, preliminary data suggests that Indian imports of Russian crude have already declined to about 30 percent lower than the August average of around 2.1 mbpd, according to data from trade intelligence firm, Kpler.
Historically, even when sanctions increased the logistical costs of shipping Russian oil, discounts offered by the Kremlin still made Russian crude commercially viable. Now, together with the looming threat of U.S. sanctions and narrowing discounts on Russian crude amid increasing Ukrainian attacks targeting refineries, New Delhi finds itself in a particularly difficult position.
Experts warn that replacing Russian crude with other suppliers will result in an increase in import bills, which would adversely impact the gross refining margins of the refining and marketing industry. This explains why many Indian refiners chose to return to purchasing Russian crude despite sanctions.
For New Delhi, caving in to the U.S. pressure will also have an adverse impact domestically and risk damaging ties with its “all-weather friend” Russia. As things currently stand, the only hope for New Delhi is pushing for the waiver option listed in the legislation, per which the President can waive the sanctions if it is “in the national interest of the United States.”
As talks with Washington over a free trade deal continue, New Delhi could potentially demand the waiver as part of the ongoing negotiations. Even if New Delhi is able to secure this waiver, it would only serve as a temporary fix. The real challenge lies in identifying India’s sources of external dependencies vis-à-vis energy security and addressing them by building state capacity.

Greece: Police bust gang using AI to clone relatives' voices for cash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:07:32 UTC
17:07:32 KST

According to the police, the organisation’s illegal proceeds from its activities are estimated to exceed 1 million euros.
A criminal organisation that used Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to clone the voices of relatives in order to make telephone scams more convincing has been dismantled by the Directorate for Combating Organised Crime.
The gang is alleged to have defrauded citizens using various pretexts, posing among other things as employees of the Hellenic Electricity Distribution Network Operator (HEDNO), mobile phone companies and fibre-optic service providers. They would then exploit voice-cloning technology to create the impression that a relative or other trusted person of the victim was on the line.
The organisation’s activities were brought to an end following a police operation by the Financial Crime Squad’s Sub-Directorate in Nea Ionia, Attica, where two of its members, aged 23 and 25, were arrested. The two suspects are believed to have acted as the gang’s "collectors" and were caught just after removing valuables worth around 30,000 euros from a home.
The case file for criminal organisation, fraud and aggravated theft also includes four more individuals, three of whom have already been identified. According to the police, the gang’s illegal gains are estimated to exceed 1 million euros.
How the AI scam worked
According to the investigation, the organisation had established clear roles, with "management" figures, "callers" and "collectors". Its operation is thought to have begun at least in early July 2026.
The "callers" searched for potential victims and contacted them using different pretexts. They usually convinced them that they had to take some action related to the installation of fibre optics or another supposedly technical procedure.
When a victim expressed doubts, the perpetrators urged them to get in touch with a relative or another trusted person, supposedly in order to confirm the process.
They then asked for the telephone number of that person and called them, pretending to represent a telecommunications company or another service provider.
During this brief conversation they recorded a sample of their voice. Using an Artificial Intelligence tool, they then created a cloned version of that voice.
The next step was to call the original victim again. This time, through voice-cloning technology, they reproduced the relative’s voice, creating the impression that this person was indeed on the other end of the line and was confirming what the scammers had previously claimed.
In this way, the perpetrators sought to dispel victims’ doubts and make the scam more convincing.
Five more incidents
So far, the gang’s involvement has been confirmed in five further cases using a similar modus operandi.
At the same time, the police investigation led to the solving of a vehicle theft reported on 14 September 2026, which, according to the findings, the organisation’s members were using as an "operational vehicle".
In total, the searches led to the seizure of a public-use vehicle and two mobile phones.
The two detainees were brought before the competent prosecutor and referred to the examining magistrate, while the investigation continues to determine the full extent of the criminal activity.
Police warn about scams using cloned voices
In light of this case, the Hellenic Police are renewing their warning about telephone scams in which perpetrators pose as employees of utilities, public services, telecommunications companies, banks or other organisations.
They place particular emphasis on the fact that recognising a familiar voice is no longer, in itself, a reliable way of confirming the caller’s identity, as the voice may have been technically manipulated or reproduced using AI.
Citizens are urged to:
- hang up immediately on suspicious phone calls,
- avoid disclosing personal or financial information,
- avoid giving details about who lives in their household or when they are away from home,
- call their relative or trusted person themselves, on a number they already know, in order to confirm the communication,
- use, wherever possible, a pre-agreed safety word or phrase,
- not open the door to strangers simply because someone has asked them to do so over the phone, even if the voice sounds like that of a relative,
- not hand over money or valuables and not place them in locations indicated to them over the phone,
- verify any scheduled work by contacting the competent organisation themselves, using its official telephone number,
- and inform the police and their relatives immediately about any suspicious call.
The police remind the public that no genuine technical inspection ever requires the handover of cash, jewellery or other valuables, nor disclosure of where such items are kept.
Special care is advised for elderly family members, as even a completely familiar voice on the phone may now have been created or reproduced using Artificial Intelligence technology.
In the event of a suspicious phone call or the presence of unknown persons at a home, citizens are urged to contact the Hellenic Police immediately on 100 or their local police station, keeping, where possible, the number from which the call was made and any other relevant information.

Personal information of nearly two million Quest Apartment Hotels customers has been compromised in a data breach, including credit card, passport and Medicare numbers.
Last month, the accommodation provider identified a cyberattack on a database system via a vulnerability in a third-party technology provider.
David Mansfield, the managing director of The Ascott Limited, which owns Quest Apartment Hotels, provided an update this week, saying a forensic data analysis revealed information relating to approximately 1,991,613 customers was affected.
The majority of information related to names and contacts, but also included:
- Vehicle registration numbers: 225,300
- Passport and/or driver licence numbers (the number only; no scanned copies of ID documents were affected): 104,268
- Credit card numbers (no CVV, including expired credit cards): 297,739
- Credit card numbers (with CVV, including expired credit cards): 46,727
- Date of birth: 3,328
- NDIS number (the number only; no scanned copies of cards or documents were affected): 271
- Medicare card number (the number only; no scanned copies of cards or documents were affected): 46
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
All the information relates to records from before June 2025.
Mansfield said the company was contacting those affected directly to inform them of which category they were in, the steps they could take, and available support.
"I recognise the concern this incident has caused. On behalf of Quest, I sincerely apologise to those who have been affected," he said.
Quest said it first identified an outage on its website on 17 August, with investigation revealing "a malicious attack" had exploited a vulnerability in a third-party service provider's software.
The company is advising customers to remain alert for suspicious emails, text messages and telephone calls, particularly communications requesting personal, financial or account information.
Quest said it was cooperating with the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian Cyber Security Centre and Victoria Police.
Last year's Annual Cyber Threat Report warned cyberattacks were a growing problem in Australia, with financial losses, ransomware attack frequency, and the number of reported data breaches all increasing.
After a major data breach involving millions of Optus customers in 2022, the federal government overhauled privacy laws, requiring companies to destroy or actively de-identify personal information as soon as it was no longer needed.
Incident raises data concerns
Paul Watters, chief executive of Cyberstronomy, which provides cyber risk expertise, said all businesses needed to have a clear understanding of the personal data they hold and why.
"Often, this is not the case," he told SBS News.
"Quest says all of the affected information came from records dating from before June 2025. That immediately raises a governance question: for each category of information, why was it still being retained?"
He said the incident could serve as a lesson for organisations.
"Audit your data holdings. Know what you have, where it is, why you are retaining it, how long you need it, and when it should be deleted or de-identified. Data you no longer hold cannot be stolen in a breach," he said.
Belinda Barnet, a Swinburne University data privacy expert, told SBS News the latest incident raised concerns about the type of data some companies were still retaining.
"Companies like Quest don't need to retain your passport after you've actually identified yourself," she said.
"We really need to have more public discussion about how [companies are] going to destroy information that's no longer needed."

Twenty women had their breasts removed unnecessarily while being treated for cancer at an NHS trust in north-east England.
The County Durham and Darlington foundation trust (CDDFT) told the BBC that the women were among hundreds of patients who came to harm during treatment at its breast unit.
The admission came after the BBC reported last year that more than 200 patients were found to have suffered harm at the CDDFT.
The broadcaster reported that the National Crime Agency was working with Durham police to investigate allegations by former patients and determine if any criminal offences had taken place.
Steve Russell, who was appointed chief executive of CDDFT last year, said: “We are deeply sorry to the women and families who have been harmed and let down by failings in our breast services.
“We recognise the profound impact this has had and have been clear that there were opportunities when, as a trust, we should have listened more carefully and acted sooner.
“Significant changes have since been made to the breast service and are bringing improvements for patients.
“Alongside this, the look-back continues to review past care, identify patients who may have experienced harm and make sure they receive appropriate information and support.
“On September 24, our trust board will meet in public to consider the future scope and timeframe of the look-back. No final decision has been made and it would not be right to pre-empt the board’s discussion.
“We will continue to be open about this work and will provide a further update following the meeting.
“Our dedicated support line remains available to anyone with concerns about their breast care on 0191 333 2126 or at cddft.breastservices@nhs.net.”
The trust has been contacted for additional comment.
The CDDFT is conducting an internal review of breast cancer cases between January 2023 and February 2025, as well as of 640 former patients who contacted a special helpline.
The BBC reported that of 514 cases reviewed by the trust so far, 315 patients had been found to have suffered harm, including 77 who were significantly harmed. One patient is known to have died.
Russell told the BBC that in some cases cancer was missed and subsequently spread.
One woman who had an unnecessary mastectomy, referred to as Jo, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “They should have done further screening and biopsies, and that would have shown that all the other areas were benign. And actually, there was very small cancer in a large breast. And actually, I didn’t need a mastectomy at all.”
“I just was in total shock, sat at the top of the stairs with the dogs, thinking, have I really heard what I’ve just heard? It was unbelievable, devastating,” she said.
“The fact that this part of your body is now gone, and you know part of what makes you a woman’s gone. It just makes you not your whole self, really. To find out that that wasn’t necessary is absolutely horrendous.”
Denise Howarth, 51, of Consett, County Durham, was diagnosed with stage one cancer in her left breast in February 2023.
She had a lumpectomy and lymph nodes removed, but at a follow-up review was told she still needed a mastectomy.
Howarth, a mother of two being represented by Hudgell Solicitors, underwent the mastectomy, followed by chemotherapy and radiology treatment.
In September last year, she was contacted by the CDDFT and told the mastectomy had not been needed.
“They called me at home to say I needn’t have had my breast removed and it was something which really knocked me off my feet, I was completely shocked,” she said.
“I’d had an awful year already as I’d lost two close relatives and my dad was really poorly so I’d never really had much time after my mastectomy to think of myself and my recovery.
“I’d just reached a point where I was beginning to focus on myself and to look forward, and then this news came like a bolt out of the blue.
“You put your trust in professional people. To be so badly let down is something I’ll never be able to come to terms with.”
On the trust’s response, Howarth said: “An apology is not enough. This is life-changing.
“I’ve lost so much confidence. I feel robbed of the person I was before. As a woman, losing a breast has a huge impact on you.
“I fear I will never be the same person again, although I have tried to be strong.”
Rachel O’Connor, part of the medical negligence team at Hudgell Solicitors, is calling for a public inquiry.
“We are currently advising a number of women who have had surgeries they have since been told were not needed,” she said.
“Breast cancer services at hospitals should be places where patients have the reassurance of exceptional care and support, from clinics and scans to surgeries and treatments.
“Sadly, at County Durham and Darlington NHS foundation trust, this has not been the case for many years, as deep-rooted, systematic failures have led to women suffering serious harm.”

U.S. Army tests a cheap missile made to intercept drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:02:02 UTC
17:02:02 KST

- Perseus Defense tested its Mk-III interceptor, built for about $2,500 each, at Yuma Proving Ground alongside U.S. Northern Command, NORAD and JIATF-401.
- The low-cost kinetic system is part of a broader Pentagon push for cheaper counter-drone options following the 2023 Langley Air Force Base drone incursion.
A counter-drone startup tested a low-cost interceptor missile at Yuma Proving Ground this month, loading it into an eight-shot launcher during a homeland-defense experiment involving U.S. Northern Command, NORAD and the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401.
Perseus Defense, a company that went through Y Combinator’s 2025 batch, said each Mk-III interceptor it fired cost roughly $2,500 to build. The company demonstrated the system to a group of distinguished visitors at the test event, showing the launcher running what it described as Lattice-level integration, a reference to Anduril Industries’ command-and-control software, following an earlier demonstration at Fort Carson’s Operation Jailbreak exercise.
The Mk-III is built to physically strike small drones rather than jam or spoof their signals, a kinetic hit-to-kill approach the company says is harder to defeat than electronic warfare against drones flying on fiber-optic links or preprogrammed waypoints that don’t rely on jammable radio signals. Perseus has said it is targeting a cost per engagement far below the $100,000-plus kinetic interceptors currently used against drones that themselves can cost as little as a few hundred dollars.
The push for that kind of low-collateral kinetic option traces back to a specific incident. In December 2023, dozens of unidentified drones flew over Joint Base Langley-Eustis in Virginia, forcing the base to temporarily relocate its F-22 fighters and exposing gaps in how U.S. installations could legally and physically respond to drone incursions over American soil. Similar sightings followed at other bases into 2024 and 2025, and the Department of War stood up JIATF-401 in 2025 specifically to speed up counter-drone capabilities for U.S. forces and installations at home.
The Perseus system was fired at Cibola Range Site 17, Yuma Proving Ground, as part of Falcon Peak 26.2, a counter-small unmanned aircraft systems experiment run by the North American Aerospace Defense Command and U.S. Northern Command. The exercise is designed to demonstrate new counter-drone technologies, expand the military’s focus on low-collateral defeat capabilities, deepen collaboration with mission partners, and give developers fast feedback to speed up the maturity of systems with potential use across the Department of War. This was the first time the campaign was held at Yuma Proving Ground rather than its previous home at Eglin Air Force Base. Other reporting on the event described a Perseus interceptor called Harpe, a 61-centimeter missile with a stated 2-kilometer engagement range fired from a launcher weighing less than 36 kilograms (79 pounds), tested alongside other short-range counter-drone systems to help U.S. Northern Command weigh mobility, cost per shot and magazine depth for base defense.
Perseus Defense was founded in 2025 by Jason Cornelius and Steve Messinger, who studied aerospace engineering together at Penn State, and the company has raised $6.5 million in seed funding.

UK says high-readiness forces ready for Suwalki crisis
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
09:00:37 BST
17:00:37 KST

The UK says high-readiness British forces could be deployed under NATO defence plans if Belarus and Kaliningrad attempted to close the Suwalki Gap, the narrow land corridor linking Poland with the Baltic states.
The position was set out in a written parliamentary answer to Labour MP Mike Tapp, who asked whether Britain had the capability to respond swiftly to an attempt to close the route. Defence Minister Louise Sandher-Jones framed the response through NATO’s collective defence arrangements rather than as a purely national UK operation.
She said: “NATO has the capability and commitment to defend every inch of Alliance territory.”
The Suwalki Gap is the stretch of territory between Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad which provides the land connection between Poland and Lithuania, and by extension the rest of the Baltic states. Its position has long made it an important part of NATO defence planning in north-eastern Europe, particularly because any attempt to sever the corridor would directly affect the Alliance’s ability to reinforce Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia by land.
Sandher-Jones said Britain had committed the overwhelming majority of its military to NATO planning, including forces held at higher readiness. She said: “The UK remains staunchly committed to NATO’s collective defence obligation, offering almost all of our Armed Forces to NATO including high-readiness forces, which can be deployed as part of NATO’s collective defence plans if necessary.”

‘A man threatened to shoot me’: the abuse pushing UK councillors out of politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:00:13 UTC
17:00:13 KST

Heather Williams has been shouted at in the street, received death threats, threats of sexual violence, and had dog faeces left on her doorstep. At one point, she didn’t leave her home alone for more than three months.
It was not how she expected her life to be when she first ran to be a Conservative district councillor in South Cambridgeshire nine years ago.
“It is very intimidating. I’ve had people threatening to rape me in my sleep, a man once threatened to shoot me,” said Williams, now opposition group leader on the council. “You do question whether you’re doing the right thing, what impact it is having on your family. Even my daughter has security protocols now.”
Williams has installed extra security measures in her home including cameras, panic alarms and an app on her phone so she can be tracked if needed.
She is not the only one – a new survey from the Local Government Association (LGA) found that over a third (35%) of councillors have made modifications to their home for security reasons.
This includes CCTV cameras, alarms, installing electric gates, removing or sealing letterboxes, reinforcing doors and locks, carrying a rape alarm, getting a dog and putting up ‘Beware of the dog’ signs (despite not having a dog). Some have even moved house.
The annual Debate Not Hate survey of more than 1,500 councillors across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland showed over half (52%) believed abuse and intimidation had increased over the past year.
It also found that women, ethnic minority and LGBTQ+ councillors were being disproportionately pushed out of politics due to the high levels of abuse and harassment.
In total, 38% of women who were considering not standing again for election said they were doing so because of abuse and intimidation – for men, the figure was 23%.
Among ethnic minority respondents, 43% said abuse had influenced their decision to not stand again, compared with 28% of white respondents. For LGBTQ+ councillors, the figure stood at 41%.
Hannah Dalton, a councillor and LGA civility in public life ambassador, said the findings showed that abuse was “a direct threat to the strength, diversity and health of our democracy”.
“We must never accept a situation where harassment and personal attacks are simply regarded as part of public service,” she said. “It is deeply alarming that most councillors believe the problem is getting worse. This toxic culture is not only affecting those currently in office, it is deterring talented and committed people from standing for election in the first place.
The majority of respondents (78%) said they felt at personal risk fulfilling their roles as councillors, with the figure rising to 85% for female, ethnic minority, LGBT+ or disabled councillors.
A quarter of councillors said they had received threats of violence, and 7% had received a death threat.
In response to the growing wave of personal attacks levelled at councillors, they are no longer required to publish their home address on council websites. Each police force also now has at least one force elected official adviser dedicated to dealing with security concerns for politicians.
But the LGA said it was not enough, and it wanted the government, police and social media platforms to do more, with “formal arrangements” on tackling such abuse.

17:00:08 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The intelligent connected new energy vehicle (NEV) industry is anticipated to contribute greatly to the upgrading of China's automobile industry, along with continuous breakthroughs in core technologies in this sector amid the artificial intelligence boom.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and eight other departments in early September jointly released a plan for the development of the intelligent connected NEV industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
The plan proposes that, by 2030, China will further consolidate its advantages across the entire intelligent connected NEV industrial chain and join the ranks of the world's auto powerhouses.
Intelligent connected NEVs are the main direction for transforming and upgrading the country's automobile industry, are typical examples of new quality productive forces, and are key components in building a modern industrial system in China, the plan notes.
This move is valued as a future-oriented strategic layout for strengthening the automobile industry which has undergone decades of constant progress in scale and core technologies and brands, with technological capabilities acting as the major driving power.
In 2025, China's automobile production and sales respectively reached 34.53 million and 34.4 million units, up 10.4 percent and 9.4 percent year on year respectively. The industry has maintained over 30 million units for three consecutive years and ranked the first globally for 17 successive years.
Of the total, production and sales of NEVs respectively reached nearly 16.63 million and 16.49 million units, ranking the first in the world for 11 years straight.
The large-scale deployment of intelligent connected vehicle technology, notably, is reshaping the core competitiveness of China's automotive industry.
In the first three quarters of 2025, 64 percent of new passenger vehicles in China were equipped with Level 2 (L2) combined driver-assistance functions. In 2026, this rate has climbed to 70 percent, and more than 30 percent of automobile models provide navigation-assisted driving functions.
What's more significant, Level 3 (L3) conditional autonomous driving has run beyond closed-road testing into commercial application. It means China's industrialization of intelligent connected vehicle sector is accelerating on all fronts, including such major shift from technical validation to commercial deployment.
Continuous breakthroughs in key technologies are generating strong momentum for auto industry upgrading. Major advances have been made in diverse areas such as batteries, charging, automotive chips and intelligent driving systems.
More importantly, some of these innovative technologies have achieved large-scale commercial application in the Chinese auto market through rapid iterative innovation.
China has developed an automotive technology ecosystem sustained by emerging technologies, innovative development models and novel business models, which lay a solid technological foundation for the country to achieve its goal of becoming one of the world's auto powerhouses.
Looking ahead, the plan notes that by 2030, in the domestic market, new energy passenger vehicles and commercial vehicles will account for 70 percent and 40 percent respectively. Also, vehicles equipped with autonomous driving functions will be applied on a large scale.
By 2030, key auto technologies will be significantly improved, with average fuel consumption of passenger vehicles reaching 3.3 liters per 100 km, and average electricity consumption of all-electric passenger vehicles reaching approximately 11.5 kilowatt-hours per 100 km. Highly automated driving will be achieved in scenarios like expressways, urban express roads and other urban roads, according to the plan.
The plan points out that enhancing technological innovation capability is a key priority in intelligent connected NEV development. With critical areas focused on energy and power systems, intelligent chassis and intelligent connectivity, China will carry out strategic, forward-looking and pioneering R&D initiatives to drive the development of the next-generation technologies for intelligent connected NEVs.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period, efforts will be made to uphold the bottom line of product quality and improve the safety and reliability of autonomous driving, said Xin Guobin, vice minister of the MIIT, at a recent media conference.
Policies concerning NEV insurance will also be optimized, while maintenance costs will be reduced to address consumer concerns and encourage consumers to purchase and use NEVs with confidence, he added. ■
