Across China: Quality violin making finds unexpected home in rural Chinese county
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:00:01 CST
17:00:01 KST

ZHENGZHOU, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Wang Jinwu picks up a violin and points to the patterns running across its back. He taps the instrument, listens to its sound, and then walks visitors through his workshop.
Wang, 54, runs a violin-making company in Xiaowangzhuang Village in Queshan County, Henan Province in central China.
Around him, workers continue their tasks in small, precise movements.
Liu Ziming, 30, is bending thin pieces of wood into the curved sides of a violin, joining them to form the body before attaching the top and back plates. Nearby, Xiong Jinduo, a mother of two in her late 30s, applies glue to thin wooden purfling and presses it into grooves along an instrument's edge.
Violin making, a craft steeped in centuries of European tradition, has found an unexpected home here in Queshan, a rural Chinese county with no history of making musical instruments.
Once a poverty-stricken county, Queshan has developed a full violin production chain, from timber treatment and component carving to painting and finishing. More than 2,600 local people now work in the industry, producing about 400,000 violins a year, according to local industry figures. About 80 percent of the violins produced in Queshan are exported, while most of the timber used for making them is imported, according to Jiang Baolin, secretary-general of the Queshan Handmade Violin Makers Association.
The story of how the industry took root here begins not with timber or a port, but with people.
Since the 1980s, villagers from Queshan began leaving for Beijing to learn violin making. Some eventually built their own workshops and businesses there. Then, from around the mid-2010s, the flow reversed, with many Queshan-born violin makers in Beijing returning home, encouraged by local incentives to develop the industry. They brought with them skills, customers and connections built over decades.
Wang was one of them.
He entered the trade almost by chance. With little schooling at the time, his initial goal was simply to work hard enough to earn a living.
Wang left Henan for Beijing at 16 or 17 and apprenticed at a violin factory. After six or seven years in factories, he began working independently in the mid-1990s. His first workshop made only four or five violins a month. Over time, he built a business and developed overseas customers.
One U.S. wholesaler has worked with him for nearly two decades. The customer now buys more than 2,000 instruments a year, roughly two-thirds of Wang's annual output.
Wang moved his factory from Beijing to Tianjin in 2017, then brought it back to Queshan in 2023. "I felt more settled once I came back home," he said.
By then, he had already built an overseas customer base, and trade fairs had become an important way to find new buyers. His company has taken part in musical-instrument exhibitions in China, the United States, Germany, Japan and Italy.
About 90 percent of his sales now go to the United States, he said, with smaller volumes shipped to countries including Italy, the Czech Republic and Finland.
A violin takes about a month and a half to complete, Wang said. The process is divided into six broad stages and many smaller tasks. Varnishing alone may involve more than 20 rounds of application, drying and sanding.
Much of the work depends on judgment that is difficult to reduce to a formula. Workers learn one stage at a time, often taking two or three months to become proficient, while mastery takes years.
Wang describes each violin as a work of art rather than a commodity.
The growth of local suppliers and supporting businesses has also shaped how the industry operates in Queshan.
Rather than relying entirely on large centralized factories, production is divided among workshops and households. Some workers specialize in a single stage and are paid by the piece. Others can take components home and arrange their own hours.
For Xiong, who also farms, that flexibility matters. She can make violin parts while staying close to her family. Liu, who has worked in the trade for nearly a decade, likewise values working close to home.
The model has helped turn a craft once learned in distant factories into a source of rural employment.
But it also exposes some of the industry's limits.
Wang said he recruited more than 10 young people after returning in 2023, but only a few stayed. Violin making requires long periods of repetitive, focused work, and some young workers prefer jobs that let them move around.
In his view, the skills themselves are not easy to standardize. Experienced makers rely not only on measurements but also on an eye and a feel honed through years of practice.
Maker Xiong Kaifeng returned to Queshan after years of making violins in Beijing and now focuses on performance-grade handmade instruments. He makes only around 20 violins and 10 cellos a year, along with fewer violas.
For makers like him, the focus is on improving quality and building recognition for Queshan's handmade instruments.
Queshan is now planning an industrial park and facilities for training, research and instrument appraisal. Local authorities also want makers to develop their own brands and move beyond contract production.
Wang is pursuing a similar direction in his own company. He wants to use better-selected timber, refine plate thickness and produce more instruments with consistently high sound quality. With what he describes as a weaker market, he is now making about 2,000 to 3,000 instruments a year, compared with more than 4,000 at one point.
One instrument Wang remains particularly proud of is a cello he made that won first prize at the First National Violin Education Equipment Exhibition in 2019. It was later sold at auction to a teacher for 80,000 yuan (about 11,838 U.S. dollars).
Returning home has not meant turning inward.
In September 2025, Wang traveled to Cremona, Italy, home to famed violin maker Antonio Stradivari, to attend the Cremona Musica International Exhibitions and Festival, an international trade show for musical instruments. During the trip, he visited local violin workshops to observe makers and study their techniques. He found that the violin-making process was slower at every stage than in his own factory, with higher standards for timber selection.
"Italian violin making has a much longer history," he said, "and there is still much for us to learn."
That may be the clearest picture of Queshan's violin industry: a craft learned elsewhere, brought home and adapted to a rural economy, while its makers continue to look outward for customers, knowledge and new ways to improve. ■

Indian Navy Augments Its Submarine Rescue Capability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

On August 31, India commissioned INS Nipun, the second dedicated Diving Support Vessel (DSV) that serves as the mothership for the two Deep Submergence Rescue Vehicles (DSRVs) in service. With this, the Indian Navy crossed a threshold in a critical operational capability – submarine rescue – that has a bearing not just for India but for the entire region.
Submarines are some of the most complex machines in existence and their operation is highly specialized. Submarine rescue takes that to another level and is a forte of a very small group of countries.
Indian Navy Chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan’s remarks at the commissioning ceremony in Mumbai aptly encapsulate this. The Nipun significantly enhances the capacity to respond to a distressed submarine, whether of the Indian Navy or that of a partner navy, he said, adding that this capability would also enable India to support submarine rescue and emerge as the “preferred submarine rescue partner” in the region.
The Indian Navy signed a deal worth 193 million British pounds (around $217 million) with U.K.-based James Fischer Defense in 2016 under which it procured two DSRVs, a Launch and Recovery System (LARS), and a LARS-integrated decompression chamber. They were operationalized at Mumbai on India’s western seaboard at the end of 2018 and at Visakhapatnam on the eastern seaboard in early 2019. Concurrently, in September 2018, the navy signed a deal with state-owned Hindustan Shipyard Limited, located at Visakhapatnam, for the construction of the two DSVs, with the first vessel to be delivered in 36 months.
Until the DSVs were completed, INS Sabarmati of the Ship Building Corporation of India acted as the interim ship for both the vessels. This left a major operational void, as it meant more time, which is the most critical factor in the event of a submarine disaster in the ocean depths.
The two vessels were launched into water in September 2022, and the first, INS Nistar, was commissioned on July 18, 2025. The induction of INS Nipun now closes that loop, significantly augmenting the Indian Navy’s specialist diving, underwater intervention, salvage, and submarine rescue support capability.
So far, the Indian Navy operated an older diving support vessel, INS Nireekshak, with limited submarine rescue capabilities. In the backdrop of the capability gaps in the past, India had signed an agreement with the United States for utilizing the U.S. Navy’s global submarine rescue flyaway kit.
The Capability
Displacing 10,000 tons, measuring over 118 meters in length, and with an endurance of 60 days, the Nistar and the Nipun were purpose-built for deep-sea diving and underwater operations for inspection and intervention and to serve as mother ships to the DSRVs. Each DSV can accommodate 25 officers and 225 sailors.
Further, the expansive deep-sea diving systems with specialized diving complex, dynamic positioning capability, and associated life-support and medical facilities enable them to conduct sustained operations at sea, according to the Indian Navy. For this, they carry a 15-ton subsea crane, a diving bell, remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), side-scan sonar, compression chambers, and a self-propelled hyperbaric lifeboat. They can undertake deep-sea diving and salvage operations up to a depth of 300 meters.
The DSRVs, in turn, can go down to a maximum depth of 650 meters and rescue 14 people in one go. They also carry a ROV and, together with the side-scan sonar, can locate a submarine at depths of up to 1,000 meters. Once a submarine is successfully located, a sub-module of the system, the Submarine Rescue Vehicle, mates with the submarine to rescue trapped personnel. The same feature can also be utilized to provide emergency supplies to a submarine.
In 2018, before induction, the DSRV was put to trials, during which it set several “firsts” for the Indian Navy. It dived to a depth of 666 meters, the deepest submergence by a manned vessel in Indian waters, and carried out ROV operations at over 750 meters and side-scan sonar operations at over 650 meters.
Given the nature of its operation, the DSRV is designed for ease of transportation. For this purpose, the entire system has been divided into 24 components, which can be easily transported by road, sea, and air. In addition to being paired with the mothership, the system can also be airlifted by heavy transport aircraft like the IL-76 and C-17 operated by the Indian Air Force, enabling swift deployment across theaters.
The Criticality
Reaching a disaster-struck submarine in the narrow time window is critical and a DSRV offers that lifeline for any submarine-operating Navy. For the Indian Navy, the order of criticality multiplies manifold, given its aging submarine fleet.
The Indian Navy operates 16 conventional submarines – six Russian Kilo-class submarines and four German HDW-class submarines, both aging fleets long awaiting replacement, as well as six newer French Scorpene-class submarines. The newest Kilo-class sub is 26 years old, and the HDW class is over 30 years old. The fleets saw life extensions to keep them going amid delayed procurements. As stated by Captain Vikas Gautam, officer-in-charge of the Submarine Rescue Unit (East), during Exercise Milan in February this year, the true measure of any navy is not only its firepower, but “its resolve and capability to bring its men and women home safely.”
Regional Assistance and Cooperative Arrangements
The maritime domain with its wide expanse is inherently complex, and submarine rescue is a restricted capability both in terms of complexity and economics. In the last few years, India has signed several cooperation agreements with countries in the region for submarine rescue, offering its capabilities, which span bilateral arrangements and multilateral engagements.
The Indian Navy also actively cooperates with the International Submarine Escape and Rescue Liaison Office (ISMERLO), established by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), which coordinates international submarine rescue responses.
In a demonstration of India’s capabilities in real time, in April 2021, India dispatched the two DSRVs to locate the missing Indonesian submarine KRI Nanggala, one with the mother ship and another airlifted in a C-17. However, they were recalled midway as the disaster-stricken submarine was located in the ocean depths. All crew onboard were dead.
In January 2021, India and Singapore signed an implementing agreement on submarine rescue support and cooperation between the two navies. In September 2024, India and South Africa signed an implementing agreement that ensures the safety of the South African Navy’s submarine crew in times of distress or accident. In October 2025, during the visit of India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh to Canberra, India and Australia, which have transformed their maritime engagement over the last decade, signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on submarine search and rescue cooperation. A month later, in November 2025, India and Vietnam signed an MoU on mutual submarine search and rescue support.
Submarine rescue has also become a major part of bilateral and multilateral exercises, underscoring its importance. In September 2025, the Indian Navy deployed the Nistar for Exercise Pacific Reach (XPR-25), hosted by the Singapore Navy in the South China Sea, which saw the participation of over 40 nations. During this event, the DSRV Tiger X carried out its maiden dive outside the Indian Ocean Region (IOR) and achieved mating with South Korea’s submarine Shin Dol-Seok.
The Indian Navy also regularly showcases its submarine rescue capabilities at multilateral engagements it hosts, like the Exercise Milan and Goa Maritime Conclave, offering assistance to countries in the region.
As the IOR and beyond see a proliferation of submarines, their search and rescue in times of crisis will be much needed. India is now well positioned to lend immediate assistance, expanding the ambit of humanitarian assistance and disaster relief efforts.

China releases 60 new wartime archives on Japanese military's "comfort woman" crime
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:59:43 CST
16:59:43 KST

CHANGCHUN, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Jilin Provincial Archives in northeast China on Friday released 60 original Japanese military documents from World War II, adding new evidence of Japan's wartime system of forced sexual slavery.
The release coincided with the 95th anniversary of the "Sept. 18 Incident." It was on Sept. 18, 1931, when Japanese troops blew up a section of the railway near Shenyang, then under their control, and accused Chinese troops of sabotage as a pretext for subsequent aggression.
The new archives came from charred historical remnants left behind after the Japanese Kwantung Army attempted to destroy them during their retreat, according to the Jilin Provincial Archives in Changchun, capital of Jilin Province.
The original Japanese military documents shed further light on the systematic and institutionalized sexual violence committed by the Japanese army, powerfully debunking the long-standing lies of Japan's right-wing forces that distort the facts surrounding the "comfort women" issue and attempt to whitewash Japan's war crimes.
Previous research has shown that some 400,000 women in Asia were forced to serve as "comfort women" -- sexual slaves for the Japanese army during World War II -- and nearly half of them were Chinese.
Lyu Chunyue, an official with the archives, said the archives now has 85 original Japanese military documents documenting the "comfort women" system. The first 25 were released in 2014 and were later included in China's documentary heritage.
The 60 newly released documents cover the establishment and authorization of "comfort stations," their daily operation, the recruitment of sex slaves and their brutal treatment, Lyu said.
The documents show that "comfort stations" were established and operated under the authority of the Japanese military, with the Japanese Kwantung Army setting up more than 20 such facilities in Northeast China.
Some archives show that military approval was required to establish new "comfort stations," and some were located inside Japanese military barracks and were restricted to military personnel.
The new archives also include records on the forced recruitment of sex slaves. A 1941 report by a Japanese military unit said that Japanese troops forcibly recruited Korean women when women could not be recruited voluntarily.
Other archives showed that "comfort women" were forcibly conscripted to the front lines under Japan's national mobilization law, thoroughly refuting the fallacy that their recruitment was voluntary.
The documents also recorded violence against the sex slaves at multiple "comfort stations."
"The release of these original archives, irrefutable proof of crimes against humanity committed by Japanese militarism, provides solid historical evidence for defending historical truth and countering historical revisionism," said Su Zhiliang, leading expert for China's bid to list "comfort women" materials on UNESCO Memory of the World Register. ■

S. Korea's public sector deficit hits record high in 2025
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:59:39 CST
16:59:39 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's public sector deficit hit a record high in 2025, driven by increased fiscal spending to boost the country's economy, central bank data showed Friday.
The public sector balance, gauged as total revenue minus total expenditure, registered a deficit of 83.1 trillion won (60.1 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, marking the largest shortfall since the Bank of Korea (BOK) began compiling the data in 2007.
The public sector encompasses the central government, local governments, and social security funds as well as non-financial and financial public corporations.
Total revenue for the public sector gained 4.7 percent from a year earlier to 1,192.1 trillion won in 2025, while total spending advanced 5.5 percent to 1,275.2 trillion won.
The faster growth in expenditure than revenue was led by two supplementary budgets aimed at stabilizing people's livelihoods, the government's proactive fiscal policy, and higher health insurance benefit payments.
After posting surpluses for six consecutive years from 2014 to 2019, the public sector logged a deficit for six straight years since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The central government's deficit worsened to an all-time high of 90.1 trillion won in 2025, up from 83.8 trillion won in 2024.
Local governments narrowed their deficit to 2.0 trillion won in 2025 from 15.5 trillion won a year earlier, supported by a substantial increase in local allocation taxes from the central government.
The social security funds saw their surplus shrink from 41.8 trillion won in 2024 to 32.0 trillion won in 2025 due to the rapidly aging population, which raised benefit payouts.
Non-financial public corporations posted a deficit of 22.1 trillion won in 2025, up from 16.7 trillion won in the prior year.
Financial public corporations swung to a deficit of 0.9 trillion won in 2025 from a surplus of 5.1 trillion won in the previous year. ■

SEOUL, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Foreign investors became net buyers of South Korean stocks for the first time in eight months, while shifting to a net outflow from the domestic bond market for the first time in four months, financial watchdog data showed Friday.
Offshore investors purchased a net 344 billion won (about 248.8 million U.S. dollars) worth of domestic listed stocks in August, according to the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS).
Foreigners shifted into net buyers in the main KOSPI market, but they offloaded shares in the tech-heavy KOSDAQ market.

Meanwhile, the domestic bond market saw net foreign outflows for the first time in four months.
Overseas investors dumped a net 3.94 trillion won worth of local listed bonds last month.
With maturing debt worth 801 billion won, net foreign disinvestment in the local bond market reached 4.74 trillion won.
The foreign ownership of domestic listed bonds stood at 330.3 trillion won at the end of August, accounting for 11.4 percent of all listed bonds in the country. ■

The carrier will be renamed KRI Sriwijaya, honouring the Srivijaya empire, a maritime kingdom based in Sumatra that became one of Southeast Asia’s dominant naval and trading powers between the seventh and 13th centuries.
“There are many disasters in this country. So we really need a vessel or platform that could carry many helicopters, because the helicopters can drop logistics quickly to remote areas,” Ali said.
However, he also noted that the ship could “be deployed for combat missions if necessary”.
Bolstering defence
The arrival of the vessel, which was commissioned by the Italian navy in 1985, comes as Prabowo has been pushing to upgrade Indonesia’s military assets and build closer defence cooperation with other countries.
Italy agreed to give Indonesia the carrier in March, after it was retired in 2014. The move was meant to bolster the two countries’ defence engagement.
Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship.
“Its condition is still very good and hopefully it can be used by the Indonesian navy for the next 15 to 20 years,” navy chief Ali said.
Indonesia’s Finance Ministry approved $450m in financing for the aircraft carrier programme in 2025. Opposition politicians worry the overall bill could be far higher.
However, Prabowo – formerly a general under the Suharto regime – has made building Indonesia’s defence assets and agreements a priority.
Jakarta signed an $8.1bn deal in 2022, when Prabowo was defence minister, to purchase 42 French-made Rafale fighter jets. India confirmed this year that it will supply the country with long-range missiles.
Indonesia has also agreed this year to a “Major Defence Cooperation Partnership” with the Trump administration in the United States, and a security treaty with Australia.

Background checks and psychological evaluations have become a requirement for buying a firearm. However, many illegal firearms remain in circulation.

Japan’s annual inflation holds at 1.9% in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:41:38 UTC
16:41:38 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Japan’s annual consumer inflation remained unchanged at 1.9% in August, staying at its highest level in seven months, official data showed Friday.
The consumer price index stood at 102.2, based on 2025 prices, according to the country’s Statistics Bureau.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile fresh food prices, eased to 1.7% from 1.8% in July, falling short of market expectations of 1.8%.
The reading remained below the Bank of Japan’s 2% inflation target for the eighth consecutive month.
The index excluding both fresh food and energy, closely monitored to assess underlying price pressures, rose 1.9% annually.
Among major components, food prices increased 3.1% year on year in August, slowing from a 3.5% rise in July.
Prices rose 4.9% for furniture and household utensils, 3% for medical care, 2.3% for transportation and communication, and 2.2% for culture and recreation.
Electricity prices fell 2.4% from a year earlier, compared with a 0.1% decline in July, while education costs decreased 3.8%.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices edged up 0.1% in August.

Rare Christian amulet holding bible scrap, ancient stone seal unearthed at Turkish site - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:41:15 UTC
16:41:15 KST

A rare early Christian gold amulet and a roughly 3,500-year-old stone seal bearing a hieroglyphic inscription were discovered during excavations by Turkish archaeologists, Turkish outlet Turkey Today reported in late July.
According to Turkey Today, researchers from Bilkent University, the University of Chicago, and Bilecik Seyh Edebali University found the artifacts during the third excavation season at the Turkmen Karahoyuk archaeological site.
The Christian amulet, which is believed to date back to the fourth or fifth century CE, according to Turkiye Today, was found within a small copper container.
Inside the amulet, archaeologists found a thin sheet of gold that is reportedly thought to carry a passage from the bible.
“Inside a copper box, we found an extremely thin gold sheet, only 0.1 millimeters thick, most likely carrying a passage from the Bible,” Turkey Today cited Michele Ruzgar Massa of Bilkent University as saying.
Amulet likely was a protective charm
Massa explained that the amulet likely belonged to a small child, and that “we can think of it as something like a nazar boncugu, a traditional evil-eye charm.”
Such amulets are rare, noted Massa, adding that a similar artifact was discovered in Germany.
The stone seal, which was also discovered at the site, bore hieroglyphic Luwian inscriptions, reported Turkey Today.
Luwian, also known as Luvian or Luish, is an ancient Anatolian language used during the Bronze and Iron Ages.
The inscription includes a personal name and an official title, which, Massa explained, indicates that it belonged to an individual who held a lower-ranking position in an organized state bureaucratic system.
The name on the seal is “Kurunti-ziti,” according to Turkey Today, related to the Hittite stag god and a guardian deity of the countryside, Kurunta.
Further, the discovery suggests that Turkmen Karahoyuk had functioned as a major administrative center at the time.
Two additional copper seals and a clay seal impression bearing a different name were also unearthed at the site.

New satellite imagery from Vantor Technologies appeared to show the Iranian regime rapidly attempting to reconstruct the Taleghan 2 facility in the Parchin military complex, the Institute for Science and International Security stated on Thursday.
The facility is located approximately 30 kilometers southeast of Tehran. It was initially destroyed in Israeli strikes in October 2024, before being partially rebuilt starting in May 2025. Israel again struck it in March 2026 during Operation Roaring Lion, and it has been heavily damaged since.
The satellite imagery appears to show the regime having erected a tarp above the hardened buried facility, which has been tied to nuclear bomb testing as part of Iran's AMAD program.
The tarp seems to be an attempt to hide reconstruction activity from satellite view or aerial reconnaissance, the institute assessed.
This assessment was boosted by significant activity being seen throughout the construction site, including various construction vehicles, such as dump trucks, bulldozers, concrete pump trucks, concrete mixers, and cranes being seen at the site in the latest satellite imagery.
The "repair and rehabilitation work began in June," the institute stated.
The first step Iran took in its reconstruction project was to repair and place concrete caps over penetration holes caused by bunker-buster heavy bombs dropped on the facility, the institute said.
Iran reinforces nuke test facility with 'concrete apron' during reconstruction project
Iran also appears to have built a new "concrete apron reinforcement on the right side of the facility," the institute said, adding that it will "provide additional blast protection from an aerial attack."
"Significant questions remain as to Iran's plans for the facility; not least is why Iran keeps rebuilding it," the institute stated.
"What is clear is that Iran remains committed to rebuilding this facility, a deeply concerning development considering the long history of nuclear weapons research and development activities that occurred there," it warned.

Saudi Arabia has conveyed through the Sultanate of Oman a new proposal to the Houthis in Yemen, including a two-week ceasefire and the opening of direct talks between Riyadh and the Houthi leadership.
According to the Lebanese newspaper Al Akhbar, which is affiliated with Hezbollah, the aim is first to discuss the Houthis' humanitarian demands and then attempt to reach a comprehensive agreement by the end of the ceasefire period.
According to sources who spoke with the Lebanese newspaper, the proposal was formulated after a series of contacts Saudi Arabia held in recent days with the United States, Egypt, Pakistan, and the Sultanate of Oman.
The sources claimed that Riyadh sought to convey a message to the Houthis that it was interested in using the period of calm to "discuss addressing all humanitarian demands," and afterward "reach a comprehensive agreement at the end of the truce."
Oman, which has played a central mediating role between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in recent years, was asked to deliver the proposal to Sanaa.
Houthis escalate, seize areas around Red Sea coast
The report comes amid a sharp escalation in fighting in Yemen and rising tensions between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia. In recent weeks, Houthi forces have seized strategic areas along the Red Sea coast, while also carrying out attacks with missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles against targets inside Saudi Arabia.
Riyadh has accused the Houthis of attacking civilian and economic facilities in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan, and Najran, as well as threatening commercial shipping in the Red Sea. In an official statement issued by Saudi Arabia last week, it was claimed that 73 civilians, including women and children, were injured in one of the waves of attacks.
US secretly holds talks with Houthis
At the same time as the Saudi contacts, secret talks were held over the weekend in Oman between US representatives and senior Houthi officials.
According to a Reuters report, the meeting took place at the US Embassy in Muscat with the assistance of the Omani government. The Houthis told the Americans that they intended to continue honoring the ceasefire reached with Washington in 2025 and that they did not intend to attack US vessels.
The Saudi move reflects an attempt to shift from a military channel to a diplomatic one as the fighting takes an increasing toll and also threatens regional trade and energy routes. According to Al Akhbar, Sanaa has not yet provided a final response to the proposal, and the Houthis continue to demand a comprehensive settlement that includes an end to the war, the lifting of the blockade, and addressing humanitarian demands. At this stage, Saudi Arabia has also not officially confirmed the details of the proposal published by the Lebanese newspaper.

"We're proud to finally talk about the extraordinary work behind this missile and how we're working with the U.S. government to rapidly scale production."
The first images of the weapon emerged in May and Australia has announced it will buy roughly $521 million worth of JATM missiles. The quantity and unit price were not disclosed.
 
The framework agreement lays the groundwork for a multiyear procurement contract aimed at strengthening the defense industrial base for the program. Lockheed said it would fund investments needed to boost output under the deal.

Retail sales bounce back across Great Britain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:40:07 UTC
16:40:07 KST

Retail sales across Great Britain unexpectedly rose last month, the latest economic indicator to defy gloomy forecasts as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to present next month’s budget.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold rose 0.5% month on month in August, defying analyst expectations of a 0.2% fall.
It marks a significant bounce back in consumer spending after a 0.5% month-on-month fall in July.
The summer heatwaves fuelled increased sales of items including fans, air-conditioning units, sports merchandise and clothing in the three months to August.
The unexpected sales boost is the latest positive update on the state of the economy for the government, after a surprise 0.4% increase in gross domestic product in July that was reported by the ONS last week.
“August’s warm weather delayed the usual shift towards autumn purchases, but retailers successfully kept consumers spending,” said Sandra Prince, the head of corporate consumer at Lloyds. “The late bank holiday weekend and back-to-school shopping are also likely to have supported demand, with online sales among the areas seeing the biggest boost.”
Across the three-month summer period sales rose 2.4% year on year, again significantly above forecasts of a 1.9% rise.
Among the strongest performers were department stores, which recorded a sales rise of 1.8% month on month in August – a bounce back after a fall in July, which the ONS attributed to stock availability problems.
Non-store retailing, primarily online shopping, rose by 1.7% month on month, a major bounce back after sales fell 3.7% the previous month due to heavy promotional activity driving June sales.
Overall, non-store retailers enjoyed a strong summer with a 5.4% sales rise across the three-month period.
Retailers selling alcohol and beverages performed well across all three months to August 2026, the ONS reported, which they attributed to promotions, the hot weather and the men’s football World Cup.
Fuel sales dropped again, down by 1.3% in August and 2.5% across the three-month period as motorists cut back on non-essential journeys after big increases in the price of petrol and diesel since the start of the Iran war in February.
UK petrol prices have hit the highest level in four years as the conflict in the Middle East intensifies.
On Thursday the Bank of England monetary policy committee voted to hold the base rate at 3.75%. However, it indicated that the latest rise in energy prices because of the conflict was likely to result in a rates increase to keep inflation in check. Inflation rose to 3.1% in August, from 2.9% in July.
“There are some challenging headwinds for consumers to navigate as we head into autumn,” said Andy Carlisle, the consumer goods and retail lead at Accenture.
“Higher energy bills, food, fuel and transport prices continue to weigh on purse strings. We’re beginning to see consumers preparing for these pressures, prioritising everyday needs while showing greater caution around discretionary and bigger-ticket purchases.”

Port CEO calls for action after dry summer costs millions of euros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:38:32 UTC
16:38:32 KST

The dry summer has cost businesses in the North Sea Port millions of euros, CEO Cas König has said. At the height of the crisis, one of the two sea locks in Terneuzen was completely closed, while the other could only be used for four hours at high tide. At one point, some companies also opted to transport their cargo by lorry rather than by ship.
This had an immediate impact on the entire maritime supply chain in Ghent and Terneuzen, both of which are downstream of the locks. Ships found it more difficult to enter or leave the port and were forced to remain moored for longer. They had to wait for the lock; then, as soon as the lock reopened, there was a rush for pilots, tugs and mooring crews.
At the deepest point, the draught, the permitted depth of a vessel below the water line, was approximately 25cm lower than in normal conditions. That meant ships had to carry lighter loads or wait longer. Due to the persistent drought, some companies switched to lorries to transport their goods.
We cannot wait and see how things go next year. We must take action
The restrictions were not only necessary for shipping. According to König, an excessively low water level can also pose risks to quays, bridges and other infrastructure.
The impact can quickly mount for businesses. “If the whole supply chain grinds to a halt, you have to be careful that their production process doesn’t come to a standstill as well,” König said. Waiting ships incur fees if they have to remain moored for longer than anticipated.
“We don’t know exactly what the financial impact is for businesses, but it certainly runs into millions,” says König.
The port’s management expects such situations to occur more frequently and wants to accelerate its climate adaptation efforts, with the relevant authorities and businesses, by implementing technical and organisational measures to tackle both drought and extreme rainfall.
The port is home to major industrial employers and production sites that depend on the smooth flow of goods in and out via the canal. Problems with water levels and draught directly affect the economic strength of Ghent’s industry.
“The situation cannot remain as it is,” says König. “We cannot wait and see how things go next year. We must take action.”

Russians fear Putin will send them to war once election is over

- Russia faces manpower shortages with high casualties and declining volunteer numbers, prompting digital summons and exit bans to enforce conscription.
- Putin links election participation to war support; the Kremlin tightly controls elections, and mobilisation efforts may focus on regions with strong loyalty to Putin.
AI generated
MOSCOW – Russians are growing fearful that President Vladimir Putin may soon order a massive new mobilisation for the war in Ukraine after this weekend’s parliamentary elections.
That fear stretches to officials in the Kremlin and army recruitment centres, who’ve been looking to open foreign bank accounts and move assets abroad while encouraging friends and relatives to leave Russia in recent months, documents seen by Bloomberg News show.
While Putin denies he has any such plans, a European security official says Russia’s preparing to draft an additional 300,000 men into the army by the end of 2026.
Unlike a previous mobilisation in September 2022, which caused a spike in public anxiety and sent tens of thousands fleeing from Russia, there may be no formal announcement this time.
That’s because the Kremlin has quietly built the digital infrastructure to summon people to the army while also closing off potential escape routes.
Three days of voting begin on Sept 18 in Russia’s first parliamentary elections since the start of the 2022 full-scale invasion.
United Russia, which campaigns as the party of Putin, is expected to retain the majority in the State Duma that it has held since 2003 in the elections that are tightly controlled by the Kremlin.
Russia is incurring massive casualties for little progress on the battlefield in Ukraine, where Putin says he has about 700,000 troops deployed.
The Kremlin needs to recruit about 400,000 people each year to replenish the army’s ranks and has relied mostly on offering huge recruitment bonuses and generous salaries to persuade people to sign military contracts.
But with the war deep in its fifth year, there are signs that the pool of volunteers is starting to dry up.
Russian regions recruited about 234,000 new contract troops between January and August, based on budget data, according to Janis Kluge, an analyst at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs in Berlin.
That compares with about 260,000 in the same period in 2025, he wrote on Substack.
Russia is restructuring military commissariats to deal with increased flows of draftees, the European official said, asking not to be identified because the matter is sensitive.
Advertising campaigns in Russia are urging men to sign military contracts to avoid the prospect of forced conscription.
Putin has called warnings of a post-election mobilisation “complete nonsense” and part of a Western information campaign against Russia.
“From the point of view of the availability of military personnel, we have no problems here,” he said in Vladivostok on Sept 3. “People are coming forward voluntarily and signing contracts.”
About 1,000 Russian soldiers are being killed in Ukraine each week in addition to those wounded, according to a person in Moscow familiar with situation.
Russia needs more front-line troops and the quality of existing recruits is extremely low, the person said, asking not to be identified because the matter is sensitive.
Ukraine’s General Staff said on Sept 15 that 301,000 Russian troops had been killed and wounded so far in 2026, with monthly losses rising to 42,000 in July and August.
It’s struggling with its own manpower challenges with about 1.5 million men on police wanted lists for evading conscription, and some 200,000 Ukrainian soldiers absent without leave.
Bloomberg News cannot independently verify the claims. Neither Russia nor Ukraine publishes official data on the numbers of their own troop casualties.
Putin continues to seek full control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, where Russian forces are making grinding assaults to try to seize a fortress belt of cities they’ve failed to conquer in fighting since 2014.
Ukraine rejects his demand to cede the territory as part of a deal to end the war.
Putin drew a direct connection between the election and the war in a televised address to the nation on Sept 16.
“Your choice and determination will show once again that millions of people are backing our fighters,” he said. “Participation in the elections is our joint contribution to Russia’s victory.”
Four other parties that are likely to gain seats in the parliamentary elections all support the war and there’s no genuine opposition.
When the Yabloko party’s “for peace and freedom” campaign appeared popular enough to clear the 5 per cent threshold for entry to the Duma, it was kicked off the ballot by Russia’s Supreme Court for supposed breaches of election rules.
“Since the key issues are being resolved on the battlefield, the State Duma won’t be that important,” said Yevgeny Minchenko, a Moscow-based political scientist who’s worked with the Kremlin. “All the parties adhere to the presidential consensus.”
The Kremlin is likely to focus mobilisation efforts in the regions showing the greatest support for Putin in the elections, according to Ekaterina Schulmann, a Berlin-based political scientist at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre.
“In places where loyalty, discipline and administrative effectiveness were demonstrated, both by voters and by the authorities, more people could be recruited,” she said. “If they manage the elections well, they can also manage mobilisation well in their region.”
European government officials say Putin has yet to make a final decision on mobilisation.
The negative public reaction to the call-up of 300,000 reservists in the 2022 draft remains etched in the memory of nervous Kremlin officials.
While that mobilisation relied on serving paper notices to draftees, Russia’s digital Unified Military Register now automatically links with tax services, police databases, medical records, property registries and border control.
Under updated regulations, an electronic summons is legally deemed to have been delivered seven days after it’s posted to the online portal regardless of whether the recipient opens it.
An automatic exit ban takes effect at border posts as soon as the notice is published to prevent people from leaving Russia.
For anyone failing to appear at a recruitment centre within 20 days, automated penalties block access to public services, including vehicle registration, real estate transactions, credit access and self-employed business status.
Some officials worried that staffing reductions of up to 15 per cent in Russia’s regions as part of budget cuts ordered by Putin earlier in 2026 could result in those let go being called up to the front, the documents seen by Bloomberg indicate.
There’s no sign that the Kremlin currently has plans to do that, according to European government officials.
Still, rumours of an impending mobilisation are stirring renewed anxiety, with reports of rising numbers of Russians crossing into neighbouring countries such as Georgia and Armenia ahead of the elections.
In August, Moscow accused Armenian officials of “provocative” statements after Yerevan indicated a readiness to welcome Russians fleeing military service.
Even as Putin insists his forces are advancing steadily in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, Russia’s summer offensive yielded a gain of just 155 sq km of territory from May to August, according to analysis by Alex Kokcharov, Bloomberg’s geoeconomic analyst for Russia, Eastern Europe and Central Asia.
The analysis based on data compiled by DeepState, a Ukrainian open-source collective with links to the country’s military, compares with 2,037 sq km in the same period in 2025.
Russia’s army has sustained roughly 33,000 casualties on average per month so far in 2026 for an average monthly gain of just 104 sq km, representing approximately 317 killed or wounded for every square kilometre taken, according to Kokcharov’s calculations.
“The military situation in recent months indicates that Russia does not have enough manpower both to concentrate forces on the main axis of advance and to reliably cover the front line,” said Kirill Rogov, head of Re: Russia, a Vienna-based research group.
“In other words, mobilisation would be necessary if the objective is to reach the borders of Donbas within six months.” BLOOMBERG

Trump administration moves to cut protections for endangered species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:30:51 UTC
16:30:51 KST

Brett Hartl, the government affairs director at the Center for Biological Diversity, said the move "stabs at the very heart of the Endangered Species Act by giving federal approval to the killing of some of America’s most beloved wildlife."
The Trump administration has issued a sweeping new directive that could see the unintentional killing of protected wildlife no longer treated as unlawful.
A memo from Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) director Brian Nesvik distributed to FWS field offices earlier this week called for a reinterpretation of "take," a term relating to the pursuit, killing or capture of a species under the 1973 Endangered Species Act (ESA).
The definition would now be altered to "affirmative conduct intentionally directed against a particular animal or animals," effectively excluding incidental harm caused by economic activities from being considered "take."
"A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel's course was not set against the whale," the memo says, quoting former Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia in a 1995 case. "Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them".
The document, which was obtained and shared by the Center for Biological Diversity, comes after a previous rule change that rescinded the definition of "harm" under the ESA.
The Interior Department confirmed the memo’s authenticity to the AFP news agency.
"The memorandum accurately reflects the US Fish and Wildlife Service's guidance for implementing the Endangered Species Act following the final rule rescinding the regulatory definition of 'harm,'" the department said.
"Under the guidance, the ESA's prohibition on 'take' continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife," it added.
The move has drawn strong criticism from environmental groups.
Brett Hartl, the government affairs director at the Center for Biological Diversity, said the move "stabs at the very heart of the Endangered Species Act by giving federal approval to the killing of some of America’s most beloved wildlife."
"The Trump administration is desperate to annihilate environmental protections, but this incredibly radical measure is both cruel and profoundly unlawful. Killing endangered wildlife is illegal, whether that’s your purpose or not," Hartl added in a press release.

Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar (AA Photo)
Türkiye plans to send the Osman Gazi floating production platform to the Sakarya Gas Field in the Black Sea in late October, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said.
Speaking at Filyos Port in Zonguldak on Sept. 17, Bayraktar said the platform’s first gas would be flared by year-end, completing the field’s second phase of development.
Once operational, Osman Gazi will add 10 million cubic meters of daily production, enough for 4 million households, he said.
Combined with existing output, this would cover the needs of 8 million households.
Bayraktar put the value of the platform’s planned daily gas output at about $10 million at current prices.
“This floating production platform will contribute $3.5 billion a year to our economy,” he said.
About 7,000 people are working on preparations at Filyos, where reactivation work has reached its final stage, Bayraktar said.
The project involves 642 kilometers of electrical cabling and nearly 30 kilometers of piping. Workers are installing about six kilometers of cable a day, he added.
The platform was sent through the Bosphorus to Filyos on May 29, 2025, to undergo preparations for deployment.

Architectural Heterotopias: Temporary Installations as Alternative Worlds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

While complex, layered with meaning, and categorized into various forms, heterotopia, a concept developed by the philosopher Michel Foucault, can broadly be understood as the manifestation of alternative realities. Unlike utopias – idealized, unreachable non-places – heterotopias are tangible, real-world spaces that operate according to their own internal logic, offering a lived alternative to dominant spatial and cultural paradigms.
Escapism, in an architectural sense, is not merely about fleeing standard realities; it is a critical tool for reimagining them under different cultural, social, and environmental conditions. Temporary installations serve as fertile testing grounds for these spatial possibilities. Often framed as sanctuaries or refuges, these works intentionally detach from pre-conceived norms – whether by seeking a return to a primal way of living or by provoking radical perceptual shifts.
Just as escapism has long driven design speculation, temporary installations allow architects to materialize not only abstract concepts, but distinct worldviews. They establish an expanded field of experimentation for designers who refuse to limit their practice to permanent, traditional construction, as seen in the projects presented below.
Related Article
Ephemeral Architecture Prototypes: The Future of Public Spaces
Room Installation / Tamara Wibowo Architects
 "Room" is a spatial meditation on duality—an architectural diptych that explores the delicate tensions between opposing realities. At its core, the installation confronts our binary understandings of space, materiality, and perception, inviting an intellectual dialogue on the boundary between nature and the built environment.
When the Earth Began to Look at Itself - Desert X Installation / Syn Architects
 To further establish an understanding of subjectivity in relation to positionality, we reference Rosi Braidotti's notion of the 'nomadic subject'. In her writings, the nomad describes an epistemological condition, a kind of knowingness (or unknowingness) that refuses fixity, that allows us to think between or 'as if', to articulate another reality. These traces inform the pathway to the proposed work and prompt the discovery process of the larger site, playing an important role in creating new kinds of relationships between subject and object.
The Waterfall that Went Silent Installation / Umeå School of Architecture
 'The Waterfall that Went Silent' is a temporary sound installation and place for reflection located in the UNESCO World Heritage site Laponia. The installation seeks to remind visitors of the roar of the waterfall Stora Sjöfallet/Stuormuorkkegårttje (part of Lule River) which nearly disappeared together with a large amount of reindeer herding lands after Sweden started hydropower developments in the valley at the beginning of the 20th century. The installation reflects on the human drive for technological progress and the need for resources and energy over the natural and cultural environment. And the values that are lost in this process.
Vessel Installation / Erazo Pugliese
 The asymmetrical "Vessel," lying on the rocks, invites visitors to experience their proximity to nature and the horizon as perceived from a terrestrial perspective: the partially fixed fabrics on the timber frame structure make one aware of the sound and intensity of the wind shifts, and framed views reestablish the relation between human-made artifacts and the landscape, while, in moments of calm it is possible to lay down or sit recalling the contemplative and existential feelings that can be experienced in nature.
Under the Same Sun Installation / Stephanie Deumer
 As part of the artist's continued exploration of simulacra and immersive environments, this work brings to life the spectacle of biological reproduction through technological and visual means. Projected live-feed footage of the aboveground landscape bathes the greenhouse with light, allowing the plants to photosynthesize and grow. The video projection and installation as a whole is powered by solar panels, which also serve as the roof to the sunken room. Taking the shape of a large puddle of water, the solar cells sit flush with the desert ground, mirage-like in appearance, and hinting at the sanctuary below.

Over 37 lakh appeals pending after Bengal SIR: EC tells Supreme Court

NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Friday told the Supreme Court that over 37 lakh appeals against the deletion or inclusion of names in West Bengal electoral rolls under the Special Intensive Revision remain pending.The poll panel told the apex court in its response affidavit that tribunals appointed by the court have disposed of only about 1.02 lakh of the 38.20 lakh appeals filed so far.This comes after a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymala Bagchi and V Mohana sought the poll panel's response to a plea seeking disclosure of assembly constituency-wise data on claims and objections filed by voters whose names were deleted during the SIR exercise.
A total of 38,20,683 appeals had been filed against orders relating to the SIR of electoral rolls. Of these, 1,02,231 appeals had been disposed of, leaving 37,18,452 pending, the poll panel said.The affidavit, however, did not provide a break-up of the appeals filed by electors whose names were deleted and those filed against the inclusion of names in the electoral rolls.Prasenjit Bose, who filed the affidavit, claimed that more than 58 lakh electors were excluded during the enumeration phase of the SIR exercise in West Bengal.
He added that while 9.64 lakh applications for inclusion (Forms 6 and 6A) and over 99,000 applications for deletion (Form 7) were received during the claims and objections phase, only around 1.82 lakh additions were reflected in the final electoral roll published on February 28.On August 25, the top court directed the Election Commission to submit data on the pendency and disposal of appeals before tribunals challenging exclusion or inclusion in electoral rolls.Observing that these appeals needed to be adjudicated in a time-bound manner, the bench had asked the poll panel to explain what steps were being taken to streamline the mechanism for disposing of pending appeals and how many additional tribunals were required.
The EC data submitted to the court showed that 34.13 lakh Form 6 applications had been filed between December 17, 2025, when the draft electoral roll was published, and August 7, 2026.Form 6 is the statutory application for inclusion of a name in the electoral roll.On April 24, the apex court asked the appellate tribunals to give out-of-turn hearings to those who made a case for urgent hearing against deletion from electoral rolls after the SIR.Approximately 700 judicial officers from West Bengal and neighbouring Odisha and Jharkhand were deployed to deal with around 60 lakh claims and objections.Later, the chief justice of the Calcutta high court, on the direction of the top court, set up 19 tribunals headed by former high court chief justices and judges to decide the appeals.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday initiated legal action against Nestle India over alleged non-compliance involving its NAN Excella Pro Stage 1 and Lactogen Pro 1 infant nutrition products.FSSAI said it examined the products and their promotional material available on e-commerce platforms. For Lactogen Pro 1, it raised concerns over a claim that the product’s “Whey Protein” was easy to digest.According to FSSAI, both products were found to be in contravention of Regulation 4(2) of the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020. The provision restricts promotional claims and material intended to increase the saleability of infant foods. The regulator also cited Section 3 of the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, which prohibits their advertisement and promotion.
FSSAI said it had sought clarifications from Nestle India regarding the claims.Separately, a sample of a follow-up formula manufactured by Nestle India was found to be sub-standard for its biotin content during laboratory analysis.
The sample was sent for re-analysis, but the referral laboratory also found it non-conforming with the prescribed biotin requirement under the 2020 regulations.In view of the alleged violations, FSSAI said three separate adjudication cases have been filed against Nestle India in relation to the products. The action covers both promotional claims and the laboratory finding concerning biotin content.

French PM vows to cut public spending by €54 billion to reduce deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:23:41 UTC
16:23:41 KST

French PM vows to cut public spending by €54 billion to reduce deficit
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Thursday that France will cut public spending by €54 billion next year to reduce the country's deficit. The announcement comes seven months ahead of the country's presidential election, and the government is wary of a new wave of demonstrations with a jump in global oil prices sparking concerns over the rising cost of living.
France's prime minister promised Thursday that the government will reduce the country's deficit next year by cutting public spending by €54 billion ($62 billion) in 2027.
But Sébastien Lecornu insisted his plans did not amount to austerity, as high fuel prices cause renewed social tensions just months before the presidential election.
Read moreFrench candidates race to claim the cost-of-living issue ahead of 2027 vote
In an interview with the Le Figaro business newspaper, he said the cuts will bring the public deficit down to 4.8 percent of gross domestic product excluding defence spending, and five percent including military spending.
The French government initially aimed to cut the deficit from 5.1 percent of GDP last year – one of the highest in the eurozone and above the three-percent limit set for EU members.
But the government acknowledged on Thursday that it will likely rise to 5.4 percent.
The 2027 budget takes "an assertive stance on cutting public spending in a country that relies too heavily on it", Lecornu told Le Figaro.
"It is a political risk, I am not unaware of that. But we are a long way from austerity!" the prime minister added.
The jump in global oil prices above $100 per barrel has led to record petrol and diesel costs in France, prompting calls to demonstrate against the high cost of living.
With a presidential election seven months away and France's economic situation worsening, the government is wary of a new wave of demonstrations like the so-called yellow vest movement that swept the country over fuel tax hikes.
Pensioners let off
Lecornu said retirees would only be asked to make a limited contribution to the cost-cutting effort.
"No pension will be reduced," he said.
"Then the debate on the pace of increases will be settled in parliament," he added.
French state pensions are normally increased in line with inflation.
Lecornu also excluded freezing the level of many benefits.
Public sector workers will not get cost-of-living adjustments.
The government will also let the income tax rate thresholds rise, bringing in more revenue from individuals.
But taxes on some companies will drop as the government is set to exclude them from an additional levy on larger businesses.
Worries about the French economy, which contracted in the first quarter and was stagnant in the second, have led to fresh concerns about the sustainability of France's public spending and debt.
Yields on government bonds have soared to levels not seen since the global financial crisis in 2008, raising the cost of financing the government's debt, which is at 117.5 percent of its GDP, to a level last seen in World War II.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

- The U.S. Army's Maneuver Battle Lab tested two tethered drone systems on an Infantry Squad Vehicle at Fort Benning from July 27 to Aug. 7, 2026.
- The drones stay powered through a physical tether, avoiding battery swaps, and the assessment will inform whether the Army adopts them as a formal program.
U.S. Soldiers and Army capability developers spent two weeks at Fort Benning testing drones that stay tethered to the ground, aiming to give small infantry units a way to see farther and keep radios working even when the terrain or enemy jamming gets in the way.
The Maneuver Battle Lab ran the assessment from July 27 to Aug. 7 at the post’s McKenna Field Landing Site, putting two commercial tethered unmanned aircraft systems, known as Te-UAS, through static tests, moving tests and emergency scenarios. The lab worked with the Army’s Air Robotics office, its Dismounted Requirements Branch, the Maneuver Future Capability Directorate and Product Lead Strategic Spectrum Warfare to design and run the trial.
A tethered drone stays connected to a ground vehicle or station by a physical cable that supplies continuous power and carries data both ways, so the aircraft never has to land for a battery swap and can theoretically stay airborne indefinitely. During the Fort Benning tests, the drones climbed to altitudes the Army considers operationally useful, and evaluators timed how fast they could go up and come back down. One test tracked a drone in “follow mode” as it stayed positioned above an Infantry Squad Vehicle-Utility moving through the training area, an Army light transport built by GM Defense to carry nine soldiers across terrain too rough for a Humvee or Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. Operators used the drones to bounce communications signals around terrain obstacles, work around signal jamming, and spot targets from a safer distance than they could on the ground.
“The Maneuver Battle Lab’s mission is experimentation,” said Tollie Strode Jr., government oversight lead for the assessment and unmanned systems team chief at the lab. “We take technology to the field, employ it in an operational context, look under the hood, kick the tires and report what we find to inform programmatic decisions.”
“This is a great opportunity for long-endurance mission sets,” said Capt. Sarah Runion, executive officer of the lab’s Live Experimentation Branch, who took part in the assessment. “Tethered UAS bring a lot of pros to the force: we don’t have to worry about battery life or anything like that, which you see on other drones. It can go through different levels of height, and it can follow you along on whatever platform you deem it on.”
Evaluators also looked at how easy the systems were to operate without extensive training. “In a matter of minutes, I was able to get [the drone] launched up in the air … and then it’s a quick, easy one-step button to bring it back down,” Runion said. “This has been a user-friendly experience.”
Mark Pagliaro, a contractor with Product Lead Strategic Spectrum Warfare, compared the setup to a mobile version of a fixed surveillance tower. “It’s similar to a very high tower,” Pagliaro said. “Having a sensor up that high in their [area of operations] is going to influence [the maneuver unit] and allow them to extend ranges and see targets farther.” He added that the simple launch process leaves operators free to focus on incoming camera feeds and data rather than piloting the aircraft.
The Maneuver Battle Lab is now compiling soldier feedback, technical performance data and details on the systems’ operational footprint into a final report for Army decision-makers. “When we develop a clear concept of operation and employment, it gives us credibility behind the numbers and information we provide to decision-makers,” Strode said. “It answers the ‘so what?’ and provides the essential analytical underpinning to determine if this technology should transition into a permanent Army program of record.”

CPO combines optical components with computing chips in the same package, shortening signal paths to reduce power consumption and transmission delays. For humanoid robots, Tbi is developing high-precision components for different parts of the machines. These include systems that control movement in the arms and legs, as well as miniature components for robotic hands.

Goldman Sachs has also raised its forecast for global humanoid robot shipments to 890,000 units in 2030 and 6.5 million units in 2035, from previous estimates of 256,000 and 1.4 million, respectively, according to CTEE.
Meanwhile, Tbi's core business in motion-control components has begun to recover. Its order visibility now extends into the first quarter of next year, while some ball screw orders have already been scheduled through the second quarter.
The company’s new plant in China’s Jiangsu province is expected to be completed by the end of this year and begin production in the first quarter of next year. Taiwan labor ministry backs removing full names from employee badges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:21:06 UTC
16:21:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The labor ministry on Friday backed calls to remove full names from employee badges, saying workplace identification rules should protect workers from harassment and threats, CNA reported.
The ministry said employee identification requirements should balance customer service needs with worker safety and avoid displaying personal information that is not necessary.
The statement followed a campaign launched on Aug. 17 by the Taoyuan Flight Attendants Union and other airline unions over privacy and safety concerns. A union survey found that nearly 40% of airline ground and cabin staff had experienced harassment linked to having their full names displayed on work badges, while more than 98% supported removing them, per CTS News.

The union also called on the labor ministry to clarify employers’ responsibility to reduce risks when identification requirements could put workers at risk.
The ministry said flight attendants may face stalking, harassment, threats, or sexual harassment while carrying out their duties. Employers must take preventive measures under workplace safety and gender equality laws and provide support and protection when they become aware of such incidents.
It also encouraged companies to review badge systems with workers and unions while meeting legal and management needs. Businesses can limit the personal information displayed as long as employees can still be identified when necessary.
The ministry urged other service-sector employers to give greater attention to worker rights, safety, and well-being and to create safer workplaces.

====================================================================================================

U.S. Marines test new AI-driven automated security system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:18:16 UTC
16:18:16 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps' MA-DOSS system automatically detected and tracked a vehicle intrusion during a live-fire exercise at Twentynine Palms on Aug. 19, 2026.
- The AI-driven system needs only two Marines and 30 minutes to set up, replacing the heavier, fixed G-BOSS surveillance towers.
A new automated security system helped Marines detect and track a vehicle that strayed toward a live-fire range during a training exercise at Twentynine Palms, California, on Aug. 19, the U.S. Marine Corps said, marking one of the first real-world uses of a system built to replace hours of manual guard duty with radar and artificial intelligence.
The system, called the Mobile All-Domain Observation and Sensing System, or MA-DOSS, was operating in support of the installation’s Provost Marshal’s Office during Service Level Training Exercise 4-26. When a vehicle approached the edge of the exercise’s alert zone, MA-DOSS detected and classified it automatically, alerting two Marine operators inside a command post. The operators confirmed the intrusion on their monitors and passed the tracking data to range safety personnel, and the live-fire event continued without interruption.
MA-DOSS pairs radar and camera sensors with artificial intelligence and machine learning software built to spot and classify targets across air, land and littoral domains at once. The system processes that data on site rather than streaming continuous video over tactical networks, which the Marine Corps says keeps bandwidth demands low while still filtering out background clutter from genuine incursions. The underlying models continue learning from what they detect, a process the program office runs in coordination with the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office, with the goal of cutting down false alarms over time.
“[AI implementation] is going to help us not just learn what the enemy’s already thrown at us, but learn what new systems may come our way in different ways and how the enemy may employ them,” said Capt. Griffen Hedrick, MA-DOSS project officer for Program Manager Ground-Based Air Defense. “So it’s not just a giant library of what they’ve done before, but predictions of the future.”
The system is meant to replace the Ground-Based Operational Surveillance System, or G-BOSS, a network of trailer-mounted towers up to 107 feet tall that the Marine Corps has used for years to watch over installations and forward bases. Those towers provide steady surveillance but are heavy and fixed in place once erected. MA-DOSS, by contrast, needs only two Marines and about 30 minutes to set up, according to the Marine Corps.
Program Manager Ground-Based Air Defense fielded two MA-DOSS Medium prototypes now in use after working with the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit and drawing on funding from the Physical Security Enterprise Analysis Group, a path meant to move faster than the traditional acquisition process. MA-DOSS is not currently an official program of record, and the Marine Corps described the Twentynine Palms demonstration as evidence supporting the case for further investment rather than confirmation of a formal program.
“In traditional security setups, maintaining that level of persistent, multi-domain awareness forces Marines to spend endless hours fixed to surveillance monitors,” said Master Sgt. Daniel Sloniker, operations chief for the Twentynine Palms Provost Marshal’s Office. “By automating detection and cueing the cameras directly to the threat, MA-DOSS eliminated screen fatigue and served as a true force multiplier, freeing our trained military policemen from passive observation so they could focus on dynamic patrols and rapid tactical response.”

ODI live: Australia tries to back up opening win over Zimbabwe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:17:41 UTC
16:17:41 KST

Travis Head has returned to his blistering best after a lean spell with a 75-ball century to help power Australia to a convincing 84-run victory over Zimbabwe in Harare and wrap up their ODI series triumph.
Stand-in captain Mitch Marsh, who cracked a fine half-century himself, saluted "a complete performance" as the world champs found a new gear following their opening win on Tuesday and moved into a 2-0 series lead with a match still to come.
Head hadn't mustered more than 26 in any of his last eight knocks in all cricket, including Tests and IPL fare, but the left-hander was back at his intimidating best on Friday as he crushed 112 off 84 balls to spearhead Australia's formidable 6-356 after being asked to bat.
In reply, the hosts never looked like challenging as the return of Josh Hazlewood (2-48), and a couple of wickets apiece for the spin trio of Adam Zampa, Cooper Connolly and part-timer Matt Renshaw, ensured Zimbabwe could muster only 272 off their 48.3 overs.
Connolly, able to bowl his left-arm spin again after five months when he was unable to do so because of back trouble, delivered another fine all-round performance.
The left-hander built on the magnificent start provided by Head and captain Mitch Marsh, who put on a thunderous opening stand of 130 off 19 overs, as he followed up with 78 off 69 balls. Rising star Ollie Peake then chipped in with 41no off 18 balls, with three sixes, to give the innings a rousing finale.
Connolly also took a catch and the final two wickets of Zimbabwe's innings off successive balls to finish with 2-25.
It also proved a landmark day for Australia's premier white-ball spinner Zampa (2-62) as he picked up his 200th ODI wicket.
The only downside for Australia, who are using this trip to Africa as a reconnaissance mission before next year's defence of their ODI World Cup, was an injury to paceman Billy Stanlake, who went down with a side strain in his fifth over.
The final match of the series will be played at Harare on Sunday before the tour rolls on to South Africa for three ODIs and three Tests.

Israeli, 23, dies in paragliding crash in Colombia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
07:16:54 UTC
16:16:54 KST

A 23-year-old Israeli man who had recently completed his military service died in a paragliding accident in Medellín, Colombia, after the glider he was riding in lost control and crashed into a cliff in a wooded area, according to local reports.
The accident occurred around noon local time Wednesday. The Colombian pilot operating the paraglider was seriously injured and taken to a hospital for treatment.
According to reports in Colombia, weather conditions are believed to have contributed to the crash. The paraglider apparently lost control before plunging into a forested area and striking a cliff.
Witnesses reported strong winds in the area shortly before the crash.
Firefighters and rescue crews were dispatched to the scene, where they recovered the Israeli traveler’s body. He was pronounced dead at the scene, while emergency personnel evacuated the injured pilot to a hospital.
Investigators from the Colombian Attorney General’s Office Technical Investigation Corps, known by its Spanish initials CTI, arrived at the crash site to conduct a forensic examination and collect evidence as authorities began investigating the circumstances of the accident.
Authorities also inspected the paragliding company involved in the flight and found that its documentation was valid and in compliance with legal requirements, according to the reports. The business was not ordered to close, though authorities said the investigation would continue to determine what caused the crash.
The Israeli was traveling in Colombia as part of the extended overseas trip commonly taken by young Israelis after completing their mandatory military service.
Following news of the accident, Rabbi Levi Vanunu, a Chabad emissary in Medellín, began working closely with the Israeli Embassy and Colombian authorities to expedite the necessary procedures for repatriating the man’s body to Israel for burial.
Israeli officials and the local Chabad representative were working to complete the bureaucratic arrangements as quickly as possible so his remains could be returned to his family in Israel.

Ireland has ruled itself out of next year's competition over the "appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza". This follows the announcement from Dutch broadcaster AvroTros, who are boycotting next year's show as it is no longer consistent with "trustworthiness, independence and humanity".
Ireland will boycott the Eurovision Song Contest for the second year in a row in protest at Israel's participation, according to Ireland's national broadcaster RTÉ.
RTÉ said in a statement: "RTÉ feels that Ireland's participation cannot be justified given the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk."
RTÉ added that they also remain "deeply concerned by the continued denial of independent access to international journalists to the territory". They also said they would not be broadcasting the competition, which will take place in Bulgaria in 2027 after singer Dara's victory for the country in May.
Ireland has won the competition seven times between 1970 and 1996, a joint record holder alongside Sweden.
Eurovision director Martin Green said he "regretted" RTÉ 's stance, but "fully respect their decision".
In 2026, RTÉ withdrew from the contest in Vienna, after the European Broadcasting Union confirmed that Israeli public broadcaster KAN would be allowed to take part.
Ireland's decision to boycott Eurovision 2027 follows that of Dutch broadcaster AvroTros, who announced last month that they would boycott next year's show as it was no longer consistent with "trustworthiness, independence and humanity". It said the competition can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.
Both Ireland and the Netherlands were among the five countries who decided to opt out of the 2026 competition, along with Spain, Iceland and Slovenia.
It remains to be seen whether Spain, Iceland and Slovenia will follow suit.
Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the last three years of Israeli bombardment. Organisations including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the United Nations have described Israel's actions as "genocide".
A report published in June by a UN independent commission found that "Israeli authorities and security forces have deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide and atrocity crimes in the Gaza Strip and war crimes in the West Bank."
A previous report last September found that Israel had committed genocide and claimed that these acts were incited by senior Israeli officials, including prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Israel has repeatedly labelled the accusations as “defamatory” and “distorted”.
Eurovision 2027 contest will take place in Burgas, Bulgaria, with the Grand Final being held at the Arena Burgas on 15 May.
